## State Buddha Sāsana
## Great Chronicle of Buddhas
## Volume 6 (Part 2)
## Chronicle of Gotama Buddha
**********
Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Saṅgha Ratana
## Chapter 44
## Section on the Apadāna of Therīs
## (1) The Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Therī
## (a) Her Past Aspiration
The future Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Therī, as a noblewoman in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, was listening to the Buddha's discourse. She saw the Buddha appoint a certain nun to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those of long standing (rattaññū)—those who know the divisions of the night—and she witnessed her being placed in that high rank.
2:
2
Having performed great meritorious deeds, she made an aspiration for that foremost position of Rattaññū. Padumuttara Buddha then gave her the prophecy.
## Life as the Leader of Water-carrying Slave Women
That woman, after performing acts of charity and observing precepts throughout her life, passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm. Later, during another Buddha-interval, she passed away from the celestial realm and became the leader of five hundred water-carrying slave women in the city of Bārāṇasī.
Then, as the rains retreat (vassa) approached, five Paccekabuddhas came from the Nandamūla cave and descended into the Isipatana Migadāya forest in Bārāṇasī. After wandering for alms in the city, they returned to the Migadāya forest and consulted among themselves, "Let us request manual labor (hathakamma) for the purpose of building small huts for the rains retreat."
(Even if a monk observing the rains retreat is one who practices the Nālaka or Moneyya practice, he must observe the retreat in a dwelling with a door, roofed with one of the five types of roofing: brick, stone, cement, grass, or leaves. If one observes the retreat without a dwelling, one commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) [Vinaya 3, p. 212]. Therefore, it is good to obtain a dwelling for the retreat when the time approaches.)
* Rattaññū person: One who has known many nights since ordination. Among such persons, the one with the highest seniority in vassa receives the foremost (Etadagga) title. One is also called Rattaññū because of knowing the divisions of the night after realizing the Four Noble Truths. Among the disciples, the first to realize the Four Noble Truths receives this special Etadagga title. Alternatively, an Arahant is called a Rattaññū. The first disciple to become an Arahant receives this special Etadagga title.
3: 3 If a dwelling is obtained, it is well. If not, one must build a rainy season dwelling even by asking for manual labor (hatthakamma). If manual labor cannot be obtained, one must build it oneself. Under no circumstances should one spend the rainy season retreat without a dwelling. — From the Commentary). Since it is the custom to seek a dwelling when the rainy season is near, the five Paccekabuddhas adjusted their robes and entered the city in the evening, standing at the gate of a wealthy merchant's house in Bārāṇasī. The woman who was the leader of the water-carrying slave women saw the five Paccekabuddhas entering the city while she was carrying a water pot on her head to the watering place. The merchant of Bārāṇasī, having heard the reason for the Paccekabuddhas' arrival, spoke dismissively, saying, "We have no opportunity to provide manual labor for you, Venerable Sirs; please proceed elsewhere." Then, as the five Paccekabuddhas were leaving the city, the leader of the slave women, entering the city with her water pot, met them face to face. She set down her water pot, bowed respectfully, and looking up, asked, "Venerable Sirs, you have only just entered the city and are already leaving. What is the reason?" The Paccekabuddhas replied, "We came to ask for manual labor (hatthakamma) for small rainy season dwellings." The woman asked again, "Did you receive it, Venerable Sirs?" The Paccekabuddhas replied, "We did not, lay devotee." The woman then asked, "Venerable Sirs, is it only the powerful and wealthy who can build and offer these rainy season dwellings, or can we
4: 4 poor people also build and offer them?" The Paccekabuddhas replied, "Lay devotee, anyone, whether powerful and wealthy or poor, can build and offer them." The woman said, "Very well, Venerable Sirs, we shall build and offer them. Please accept the alms-food I now invite you to tomorrow." After inviting them, she took up her water pot again and, instead of going into the city, stood on the path to the watering place. As each of the other water-carrying slave women arrived, she called them together, saying, "Friends, sit here." When all five hundred slave women were assembled, she asked, "Mothers, do you wish to always perform the work of others' slaves, or do you wish to be free from slavery?" All the slave women replied with one voice, "O friend, we wish to be free from slavery this very day." The leader then urged them, "If that is so, I have invited five Paccekabuddhas, who could not obtain manual labor (hatthakamma), for a meritorious deed tomorrow. Let your husbands donate their manual labor (hatthakamma) for just one day." The slave women agreed, saying, "Very well," and in the evening, they told this to their husbands who had returned from working in the forest. The husbands all agreed and assembled at the door of the head slave's house.
5: 5 Then, the leader of the slave women urged those men, saying, "Friends, tomorrow, donate your manual labor (hatthakamma) to build rainy season dwellings for the five Paccekabuddhas," explaining the benefits of the deed. She even used firm words of advice and warnings to those who were reluctant, making them all agree. The next day, after offering alms-food to the Paccekabuddhas, the leader of the slave women gave a signal to the men to provide their manual labor. The five hundred men immediately entered the forest, collected timber, and built five rainy season dwellings—one for every hundred men—complete with walkways (caṅkama) and day-quarters. They provided everything needed, such as couches, benches, drinking water, and washing water. They requested and received a commitment from the Paccekabuddhas to reside in those dwellings for the three months of the rainy season, and then they took turns offering alms-food. To any slave woman who could not afford to offer alms on her turn, the leader provided the necessary provisions from her own house. Having thus served and supported them for the three months of the rainy season, as the end of the retreat approached, the leader of the slave women had each woman weave a piece of cloth. According to this plan, five hundred pieces of coarse cloth were produced. From those five hundred coarse cloths, the leader exchanged them and prepared three sets of fine triple robes (ticīvara)—consisting of the outer robe, the upper robe, and the inner robe—
6:
6
She prepared three sets of fine robes for each and offered them. While the women were watching, the Paccekabuddhas flew through the air to Mount Gandhamādana.
## Life as the Leader of Weavers
All those slave women performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives and, upon passing away, were reborn in the celestial realm. The eldest among those five hundred goddesses passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn in the house of the chief weaver in a weavers' village near Bārāṇasī. One day, the five hundred Paccekabuddhas, who were the sons of Queen Padumavatī, came to the gate of the royal palace at the invitation of the King of Bārāṇasī. Finding no one even to look at them (let alone provide seating or alms), they left the city and arrived at that weavers' village. As soon as the chief weaver woman saw the Paccekabuddhas, she felt love and devotion. She paid homage with respect and offered alms-food. After the five hundred Paccekabuddhas had finished their meal, they departed for Mount Gandhamādana.
## (b) Becoming a Nun in the Final Life
That chief weaver woman, after performing meritorious deeds throughout her life and wandering through the celestial and human realms, was born as the younger daughter of the Great Sakyan King Mahāsuppabuddha of Devadaha, long before our Buddha appeared. That young princess was named "Gotamī".
7: 7 She was the younger sister of Princess Mahāmāyā. Brahmins learned in the Vedas and the reading of marks examined the characteristics of the two princesses and prophesied, "The sons born from the wombs of these two sisters will become Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti)." When they reached the proper age, King Suddhodana married both sisters, Mahāmāyā and Gotamī, and brought them to his golden palace in Kapilavatthu. Upon reaching the palace, Princess Mahāmāyā was appointed to the position of Chief Queen (Aggadevi Mahesī). Later, our future Buddha (Bodhisatta) passed away from the Tusita heaven and took conception in the womb of Chief Queen Mahāmāyā. Seven days after giving birth to the Bodhisatta (on the 7th day after the full moon of Kason, in the Great Era year 68), Queen Mahāmāyā passed away and was reborn as the deva Santusita in the Tusita heaven. After Queen Mahāmāyā passed away, King Suddhodana elevated the younger sister, Queen Gotamī, to the position of Chief Queen. Two or three days after Queen Mahāmāyā gave birth to the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, Queen Mahāpajāpatigotamī, the younger sister of Mahāmāyā and foster mother of the Bodhisatta, gave birth to Prince Nanda. When Queen Mahāmāyā passed away, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha was only seven days old, and Prince Nanda was only four or five days old. When Queen Mahāmāyā passed away, the foster mother Mahāpajāpatigotamī gave her own biological son
8:
After handing over Prince Nanda to the nurses, she personally took care of all the needs of the Bodhisatta (her nephew) and nursed him with her own milk.

At a later time, the Bodhisatta went forth, attained Omniscient Buddhahood, and while benefiting the world of sentient beings, eventually arrived at the royal city of Kapilavatthu for the first time. On the following day, he entered the city for alms. At that time, his father, King Suddhodana, heard the Dhamma while the Buddha was on his alms round and became a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer). Subsequently, on the second day, Prince Nanda was ordained as a monk, and on the seventh day, Prince Rāhula was ordained as a novice. (The details of these events have been described previously.)

At another time (during the fifth vassa), the Blessed One was residing at the Kūṭāgāra Hall in the Great Wood (Mahāvana) near the city of Vesālī. At that time, King Suddhodana attained Arahatship under the royal white umbrella within the golden palace of Kapilavatthu and attained Parinibbāna on that very day. Then, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī felt a strong desire to ordain. Following this, five hundred Sakyan princesses, who were the former wives of the five hundred monks mentioned in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, became of one mind and consulted together, saying, "Let us go to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and all of us will become bhikkhunīs in the presence of the Buddha." With the Great Foster Mother as their leader, they approached the Buddha, desiring to become bhikkhunīs. Although the Great Foster Mother had previously requested the Blessed One for the status of a bhikkhunī (nun),
9:
she had not received permission. Therefore, on this occasion, she called for a barber to shave her hair, donned saffron-dyed robes, and accompanied by those five hundred Sakyan princesses, traveled on foot to the city of Vesālī. After seeking the assistance of the Venerable Ānanda Thera and having him plead with the Blessed One, she received the status of a novice and a bhikkhunī by accepting the Eight Garudhammas (Heavy Rules). As for the five hundred Sakyan princesses, they became bhikkhunīs who were ordained by one side (the Bhikkhu Saṅgha) alone, known as Ekatoupasampanna-bhikkhunīs. (The details of this section should be looked up and noted in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Chapter 23, starting from page 414.)

After becoming a bhikkhunī, the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī attained Arahatship upon hearing the Saṅkhitta Sutta (found in Aṅguttara Nikāya 3, 106). As for the five hundred Sakyan bhikkhunīs, they later heard the Nandakovāda Sutta (found in Majjhima Nikāya 3, 314) and, according to their respective inclinations, some became Sotāpannas, some Sakadāgāmīs, some Anāgāmīs, and some became Arahats.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

At another time, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery and was assigning bhikkhunīs to their respective positions (Etadagga), he declared regarding the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ rattaññūnaṃ yadidaṃ mahāpajāpatigotamī = Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who are of long standing (rattaññū), Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is the foremost."
10:
Thus, the Buddha praised her and placed her in the pre-eminent position of Etadagga in the category of "Rattaññū," meaning those who have known the long passage of nights, or those of the greatest seniority in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha.

(In this context, her original name by lineage was "Gotamī," meaning a princess of the Gotama clan. On the day she was named, wise Brahmins skilled in the Vedas and physiognomy examined the princess's marks and prophesied: "If this princess gives birth to a daughter, that daughter will become the Chief Queen of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch). If she gives birth to a son, that son will become a Cakkavatti." Thus, whether she bore a daughter or a son, in both ways, the offspring of this princess would be of the highest and most noble rank. At that time, they gave her the significant name "Mahāpajāpatī," meaning the mistress of noble offspring. Combining the lineage name and the significant name, this Elder is referred to in the scriptures as "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Therī." — From Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 4, page 219.)

## The Parinibbāna of Gotamī Therī

Then one day, while the Great Foster Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was residing in the bhikkhunī monastery within the city of Vesālī, and the Blessed One was staying at the Mahāvana monastery in the same city (at that time, the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was 120 years old; during the Buddha's time, bhikkhunī monasteries had to be built within cities or villages), she went on her alms round in Vesālī in the morning. After finishing her meal, she entered the Attainment of Fruition (Phalasamāpatti) for a period at her usual daytime resting place. Upon emerging from that attainment, she reflected on her practice.
11:
Reflecting with great joy and examining her own life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), she realized that her life-force was exhausted. She thought, "It would be well if I were to go to the Mahāvana monastery, inform the Blessed One and ask for permission to attain Parinibbāna, take leave of the noble members of the Saṅgha, including the two Chief Disciples and other elders who are worthy of mental cultivation, and then return to this bhikkhunī monastery to attain Parinibbāna." Just as this thought arose in the mind of the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, a similar thought arose in the minds of the five hundred Sakyan bhikkhunīs.

(Note: The inspiring and detailed account of the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī's Parinibbāna can be found in (1) the "Chiddapidhānanī" written by the Most Venerable Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw, under Matika heading No. 12; and (2) in the Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Therī Apadāna of the Khuddaka Nikāya, Apadāna Pāḷi, page 260, along with its Burmese translation. In this text, however, only a brief summary will be presented.)

The thought arose in the mind of the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī: "I shall not have the opportunity to witness the Parinibbāna of my son, the Buddha, the two Chief Disciples, my grandson Venerable Rāhula, my nephew Venerable Ānanda, or my son Venerable Nanda. Before the Buddha, the two Chief Disciples, Venerable Mahā Kassapa, Venerable Ānanda, Venerable Nanda, and Venerable Rāhula attain Parinibbāna, I shall relinquish my life-force early, obtain the Buddha's permission, and attain Parinibbāna." Similarly, this thought arose in the minds of the five hundred Sakyan bhikkhunīs.
12:
At that moment, a great earthquake occurred, and untimely thunder roared from the sky. The guardian deities of the monastery wept. When the five hundred bhikkhunīs went to the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and reported these events, the Elder told them of her own intention. The five hundred bhikkhunīs also shared that they had the same intention. Then, all the bhikkhunīs asked the guardian deities for forgiveness for any faults, took a final look at the bhikkhunī monastery, and the Elder recited this verse:

"Na jarā maccu vā yattha, appiyehi samāgamo.
Piyehi na viyogotthi, taṃ vajissaṃ asaṅkhataṃ.
= I shall go to the Unconditioned state (Nibbāna), where there is no aging or death, where there is no suffering of meeting with the unpleasant, and no suffering of parting from the beloved."

Upon her reciting this verse, all the deities and humans who were not yet free from passion wept bitterly. (The poetic description of their weeping should be looked up in the Pāḷi texts.)

When the bhikkhunīs came out onto the main city street, devout lay followers (upāsikās) came out of their houses, prostrated at the feet of the Elder Gotamī, and wept piteously. (The detailed description of their weeping should be looked up in the Pāḷi texts.) The Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī also had to preach the Dhamma to dispel the grief of those lay followers. (The manner of her preaching should be taken from the Pāḷi texts; this applies to subsequent sections as well.)
13:
After comforting the lay followers of Vesālī by preaching the Dhamma in nine and a half verses, the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī reached the presence of the Blessed One. She addressed him with many verses (16 verses) starting with "Ahaṃ sugata te mātā, tvaṃ ca vīra pitā mama" (I am your mother, O Sugata, and you, O Hero, are my father), requested permission to attain Parinibbāna, and paid her respects. After the Blessed One spoke the verses of permission, she praised the Buddha again with five verses.

Following this, she respectfully paid homage to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, Venerable Rāhula, Venerable Ānanda, and Venerable Nanda. She then pointed out the faults of the five aggregates with two verses starting with "Āsīvisālayasame" and again requested permission to attain Parinibbāna. Although Venerable Nanda and Venerable Rāhula, being Arahats, experienced only spiritual urgency (Dhamma-saṃvega), Venerable Ānanda, being a Sekha (one still in training), wept bitterly while reciting the verse starting with "Hā santiṃ gotamī yāti" (Alas, Gotamī goes to peace). The Elder preached words to dry his tears to her nephew Venerable Ānanda, and then the Blessed One said:

"Thīnaṃ dhammābhisamaye, ye bālā vimatiṃ gatā.
Tesaṃ diṭṭhippahānatthaṃ, iddhiṃ dassehi gotami.
= O Gotamī, my foster mother... in order to dispel the wrong views of those foolish ones who have doubts regarding the realization of the Four Noble Truths by women in this, my Dispensation, display your psychic powers."

Urged thus, the Elder, who was 120 years old, performed the various psychic powers (iddhividha) such as becoming many from being one, becoming one from being many, appearing and disappearing, and passing through walls and mountains without obstruction.
14:
14

In addition to displaying powers such as traveling through the air, she performed a miracle by making Mount Meru the handle and the great earth the canopy of an umbrella, turning it upside down and holding it in the sky while walking in meditation. She also manifested a vision of the entire world-system (okāsaloka) being covered in smoke, as if six suns had risen. After displaying many such psychic powers (iddhi), she descended from the sky, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat in a suitable place, saying: "O Son and Buddha, your foster mother is now 120 years old. I am very aged. This is enough for me. O Son and Buddha, please allow me to enter Parinibbāna."

At that time, the assembled audience was greatly amazed and asked: "O Venerable Gotamī Therī, what kind of meritorious deeds (adhikāra-kusala) did you perform in the past to be endowed with such incomparable power and effort?" In response, she recounted her practice (Apadāna) starting from the time of Padumuttara Buddha until her final birth, explaining it in detail through many verses.

Then, the five hundred bhikkhunīs also flew into the sky and displayed various beautiful miracles, appearing like stars gathered and strung together. They descended from the sky and, with the Buddha's permission, paid homage to him. Sitting in suitable places, they spoke of the great gratitude they owed to the foster mother, Gotamī Therī, and requested the Buddha's permission to enter Parinibbāna.

The Buddha said: "Yassa dāni kālaṃ vo maññatha—O bhikkhunīs, you yourselves know the time for your Parinibbāna." When he said this, all those bhikkhunīs paid homage to the Buddha...
15:
15

...paid homage, rose from their seats, and departed. The Buddha, accompanied by a large crowd, followed his foster mother as far as the main gate of the forest monastery. Upon reaching the gate, the foster mother prostrated at the Buddha's feet, paying her final respects along with the five hundred bhikkhunīs. They then went to the bhikkhunī monastery within the city of Vesālī, where all the bhikkhunīs sat in a half-cross-legged position in their respective dwellings. (Half-cross-legged means sitting with the left leg placed as in a cross-legged position and the right leg tucked in; try sitting this way).

At that time, the laywomen (upāsikās) who were devoted to the Dispensation, knowing that they were about to enter Parinibbāna, came to pay homage and worship. They beat their breasts and fell to the ground like uprooted creepers, weeping. The foster mother, the Great Therī, gently stroked the head of the leading laywoman and said:

"Alaṃ puttā visādena, mārapāsānuvattinā.
Aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ sabbaṃ, viyogantaṃ calācalaṃ.

My daughters, there is no benefit in the distress of weeping and wailing, which is but following the snare of Māra. All conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are impermanent. They end in separation and are constantly trembling and changing."

After teaching and admonishing them thus, she sent them back to their homes. She then entered the eight mundane meditative attainments (samāpatti) in both forward and reverse order, from the first fine-material absorption (rūpāvacara-pathama-jhāna) up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and back down to the first absorption. Then, starting again from the first absorption...
16:
16

...up to the fourth absorption, and after emerging from the fourth absorption, she attained the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu), becoming completely extinguished like a lamp when the oil and wick are exhausted. The remaining five hundred Sākyan bhikkhunīs also attained Nibbāna and were extinguished in the same way.

At that moment, there were great earthquakes, meteors falling from the sky, the thundering of celestial drums, the wailing of deities, a rain of flowers, and the shaking of Mount Meru like a dancer in the middle of a festival. The ocean roared as if in grief. Nagas, Asuras, Devas, and Brahmas were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and uttered words of urgency such as: "Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, yathāyaṃ vilayaṃ gatā" (Impermanent indeed are conditioned things, as they have thus gone to destruction). Many other wondrous and diverse events occurred.

Then, the Devas and Brahmas approached the Buddha and informed him that the foster mother Gotamī Therī and the five hundred Sākyan princesses who were bhikkhunīs had entered Parinibbāna. The Buddha sent Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Go and inform the monks." The Buddha himself, accompanied by a large assembly of monks, went there. (1) At the very front were humans, Devas, Nagas, Asuras, and Brahmas. (2) Following them were five hundred golden biers created by Vissakamma, upon which the bodies of the five hundred bhikkhunīs were placed along with their couches, carried by deities. (3) Then, the bier of the foster mother Gotamī Therī was carried by the Four Great Kings. (4) Finally, the Buddha followed along with the Saṅgha. According to this order, the entire path was covered with celestial canopies and decorated with banners and flags.
17:
17

Flower carpets were strewn on the ground, celestial lotuses (paduma) hung from the sky, and various fragrant flowers, sweet music, songs, and dances were offered in worship as they proceeded to the cemetery grounds. 

During the procession, the moon and sun were both visible to the people. The stars and constellations were also shining brightly. Although it was noon, the sun remained as cool as the moon. The wonders at the Buddha's own Parinibbāna and cremation were not as numerous as those at the foster mother's Parinibbāna and cremation. At the Buddha's Parinibbāna, he did not personally supervise or arrange it, nor did Venerable Sāriputta and others. However, at the Parinibbāna of the foster mother Gotamī, both the Buddha and Venerable Sāriputta and others personally supervised and arranged the events.

Upon reaching the cemetery, the body was placed on a pyre of fragrant wood and cremated. Venerable Ānanda, holding the relics (dhātu) of Gotamī Therī, said:

"Gotamī nidhanaṃ yātā, ḍayhañcassā sarīrakaṃ.
Saṅketāṃ buddhanibbānaṃ, na cirena bhavissati.

Gotamī, known as the foster mother, has reached the end and entered Nibbāna. Her physical body, the product of seasonal change, has been consumed by fire. By this sign, which is noted with certain apprehension, the Parinibbāna of our teacher, the Buddha, will surely take place before long."
18:
18

After uttering these words of spiritual urgency, he placed the foster mother's relics in her alms-bowl and offered them to the Buddha. Then, the Buddha took the relics of his foster mother in his hands, showed them to the assembled crowd of humans, Devas, and Brahmas, and said:

"Mahato sāravantassa, yathā rukkhassa tiṭṭhato.
Yo so mahattaro khandho, palujjeyya aniccatā.
Tathā bhikkhunisaṅghassa, gotamī parinibbutā.

Just as a large, solid, and firmly standing tree has a main branch that is very extensive and great, and that great branch might break and fall because its inherent nature is impermanent; so too, Gotamī, who was like the main trunk of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha—which is like a great tree—has now attained Nibbāna and is extinguished."

He taught and admonished them with ten such verses. (The Pali and meaning of these verses should be read in the Chiddapidhānanī text for inspiration).

This is the story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Therī.

## (2) The Story of Khemā Therī

(The story of this Khemā Therī is briefly explained in the Aṅguttara Commentary, the Therīgāthā Commentary, and the Dhammapada Commentary. In the Apadāna Pali, however, Khemā Therī herself...
19:
19

...recounts it in detail. Therefore, I shall write the story of Khemā Therī by coordinating it with the three commentaries, while taking the Apadāna Pali as the primary source.)

## (a) The Therī's Past Aspiration

One hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, this future Khemā Therī was born as the daughter of a wealthy man in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī. One day, she heard the Dhamma preached by the Buddha, developed faith, and became a lay follower (upāsikā) established in the Three Refuges.

Later, after asking permission from her parents, she served and offered alms-food to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for seven days. At the end of the seven days, she heard and saw Padumuttara Buddha appointing Sujātā Therī to the foremost rank (etadagga) in wisdom. Feeling joyful and inspired, she performed further meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that same rank of being foremost in wisdom. Padumuttara Buddha then gave her a prophecy, saying that after one hundred thousand aeons, she would become Khemā Therī, the one foremost in wisdom in the Dispensation of this Buddha.

## Being a Celestial Queen and Human Queen for Many Lives

That daughter of the wealthy man performed meritorious deeds throughout her life. When she passed away from that life, she became the chief queen in the five great celestial realms—Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, Tusita, Nimmānarati, and Paranimmitavasavatti—in succession. Furthermore, when she passed away from the celestial realms and was reborn in the human world, she became the chief queen of Universal Monarchs and independent kings. In this way, in every life she was born into, whether in the celestial or human realms...
20:
20

...she became a great celestial queen or a great human queen, enjoying and experiencing celestial and human pleasures alternately for many aeons.

## Life as a Brahmacārinī Bhikkhunī

After wandering through many aeons enjoying celestial and human pleasures, ninety-one aeons ago, when Vipassī Buddha appeared in the world, she was born as a woman of good family. When she approached the Buddha and heard the Dhamma, she developed great faith and became a bhikkhunī. For ten thousand years, she practiced the holy life (brahmacariya), becoming one who strove in meditation, was full of great learning (bahussuta), was expert in the law of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), was courageous regarding the Four Noble Truths, and was a subtle and excellent preacher of the Dhamma (dhammakathika). Thus, she followed and practiced the three trainings of the Dispensation.

When she passed away from that life, she ascended to the Tusita heaven. Due to the merit of her diligent efforts in the Dispensation of Vipassī Buddha, in every life she was born into, she possessed wisdom, virtue, wealth, and property superior to others, and had a clever retinue. She easily obtained and enjoyed many pleasant celestial and human riches. Furthermore, due to the power of that practice of merit, in every human and celestial life, she became a celestial or human queen who was highly regarded and cherished by her lords and rulers.

## Life as a Donor of a Monastery

During the time of Koṇāgamana Buddha in this Bhadda-kappa, she was a wealthy woman in the city of Bārāṇasī (her name is not mentioned; she should simply be remembered as Khemā)...
21:
The women Dhanañjānī and Sumedhā, along with their friend, became fellow donors. Together, the three of them acted as sponsors and built a great Saṅgha monastery complex (ārāma) and a communal dwelling (saṅghika-vihāra) as an offering. After passing away from that life, all three enjoyed high-class celestial and human pleasures in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and the human realm.

## Life as the Eldest Daughter of King Kikī
During this very Bhadda-kappa (Fortunate Aeon), when the Buddha Kassapa appeared in the world, King Kikī of Bārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāsi was a primary supporter and attendant of the Buddha. King Kikī had seven daughters, as mentioned in the verse:

Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā ca, Paṭācārā ca Kuṇḍalā.
Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, Visākhā hoti sattamī—

According to this verse, those who would eventually become (1) Khemā Therī, (2) Uppalavaṇṇā Therī, (3) Paṭācārā Therī, (4) Kuṇḍalakesī Therī, (5) Kisāgotamī Therī, (6) Dhammadinnā Therī, and (7) the great lay-supporter Visākhā in the dispensation of our Buddha, were then the seven princesses:

Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā ca, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā.
Dhammā ceva, Sudhammā ca, sattamī Saṅghadāyikā—

Namely, (1) Princess Samaṇī, (2) Princess Samaṇaguttā, (3) Princess Bhikkhunī, (4) Princess Bhikkhudāyikā, (5) Princess Dhammā, (6) Princess Sudhammā, and (7) Princess Saṅghadāyikā. Among these seven daughters, the noble lady who was the future Khemā Therī was the eldest, Princess Samaṇī.
22:
That Princess Samaṇī, having heard the Dhamma of the Buddha Kassapa, felt a strong desire to ordain as a bhikkhunī. Although she requested permission from her father, the King, she did not receive the opportunity to become a bhikkhunī. At that time, all seven sisters practiced maidenly celibacy (komāri-brahmacariya) for twenty thousand years, remaining unmarried throughout their lives. They observed the Uposatha precepts and served the Buddha Kassapa with the four requisites until the end of their lives.

On one occasion, the Buddha Kassapa preached the wonderful Mahānidāna Sutta. (The Mahānidāna Sutta is the second discourse in the Mahāvagga of the Dīgha Nikāya; one should refer to that text). Upon hearing this Mahānidāna Sutta, Princess Samaṇī developed great faith, studied it, memorized it, and recited it frequently.

Due to those meritorious deeds, when she passed away from her life as Princess Samaṇī, she became a chief queen in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

## (b) Ordaining as a Bhikkhunī in Her Final Life
In this final existence, that noble lady was born as the daughter of King Maddarāj in the city of Sāgala. Because she was born bringing peace and safety to all citizens, she was named Princess "Khemā." When Princess Khemā reached maturity, she became the dearly beloved chief consort of King Bimbisāra, and she was extremely intoxicated with the beauty of her own physical form.
23:
When the Blessed One was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha, Queen Khemā heard reports that "the Buddha preaches the Dhamma by pointing out the faults of physical beauty." Being one who was intoxicated with her own beauty, she thought, "If I go, the Buddha will surely point out the faults in my physical form as well." Out of fear, she avoided going to pay respects to the Blessed One.

## King Bimbisāra's Skillful Means
King Bimbisāra reflected, "I am the foremost supporter and attendant of the Blessed One. Yet, I cannot accept that the chief consort of a noble Ariya like myself does not go to pay respects to the Blessed One." He then commissioned poets to compose songs (gīti-gāthā) praising the Veḷuvana Monastery. He commanded famous singers to sing these verses repeatedly in the vicinity where Queen Khemā would hear them.

## Four Verses Praising the Veḷuvana Garden
(1) Rammaṃ veḷuvanaṃ yena, na diṭṭhaṃ sugatālayaṃ.
Na tena nandanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, iti maññāmashe mayaṃ.

If any person has not seen the delightful Veḷuvana, which is the residence of the Sugata (the Buddha), the pinnacle of the three worlds, then that person has not truly seen the Nandana grove, the supreme garden where the devas rejoice. This is what we believe.

(2) Yena veḷuvanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, nara-nandana-nandanaṃ.
Sudiṭṭhaṃ nandanaṃ tena, amarinda sunandanaṃ.

If any person has clearly seen the Veḷuvana garden—which is cherished by King Bimbisāra, the delight of the people, and which the Buddha, loved by the whole world, finds pleasing—then that person has truly seen the Nandana grove, the celestial garden so greatly loved by Sakka, the lord of the devas.
24:
(3) Vihāya nandanaṃ devā, otaritvā mahītalaṃ.
Rammaṃ veḷuvanaṃ disvā, na tappanti suvimhitā.

Many devas from Tāvatiṃsa, having left and abandoned the Nandana grove, descend to the surface of the earth in the land of Jambudīpa. When they see the delightful Veḷuvana garden with their own eyes, they are greatly amazed; they find peace, forget their celestial luxuries, and can never see enough of it.

(4) Rājapuññena nibbattaṃ, buddhapuññena bhūsitaṃ.
Ko vattā tassa nissesaṃ, vanassa guṇasañcayaṃ.

This Veḷuvana garden arose through the merit of the King and is adorned by the power and glory of the Buddha. What wise poet could ever fully describe the entire collection of virtues of this supreme bamboo grove?

When Queen Khemā heard these songs, although she had visited the Veḷuvana garden in the past to enjoy herself with the King, it felt as if she had never been there. A strong and extraordinary desire to go and see it arose in her. She requested permission from King Bimbisāra and, with great ceremony, planned to enter the garden at a time when the Buddha would be out for alms to avoid meeting him. She wandered through the Veḷuvana garden, a place where noble yogis delight, observing the various flowers, fruits, and buds, the buzzing bees, the singing cuckoos, the dancing peacocks, and the quiet, secluded walkways, pavilions, monasteries, and rest houses.
25:
While wandering, Queen Khemā saw a young yogi monk sitting under a tree, striving diligently in his monastic practice. She mistakenly thought, "At such a beautiful age, one should enjoy the pleasures of the senses; only when one is old and frail should one practice the Dhamma."

Thinking that the Buddha was not present, she approached the Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber). However, the Buddha, knowing beforehand that Queen Khemā would come, did not go out for alms. He remained in the Gandhakuṭī and, through his psychic power, created a vision of a young woman (iddhirūpa) far more beautiful and graceful than Queen Khemā herself, standing and fanning him. Queen Khemā saw the Blessed One face-to-face.

Queen Khemā abandoned her attachment to her own beauty and gazed intensely at the beauty of the created young woman. Even as she looked, by the Buddha's will, that young woman began to age—her skin wrinkled, her hair turned white, her teeth broke, her complexion faded, her breasts sagged and withered, her skin became parched and shriveled, her limbs became awkward, her joints and veins became prominent, and her body bent over. Gasping for breath and trembling, her eyes rolled back, and she collapsed and died. Seeing this, a powerful sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in Queen Khemā's mind:

"Dhīratthu rūpaṃ asuci, ramante yattha bāliyā.

Woe to this physical form! In its own nature, it is impure. It is truly loathsome. Yet, foolish women, blinded by lack of wisdom, take delight in such an impure and disgusting body!"

Then, the Blessed One preached these verses of Dhamma to Queen Khemā:
26:
(1) Āturaṃ asuciṃ pūtiṃ, passa kheme samussayaṃ.
Uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ, bālānaṃ abhinanditaṃ.

Khemā, look closely at this body—afflicted by pain, impure, putrid, oozing from above and leaking from below, yet greatly cherished and delighted in by the foolish.

(2) Asubhāya cittaṃ bhāvehi, ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ.
Sati kāyagatā tyatthu, nibbidābahulā bhava.

Develop a meditative mind that is one-pointed and well-concentrated, for the purpose of perceiving the body as unattractive and loathsome (asubha). Let mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) be established in you. Be full of revulsion (nibbidā) toward it.

(3) Yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ, yathā etaṃ tathā idaṃ.
Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, kāye chandaṃ virājaya.

Khemā, as this body [of the vision] is, which has aged and decayed, so too will that body of yours age and decay. As that body of yours is, so is this one. Dispel all desire for the body, both internally and externally.

Upon hearing this Dhamma teaching, the Buddha, seeing that Queen Khemā's mind was clear, joyful, and firm, preached the Mahānidāna Sutta (which she, in her past life as Princess Samaṇī during the time of Kassapa Buddha, had studied and memorized). When she heard the Mahānidāna Sutta, Queen Khemā remembered what she had studied before and, at that very place, reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) = she became a Sotāpanna.

After becoming a Sotāpanna, Queen Khemā wished to apologize for her past mistake of being deluded by pride in her beauty. Prostrating at the feet of the Buddha, she spoke these five verses of apology:

(1) Namo te sabbadassāvi, namo te karuṇākara.
Namo te tiṇṇasaṃsāra, namo te amataṃ dada.

Sabbadassāvi = O Buddha, who sees and knows all things without exception. Te = To you, the Lord Buddha. Namo = I pay respectful homage. Karuṇākara = O Buddha, who is the source of Great Compassion. Te = To you, the Lord Buddha. Namo = I pay respectful homage.

## Khemā Therī Becoming an Arahant
After obtaining the status of a Bhikkhunī (nun), on the fifteenth day, while performing her duties at the Uposatha hall, Khemā Therī saw the lighting and extinguishing of a lamp. Gaining a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and again contemplating the arising and passing away of mental and physical phenomena (saṅkhāra), she reached the Path and Fruit of Arahantship, adorned with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) and the six higher powers (abhiññā), and became an Arahant Therī. (This account of Khemā Therī becoming an Arahant is written according to the Khemā Therī Apadāna;
34:
34
(The Aṅguttara Commentary and Dhammapada Commentary provide a different explanation; however, to avoid confusion, it is not presented in this text.)

As Khema Therī was a student of both Pariyatti (scriptural study) and Paṭipatti (practice), she was exceptionally skilled and proficient in the seven stages of purification (visuddhi). Furthermore, she was matchless in her courage regarding the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu) and was highly learned and expert in the methods of Abhidhamma. Thus, she was an outstanding individual of great wisdom, accomplished in both Pariyatti and Paṭipatti. This matter can be understood by referring to the Khema Sutta (found in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Saḷāyatana Vagga, 10-Abyākata Saṃyutta, Vol. 2, page 544). The summary of the Khema Sutta is as follows:

## Khema Therī Preaches the Subtle Dhamma to King Kosala

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, Khema Therī was wandering through the Kosala country and was staying at a place called Torana, situated between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, while traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, stopped for a night's rest at that place called Torana. Then, King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a man, saying, "Come, good man, go and find out if there is any recluse (samaṇa) or brahmin (brāhmaṇa) in this Torana area whom I should visit today."

Following the King's command, that man searched throughout the entire Torana area but did not find any recluse or brahmin whom the King should visit, except for [Khema Therī] who was residing in that Torana area.
35:
35
Having seen the Elder Khema, the man returned to the King and said to King Kosala:
“Great King, in this Torana area, there is no ascetic or brahmin whom you should visit. However, there is a nun named Khema, a disciple of the Blessed One. A good report of her fame has spread: ‘She is wise, skilled, learned, eloquent, and possesses good insight.’ I would like the Great King to visit the nun Khema.”

Following the man's report, King Kosala went to the nun Elder Khema, paid homage to her, and sat down at a respectful distance. Then, the King and the nun Elder Khema engaged in the following dialogue:

(King)
“Venerable lady, does a being exist after death?”

(Elder Theri)
“Great King, the Blessed One has not declared this: ‘A being exists after death.’”

(King)
“Venerable lady, if that is so, does a being not exist after death?”

(Elder Theri)
“Great King, the Blessed One has also not declared this: ‘A being does not exist after death.’”

(King)
“Venerable lady, does a being both exist and not exist after death?”

(Elder Theri)
“Great King, the Blessed One has also not declared this: ‘A being both exists and does not exist after death.’”

(King)
“Venerable lady, if that is so, does a being neither exist nor not exist after death?”

(Elder Theri)
“Great King, the Blessed One has also not declared this: ‘A being neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”

This was the first level of dialogue between King Kosala and Elder Khema. Then, moving to the next level, they continued their dialogue as follows:

(King)
“Venerable lady, when I asked, ‘Does a being exist after death?’, you replied, ‘Great King, the Blessed One has not declared this: “A being exists after death”’ (1). When I asked, ‘Venerable lady, if that is so, does a being not exist after death?’, you replied, ‘Great King, the Blessed One has also not declared this: “A being does not exist after death”’ (2). When I asked, ‘Venerable lady, does a being both exist and not exist after death?’—

“—you replied, ‘Great King, the Blessed One has also not declared this: “A being both exists and does not exist after death”’ (3). When I asked, ‘Venerable lady, if that is so, does a being neither exist nor not exist after death?’, you replied, ‘Great King, the Blessed One has also not declared this: “A being neither exists nor does not exist after death”’ (4). Venerable lady, what is the cause, what is the reason why the Blessed One has not declared these four points?

(Elder Theri)
“Great King, if that is so, I will question you in return on this matter. Answer as you please. Great King, what do you think? Do you have any accountant, or any calculator, or any statistician who is able to count the grains of sand in the river Ganges, saying: ‘There are this many grains of sand,’ or ‘There are this many hundreds, this many thousands, or this many hundreds of thousands of grains of sand’?”

(King)
“No, venerable lady.”

(Elder Theri)
“Great King, do you have any accountant, or any calculator, or any statistician who is able to count the drops of water in the great ocean, saying: ‘There are this many measures of water,’ or ‘By measure of drops, there are this many hundreds,

this many thousands, or this many hundreds of thousands’?”

(King)
“No, venerable lady. Why? Because the great ocean is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom.”

(Elder Theri)
“Even so, Great King, that form by which one describing a being might describe him—that form has been abandoned by the Blessed One, cut off at the root, made like a palmyra stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. The Blessed One is free from the designation of ‘form’; he is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom like the great ocean. For such a Blessed One, the statement ‘A being exists after death’ does not apply. The statement ‘A being does not exist after death’ does not apply. The statement ‘A being both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply. The statement ‘A being neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply. (This means that for the Blessed One, one should not say a being exists after death, nor should one say he does not exist. One should not say he both exists and does not exist, nor should one say
