he neither exists nor does not exist. It is very deep.)

“That feeling by which one describing a being might describe him... (etc.), that perception... (etc.), those mental formations... (etc.), that consciousness by which one describing a being might describe him—that consciousness has been abandoned by the Blessed One, cut off at the root, made like a palmyra stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. The Blessed One is free from the designation of ‘consciousness’; he is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom like the great ocean. For such a Blessed One, the statement ‘A being exists after death’ does not apply... (etc.). The statement ‘A being neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.”

(This was the second level of dialogue between King Kosala and Elder Khema; the explanation will be provided later.)

Then King Pasenadi Kosala, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the nun Khema, rose from his seat, paid homage to her, and departed respectfully. Later, on another occasion, King Pasenadi Kosala approached the Blessed One and asked him the same questions he had asked Elder Khema. The Blessed One answered him in exactly the same way as Elder Khema had answered. (The dialogue can be seen in the Burmese translation of the Pitaka.)

When King Pasenadi Kosala saw that the Blessed One's answers and Elder Khema's answers were identical (not differing by even a single letter or syllable), he was greatly amazed and said:
40:
40
“Venerable sir, it is wonderful! Venerable sir, it is marvelous! How the meaning and the phrasing of the Teacher and the disciple coincide, agree, and do not diverge. Venerable sir, once I approached the nun Khema and asked her about this matter. That lady answered me with these very words and these very phrases, just as the Blessed One has answered now. Venerable sir, it is wonderful! Venerable sir, it is marvelous! How the meaning and the phrasing of the Teacher and the disciple coincide, agree, and do not diverge.” Having said this, he asked permission to depart, and greatly rejoicing in the Blessed One's words, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed. This is the summary of the Khema Sutta.

(In this regard: Regarding the second level of questioning about why the Blessed One did not declare whether a being exists after death, does not exist, both, or neither—

(1) If one answers according to the third sutta of the Avyākata Saṃyutta: Since in the ultimate sense only the five aggregates exist and there is no ‘being’ (apart from the five aggregates), the Blessed One does not declare the existence or non-existence of a being. This is a valid explanation.

(2) Or, according to the fourth sutta of the Avyākata Saṃyutta: These four types of wrong views regarding the existence or non-existence of a being occur only in the mind of one who does not know the nature of the Four Noble Truths in relation to the five aggregates. In the mind of one who knows the nature of the Four Noble Truths,
41:
41
these four wrong views do not occur. Since the Blessed One has fully and completely realized the nature of the Four Noble Truths, these four wrong views do not exist in him at all; because they do not exist, he does not declare them. This is also a valid explanation.

(3) Or, according to the fifth sutta of the Avyākata Saṃyutta: These four wrong views occur only in the mind of one who is not free from craving and desire for the five aggregates. In the mind of one who is free from craving and desire for the five aggregates, these four wrong views do not occur. Since the Blessed One is completely free from craving and desire (along with habitual tendencies) for the five aggregates, these four wrong views do not arise at all; because they do not arise, he does not declare them. This is also a valid explanation. (Furthermore, the sixth sutta of the Avyākata Saṃyutta provides four reasons for the answer, which are also clear and valid.)

Despite these explanations, the essence of Elder Khema's intended answer is: “Great King, for the Blessed One, the five aggregates—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—by which one might designate a ‘being’ after death, have been abandoned (by abandoning their cause, samudaya). For the Blessed One, there will be no new aggregates after the final death-consciousness (parinibbāna-cuti-citta). Thus, the Blessed One is free from the future collection of the five aggregates, as they will not arise anew. For this reason, the designation of a ‘being’ or ‘person’ as having such a nature has ceased; therefore, he is free from the designation of future aggregates. Great King, the Blessed One is deep in his virtues and his disposition (ajjhāsaya), just like the great ocean. For the Omniscient Buddha who is thus deep in virtue and disposition, since the five aggregates by which one might designate a ‘being’ after death no all longer exist, the designation ‘being’ no longer exists. For the Blessed One who sees this absence, all four points—such as ‘a being exists after death’—[do not apply]."
42:
should no longer be spoken of; therefore, these four points were 'greatly left undeclared' by the Blessed One.

If that is the case, one might ask: "Since there is no new aggregate to be formed after the death and passing away (parinibbāna-cuti) of the Blessed One, if it is not taught for the first question—'Does a being exist after death?'—then for the second question—'Does a being not exist after death?'—should it not be answered and admitted as 'Yes, he does not exist'?"

The answer is: To admit and answer in such a way is also not appropriate, because the question itself asks about the designation 'being' (satta), which does not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha). Thus, one should not admit 'Yes, he does not exist.' This is the explanation. (Extracted from the Commentary)

These questions and answers are indeed very subtle and profound. There is a special reason why the Elder Nun Khemā answered so subtly. That special reason is that in the first level of the four questions, the questioner, King Kosala himself, intended to include the Blessed One within the term 'being' (satta). Knowing the King's intention and aim, the Elder Nun Khemā answered by profoundly pointing out only the matters related to the Blessed One. (This Khemā Sutta is very subtle; therefore, the virtuous should not be satisfied with just this much and should inquire further from the wise.)

## (C) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

As mentioned above, the preaching of this Khemā Sutta to King Kosala in the place called Toraṇa, between the city of Sāvatthī and the city of Sāketa, was the most immediate cause for the Elder Nun Khemā to receive the title of Etadagga in wisdom. Therefore, at a later time, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, when he was appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions of Etadagga (the foremost rank), he declared regarding the Elder Nun Khemā:
43:
“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ yadidaṃ khemā = Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who possess great wisdom, the Elder Nun Khemā is the most outstanding and the foremost.”

Thus praising her, he placed her in the most outstanding and foremost position—the rank of Etadagga—in the category of “Mahāpañña = Great Wisdom.” For this reason, the Elder Nun Khemā herself joyfully recited these following verses in her Apadāna:

(1) Tato toraṇavatthusmiṃ,
raññā kosalasāminā.
pucchitā nipuṇe pañhe,
byākarontī yathātathaṃ.

Tato = After becoming an Arahant. Ahaṃ = I, the Elder Nun named Khemā. Toraṇavatthusmiṃ = In the place named Toraṇavatthu between the city of Sāvatthī and the city of Sāketa. Kosalasāminā = By King Pasenadi Kosala, who rules over the entire Kosala country with great glory and power. Pucchitā = Being asked out of a desire to know. Nipuṇe pañhe = Subtle questions. Yathātathaṃ = Exactly as they are, without distortion. Byākarontī = I have analyzed and answered.

(2) Tadā sa rājā sugataṃ,
upasaṅkamma pucchatha.
tatheva buddho byākāsi,
yathā te byākatā mayā.
44:
Tadā = At that time. Sa-so rājā = That king named Kosala. Sugataṃ = To the presence of the Blessed One upon returning to Sāvatthī. Upasaṅkamma = Having approached. Pucchatha = Asked the profound questions again. Tadā = When he asked thus. Te = Those subtle questions. Mayā byākatā yathā = Just as they were analyzed and answered by me. Tatheva = In that very same way. Buddho = The Blessed One, known as the Omniscient Buddha, the Supreme One of the world. Byākāsi = Answered with the same meaning, without any difference in sense, word, or syllable.

(3) Jino tasmiṃ guṇe tuṭṭho,
etadagge ṭhapesi maṃ.
mahāpaññānamaggāti,
bhikkhunīnaṃ naruttamo.

Naruttamo = The Supreme One among men, the unique Leader. Jino = The Conqueror of the five Maras, the Blessed One himself. Tasmiṃ guṇe = Regarding that quality of preaching and expounding the Dhamma. Tuṭṭho = Being greatly pleased and satisfied. Maṃ = Me, who is called Khemā Therī. Mahāpaññānaṃ = Among those who possess great wisdom. Bhikkhunīnaṃ = Among your many female disciples. Aggāti = As the most outstanding and foremost. Etadagge = In the rank of Etadagga. Ṭhapesi = He praised and appointed me.

This is the account of the Elder Nun Khemā.
45:
## (3) The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā

## (A) The Theri's Past Aspiration

The Bodhisatta (future) of this Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā was a daughter of a good family (a merchant's daughter) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Blessed Buddha Padumuttara. One day, she went with a group of people to the presence of the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma. There, she saw the Blessed One appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the most outstanding and foremost rank—the position of Etadagga—in the category of great psychic powers. She then offered a great donation (Mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha. Placing seven bundles of blue lotuses at the feet of the Blessed One, she made an aspiration for that very same rank of Etadagga in great psychic powers. The Blessed Buddha Padumuttara also granted her the prophecy (byādika).

## Offering Lotus Flowers to a Paccekabuddha

That merchant's daughter respectfully served and attended to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha for the rest of her life in that existence. When she passed away from that life, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. When she passed away from that heaven, she was reborn as a human in the world of men and offered alms-food along with a lotus flower to a Paccekabuddha.

## Life as a Merchant's Daughter Again

Ninety-one aeons (kappas) ago from this present Bhadda Kappa, that lady of good family was again a merchant's daughter in the city of Bārāṇasī. She respectfully invited the Saṅgha led by the Blessed Buddha Vipassī and offered a great donation.
46:
She worshipped the Blessed Buddha Vipassī with lotus flowers and made an aspiration in her mind for a beautiful and graceful physical appearance.

## Life as the Daughter of King Kikī

That merchant's daughter, performing meritorious deeds throughout her life in that existence, wandered between the realms of devas and humans. During the time of the Blessed Buddha Kassapa in this Bhadda Kappa, she became Princess Samaṇaguttā, the second among the seven daughters of King Kikī (mentioned earlier). Like the Bodhisatta of the Elder Nun Khemā, she practiced the life of celibacy (komāri-brahmacariya) for twenty thousand years and built a large monastery complex (pariveṇa) for the Saṅgha. When she passed away from that life, she was reborn again in the deva realm.

## Life as Ummādantī

When that goddess passed away from the deva life, she was reborn as a lady of good family in a noble clan in the human world and offered a golden-colored, smooth, and bright cloth to an Arahant Elder, a disciple of the Blessed Buddha Kassapa who was worthy of special offerings. (The detailed story can be found in the Ummādantī Jātaka of the Paṇṇāsa Nipāta in the 550 Jātaka stories).

When she passed away from that life, she became the daughter of a wealthy brahmin named Tiriṭivaccha in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the Sivi Kingdom. She was the merchant's daughter Ummādantī, who possessed extremely beautiful and graceful features. (The detailed story of this Ummādantī can be found in the Ummādantī Jātaka of the Paṇṇāsa Nipāta in the 550 Jātaka stories).
47:
## Life as a Woman Guarding the Field

When she passed away from the life of the merchant's daughter Ummādantī, she was reborn as a farmer's daughter in a small village. One day, while going to the field hut, she saw a Paduma lotus flower that had bloomed early in the morning in a pond along the way. She went down into the pond and picked that Paduma lotus, as well as a Paduma lotus leaf to hold popped rice (when she reached the field hut). Upon reaching the field hut, after harvesting the stalks of sali rice, she sat inside the hut and roasted the rice. She then counted the grains of popped rice one by one until they reached five hundred (500).

At that moment, a Paccekabuddha who had arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana arrived and stood not far from the girl. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, the girl took the popped rice along with the Paduma lotus, descended from the field hut, placed the popped rice into the Paccekabuddha's bowl, covered the bowl with the Paduma lotus, and offered it.

After the Paccekabuddha had walked a short distance, the girl thought, "Monks do not have a need for flowers; I will take the flower back and wear it." She followed him, asked for the flower back from the Paccekabuddha's hand, but then thought again, "Oh, if the Venerable Paccekabuddha did not want the flower I offered, he would not have allowed me to place it on the bowl when I offered it. Surely, the Venerable Paccekabuddha must have a use for the flower I offered." Thinking thus, she went back again and placed the Paduma lotus on the Paccekabuddha's bowl.
48:
She offered it again. (The fact that this action was not straightforward will become evident later in the results within the cycle of rebirths.)

After offering the Paduma lotus and asking for forgiveness from the Paccekabuddha, she made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, as a result of offering these grains of popped rice, may I have as many beloved sons as the number of these grains. Furthermore, as a result of offering the Paduma lotus, in every realm where I am born, may Paduma lotuses miraculously rise from the ground at every step I take."

(According to the Apadāna of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā)—When the woman guarding the field offered the popped rice and lotus and made her aspiration, five hundred (500) men guarding the field also offered honey to the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration to become the five hundred sons of that girl.

While the girl was watching, the Paccekabuddha traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana. He placed that Paduma lotus as a foot-wiper at the base of the stairs where Paccekabuddhas step at the Nandamūla Cave.

## Life as Padumavatī

Due to the result of that meritorious deed, when she passed away from that life, she was reborn spontaneously (upapatti-paṭisandhi) in the deva realm. From the time she was born in the deva realm, at every step that goddess took, a large Paduma lotus rose from the ground to support her foot. When she passed away from that deva life, she was reborn in the human world near the foot of a mountain.
49:
Inside a large lotus pond, within the heart of a lotus, a moisture-born (saṃsedaja) rebirth took place. A certain hermit was living in dependence on that pond. When the hermit went to the pond early in the morning to wash his face, he saw that particular Paduma lotus (in which the woman was conceived) and thought: "This lotus is exceptionally larger than the others. While other lotuses have bloomed, this great lotus remains only as a bud; there must surely be a special reason for this." Thinking thus, he descended into the water and plucked that great Paduma lotus bud.

As soon as the hermit plucked it, the great lotus bud bloomed. The hermit saw a young maiden lying within the heart of the Paduma lotus. From the moment he saw her, he felt a fatherly love for her. He took the maiden along with the Paduma lotus to his leaf-hut hermitage and laid her on a small couch. Then, due to the power of the maiden's merit, milk began to flow from the hermit's thumb. When that first lotus withered, the hermit plucked another fresh lotus and laid the maiden in that new lotus.

Later, from the time the young maiden was able to run and play, a Paduma lotus would miraculously spring up from the earth at every single step to receive her feet. The complexion of her skin was also exceedingly beautiful, like a heap of saffron (kuṅkuma). The young maiden surpassed human beauty but did not quite reach the beauty of a goddess. Because she was found in the heart of a Paduma lotus, her name was given—
50:
—by her father, the hermit, as "Padumavatī." When her father, the hermit, went into the forest to search for fruits, Padumavatī would remain alone in the leaf-hut hermitage.

## Becoming the Chief Queen Padumadevī

When the maiden Padumavatī reached the age of maturity, one day while her father was away in the forest searching for fruits, a hunter arrived at the hermitage. Upon seeing the maiden Padumavatī, he thought, "There is no such exquisite beauty among humans; I shall investigate to know about this maiden." He sat waiting for the hermit's return. When her father returned from the forest, Padumavatī went out to meet him and took the carrying pole and water jar from his hands. She then dutifully performed the services she had to do for her father who was seated in the hermitage.

Only then did the hunter realize that the maiden was indeed a human being. He paid homage to the hermit and remained seated. After the hermit had entertained the hunter with large and small forest fruits and drinking water, he asked, "Young man, will you stay in this forest or will you return?" When the hunter replied, "I shall return, Venerable Sir; there is nothing for me to do in this forest," the hermit asked again, "When you reach the city from this forest, will you be able to remain without speaking of what you have seen here?" Then the hunter, speaking to please him, said, "If the Venerable One does not wish it, why—
51:
—would I speak of it? I shall not, Venerable Sir." After paying homage to the hermit, he departed, marking the branches and trees along the way so that he might remember the path when he returned.

When the hunter reached the city of Vārāṇasī, he went to have an audience with the King. When the King of Vārāṇasī asked, "Friend hunter, why have you come before me?", the hunter replied, "Your Majesty, I, your forest hunter, have come because I saw a wonderful woman-treasure (itthi-ratana) at the foot of a mountain." He then reported the entire matter. After hearing the hunter's words, the King quickly went to the foot of the mountain and, having built a temporary pavilion not far from the hermitage, he went to the hermitage together with the hunter and other royal attendants at a time when the hermit had finished his meal and was seated. He paid homage to the hermit, engaged in polite conversation, and sat in a suitable place.

Then the King placed the requisites for a hermit monk that he had brought at the hermit's feet and spoke testingly, "Venerable Sir, what will you do in this forest? Let us go." The hermit replied, "Great King, you yourself may go." When the King said, "Venerable Sir, very well, I shall return; however—
52:
—we have heard that there is a woman, a member of the opposite sex (visabhāga-parisā), near the Venerable Sir. This woman, this member of the opposite sex, is not suitable for hermits and monks. I wish for that woman to follow along with me," he said directly.

Then the hermit, expressing his concern, said, "The minds of men are difficult to satisfy. How will my daughter be able to live among the King's harem and queens? I do not think she can." To reassure the hermit, the King replied, "Venerable Sir, from the moment we are drawn by affection and take delight in her, I shall place her in the position of the leader of the other women of the harem—the position of Chief Queen—and look after her."

Upon hearing the King's words, the hermit called his daughter by the name he had given her since childhood, "Dear daughter Padumavatī!" With just that single call, the maiden Padumavatī came out from the leaf-hut, paid homage to her father, and stood there. When her father said, "Dear daughter, you have reached maturity. From the moment the King has seen you, it is no longer suitable for you to stay in this place. Go together with the King, my daughter," Padumavatī replied, "Very well, father," and without refusing her father's words, she paid homage, wept, and remained standing. The King of Vārāṇasī, thinking, "I shall win the heart of Padumavatī's father," placed Padumavatī upon a heap of gold, silver, and jewels right there and performed the consecration (abhiseka) ceremony.
53:
53
## The Other Queens' Jealousy of Padumadevī Due to the King's Great Affection

Thereafter, the King took Padumavatī as his consort and brought her to his city. From the moment of their arrival, he did not even look at the other concubines and queens, but lived in delight and enjoyment only with Queen Padumavatī. The other royal women, being severely oppressed by jealousy, desired to break the King's love for Queen Padumavatī. They said, "Great King, this Padumavatī is not a real human being. Where have you ever seen Paduma lotuses miraculously springing up under the feet of humans as they walk? Surely, this Padumavatī is an ogress (yakkhinī). Great King, please expel her from the golden palace immediately." Thus they spoke words of jealousy (issā). When the King heard the words of those women, he remained silent without giving any reply.

Later, at one time, the border regions of the King of Bārāṇasī were on the verge of ruin due to a rebellion. The King, knowing that Padumavatī was pregnant, left her at the golden palace and went to the border region. At that time, those royal women, seeing a good opportunity, gave bribes to Queen Padumavatī's attendant and instructed her, "As soon as Padumavatī's son is born, remove him to a secluded place, smear another log of wood with blood, and place it near Padumavatī."

Queen Padumavatī soon gave birth, being delivered from her pregnancy. Prince Mahāpaduma...
54:
—was the only one conceived in the mother's womb. The remaining four hundred and ninety-nine princes became moisture-born (saṃsedaja) princes while Prince Mahāpaduma was lying down after being born from the mother's womb. They were conceived as moisture-born beings in the drops of blood.

At that time, the maidservant, knowing that "Queen Padumavatī has not yet regained consciousness," smeared a log of wood with blood, placed it near Queen Padumavatī, and informed those royal women that the Queen had given birth. All five hundred of those royal women each secretly took one prince. They sent people to the turners to bring five hundred boxes (karanda), placed the young princes they had taken into the boxes respectively, and sealed them with their marks on the outside.

Queen Padumavatī regained consciousness and asked the maidservant, "O mother, how is it? Have I safely given birth?" The wicked maidservant, threatening and scowling at Queen Padumavatī, muttered, "Where would the Queen get a son?" and saying, "This is indeed what was born from the Queen's womb," she placed the blood-smeared log she had prepared before Queen Padumavatī. Seeing that log, Queen Padumavatī was distressed and said in grief, "Mother, split that log and remove it quickly. If anyone sees it, it will only be a cause for shame." Hearing the Queen's words, that wicked maidservant—
55:
Like one seeking benefit, he split the log of wood and threw it into the stove.

The King also returned from the border regions and, while waiting for an auspicious astrological time, resided in a temporary leaf-hut palace constructed outside the city. At that time, those five hundred queens and concubines came to welcome the King and spoke slanderous words, saying, "Great King, you did not believe us; all that we submitted to you has become as if it were groundless. If Your Majesty does not believe us, please summon and question Queen Padumavatī's servant woman. Your most beloved Queen Padumavatī has given birth to a large log of wood."

Without questioning, investigating, or reflecting on the matter, the King misunderstood, thinking, "Padumavatī must be of the race of ogres (yakkhinī)," and banished Queen Padumavatī from the palace.

As for Queen Padumavatī, as soon as she had to leave the golden palace, the lotus flowers vanished. Her complexion also deteriorated and became unsightly. Padumavatī traveled alone and helpless along the way. Then, an old woman, seeing Padumavatī, felt a motherly love for her and asked, "Daughter, where are you going?"

Padumavatī replied, "O mother, I am a stranger. I am wandering and searching in the hope of finding a place to stay." The old woman then said, "Daughter, if that is so, come along to my house," and she took her in, provided her with a place to stay, and fed her.
56:
## The Great Deception of the King's Women Revealed

While Queen Padumavatī was living in the old woman's house in this manner, those five hundred royal women, being of one mind, addressed the King, saying, "Great King, while Your Majesty went to war, we made a vow to the deity guarding the Ganges River, saying, 'If our King returns victorious from the war, we shall perform an offering to you, the deity of the Ganges, and then enjoy ourselves playing in the water.' Great King, let us inform the deity of the Ganges of the news of Your Majesty's victory."

The King, delighted by the words of those royal women, went to the Ganges River to play in the water.

The five hundred royal women also brought the caskets they had taken, keeping them covered. When they reached the landing stage of the Ganges, in order to hide the caskets, they jumped into the water while still wrapped in their upper robes and let the caskets float away. The five hundred caskets floated away in a single group and became entangled in a net that had been spread and set downstream. Later, when the King came out of the water after playing, those who lifted and gathered the net found the caskets to be extraordinary and presented them to the King.

When the King saw the caskets, he asked, "Friends, what items are inside these caskets?" The royal attendants who presented the caskets replied, "Great King, we do not know what is inside the caskets; we found them to be extraordinary and have presented them to you." The King ordered the caskets to be opened and inspected. First, he happened to open the casket where Prince Mahāpaduma was residing.
57:
Remarkably, on the very day those five hundred princes were placed in the caskets, milk began to flow from their thumbs due to the power of the princes' merit. In order to dispel the King of Bārāṇasī's doubt, Sakka, the King of Devas, had letters inscribed inside the caskets:

"These princes are the sons of the King of Bārāṇasī, born from the womb of Queen Padumavatī. This being so, the five hundred royal women, who are enemies of Queen Padumavatī, placed the princes in caskets and set them adrift in the water. Let the King of Bārāṇasī know this fact."

As soon as the caskets were opened, the King read the letters and saw the princes. He himself embraced Prince Mahāpaduma and said, "Friends, quickly harness the chariots! Adorn the state horses! Today, after entering the city, I shall show my love to certain women." Having said this, he rode the chariot into the city palace. Upon ascending the palace, he had a bag of a thousand silver coins tied to the neck of the state elephant and had a drum beaten, proclaiming, "Whoever finds Queen Padumavatī, let that person take these thousand silver coins!"

Hearing the sound of the drum, Padumavatī informed the old woman, her mother, saying, "O mother, please take the bag of a thousand silver coins from the neck of the elephant." The old woman said, "Daughter, I do not dare take such a sum of money." When Padumavatī spoke repeatedly for a second and third time for her to take it,
58:
when she was told repeatedly to take it, the old woman asked, "Daughter, what should I say to take it?" Padumavatī said, "O mother, say, 'My daughter has seen Queen Padumavatī,' and take it." Thinking, "Whatever happens, let it be," the old woman went to where the King's men were beating the drum and requested the bag of a thousand silver coins. When the King's men asked, "O grandmother, have you seen Queen Padumavatī?", the old woman replied, "I have not seen her, but my daughter says she has seen Queen Padumavatī."

The royal attendants said, "O grandmother, where is your daughter now?" and followed the old woman. When they saw and recognized Queen Padumavatī, they prostrated themselves at the Queen's feet. Only then did the old woman realize, "This woman is Queen Padumavatī," and she spoke words of compassionate anger, saying, "The royal woman has done a heavy task indeed! While this royal woman is the Chief Queen of such a King, she has been living in such a place as this, unprotected."

The King's men surrounded the house where Queen Padumavatī lived with white cloth curtains, stationed guards at the door, and reported the matter to the King. The King sent a golden palanquin. Queen Padumavatī said, "I cannot return to the golden palace in such an obscure manner. Only after having exquisite and wonderful floorings spread from the house where I live to the golden palace, and having a cloth ceiling decorated with golden stars hung above them,
59:
and when all the ornaments for a queen to adorn herself have been sent, will I go on foot. In this way, the citizens shall see my prosperity and happiness." The King gave the order, "Act and arrange according to Queen Padumavatī's wishes." Thereafter, Queen Padumavatī, having adorned herself with all the ornaments, set out, saying, "I shall now go to the golden palace."

At that time, at every spot where Queen Padumavatī stepped, wonderful Paduma lotuses burst forth from the ground, breaking through the exquisite floorings. Queen Padumavatī, demonstrating her glory to the multitude of people, ascended to the King's golden palace. Then, she had all the exquisite floorings given to the old woman as payment for her care.

## Padumavatī's Great Magnanimity

The King summoned all those five hundred queens and concubines together and said to Queen Padumavatī, "My Queen, I give these five hundred queens and concubines to you to be your slave-servants." Queen Padumavatī submitted, "Very well, Great King. I wish for all the citizens to be informed that these five hundred royal women have been given to me." The King then had a drum beaten, proclaiming, "The five hundred queens and concubines who wronged Queen Padumavatī have been given by me to be the slave-servants of that Queen Padumavatī." Queen Padumavatī, reflecting and knowing, "Now all the citizens well know that those five hundred queens and concubines are slave-servants," asked, "Great King, does your servant
60:
have the right to make her own slave-servants free from the status of being slaves of the King?" The King replied, "My Queen, to do so is according to your own wish." Then Queen Padumavatī submitted, "Great King, if that is so, please summon those same drum-beating attendants and have them proclaim again, 'Queen Padumavatī has released from slavery all five hundred royal women whom the King gave to her as slaves.'"

After Queen Padumavatī had released those five hundred royal women from slavery, she entrusted four hundred and ninety-nine princes into the hands of those queens and concubines to be cared for and fed, while she herself took only Prince Mahāpaduma.

## The Five Hundred Princes Become Paccekabuddhas

Later, when the five hundred princes reached the age for frolicking and playing, their royal father had various places for the princes to play (various playgrounds) constructed within the auspicious royal garden. When the princes were sixteen years of age, they all gathered and were playing joyfully in the auspicious square pond covered with Paduma lotuses within the royal garden. While doing so, they saw with their own eyes new Paduma lotuses blooming brilliantly and old Paduma lotuses snapping from their stalks and falling one by one. Prompted and urged by the merit of their perfections (pāramī) for Paccekabodhi—
61:
61
“Even to this non-sentient thing, such decay comes; how much more so to our bodies? This body, too, will surely have such a destination.
= This lotus flower, which blooms beautifully due to the influence of karma, the essence of the earth, the moisture of the water, and the season, eventually withers, ages, and falls away as the danger of decay reaches it. Our bodies, which are formed by the combination of the four causes and are tender and moist—how could that terrifying danger of decay not reach them? Our bodies, which wither and deteriorate, will also one day fall away and drop to the ground just like this lotus flower. It is indeed certain and inevitable.”

Taking this as their object for Vipassanā meditation, they became Paccekabuddhas (Self-Enlightened Ones who, without a teacher, contemplate the three characteristics of mental and physical phenomena and attain the four Path-knowledges). They rose from their seats and, using their psychic power of Iddhividha, sat cross-legged upon the pericarp of the lotus flowers.

Afterward, the attendants who had come with the princes, realizing that much of the day had passed, addressed them, saying, “O Princes, please consider the time to return to the golden palace.” Those five hundred Paccekabuddhas remained silent and gave no answer. The attendants returned to the palace and reported to the King of Bārāṇasī, the father, “Your Majesty, the princes are sitting upon the pericarps of the lotus flowers. Although we told them to return to the golden palace, they did not utter a single word.”
62:
62
Then, the royal father gave the command, “Let my sons stay as they wish.”

The five hundred Prince Paccekabuddhas, though guards were stationed throughout the night, remained sitting upon the lotus pericarps until dawn. The next day, the attendants approached them again and said, “O Princes, please consider the time to return to the golden palace.” When the five hundred Prince Paccekabuddhas replied, “We are not princes; we are Paccekabuddhas,” the attendants spoke plainly according to their knowledge, saying, “Sirs, you speak a very heavy word. Those called Paccekabuddhas are not like you. Paccekabuddhas keep their hair and beards only two finger-breadths long and are adorned with the eight requisites. As for you, you have long hair and beards and are wearing the ornaments of princes; how can you be Paccekabuddhas?” Then, the five hundred Paccekabuddhas stroked their heads with their right hands. At that very moment, their lay appearance vanished, and they were already clad in the eight requisites. Thereafter, while the people were watching, the five hundred Paccekabuddhas traveled through the air to the Nandamūla Cave.

## Life as a Housewife Working with Her Own Hands
Queen Padumavatī also fell into great distress and anxiety, thinking, “Alas, from being a mother of sons, I have now become a mother without sons.”
63:
63
Due to the weight of that distress and anxiety, she passed away from that life and was reborn in a family that earned their living by manual labor in a small village at the gate of the city of Rājagaha. Later, she married and went to live at her husband's house. One day, while she was taking gruel to her husband in the field, she saw eight of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas (who were her sons in the previous life) traveling through the air during their alms-round. She went quickly and spoke to her husband, the farmer, “O Lord, behold the Paccekabuddhas! Let us invite these noble Paccekabuddhas and offer them a meal.” The simple farmer said, “My dear, those are called 'monk-birds' (meaning birds that look like monks). In other places (or at other times, according to the Sri Lankan version), they fly and wander in the sky just like this. They are not Paccekabuddhas; they are just birds.”

While the husband and wife were talking, the eight Paccekabuddhas descended to the ground not far from them. That housewife offered her own portion of rice and food for that day to the eight Paccekabuddhas and invited them, saying, “Venerable Sirs, please accept my alms-food tomorrow as well, all eight of you.” The eight Paccekabuddhas said, “Very well, laywoman. Let your offerings be only for eight, and let there be only eight seats. However, if you see many other Paccekabuddhas besides us,
64:
64
your heart will have even greater faith and devotion.” The housewife (the former mother) prepared eight seats and the offerings for eight people the next day and sat waiting.

The eight invited Paccekabuddhas informed the remaining four hundred and ninety-two Paccekabuddhas, saying, “Venerable Sirs, who have ceased suffering, do not go elsewhere today; please come and show favor to your mother.” Hearing the words of the eight Paccekabuddhas, all five hundred Paccekabuddhas traveled through the air and appeared at the door of their mother's house. Because the mother had recognized them from before, she was not at all shaken even though she saw so many Paccekabuddhas (despite the concern that the offerings might not be enough). She invited all five hundred Paccekabuddhas into the house and had them sit in the seats (the eight seats).

When the eight Paccekabuddhas sat down in order, the ninth Paccekabuddha created eight more seats and sat in the first of those seats. As the seats increased and expanded, the house also increased and expanded accordingly. (This is a matter of psychic power).

In this way, when all five hundred Paccekabuddhas were seated, the former mother offered the food she had prepared for eight people to all five hundred Paccekabuddhas. It was sufficient for all of them as they desired.
65:
65
After offering the food, she brought eight blue lotuses and placed them at the feet of the eight Paccekabuddhas she had originally invited. She then made an aspiration, saying, “Venerable Sirs, in whatever life I am reborn in Saṃsāra, may my body's complexion be like the color of the heart of these blue lotuses.” The five hundred Paccekabuddhas gave their blessing to their mother and returned to Mount Gandhamādana.

## (b) Becoming a Nun in Her Final Life
That woman performed meritorious deeds throughout her life. After passing away from that life, she was reborn in the celestial realm. During the time when our Supreme Buddha appeared, she was conceived in a wealthy merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī. Because the complexion of the merchant's daughter was like the heart of a blue lotus, she was named “Uppalavaṇṇā.” When Uppalavaṇṇā reached the age of maturity, all the kings and wealthy men throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa sent messengers with letters to her father, the great merchant, asking, “Please give your daughter to us.” There was no king or merchant who did not ask for her.

Then, the father thought, “With only one daughter, I will not be able to satisfy the minds of all those who want her. Therefore, I shall use a stratagem.” He summoned his daughter and asked, “Dear daughter, would you be able to become a nun?” Since Uppalavaṇṇā herself was a *pacchimabhavika* (one in her final birth in Saṃsāra), the words spoken by her father
66:
66
were like fragrant oil, refined a hundred times, being poured over her head. Therefore, she joyfully replied to her father, “I will become a nun, father.”

The great merchant honored his daughter Uppalavaṇṇā with great ceremony, took her to the nunnery, and had her ordained. Not long after Uppalavaṇṇā Bhikkhunī was ordained, her turn came to perform duties in the Uposatha hall. Uppalavaṇṇā Bhikkhunī lit a lamp and swept the Uposatha hall. Then, taking the flame of the lamp as her meditation object, she stood and looked at the tip of the flame repeatedly, developing the fire kasina (tejo-kasiṇa). Before long, she attained the Tejo-kasiṇa Jhāna. Based on the concentration of that Tejo-kasiṇa Jhāna, she practiced Vipassanā meditation and soon reached the Fruit of Arahantship, becoming an Arahant Therī. Simultaneously with reaching the Fruit of Arahantship, she became one who had mastered the five proficiencies (vasībhāva) in psychic powers, as she had previously aspired.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Foremost (Etadagga)
Later (when the Buddha reached His seventh rainy season), on the day the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle, Uppalavaṇṇā Arahant Therī boldly spoke like the roar of a lion, saying, “Supreme Buddha, let me perform a miracle.” (The details of her request can be found in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, page 517). The Supreme Buddha...
67:
67
Based on this background, on another occasion while residing at the Jetavana monastery, when the Buddha was appointing bhikkhunīs to various positions (ṭhānantara), he praised the Arahant Therī Uppalavaṇṇā:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ iddhimantīnaṃ yadidaṃ uppalavaṇṇā = Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who possess psychic powers (iddhi), Uppalavaṇṇā is the foremost.”

Thus, he placed her in the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being “foremost among those with psychic powers (iddhimantī).”

This is the account of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī.

## (4) The Account of Paṭācārā Therī
## (a) The Therī's Aspiration in the Past
This future Paṭācārā Therī was also born as a daughter of a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's discourse, she saw the Buddha appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being foremost among those who are versed in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara). Feeling inspired, she performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made an aspiration for that same position of being foremost among those who carry the Vinaya Piṭaka. Padumuttara Buddha also gave her the prophecy (byādika) as in the previous cases.
68:
68
## Her Life as the Daughter of King Kikī
That wealthy man's daughter performed meritorious deeds throughout her life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was the third of the seven daughters of King Kikī mentioned earlier, named “Bhikkhunī.” For twenty thousand years, she practiced the maidenly celibacy (komāribrahmacariya) and built a large monastery complex (saṅghārāma parivena) for the Saṅgha.

## (b) Becoming a Nun in Her Final Life
After performing meritorious deeds throughout her life, she passed away from that existence and was reborn in the deva realm. She enjoyed divine pleasures (sampatti) for an incalculable period between the appearance of two Buddhas. During the time when our Buddha appeared, she was reborn as the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the city of Sāvatthī.

When she reached the age of maturity, she fell in love with a servant in her own house. Later, when her parents were about to marry her to a son of a merchant of equal status and class, and she was about to be taken to his house, she spoke to the servant she loved: “From tomorrow onwards, you will not have the chance to see me even through a hundred gates, as I will be taken to the house of the merchant's son my parents have chosen. If you have any intention, take me away now and flee.” The servant agreed, saying, “Very well, let it be so.”
69:
69
Taking suitable gifts and wealth, he led the merchant's daughter away. They fled three or four yojanas from Sāvatthī and lived in a small village.

Later, she became pregnant. When the pregnancy was mature, she said to her husband, “My lord, this place is a place without any refuge for us. Therefore, let us return to my parents' house.” Because the husband did not dare to return, he delayed the time, saying, “We shall go today, we shall go tomorrow.” Knowing her husband's nature, she thought, “This fool will not take me to my parents,” and while her husband was away on a journey, she decided, “I will go to my parents' house alone,” and set out on the journey.

When the husband returned home and did not find her, he asked the neighbors and learned that she had returned to her parents' house. Thinking, “Alas, because of me, this lady of good family has become helpless,” he felt great compassion and followed her closely. He caught up with her on the way. For her, the birth of the child occurred right there on the road. Then both husband and wife consulted and agreed: “The purpose for which we were going to the parents' house—the birth of the child—has already been completed on the way. What is the use of going there now? There is no further need.” Thus, they returned to their small forest village.
70:
70
Later, she became pregnant again. When the pregnancy was mature, she spoke to her husband about returning to her parents' home as before, but the husband delayed as before, saying, “We will go today, we will go tomorrow.” So she set out for her parents' house alone, and her husband followed and caught up with her on the way as before.

Immediately after she gave birth on the road, a great storm arose from all four directions and rained heavily. She said to her husband, “My lord, a great storm has arisen and is raining heavily from all four directions in the night. Please make an effort to build a shelter for us (according to the Sinhalese version—a place not wet by rain).” The husband comforted her, saying, “Very well, I will build it.” He gathered whatever sticks and branches he could find to build a makeshift hut. Thinking, “I will bring grass for the roof,” and not knowing in the darkness whether there was an anthill or not, he began to pull grass at the base of an anthill.

At that moment, a cobra lying in the anthill bit him on the foot. The man fell and died right there. The merchant's daughter, waiting and thinking, “He will come now, he will come now,” passed the three watches of the night. She thought, “Surely this man has abandoned me on the road, thinking 'this woman is helpless'.”
71:
71
When the light of dawn appeared, she followed his tracks and looked here and there. She found her husband fallen dead near the base of the mountain (or anthill). Crying bitterly, “Because of me, my husband has perished,” she carried the younger son on her hip and led the elder son by the hand, continuing along the road. On the way, she encountered a small river (or stream) that appeared deep but was shallow. Thinking, “I cannot carry both sons across at the same time,” she left the elder son on this bank, carried the younger son to the other bank, laid him on a cloth, and planned, “I will return to fetch the elder son and cross this river.” She then waded back into the river.

When she reached the middle of the river, a hawk, thinking “this object is a piece of meat,” flew down swiftly to snatch the younger child. Because she was far away, she could only stretch out her hands and make a sound to drive the hawk away. Seeing his mother's gesture of stretching out her hands, the elder son thought, “My mother is calling me,” and ran into the river. He was swept away by the current and died. Before she could reach him, the hawk snatched the younger son and flew away. The distressed woman was overcome with great grief on the road:

“Ubho puttā kālaṅkatā,
Panthe mayhaṃ patī mato.”
72:
72
“Both my sons have passed away,
My husband is dead on the path.”

(The verse means: Of me, who is known by the name Paṭācārā because I have failed in my duties of restraint, both sons—the elder and the younger—have perished, one by drowning and one taken by a hawk. On the path where there is no refuge, my husband, my support, has died.)

Uttering this half-verse of lamentation, she headed towards the city of Sāvatthī. Although she reached Sāvatthī and was near her parents' house, she could not recognize it due to the intensity of her grief. She asked people she met nearby, “There is a merchant's house of such description in this area; which house is it?” Those people replied, “Lady, what can you do by asking about that merchant's house? You can do nothing. That merchant's family home collapsed last night due to a violent wind. All the members of the merchant's family perished inside that collapsed building. When they died, the great and small members of that family were cremated together on a single funeral pyre. (Pointing to where the smoke was rising) Look, Lady, at that column of smoke rising up.” Upon hearing these sorrowful words, Paṭācārā could only say, “Oh, what are you saying?” and being unable to even keep her clothes on, she raised both arms in her naked state,
73:
73
Crying out and raising her arms, she went towards the place where the funeral pyre of her parents and relatives was. Wishing to complete the previous half-verse of lamentation with another half-verse, she wailed:

“Ubho puttā kālaṅkatā,
Panthe mayhaṃ patī mato.
Mātā pitā ca bhātā ca,
Ekacitakasmiṃ ḍayhare.”

(The verse means: Of me, the daughter of a good family who is known by the name Paṭācārā because I have failed in my duties of restraint, both sons have perished—one drowned and one taken by a hawk. On the path where there is no refuge, my husband has died. My mother, my father, and my brother who was born from the same womb, have all perished in the collapsed house and are now being cremated on a single funeral pyre.)

Thus she lamented.

## How She Got the Name Paṭācārā
Because she was wandering around in her naked state, even when someone offered her a cloth (htamein) to cover her shame, she did not remember to wear it and only tore it into pieces and threw it away. Then, wherever people saw her,
74:
She wandered around in a circle. At that time, she was named "Patācārā" because she wandered about without wearing a cloth (paṭa). Furthermore, because she did not wear clothes, the behavior of those without shame was evident in her. Thus, she was called "Patācārā" because she had fallen away from the conduct of the modest and the conduct of the shameless was manifest in her.

The wealthy man's daughter, Patācārā, unable to control her mind and in her natural state of birth, wandered aimlessly, wailing only the verses of lamentation mentioned before. When people saw her, they said, "Hey, go away, you madwoman!" Some threw rubbish on her head, some scattered dust on her, and some threw stones at her.

## Receiving the Sprinkling of the Cool Water of the Deathless

While the Buddha was sitting in the midst of a large assembly at the Jetavana monastery preaching the Dhamma, he saw Patācārā wandering about in such an unsettled state. Seeing that the time for her wisdom to ripen had come, he made a solemn determination (adhiṭṭhāna) so that Patācārā would come towards the monastery. When the audience saw Patācārā coming, they said, "Do not allow this madwoman to come to this place." The Buddha said, "Do not forbid Patācārā." When she came near, he spoke with great compassion, saying, "Dear daughter, regain your mindfulness."
75:
At 그 moment, by the power of the Buddha, Patācārā regained her mindfulness. Realizing that her garment had fallen off (that she was without it), she felt great shame and dread. She sat down, crouching and bending her waist, covering herself as much as possible. At that time, a man threw her an upper garment. Patācārā wore that cloth, approached the Buddha, and respectfully paid homage with the five-point prostration, saying:

"Venerable Sir, please be my refuge. A hawk has snatched away one of my sons (the younger one). The other (the elder one) was swept away and drowned by the turbulent river water. My husband passed away on the journey. My parents and my brother also died when their house collapsed, and they have been cremated on a single funeral pyre, Venerable Sir."

Thus, she explained the cause of her sorrow.

The Buddha said, "Dear daughter Patācārā, do not be overwhelmed by various thoughts. You have come to the presence of one who can be your refuge and reliance. Just as you are now shedding tears because of the death of your sons, husband, parents, and brother, even so, the tears you have shed due to the death of sons, husbands, parents, and brothers throughout this incalculable Saṃsāra are far more than the water in the four great oceans." Thus, he pointed out the Dhamma, saying:
76:
Catusu samuddesu jalaṃ parittakaṃ,
Tato bahuṃ assujalaṃ anappakaṃ.
Dukkhena phuṭṭhassa narassa socanā,
Kiṃ kāraṇā amma tuvaṃ pamajjasi.

"Dear daughter Patācārā, the water in the four oceans of the four directions—east, west, south, and north—is very little compared to the tears of a single being. The tears that have flowed and trickled due to the grief of a person who has not yet removed the defilement of anger, being afflicted by both physical and mental suffering from the loss of children, husband, parents, and brothers, are many times more in number than the water in those four great oceans. Dear daughter Patācārā, for what reason are you negligent and forgetful? Do not be negligent; hold fast to mindfulness and do not be heedless."

Thus, he preached the verse of Dhamma that dispels sorrow.

When the Buddha had thus preached the discourse on the incalculable nature of Saṃsāra (Anamatagga-pariyāya-kathā), the sorrow in Patācārā's mind was greatly thinned. Then, the Buddha, seeing that Patācārā's sorrow had diminished, said, "Dear daughter Patācārā, for one who must go to the next world, children, husbands, and such...
77:
...cannot be a protection, nor can they be a hiding place or a refuge. Therefore, even if those children, husbands, and others are alive, they are as if non-existent for one who must go to the next world. Therefore, a wise person should purify his own virtue and well-complete the path of good practice leading to Nibbāna." Expressing this meaning, he said:

Na santi puttā tāṇāya, na pitā nāpi bandhavā.
Antakenādhipannassa, natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā.

"Dear daughter Patācārā, for one who is oppressed by Death (Antaka) when the time has come, sons and daughters cannot provide protection by repelling the enemy of Death. Parents, the great benefactors, cannot. Even relatives and friends bound by affection cannot. Among relatives—parents, daughters, sons—there is no such thing as being able to protect by repelling and removing the enemy of Death."

Etamatthavasaṃ ñatvā, paṇḍito sīlasaṃvuto.
Nibbānagamanaṃ maggaṃ, khippameva visodhaye.

"A wise person, who considers and foresees the future, having understood this reason—that there is not a single person who can protect when the enemy of Death arrives—and being restrained by virtue so as not to break his conduct...
78:
...should quickly clear the path of the eightfold constituents leading to Nibbāna through daily practice."

He preached with these verses. At the end of the teaching, Patācārā, the wealthy man's daughter, completely burned away defilements as numerous as the dust of the great earth with the fire of the wisdom of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala); she became a Sotāpanna Ariya.

After becoming a Sotāpanna, Patācārā requested the Buddha to ordain her as a nun. The Buddha had her taken to the bhikkhunīs and ordained. After attaining the state of a nun, while Bhikkhunī Patācārā was practicing Vipassanā for the sake of the higher paths, one day, while pouring water from a jar to wash her feet, the water flowed to a short distance and stopped. When she poured a second time, it reached a little further than the first and stopped. When she poured a third time, it reached a little further than the second and stopped.

## Patācārā Therī Becomes an Arahant

Patācārā Therī took those three distances reached by the water as her object of meditation, and having partitioned the three stages of life with wisdom, she reflected:
79:
"Like the water I poured the first time, these beings can pass away and die in the first stage of life. Like the water poured the second time, which reached a little further than the first water and stopped, they can pass away and die in the middle stage of life. Like the water poured the third time, which reached a little further than the second water and stopped, they will certainly pass away and die in the last stage of life."

Thus, she remained reflecting with penetrating wisdom. Having taken the object of meditation and reflected in this way, Patācārā Therī meditated on the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), thinking, "Just as all three types of water have the nature of being exhausted and destroyed, so too the life-continuum (āyu-saṅkhāra) of beings has the nature of being exhausted and destroyed." Following that characteristic of impermanence, she investigated and reflected on the characteristics of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) and non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa). While developing Vipassanā, desiring suitable weather, she entered her cell in the monastery. To dispel the darkness, she entered the room holding an oil lamp. After placing the lamp in its proper place, while sitting on the small couch, she pulled the wick towards the oil with a needle to extinguish the lamp.

At that time, the Buddha, while sitting in the Gandhakuṭī, sent forth his radiance and appeared as if standing before the Therī, saying:

"Dear daughter Patācārā, this matter that you are considering is true just as you consider it. All beings indeed...
80:
...have the nature of passing away and dying. Therefore, rather than living a hundred years without seeing the arising and falling of the five aggregates with wisdom, living for even a single day or a single moment while seeing the arising and falling of the five aggregates with wisdom is truly praiseworthy and noble."

Expressing this meaning, he preached this Dhammapada verse:

Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve,
apassaṃ udayabbayaṃ.
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo,
passato udayabbayaṃ.

"Dear daughter Patācārā, if a person should live for a hundred long years without knowing or seeing the arising and falling of the two groups of mind and matter with the eye of Vipassanā wisdom, then the life of one who lives for even a single day while observing, reflecting, and knowing the arising and falling of the two groups of mind and matter with the eye of Vipassanā wisdom is far more praiseworthy and noble."

At the end of the verse, Patācārā Therī reached the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala) together with the four analytical insights (Paṭisambhidā). She became an Arahant Therī who had attained the analytical insights.
81:
81
## (c) Attaining the Title of Etadagga
After Paṭācārā Therī became an Arahant with the exhaustion of all taints (āsavas), she studied the entire Vinaya Piṭaka in detail under the Blessed One and was accustomed to preaching and answering matters concerning the Vinaya according to the truth. Therefore, at a later time while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, when the Blessed One was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions of rank (ṭhānantara), he praised the Arahant Paṭācārā Therī, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ paṭācārā = Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who are bearers of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara), Paṭācārā is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed her to the pre-eminent (Etadagga) position of being the foremost in the category of “Vinayadhara = Bearer of the Vinaya.”

This is the account of Paṭācārā Therī.

## (5) The Story of Dhammadinnā Therī
## (a) The Therī’s Past Aspiration
This noble lady, the future Dhammadinnā Therī, was a poor working woman in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Being a wise person of mature wisdom and a keeper of virtue, one day, while going to fetch water, she saw the Venerable Sujāta, the Chief Disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara,
82:
82
entering for alms. With a heart full of faith and devotion, she personally offered the cake she had brought for her own consumption to the Great Elder. To show his favor to the woman, the Great Elder accepted the cake and partook of it while sitting right there.

At the time of receiving that cake offering, the Venerable Sujāta had just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Therefore, that meritorious deed was capable of yielding results in a very short time.

Not being satisfied with merely offering the cake, the working woman (servant) sold her hair for whatever she could get, invited the Venerable Sujāta to her home, and offered him a choice meal. When her master, the treasurer, heard of this, he was greatly delighted and pleased, and he gave her in marriage to his son, making her his daughter-in-law.

One day, this daughter-in-law of the treasurer went with her mother-in-law to the presence of the Blessed One Padumuttara. While listening to the Dhamma after paying respects, she saw the Blessed One Padumuttara appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the pre-eminent (Etadagga) position of being “Dhammakathika = Foremost in Preaching the Dhamma.” Greatly delighted, she made a grand offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and made an aspiration for that same Etadagga position. The Blessed One Padumuttara then gave her the prophecy (byādika) that her aspiration would be fulfilled during the time of our Blessed One.
83:
83
## Life as the Treasurer’s Wife
That daughter-in-law of the treasurer performed meritorious deeds until the end of her life. After passing away from that life, she wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Ninety-two aeons ago from this present world, during the time when the Blessed One Phussa appeared, she became the wife of the treasurer for the three princes who were half-brothers of the Buddha. She was a person of great and intense faith; if asked for one thing, she would give two. (The story of this treasurer and his wife can be found in the Mahā-Buddhavaṃsa, Volume II, starting from page 607).

## Life as King Kikī’s Daughter
That treasurer’s wife performed meritorious deeds until the end of her life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, she became the sixth daughter named “Sudhammā” among the seven daughters of King Kikī mentioned previously. She practiced the holy life of celibacy (komāri-brahmacariya) for twenty thousand years and built a large monastery complex (parivena) for the Saṅgha of monks.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
That princess performed meritorious deeds until the end of her life. After passing away from that life, she was reborn in the deva realm. For an incalculable period between the appearance of two Buddhas, she wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time when our Blessed One appeared, she was born as the daughter of a treasurer in the city of Rājagaha. When she reached the age of maturity,
84:
84
her parents gave her in marriage to the treasurer Visākha. She arrived at Visākha's house and became well-known as the treasurer’s wife, Dhammadinnā.

The treasurer and his wife, who had great faith during the time of the Blessed One Phussa ninety-two aeons ago, became the treasurer Visākha and the treasurer’s wife Dhammadinnā in the time of our Blessed One. The treasurer Visākha was one among the one hundred and ten thousand persons who attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) when the Blessed One first arrived at the city of Rājagaha (on the full moon day of Phussa in the year 103 of the Great Era) and preached to King Bimbisāra, who had come with a following of one hundred and twenty thousand people to see the Buddha. He was also a treasurer who was a very close friend of King Bimbisāra.

From the very first time he saw the Blessed One, the treasurer Visākha was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Later, upon hearing the Dhamma again one day, he reached the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala). Subsequently, hearing the Dhamma again on another day, he was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). After becoming an Anāgāmī Ariya, when he returned home, he did not return as he had on other past days—looking here and there, smiling and cheerful—but instead, on the day he became an Anāgāmī, he returned with very calm faculties and a very peaceful mind.

The treasurer’s wife Dhammadinnā opened the lion-supported window and looked out toward the street. Seeing the manner in which the treasurer Visākha was coming with such great composure, she thought, “What special reason could there be for my lord, the treasurer Visākha, to be coming with such great composure?”
85:
85
Thinking thus, she wished to welcome the treasurer and stood at the head of the stairs, extending her hand for him to take. On other past days, the treasurer Visākha used to take Dhammadinnā’s hand to ascend the house, but on that day, he kept his hand withdrawn. The treasurer’s wife thought, “I shall know at the time of the morning meal,” and composed her mind. Although the treasurer Visākha used to eat together with Dhammadinnā in the past, on that day, he did not call or invite her, but ate alone with great composure, like a monk practicing meditation. The treasurer’s wife thought, “I shall know in the evening,” and calmed her mind.

When evening came that day, the treasurer Visākha did not enter the auspicious bedchamber but had another room cleaned, a suitable couch (kappiya-khaṭṭa) prepared, and slept alone. Only then did Dhammadinnā think, “Could there be some external longing or affection for this treasurer? Or has someone caused a rift between us? Or is there some fault of mine?” Feeling very distressed, after a day or two had passed, she thought, “By now, I should be able to know,” and went to attend to the treasurer Visākha, paid respects, and stood there. Then, the treasurer Visākha and the treasurer’s wife Dhammadinnā questioned and answered each other as follows:
86:
86
(The Treasurer)
“Dhammadinnā, why have you come at an unusual time?”

(The Treasurer’s Wife)
“It is true, my lord, I have come at an unusual time. My lord is not as before. How is it? Is there some external longing or affection on my lord’s part apart from me?”

(The Treasurer)
“There is none, Dhammadinnā.”

(The Treasurer’s Wife)
“If not, is there someone who has caused a rift?”

(The Treasurer)
“There is no such person who has caused a rift either.”

(The Treasurer’s Wife)
“If so, is there any fault of mine?”

(The Treasurer)
“There is no fault of yours either, Dhammadinnā.”

(The Treasurer’s Wife)
“If that is the case, why does my lord not even speak words of greeting or response in the natural manner of a husband and wife?”

When asked directly like this, the treasurer Visākha thought, “This Supramundane Dhamma (Lokuttara Dhamma) that I have realized is a very heavy and profound Dhamma, not something to be revealed like common talk or local matters. It is a Dhamma that should be kept private. However, if I do not answer, this treasurer’s wife Dhammadinnā might die right here of a broken heart.” Considering this, he said:
87:
87
“Dhammadinnā, because I have heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, I have attained and realized the Supramundane Dhamma (Lokuttara Dhamma). For one who has attained and realized such Supramundane Dhamma, worldly behaviors of this nature are no longer appropriate at all. If you so desire (agree), there are forty crores of wealth brought from your side and forty crores from my side, totaling eighty crores of wealth in this house. You shall be the owner of these eighty crores of wealth and remain in the position of my mother or my elder sister. I shall live on just the food you provide. If you do not wish to do this, then take these riches and return to your parents’ house. If you have no external longing, I shall keep you in the position of a younger sister or a daughter and look after you.”

Thus he spoke openly and extensively. When the treasurer’s wife Dhammadinnā heard these words, she thought, “It is not possible for an ordinary man to speak like this. Surely, this lord has realized the Supramundane Dhamma with penetrative insight. Specifically, what I want to know is: is this Supramundane Dhamma only for men to realize, or are women (mātugāma) also capable of realizing it with penetrative insight?” Having thought thus, she asked the treasurer Visākha, “My lord, how is it? Is this Supramundane Dhamma attainable only by men?”
88:
She asked directly, "Can women also attain this?"

Then the merchant Visākha replied, "What are you saying, Dhammadinnā? Anyone who strives and practices the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti) can receive this supramundane (lokuttara) inheritance. Anyone who possesses the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of previous merit for the Path and Fruit (magga-phala) can receive this supramundane Dhamma."

When he answered thus, the merchant's wife Dhammadinnā requested permission, saying, "Noble sir, if that is so, please grant me permission to become a bhikkhunī."

Then the merchant Visākha said, "Very well, lady. I also wish for you to be established in this supramundane path. However, not knowing your heart's desire, I did not speak of it or encourage you." Having said this, he immediately went to King Bimbisāra, paid homage, and stood there.

When King Bimbisāra asked, "Merchant, why have you come at an unusual time?", the merchant Visākha replied, "Great King, the merchant's wife Dhammadinnā says she will become a bhikkhunī."

The King asked, "What should be provided for the merchant's wife Dhammadinnā?" The merchant Visākha replied, "She desires nothing else, Your Majesty. However, she should have a golden palanquin, and I wish for the city to be cleaned and cleared."

As requested by the merchant Visākha, the King provided a golden palanquin and ordered the city to be cleaned.
89:
## The Grand Ordination as a Bhikkhunī

The merchant Visākha had Dhammadinnā bathed with scented water and adorned with all kinds of ornaments. He had her sit upon the golden palanquin, surrounded by all her relatives. Then, making offerings with many perfumes and flowers as if perfuming the entire city, they went to the bhikkhunīs' monastery. He addressed them, "Venerable ladies, please ordain my partner Dhammadinnā as a bhikkhunī."

The bhikkhunīs (thinking she was being sent away due to some fault) said, "Lay follower, you should forgive mistakes made once or twice." Visākha replied, "Venerable ladies, Dhammadinnā has no fault whatsoever. Dhammadinnā is one who wishes to become a bhikkhunī out of faith and devotion."

Then, a senior nun (therī) who was skilled in the Vinaya taught Dhammadinnā the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in the skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), shaved her hair, and ordained her. The merchant Visākha addressed the Therī Dhammadinnā, saying, "Venerable lady, may you delight in the Sāsanā. The Blessed One has clearly taught the Dhamma which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end." After paying homage, he returned home.

From the day she was ordained, the Therī Dhammadinnā received many gains and offerings. Because of these abundant gains and offerings, she found no opportunity to practice the recluse's Dhamma.
90:
(This collection of words is from the commentary on the Cūḷavedalla Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya Mūlapaṇṇāsa).

After becoming a bhikkhunī, Dhammadinnā reflected, "This merchant Visākha, while still living in the household, has worked towards the end of the suffering of saṃsāra. Now that I have attained the status of a bhikkhunī, it is only proper that I also strive and practice to reach the end of the suffering of saṃsāra." She went to her teachers and preceptors and said, "Venerable ladies, my mind does not find delight in this place crowded with the five sense objects. I wish to go to a small village monastery in the forest."

Because she was one who had left a great family to become a nun, the senior nuns could not refuse her wish to live in a forest monastery. Thus, they accompanied the Therī Dhammadinnā to a small village monastery.

Because the Therī Dhammadinnā was one who had investigated conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) with wisdom in past lives, it was not long before she attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) through her diligent practice. Then, the Therī Dhammadinnā reflected, "My task as a monastic has reached its summit. What is the use of staying in this forest? There is nothing more to be done. I shall return to Rājagaha. There, many of my relatives will be able to perform meritorious deeds by relying on me." Having reflected thus, she invited her teachers and preceptors and returned to Rājagaha.
91:
## Visākha Asks Questions

The merchant Visākha heard the news that "Therī Dhammadinnā has returned to Rājagaha." He thought, "Dhammadinnā went to the countryside shortly after ordaining, and now she has returned so soon. What could be the reason? I shall go myself to find out." In the evening, he went to the Therī Dhammadinnā, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He thought, "To ask 'Lady, do you delight in the Sāsanā or not?' is not the way of the wise. I shall ask questions concerning the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā). By her answers to these questions, I shall know whether she delights in the Sāsanā or not."

Having reflected thus, he asked questions starting with the five aggregates. (The full details of Visākha's questions and Therī Dhammadinnā's answers can be found in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka, Mūlapaṇṇāsa, 5-Cūḷayamakavagga, 4-Cūḷavedalla Sutta, starting from page 385).

The Arahant Therī Dhammadinnā answered every group of questions correctly and without hesitation, like cutting a lotus stalk with a sword or like a swift horse. The merchant Visākha, recognizing the sharpness of her wisdom, asked everything that should be asked regarding the three lower paths (magga) which he himself had attained and understood. Then, based on what he had heard and learned (though not personally attained), he asked a question regarding the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). The Therī Dhammadinnā, knowing that Visākha's scope of questioning should only go as far as the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala),
92:
realized that "Now the merchant Visākha has run past the boundary of what he should ask." Wishing to stop him, she said:

When Visākha asked, "Lady, what is the counterpart of peace, which is Nibbāna?"

She replied, "Lay follower Visākha, you have overstepped the question. You are not able to grasp the limit of questions. (Meaning: Nibbāna is a Dhamma without a counterpart. By asking for the counterpart of the peerless Nibbāna, you cannot grasp the measure of the question). Indeed, Visākha, the holy life of the three trainings (sikkhā) in the Sāsanā merges into Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its destination, and has Nibbāna as its culmination. Visākha, if you wish (if you are not yet satisfied and want to ask further), approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it."

She spoke thus decisively. Then, the merchant Visākha went to the Blessed One and reported the entire conversation—how he had asked and how the Therī Dhammadinnā had answered. When the Blessed One heard Visākha's words, he said, "In my daughter Therī Dhammadinnā, there is no longer any craving (taṇhā) or greed for the aggregates of the past,
93:
future, or present." He then spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:

*Yassa pure ca pacchā ca,*
*majjhe ca natthi kiñcanaṃ;*
*Akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ,*
*tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.*

"Householder Visākha, for whom there is nothing—no 'mine' or preoccupation called the attachment of craving—in the past aggregates that have occurred, in the future aggregates that will arise, or in the present aggregates between the past and future; who is without such preoccupations as passion and so forth; who has no clinging to anything whatsoever—that noble person, I, the Teacher of the three worlds, call a Brāhmaṇa, a holy person, because they have discarded all evil."

(At the end of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. From Dhammapada Commentary 2, page 452).

Afterwards, the Blessed One gave his approval to the Therī Dhammadinnā and said to the merchant Visākha, "Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is wise. Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has great wisdom. Visākha, if you had asked me about that matter, I would have explained it
94:
in the same way that the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has explained it. That is indeed the meaning of that question. You should remember the meaning just as the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has explained it."

(This incident led to the Therī Dhammadinnā receiving the pre-eminent (etadagga) title of 'Dhammakathika'—one who is most skilled and excellent in preaching the Dhamma).

(Note: Because of this confirmation by the Blessed One, the entire Cūḷavedalla Sutta is no longer considered a discourse spoken by a disciple (sāvaka-bhāsita), but a discourse spoken by the Victor (jina-bhāsita). For example, a letter written by officials is not called a royal decree until it is stamped with the king's seal; as soon as it is stamped, it is called a royal decree. Similarly, because the Blessed One set his seal of approval by saying, "I would have explained it in the same way," this entire Cūḷavedalla Sutta is to be understood as a Jina-bhāsita Sutta spoken by the Buddha. The same applies to other suttas of this nature).

## (C) Attaining the Pre-eminent Title

At a later time, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, as he was assigning the various pre-eminent (etadagga) positions to the bhikkhunīs, he took this Cūḷavedalla Sutta as the basis and declared the Therī Dhammadinnā in this Sāsanā:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ dhammadinnā."
"Monks, among my female disciples who are speakers of Dhamma, Dhammadinnā is the foremost."
95:
“Among my female disciples, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is the foremost, the most excellent.”

Thus, the Buddha praised her and appointed her to the rank of Etadagga, the foremost in the category of being a speaker of Dhamma (Dhammakathika).

This is the account of Dhammadinnā Therī.
**********
## (6) The Account of Nandā Therī
(In this context, Nandā Therī refers to Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī. Her story has been extensively detailed in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume IV, page 344, in the chapter “Appendix to the Burmese Translation of the Vijaya Sutta.” In this Chapter 44, I shall describe it briefly as it appears in the Aṅguttara Commentary.)

## (a) The Therī’s Past Aspiration
The future Nandā Therī was born as a daughter of a wealthy family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha’s discourse, she saw the Buddha appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the rank of Etadagga, the foremost among those who dwell in meditative absorption (jhāna). She performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very rank. The Buddha also gave her a prophetic assurance (byādika).

## (b) Ordination in Her Final Life
