After that life, she wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In this final existence, she was born as the younger sister (and betrothed) of Prince Nanda.
96:
She became Princess Nandā. She was also called Princess Abhirūpanandā. Later, because she possessed an exceedingly beautiful physical form, she became known by the name Janapadakalyāṇī (the Beauty of the Land).

This Janapadakalyāṇī Abhirūpanandā, the biological daughter of the Great Foster Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, heard the news after our Buddha attained Enlightenment and eventually returned to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, ordained Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula, and departed. After King Suddhodana attained Parinibbāna, she heard: “My mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and my sister-in-law Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, have left the household life and become bhikkhunīs in the presence of the Buddha.” She reflected, “For me, from the time my mother and sister-in-law became bhikkhunīs, what business is there left for me in this golden palace? There is none.” Thus, she went to the presence of the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and was ordained as a bhikkhunī.

From the day she became a bhikkhunī, she thought, “The Buddha disparages physical beauty,” and thus she did not go to attend upon the Buddha. Even when her turn came to receive the exhortation (ovāda), she did not go herself but sent another bhikkhunī in her place to bring back the instruction. The Buddha, knowing well that Nandā Therī was intoxicated with pride in her beauty, issued a further decree: “Bhikkhunīs must come in person to receive their own exhortation; they must not send another bhikkhunī as a representative.”
97:
At that time, Rūpanandā Therī, seeing no other way to avoid it, reluctantly went to the Buddha to receive the exhortation.

To suit the temperament of Rūpanandā Therī, the Buddha had beforehand used his psychic power to create a vision of a beautiful woman holding a palm-leaf fan and fanning him. When Rūpanandā Therī saw this created vision of the beautiful woman, she thought, “Oh, I have been negligent and failed to come to the Buddha for no good reason. Even women as beautiful as this are moving about near the Buddha, serving him intimately. Compared to the beauty of this woman, my own beauty does not even equal a sixteenth part of a sixteenth part (1/256th). Because of my ignorance and wickedness, I have failed to come to the Buddha for so long.” Thinking thus, she stood there staring intently at the vision of the beautiful woman.

Because Rūpanandā Therī was one who had fulfilled past merits, the Buddha preached the verse from the Dhammapada beginning with “Aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ kataṃ” (A city made of bones), and followed it by preaching the Vijaya Sutta from the Sutta Nipāta, beginning with “Caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ, nisinno uda vā sayaṃ.” Rūpanandā Therī repeatedly reflected on the discourse of the Vijaya Sutta and diligently practiced the meditation on emptiness (Suññata-kammaṭṭhāna). Within two or three days, she attained the Fruit of Arahantship.
98:
(The detailed account should be sought in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume IV, starting from page 344.)

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
From the time she attained Arahantship, Rūpanandā Therī became pre-eminent and outstanding among the bhikkhunīs who delighted in meditative absorption (jhāna). Therefore, later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery and was appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective ranks of Etadagga, he spoke in praise of Nandā Therī:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ jhāyīnaṃ yadidaṃ nandā = Monks, among my female disciples who are habitual practitioners of jhāna, Nandā is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed her to the rank of Etadagga, the foremost in the category of “Jhāyī,” meaning those who habitually enter into and delight in meditative absorption.

This is the account of Nandā Therī.
**********
## (7) The Account of (Bahupputtika) Soṇā Therī
## (a) The Therī’s Past Aspiration
The future (Bahupputtika) Soṇā Therī was born as the daughter of a wealthy man in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha’s discourse, she saw the Buddha
99:
appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the rank of Etadagga, the foremost in the category of “Āraddhavīriya,” meaning those of intense and sharp energetic effort. Seeing this, she was filled with admiration and, after performing great meritorious deeds, she made an aspiration for that rank of Āraddhavīriya Etadagga. Padumuttara Buddha also gave her the prophetic assurance.

## (b) Ordination in Her Final Life
That daughter of the wealthy man wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the period when this Buddha appeared, she was born as the daughter of a wealthy man in the city of Sāvatthī. When she reached the age of maturity, she went to the house of her husband, a wealthy man’s son. She gave birth to ten children and thus became famous as “Bahupputtika Soṇā” (Soṇā of many children).

Later, when her husband, the wealthy man’s son, became a monk, the lady Bahupputtika Soṇā married off her ten grown children and distributed all her wealth among them as inheritance. She did not keep even a small amount for herself. Her sons and daughters treated her with kindness and care for only two or three days. After those few days, they began to speak to her in a dominating and overbearing manner.

Realizing that her children no longer respected her, Bahupputtika Soṇā reflected, “What is the use of me living in the household life? There is nothing left to do.” Thus, she left the household life and was ordained as a bhikkhunī. After her ordination, the teacher bhikkhunīs,
100:
on account of a certain fault, imposed a suitable penalty on her, saying, “This Bahupputtika Soṇā Bhikkhunī does not know the duties and does what is improper.” When her children saw their mother, Bahupputtika Soṇā Therī, undergoing the penalty, they mocked and ridiculed her wherever they met her, saying, “This old woman still does not even understand the monastic discipline to this day.”

Upon hearing the mocking words of her children, Bahupputtika Soṇā Therī was struck with great spiritual urgency (saṃvega). She reflected, “I must act to make my destiny pure.” Thus, whether sitting or standing, she meditated on and recited the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). (Bahupputtika Soṇā Bhikkhunī reflected, “Since I have become a bhikkhunī only in my old age, it is proper that I should be diligent.” While performing the major and minor duties for the other bhikkhunīs, she resolved, “I shall practice the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night.” She would hold onto a pillar on the ground floor of the mansion with her hand and, without letting go, she would practice the Dhamma. When she became exhausted and went for walking meditation, she thought, “In the dark, my head might strike against a tree or something.” Thus, she would hold onto a tree with her hand and, without letting go, she would walk around it in meditation, practicing the Dhamma with intense effort. — From the Therīgāthā Commentary.)

## Becoming Known as Āraddhavīriya Soṇā Therī
Because that (Bahupputtika) Soṇā Therī practiced the Dhamma with such great effort, without sleeping or resting as described,
101:
whereas she was previously known by the name Bahupputtika Soṇā Therī, she later became famous as “Āraddhavīriya Soṇā Therī,” meaning Soṇā Therī of sharp and intense energetic effort.

## Attaining Arahantship
One day, when the bhikkhunīs were going to the Jetavana Monastery to receive exhortation, they left a message for the elder bhikkhunī Āraddhavīriya Soṇā, saying, “O Lady Soṇā, please set some water to boil for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.” Before setting the pot of water to boil, the elder bhikkhunī Soṇā first walked back and forth near the kitchen, reciting the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra) and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā). While the Buddha was residing within the Gandhakuṭī of the Jetavana Monastery, he spoke:

Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ dhammamuttamaṃ.
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato dhammamuttamaṃ.

“Soṇā, my dear daughter. Though one should live for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma (the ninefold supramundane Dhamma), the life of one who lives for a single day seeing the supreme Dhamma is indeed better. For such a person, even a single day of life seeing the supreme Dhamma is superior to a hundred years of life in which the continuity of the aggregates is maintained without such vision.”
102: “Jīvitaṃ = Life, continuing through the sequence of the aggregates, seyyo = is indeed noble and most praiseworthy.” He recited and preached this verse of radiance. At the conclusion of the verse of radiance, the elder nun Soṇā Therī attained the Fruit of Arahatship (became an Arahat). She then reflected: “I have attained the Fruit of Arahatship. If people who come here, unaware of this fact, should speak disparagingly or critically of me without investigation, they would accumulate much demerit. Therefore, it is proper for me to perform an act so that others may know my attainment.” Having considered this, she placed a water pot (a pot for boiling water) on a tripod, but left it as it was without lighting a fire beneath it. When the fellow nuns returned from the monastery, they looked toward the tripod and, seeing no flames, they spoke critically: “Even though we instructed this old woman to boil water for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, she has not even lit a fire under the tripod until now.” Then the elder nun Soṇā Therī spoke wondrous words: “Sisters, what is it to you? Those bhikkhunīs who wish to bathe with hot water, let them take the water from that pot and bathe.” When she spoke these amazing words, the fellow nuns thought, “There must surely be a special reason for this old woman to speak such wondrous words,” and they went toward the water pot.
103:
103
When they dipped their hands into the water to test it, they found it to be warm. They brought another empty pot and drew water from the pot on the tripod. Every time they drew water, the place where the water was taken from was immediately refilled as before.
Only then did all the fellow nuns clearly realize that Therī Soṇā had attained the fruit of Arahantship. First, the junior nuns prostrated themselves at the feet of the Elder Therī with the five-point prostration and apologized, saying, "Noble Lady, for so long we have failed to investigate and reflect, and have spoken wrongly to you, bullying and overbearing. Please forgive us." The senior nuns also sat in a crouching position and apologized, saying, "Noble Lady, please forgive us."
## (c) Receiving the Foremost Title (Etadagga)
From that time on, the virtues of the Elder Therī became widely famous: "Although she ordained only in her old age, because of her intense and ardent effort, Therī Soṇā has attained the fruit of Arahantship in a short time." Later, while the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana monastery and appointing the Elder Nuns to their respective foremost positions, he declared of Therī Soṇā:
"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ āraddhavīriyānaṃ yadidaṃ soṇā" — "Monks, among my nun disciples who are energetic, Soṇā is the foremost."
104:
"Among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who are energetic and exert great effort, the bhikkhunī named Soṇā is the most excellent, the foremost."—

Having praised her thus, the Buddha placed her in the foremost rank (Etadagga) in the category of "those who possess great energy" (Āraddhavīriya).

This is the account of Soṇā Therī.

**********

## (8) The Account of Sakulā Therī

(The name of this Therī is mentioned as "Bakulā" in the Saṭṭha-mū Aṅguttara Commentary. However, in the Sri Lankan edition, it is mentioned as "Sakulā". In the Saṭṭha-mū Therīgāthā Commentary, it is also mentioned as "Sakulā". Therefore, following the more common usage in the Sri Lankan edition and the Therīgāthā Commentary, she is referred to as "Sakulā Therī" in this Mahā Buddhavaṃsa. The details of this Therī are also more complete in the Therīgāthā Commentary, so her account will be presented here according to that text.)—

## (a) The Therī's Past Aspiration

The future Sakulā Therī was born as a daughter of King Ānanda in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. She was a half-sister of Padumuttara Buddha and was named Nandā. When Princess Nandā reached the age of discretion, she was listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha one day. She saw Padumuttara Buddha appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost rank (Etadagga) in the category of "those who are proficient in the divine eye" (Dibba-cakkhuka). Inspired by this, she performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) with great effort and...
105:
...she herself made an aspiration for that foremost rank of Dibba-cakkhuka. Padumuttara Buddha also delivered a prophecy that the princess's aspiration would be fulfilled during the dispensation of our Buddha. (The detailed account should be sought in the Sakulā Therī Apadāna in the Myanmar translation of the Piṭaka).

## Life as a Wandering Nun (Paribbājikā)

Princess Nandā performed many meritorious deeds throughout that life until its end. After being reborn in the celestial realms, she wandered through the rounds of rebirth only in the happy states of humans and devas. During the time when Kassapa Buddha appeared, she was born into a Brahmin family and became a wandering nun (paribbājikā), living a solitary life. (After Kassapa Buddha attained Parinibbāna and the relic stupa was built), one day, while wandering for oil as alms and having received oil, she performed an offering of oil lamps throughout the night at the Buddha's stupa.

## (b) Ordination in Her Final Life

When that wandering nun passed away from that life, she became a goddess with exceptionally pure divine eyes in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. She wandered through the celestial realms for an entire interval between Buddhas (buddhantara). During the time our Buddha appeared, she was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī and was named "Sakulā". When the young Brahmin lady Sakulā reached the age of discretion, she became a faithful lay follower (upāsikā) in the Sasana during the water-pouring ceremony for the donation of the Jetavana monastery to the Buddha. Later, from an Arahant Elder...
106:
...she heard the Dhamma and, being deeply moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she entered the order as a nun. After ordaining, she practiced the Dhamma of a recluse diligently and without negligence, and before long, she attained the fruit of Arahantship and became an Arahant Therī.

## (c) Receiving the Foremost Title

From the time she attained Arahantship, Sakulā Therī became exceptionally proficient in the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) through special practice, as she had aspired in the past. Thus, at a later time, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery and was appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective foremost ranks, he declared regarding Sakulā Therī:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ dibbacakkhukānaṃ yadidaṃ sakulā = Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who are proficient in the divine eye, Sakulā is the most excellent, the foremost."

Having praised her thus, he placed her in the foremost rank (Etadagga) in the category of "those who are proficient in the divine eye" (Dibba-cakkhuka).

This is the account of Sakulā Therī.

**********

## (9) The Account of Kuṇḍalakesā Therī

## (a) The Therī's Past Aspiration

The future Kuṇḍalakesā Therī was born as the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's...
107:
...Dhamma discourse, she saw Padumuttara Buddha appoint Subhā Therī to the foremost rank (Etadagga) in the category of "those who possess swift realization" (Khippābhiññā). Inspired by this, she performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made an aspiration for that foremost rank of Khippābhiññā. Padumuttara Buddha also delivered a prophecy that the merchant's daughter's aspiration would be fulfilled during the dispensation of our Buddha.

## Life as the Daughter of King Kikī

That merchant's daughter wandered through the celestial and human realms for a period of one hundred thousand aeons. During the time when Kassapa Buddha appeared, she was the fourth daughter named "Bhikkhadāyikā" among the seven daughters (mentioned previously) of King Kikī, the ruler of Bārāṇasī in the Kāsī kingdom. For twenty thousand years, she observed the ten precepts and practiced the celibate life (komāri-brahmacariya) without seeking a partner, and she built and donated a large monastery complex for the Saṅgha to reside in.

## (b) Ordination in Her Final Life

That Princess Bhikkhadāyikā wandered through the celestial and human realms for an entire interval between Buddhas (buddhantara). During the time our Buddha appeared, she was born as the daughter of a wealthy merchant named Bhaddā in the city of Rājagaha. On the same day Bhaddā was born, a son was born to the royal chaplain (purohita) in that same city of Rājagaha. At the time the chaplain's son was born, all the weapons in the entire city, starting from the King's palace, emitted a brilliant glow.
108: The great chaplain went to the palace early in the morning and first asked the King, “How is it, Great King? Did you sleep and live in comfort?” The King replied, “Teacher, how could there be comfortable sleep for me? I did not sleep well at all. Throughout the entire night, I saw all the weapons in the golden palace emitting a brilliant glow, and we were filled with great fear.” The chaplain then said, “Great King, do not be anxious or troubled with various thoughts because of the brilliant glowing of those weapons. It was not only in Your Majesty’s golden palace that the weapons glowed. This phenomenon of weapons emitting brilliant flashes occurred throughout the entire city.” The King asked again, “Teacher, why did the weapons glow in such a manner?” The chaplain replied, “Great King, a son was born in our house under the thief constellation (coranakkhatta). This boy was born as an enemy to the whole city. This brilliant glowing of weapons is the omen (pubbanimitta) that this boy will be an enemy to the whole city. There is no danger to Your Majesty. However, if Your Majesty wishes to remove him, we shall dispose of the boy.” Then the King said, “If there is no danger of him harming us, there is no need to remove or dispose of the boy.”
109:
The great chaplain thought, "My son has brought his own name with him," and after reflecting, he named the son "Sattuka". In the merchant's house, the daughter Bhaddā grew up day by day. In the chaplain's house, the youth Sattuka also grew up day by day. From the time the youth Sattuka was able to run and play by his own strength, he would steal every single object he encountered wherever he went, filling his parents' house. Although his father, the great chaplain, spoke a thousand reasons and admonished the wicked young Sattuka not to steal, he was unable to stop him.

## The Outbreak of the Criminal Sattuka in Rājagaha

Later, when the wicked Sattuka reached adulthood, the father, the great chaplain, realized clearly that there was no way to stop him from stealing and committing crimes. He gave him two dark-colored garments, tools for breaking through and cutting walls and fences, and a travel mechanism (a rope ladder). He then said, "Live your life by this theft alone," and giving up on him, he drove the wicked son Sattuka out of the house and abandoned him.

From that day on, the criminal Sattuka would throw his rope ladder, climb onto the palaces of wealthy families, cut through and break into walls and fences, and rob all the wealth and property kept in others' houses as if they were his own. In the entire city of Rājagaha, there was no place where the criminal Sattuka did not steal or hide...
110: ...or plundered. Every single house was full of holes because the villain Sattuka had broken in. One day, while the King of Rājagaha was touring the city in his chariot, he saw the holes in the house walls and asked the charioteer, "Friend charioteer, why are there holes in every house in this city?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, in this city, a villain named Sattuka is plundering and stealing the wealth of noble families by cutting and breaking through house walls. That is why there are holes in every house." Then the King summoned the City Warden and asked, "Is it true that there is a wall-boring thief and villain named Sattuka in this city of Rājagaha? Why have you not captured that villain?" The City Warden replied, "Your Majesty, we are unable to find that villain with the stolen goods." The King then strictly ordered the City Warden, "If you can capture that villain Sattuka today, you shall live. If you cannot capture him, you shall face the royal authority and punishment." The City Warden, accepting the command saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," stationed his spies and royal officers throughout the city. He caught the villain Sattuka red-handed with the stolen goods while he was in the act of boring through a wall and stealing others' property, and presented him to the King. The King issued an order, "Take this villain Sattuka out through the south gate of the golden city and execute him." (This event should be understood as occurring during the reign of King Ajātasattu.)
111:
...(it should be understood thus). The city official accepted the King's command and, at every four-way intersection, had the criminal Sattuka whipped a thousand times. With his hands tied behind his back, he was led toward the southern gate.

## The Affection of the Merchant's Daughter Bhaddā

At that time, the merchant's daughter Bhaddā, hearing the loud noise of the crowd from the street, opened the lion-supported window (sīhapañjara) and looked out. Seeing the criminal Sattuka being led away while being whipped, she was overcome by a mixture of love and grief (due to the connection of having lived together in the past). She clutched her breast with both hands and went to lie face down on her auspicious bed. Notably, Bhaddā was the only daughter of the wealthy merchant and his wife, and they loved her dearly. Therefore, Bhaddā's relatives could not bear to see even a slight change in her countenance.

Then, her mother, the merchant's wife, seeing Bhaddā lying face down on the bed, asked, "Daughter, what are you doing?" When Bhaddā asked, "O mother, did you see that thief being led away to be executed?", the mother replied, "Yes, I saw him, dear daughter." Then Bhaddā spoke directly, "O mother, I will only live if I get that man; if I do not get him, there is only death for me." Her parents and relatives tried to...
112:
...persuade and reason with her in various ways, but when they could not succeed, they finally remarked, "Living is still better than death."

After that, the wealthy merchant went to the city official and, after giving a bribe of a thousand pieces of silver, spoke privately, "Lord official, my daughter has a heart full of desire for that criminal Sattuka. I want you to release this criminal Sattuka by some possible means or stratagem." The city official agreed, saying "Very well," and continued to hold the criminal Sattuka as if still under arrest. He prolonged the matter here and there until sunset. When the sun had set, he had a prisoner brought out from the jail, released the bonds of the criminal Sattuka, and had him sent secretly to the merchant's house. Then, using the same bonds that had bound Sattuka, he bound the prisoner, led him out through the southern gate, and executed him.

## Parental Love is Truly Great

The merchant's servants brought the criminal Sattuka and arrived at the merchant's house. Upon seeing Sattuka, the merchant thought, "I will now fulfill my daughter's wish," and had the criminal Sattuka bathed with scented water, dressed in a full set of ornaments, and sent him to his daughter's palace. The merchant's daughter Bhaddā, joyfully thinking, "My plan has succeeded and is fulfilled," adorned herself most beautifully with many ornaments and attended to and served the criminal Sattuka.
113: ## Sattuka's Devious Plot. After two or three days had passed, the villain Sattuka wickedly plotted, "All the ornaments and wealth of this merchant's daughter must become mine. I must find a way to take these ornaments." While sitting comfortably near her, he said with a serious face, "Lady, I have something to tell you." The merchant's daughter, as if receiving a thousand gains, joyfully and with great expectation replied, "Speak boldly, my lord." Then the villain Sattuka said to Bhaddā, "Bhaddā, you may think, 'Because of me, this Sattuka has gained his life.' In truth, when I was captured, I made a humble vow to the mountain deity of Corapapāta, 'If I gain my life, I will offer a sacrifice to you, O Lord Deity.' I have gained my life because of that mountain deity of Corapapāta. You, Bhaddā, must quickly prepare the offerings for the sacrifice." Bhaddā, the merchant's daughter, with the intention of fulfilling the wish of her lord and husband Sattuka, had the offerings prepared. Dressed in full attire, she rode with Sattuka in a single carriage to Mount Corapapāta. With an honest heart, thinking, "I shall perform the sacrifice to the mountain deity," she made efforts to climb the mountain with their attendants.
114:
114
"For me, there will be no opportunity to seize the ornaments of this merchant's daughter," he thought. Thus, he made his companions stay at the foot of the mountain and, making the merchant's daughter Bhaddā carry the offerings for the ritual alone, he climbed the Corapapāta mountain.

## Sattuka's Intentions Become Clear

When the two of them climbed the mountain, Sattuka did not speak any endearing words to Bhaddā at all, but spoke only harsh and coarse words. Bhaddā, being a clever woman, understood the wicked intention of the villain Sattuka just by the manner of his speech. When they reached the top of the mountain, the villain Sattuka spoke rudely, "Bhaddā, take off your outer garment and wrap all the ornaments you are wearing into a bundle in this cloth."

Though the clever Bhaddā asked gently and endearingly, "O Lord, what fault have I committed?", Sattuka, acting like the villain he was, spoke vulgarly, "You fool! Do you think I came here to make an offering to the spirits? (I did not). I am one who would even dare to tear out and eat the liver of the deity guarding this mountain (let alone make an offering). In truth, I have come to this mountain top under the pretext of making an offering because I want to seize your ornaments."

## Bhaddā's Cleverness

The very clever and wise Bhaddā said, "Lord, to whom do these ornaments belong? (meaning, they belong to you). And to whom do I belong?"
115:
“...meaning, it is indeed your property.” When she spoke thus, the thief Sattuka replied curtly, “We do not understand such talk; your property is one thing, and mine is another.” Then Bhaddā, the merchant's daughter, spoke cleverly, “Very well, my lord. I have one special request; I wish for you to fulfill one desire of my heart. While I am still adorned as I am now, I wish for you to allow me to embrace and cherish you, circling you from the front and from the back.” The thief Sattuka accepted, saying, “Very well.”

Knowing that the thief Sattuka had accepted, Bhaddā, without wasting time, embraced and cherished him from the front, and then, while pretending to embrace and cherish him from behind, she pushed the thief Sattuka with all her might into the mountain cleft. The thief Sattuka tumbled down the mountain and, before even reaching the ground, was dashed to pieces in mid-air, meeting a miserable end.

(In this regard: At the moment she pushed the thief Sattuka off the mountain, there arose in Bhaddā's mind a consciousness rooted in hatred (dosamūla-cittuppāda) dominated by the intention to kill (pāṇātipāta-cetanā). However, before and after that moment, when she was planning and reflecting on how to escape the danger to her life, it should be specially noted that there arose in her mind great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala-cittuppāda) dominated by the wisdom of skillful means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa). This was a special instruction given by the great teacher U Lin to Saya Tun before his passing.)
116:
116
## The Mountain Deity Praises Bhaddā's Wisdom in Expedients

Seeing the extraordinary action performed by the merchant's daughter Bhaddā, the deity guarding the Corapapāta mountain recited these two following verses (gāthās) in praise of her wisdom and virtue:

(1) Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu,
Puriso hoti paṇḍito.
Itthīpi paṇḍitā hoti,
Tattha tattha vicakkhaṇā.

(In the first line of this verse, the Aṅguttara Commentary has "Na so sabbesu ṭhānesu," but the Apadāna and Dhammapada texts quoted in the Therīgāthā Commentary have only "Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu." That version is smoother in meaning.) The translation is: In all matters and in every situation, it is not only a man of noble birth who can be a wise person (paṇḍita). If a woman is one who can see clearly and deliberate well in various affairs, she too can be a wise person.

(2) Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu,
Puriso hoti paṇḍito.
Itthīpi paṇḍitā hoti,
Lahuṃ atthavicintikā.
117:
In all matters and in every situation, it is not only a man of noble birth who can be a wise person (paṇḍita). A woman, too, can be a wise person if she is one who can quickly reflect upon and devise a good way to achieve a beneficial result without deviating.

## Bhaddā the Merchant's Daughter Becomes a Wandering Nun

Thereafter, Bhaddā reflected, “I can no longer return home in this manner; it is not possible to go back. From this mountain, I shall go wherever I face and enter into whatever form of monkhood I find.” As she wandered aimlessly, she arrived at a monastery of the Nigaṇṭhas (naked ascetics) and requested the Nigaṇṭha teachers to ordain her. Then, when the Nigaṇṭha teachers asked her, “In what way do you wish to be ordained? Do you wish for the inferior ordination or the noble ordination?” Bhaddā, acting as one in her final birth (pacchimabhavika), replied, “Please grant me only the highest form of monkhood in your dispensation.”

## Acquiring the Name Kuṇḍalakesā

The Nigaṇṭha teachers agreed, saying, “Very well,” and ordained her by plucking out her hair with the shell of a palm-nut. (In their belief, shaving the hair with scissors or a knife for ordination was considered the inferior way, while plucking out the hair with a palm-nut shell while enduring the pain was considered the noble way. Therefore, to make her a noble nun, they plucked her hair with a palm-nut shell.) Because her hair had been painfully plucked out with a palm-nut shell, when the new hair grew back, it grew in clusters, curling like earrings. For that reason, from that time on, she became known as “Kuṇḍalakesā,” meaning “one with hair curled like earrings.”
118:
## Kuṇḍalakesā Becomes a Proponent of the Nigaṇṭha Doctrine

After the Nigaṇṭha nun Kuṇḍalakesā had learned all the arts and sciences from the Nigaṇṭhas where she was ordained, being one possessed of perfections (pāramī), she realized, “For these Nigaṇṭhas, there is no higher or more noble Dhamma than this doctrine.” She then left the Nigaṇṭhas and wandered through various villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Wherever there were wise men, she went to them and learned all the arts and sciences they knew, becoming their pupil. At that time, because she had mastered the arts in many places, there was almost no one capable of competing with the Nigaṇṭha nun Kuṇḍalakesā in debate.

Becoming a renowned debater and finding no one who could defeat her in argument, Kuṇḍalakesā would make a heap of sand at the entrance of the village or market town she entered, plant a rose-apple (jambu) branch upon it, and instruct the local children nearby, “Let anyone who is capable of competing with me in debate and finding fault in my doctrine trample and crush this rose-apple branch.”
119:
119
Having given instructions and established the challenge, she left it there. When no one had stepped on or crushed that rose-apple (jambu) branch for seven days, the female ascetic Kuṇḍalakesī took the branch and departed for another place.

## The Venerable Sāriputta Disciplines Kuṇḍalakesī

At that time, our Blessed One had appeared in the world and was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. The female ascetic Kuṇḍalakesī (the one-clothed ascetic) also wandered through various villages, market towns, and royal capitals in due course. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, as she was about to enter the city, she followed her previous custom by planting the rose-apple branch in a sand pile, giving the challenge to the nearby children as mentioned before, and then entered the city.

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, after the other monks had entered for alms (having performed his usual duties such as: walking through the entire Jetavana Monastery to neatly arrange any misplaced requisites to make them pleasing to the eye, providing drinking and usable water in monasteries that lacked it, sweeping and cleaning monasteries that were dusty, and visiting various sick monks to offer words of encouragement and seek suitable medicine and food for them), entered the city alone for alms. Seeing the rose-apple branch planted in the sand pile, he asked the nearby children, "Why is this rose-apple branch planted here?"
120:
The children reported everything the Nigaṇṭha nun Kuṇḍalakesā had said without omission. Then, the Venerable Sāriputta said, “Children, if that is the case, take this rose-apple branch and trample and crush it.” Upon hearing the Elder's words, some of the children did not dare to trample or crush it, but some brave children, as soon as they heard the Venerable Sāriputta's words, were emboldened and trampled and crushed the rose-apple branch until it was reduced to powder.

When Kuṇḍalakesā came out after finishing her meal in Sāvatthī and saw her rose-apple branch crushed and trampled, she asked the children nearby, “Whose doing is this?” The children then told Kuṇḍalakesā that the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, had ordered them to trample and crush it. Then Kuṇḍalakesā thought, “One who does not know their own strength would not be able or dare to have this rose-apple branch crushed and trampled. Without a doubt, the Elder who ordered this branch crushed must be a great person. Furthermore, it would not be fitting for me to go alone with few companions. It would be better to enter the city and inform the public that ‘the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta Thera, and I shall engage in a debate.’” She acted according to this plan. In the city of Sāvatthī, which had eighty thousand households, the news spread from one person to another in a short time.
121:
The Venerable Sāriputta, having finished his meal, sat at the foot of a tree (waiting for Kuṇḍalakesā to arrive). Then Kuṇḍalakesā, surrounded by a great crowd of people, approached the Elder. After exchanging polite greetings, she stood in a suitable place and engaged in a dialogue with the Elder as follows:

(Kuṇḍalakesā)
“Venerable Sir, did you order my rose-apple branch to be crushed and trampled?”

(Venerable Sāriputta)
“Yes, I ordered it to be crushed and trampled.”

(Kuṇḍalakesā)
“Venerable Sir, if that is so, let there be a debate between you and me.”

(Venerable Sāriputta)
“Let it be so, young nun.”

(Kuṇḍalakesā)
“Who shall ask first, and who shall answer, Venerable Sir?”

(Venerable Sāriputta)
“The right to question belongs to us first (as the challengers). However, you, young nun, should be the one to ask first about the things you know.”

With the Elder's permission, Kuṇḍalakesā asked all the doctrines she knew. The Elder [answered] them all.
122:
He solved the problems. After that, the Elder began a conversation and spoke with Kuṇḍalakesā as follows:

(Venerable Sāriputta)
"O female wandering ascetic, you have asked me many questions (and I have answered them); now I shall ask you one question."

(Kuṇḍalakesā)
"Please ask, Bhante."

(Venerable Sāriputta)
"Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ? = O female wandering ascetic, what is the one thing (that should be known through the three types of full understanding)?"

(Kuṇḍalakesā)
"I do not know, Bhante."

(Venerable Sāriputta)
"O female wandering ascetic, if you do not know even this much (which the young novices in our Dispensation study), what other Dhamma could you possibly know? You will not be able to know anything else."

When the Elder spoke thus, Kuṇḍalakesā, being a person of perfections (pāramī), prostrated at the Elder's feet and said, "Bhante, I take refuge in you and shall serve you."

The Elder said to Kuṇḍalakesā, "There is no need to take refuge in me or serve me. The Buddha, the Supreme Being in the entire world including the devas, is residing in the Gandhakuṭī of the Jetavana Monastery. You should take refuge in and serve that Blessed One."

Kuṇḍalakesā replied, "Very well, Bhante, I shall follow your instruction." In the evening, at the time when the Buddha was preaching the Dhamma, she went to the Buddha.
123:
She approached the Buddha, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and stood in a suitable place. The Blessed One, perceiving that Kuṇḍalakesā's wisdom was mature, recited this verse:

“Sahassamapi ce gāthā,
Anatthapadasaṃhitā.
Ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyo,
yam sutvā upasammati.”

“Sahassamapi ce gāthā = Even if there be a thousand verses; Anatthapadasaṃhitā = if they are composed of meaningless words and phrases such as descriptions of rain or mountains; Na seyyo = they are by no means praiseworthy or noble. Yaṃ = That single verse, such as 'Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ', etc.; Sutvā = which, when heard with the ear of faith; Upasammati = completely calms all the heat of defilements; Taṃ ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ = that single excellent Dhamma verse that leads to the cessation of defilements; Seyyo = is especially praiseworthy and noble.”

At the end of the verse, while still standing, Kuṇḍalakesā attained Arahatship together with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). She then requested the Blessed One to ordain her as a bhikkhunī. The Blessed One accepted and permitted her ordination. Kuṇḍalakesā then went to the bhikkhunī convent and was ordained.
124:
## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
Later, among the fourfold assembly of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen (upāsakas), and laywomen (upāsikās), words of praise arose: "This Therī Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā is truly great; she attained Arahatship at the conclusion of just one four-line verse." The Blessed One, taking this as the occasion, praised Therī Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ yadidaṃ bhaddā kuṇḍalakesā = O monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who possess quick intuition (khippābhiññā) in attaining the Path and Fruit, Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Quick Intuition."

This is the story of Therī Kuṇḍalakesā.
**********
## (10) The Story of Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī
(The story of this Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī is connected with the story of Venerable Mahā Kassapa. Since the detailed account has already been explained in Chapter 43, starting from page 100, only a brief account of this Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī is given in the Commentary. The pious readers of the Buddha's lineage should review and read the account of (4) Venerable Mahā Kassapa in Chapter 43, page 100 of this sixth volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas. Here, I shall describe it briefly according to the explanation in the Commentary.)
125:
## (a) The Therī's Past Aspiration
The future Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī was a noblewoman in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. She was the wife of the merchant Videha. While listening to the Buddha's sermon, she saw the Blessed One appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who could recollect past existences. Inspired by this, she performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position.

## Life as a Merchant's Wife
That merchant's wife wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. As mentioned on page 111, she became a merchant's wife in the city of Bārāṇasī. While she was quarreling with her sister-in-law, a Paccekabuddha came for alms. After the sister-in-law offered alms and made an aspiration that offended the merchant's wife, the latter, unable to bear it, took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha's hand, threw away the food, and filled it with mud. However, upon being rebuked by the villagers who saw this, she felt remorse and shame. She took the bowl again, threw away the mud, washed it clean, rubbed it with scented powder, and filled it with catumadhu (four sweet foods). On top of that, she poured ghee as white as a lotus stalk, making it shine brilliantly. She then offered the bowl to the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: "Just as this alms-food shines brilliantly, may my body also be radiant."
126:
All these events should be understood according to the method already described in the "Story of Venerable Mahā Kassapa."

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
Specifically, when they renounced the world in their final life, Venerable Mahā Kassapa took the right path and went to the Bahuputtaka banyan tree where the Buddha was. This young lady, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, because women were not yet permitted to ordain, took the left path and went to the park of the female wandering ascetics (paribbājikā) and became one herself. Bhaddā Kāpilānī lived as a female wandering ascetic for five years. This is known from her Apadāna: "Pañca vassāni nivasiṃ, paribbājavate ahaṃ."

When Bhaddā Kāpilānī had been a paribbājikā for five years, the Great Foster Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī requested and received permission to establish the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and was ordained herself. At that time, Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī received ordination from Therī Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Later, by diligently practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), she attained Arahatship and became an Arahant Therī.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
After becoming an Arahant, Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī became especially proficient in the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati abhiññā), in accordance with her past aspiration. Therefore, at a later time, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery,
127:
and was appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective foremost positions, he praised Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantīnaṃ yadidaṃ bhaddā kāpilānī = O monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who can recollect past existences, Bhaddā Kāpilānī is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Recollecting Past Lives."

(Note: The name given by her original parents was Bhaddā. When she reached maturity and was married by her parents to the youth Pippali, the future Mahā Kassapa, she became known as Kāpilānī because she was the daughter-in-law of the Brahmin Kapila, Pippali's father.)

This is the story of Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī.
**********
## (11) The Story of Therī Bhaddakaccānā (Yasodharā)
(The story of this Therī Bhaddakaccānā, also known as Yasodharā, is as well-known as the saying "water follows the land" whenever the story of the Buddha is told. Therefore, just as the Commentary explains her story very briefly, I shall also present it briefly in this text according to the Commentary.)

## (a) The Therī's Past Aspiration
The future Therī Bhaddakaccānā (Yasodharā) was also a noblewoman during the time of Padumuttara Buddha in
128:
the city of Haṃsāvatī. Later, while listening to the Buddha's sermon, she saw the Blessed One appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Attaining Great Supernormal Powers" (Mahābhiññāppatta). She performed meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
That noblewoman wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the time when our Buddha appeared, she was born as the daughter of King Suppabuddha the Sakyan, the maternal uncle of the Bodhisatta, and was named Bhaddakaccānā.

When Princess Bhaddakaccānā (Yasodharā) reached maturity, she became the chief consort of Prince Siddhattha, the Bodhisatta, as previously described. Later, the chief consort Bhaddakaccānā (Yasodharā) gave birth to a son, Rāhula. On the very day Prince Rāhula was born, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha renounced the world. After attaining Omniscient Buddhahood at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree and benefiting the world of beings, he eventually arrived at the city of Kapilavatthu and blessed his relatives.

Later (in the fifth year after the Buddha's enlightenment), when his father King Suddhodana attained Arahatship under the white parasol and passed away into Parinibbāna on that very day, the Great Foster Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī...
129:
Together with the five hundred Sakyan princesses (who were the former wives of the five hundred monks mentioned in the Mahāsamaya Sutta), she entered the monastic life in the presence of the Blessed One. At that time, Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, and Princess Janapadakalyāṇī also entered the monastic life under the Great Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatigotamī.

Bhaddakaccānā = From the time she became a nun, she became well-known as "Bhaddakaccānā Therī." After her ordination, Bhaddakaccānā Therī diligently practiced insight meditation (Vipassanā) and before long, she attained the Fruit of Arahatship and became an Arahat.

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

After attaining Arahatship, Bhaddakaccānā Therī became exceptionally proficient in the supernormal powers (Abhiññā). While sitting in a single cross-legged posture, she could recall everything that had occurred within one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappas) through a single act of advertence. When the fame of Bhaddakaccānā Therī’s virtues became widespread, the Blessed One, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, assigned the various Etadagga titles to the nuns and declared concerning Bhaddakaccānā Therī:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ mahābhiññāppattānaṃ yadidaṃ bhaddakaccānā = Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who have attained great supernormal powers, Bhaddakaccānā is the foremost.”
130:
Thus, the Buddha praised her and appointed her to the pre-eminent Etadagga position in the category of "Mahābhiññāppattā = those who have attained great supernormal powers."

(A special note here: In the era of a single Buddha, only four disciples usually appear who attain great supernormal powers. Other disciples do not reach the state of Mahābhiññā. Indeed, other disciples can only recall up to one hundred thousand aeons; they cannot recall beyond that. However, disciples who have reached the state of Mahābhiññā can recall events within one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons. In the Dispensation of our Blessed One, only these four—1, 2: the two Chief Disciples, 3: Ven. Bākula, and 4: Bhaddakaccānā Therī—could recall one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons. Therefore, this Bhaddakaccānā Therī received the "Mahābhiññāppatta-Etadagga" title. The original name of this elder nun was Bhaddakaccānā; she was also called Bhaddakañcanā because she possessed a complexion as extremely noble as gold. This is a special point to note.)

This is the account of Bhaddakaccānā Therī.

**********

## (12) The Account of Kisāgotamī Therī

## (a) Her Aspiration in the Past

The future Kisāgotamī Therī was an ordinary woman in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's discourse, she saw the Buddha appoint a nun to the Etadagga position of "Lūkhacīvaradhara = those who wear coarse robes." Inspired by this, she performed meritorious deeds to the best of her ability and made an aspiration for that same Etadagga position of wearing coarse robes.
131:
Padumuttara Buddha also gave her the prophecy that her aspiration would be fulfilled in the Dispensation of our Buddha.

## Her Life as the Daughter of King Kikī

For one hundred thousand aeons, that woman wandered through the celestial and human realms without falling into the four lower worlds. During the time of Kassapa Buddha in this Bhadda-kappa (Fortunate Aeon), she became the fifth daughter named "Dhammā" among the seven daughters of King Kikī of Bārāṇasī. She practiced the maidenly holy life (komāribrahmacariya) for twenty thousand years.

## (b) Ordination in her Final Life

After passing away from that life, Princess Dhammā was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In this final existence, she was born into a family in Sāvatthī that was originally of the merchant class but had become poor due to an economic decline. Her name was Gotamī. Because she had a particularly lean and slender body, she was called "Kisāgotamī = Lean Gotamī."

(I shall further extract and present how Kisāgotamī became the daughter-in-law of a wealthy merchant from the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume I, pages 443 and 444:)

## Wealth Vanishes when Merit is Exhausted

“Yadā kamma-kkhayo hoti, sabbametaṃ vinassati.
= When the force of kamma is exhausted, all wealth tends to perish.”
132:
In accordance with the teaching in the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, the forty crores of gold and silver wealth in the house of a certain merchant in Sāvatthī turned into mere charcoal (because the force of that merchant's merit had been exhausted). Seeing this occurrence, the merchant was overcome with great grief; unable to eat, he just lay on his couch. A friend of the merchant came to the house and asked, "Friend, why are you so grieved?" Upon hearing the reason, he said, "Friend, do not worry. I have thought of a strategy. I want you to carry out this strategy." When the merchant asked, "Friend, what must I do?", the friend explained the following method and strategy:

"Friend, spread a mat in your home market (a place inside your house suitable for a shop and visible to many people). Sit there like a merchant selling goods, with the charcoal piled up on the mat.

Among the people passing in front of your house, if someone says, 'Merchant, other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, but you are selling charcoal,' just say briefly (without long explanation), 'What else should I do if I don't sell my own property?' (This means those people are not possessors of great merit).

However, if someone says, 'Merchant, other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so on,
133:
but you are selling gold and silver,' then ask them, 'Where is the gold and silver?' If that person says, 'These items here,' then you should say, 'Please bring those items to me,' and receive them with both your hands. (That person is a possessor of great merit). In this way, the property given by that person will become gold and silver in your hands, just as it was originally.

I want to give a special reminder: if the person who speaks thus is a maiden, you should take that maiden into your house for your son (as a wife) and entrust those forty crores of gold and silver to that daughter-in-law. Then, you may use the wealth as managed and given by her.

If the person who speaks thus is a young man, give your daughter who has reached marriageable age to that young man, entrust the forty crores of gold and silver to that son-in-law, and then use the wealth as managed and given by him."

Thus, he provided this excellent method and strategy.

## Kisāgotamī, the Possessor of Merit

The merchant whose wealth had vanished said, "This is an excellent method," and as his friend had instructed, he sat as if selling charcoal piled up in a place suitable for a shop inside his house, where it was visible to many passersby. To those people (who were not possessors of merit) who asked, "Merchant, other people
134:
sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, but why are you selling charcoal (which does not suit your status)?", the merchant simply gave a brief reply, "What else should I do if I don't sell my own property?"

Then one day, Kisāgotamī, the daughter of a formerly wealthy family mentioned earlier, arrived at the door of that home market on some business of her own. Upon seeing the merchant, she said, "O father, how is this? Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, but you are selling gold and silver!" The merchant asked, "Daughter, where is the gold and silver?" When Kisāgotamī said, "Father, are you not sitting and holding that very gold and silver?", the merchant said, "Daughter, please bring that gold and silver to me." Kisāgotamī took a handful and poured it into the merchant's two hands. All those items became only silver and gold, just as they were originally.

## Kisāgotamī Becomes the Merchant's Daughter-in-law

Then the merchant asked Kisāgotamī, "Daughter, what is the name of your house?" When Kisāgotamī replied, "It has such and such a name," and after he learned that she did not yet have a husband, he stored away the wealth that had been charcoal. He then took Kisāgotamī for his son (as a wife) and entrusted the forty crores of wealth to her. At that time, everything became
135:
entirely silver and gold, just as it was originally. (This passage is from the Dhammapada Commentary).

Later, Kisāgotamī gave birth to a son. At that time (although they had previously looked down on her as the daughter of a poor family), because a son was born, the entire household came to treat her with love and cherish her. However, Kisāgotamī's son died just at the age when he could run and play about. Consequently, great grief arose within Kisāgotamī, who had never experienced the sorrow of losing a child before. Kisāgotamī thought, "I, who was once poor and lacked gain and honor in this house, reached a state of being honored and cherished from the time my son was born. These people might try to discard my son's body outside the city." Thinking thus, she took her son's corpse in her arms and went from house to house, repeatedly saying, "Please give me medicine to bring my son back to life" (wandering like one driven mad by grief).

In every place she was seen, people snapped their fingers and mocked her, saying, "Where have you ever seen or heard of medicine that brings the dead back to life?" Kisāgotamī could not gain any sense or awareness from the words of those people. Then, a wise man saw Kisāgotamī and reflected, "Oh, this young woman must have reached a state of mental distraction due to the grief for her son. No one else will know the medicine for this young woman; only the Blessed Buddha will know it."
136:
136
"Dear daughter, there is no one else besides the Buddha who can know the medicine to bring your son back to life. Indeed, the Buddha, the Supreme Being in the world including the devas, is currently residing at the Jetavana Monastery on the outskirts of Sāvatthī. Dear daughter, go only to that Blessed One and ask him," he said, giving her advice and encouragement.

## The Excellent Expedient Given by the Buddha to Quell Sorrow

Then Kisāgotamī thought, "This noble wise man speaks the truth." Clutching the corpse of her son, she went to the Buddha while he was sitting on the Dhamma-throne to preach. Standing at the edge of the assembly, she cried out, "O Blessed One of great glory, please give me the medicine to bring my son to life."

The Buddha, seeing Kisāgotamī's past merit which served as a supporting condition (upanissaya) for attaining the Paths and Fruits, said, "Dear daughter Gotamī, you have done well to come here for the medicine to bring your son to life. It is very good that you have come here to obtain the medicine for your son's life. Dear daughter, go; enter the city of Sāvatthī, go through the whole city starting from the outermost house, and bring back a small amount of mustard seed from a house where not a single person has ever died."

(In this matter, one should note the Buddha's instruction. The Buddha's instruction was: "Not a single person...")
137:
Kisāgotamī, thinking that if she obtained those mustard seeds her son would come back to life, replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and with great hope, she entered the city. At the very first house she encountered, she said to the householders, “The Buddha has sent me to fetch a few mustard seeds for the medicine to bring my son back to life. Please give me a few mustard seeds.” The householders said, “Take them, Gotamī,” and when they brought out the mustard seeds to give her, Kisāgotamī asked, “I cannot take them without asking this: Has anyone ever died in this house before?” The householders replied, “What are you saying, daughter Gotamī? Who could possibly count those who have died in this house before? They are beyond counting.” Then Kisāgotamī said, “If that is the case, it is enough. I will not take these mustard seeds. The Buddha told me to bring mustard seeds only from a house where no one has died,” and she left that house.

In this manner, Kisāgotamī visited two or three houses. After entering the third house, she thought, “This must be the case for the whole city. The Buddha, who desires the welfare of beings, must have seen this.”
138:
With a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she left the city from that third house and went to the cemetery. Holding the corpse of her young son, she said, “Dear son, I mistakenly thought that this nature of death happened only to you. In truth, this nature of death has not happened only to you; it is a nature common to all people.” After saying this, she abandoned the corpse of her son in the cemetery and recited this verse:

‘Na gāmadhammo no nigamassa dhammo,
Na cāpiyaṃ ekakulassa dhammo.
Sabbassa lokassa sadevakassa,
Eseva dhammo yadidaṃ aniccatā.’

(The meaning of this verse will be written later). Then she went to the Buddha. The Buddha asked her, “Dear daughter Gotamī, did you obtain the mustard seeds?” Kisāgotamī replied, “Bhante, the matter to be done with mustard seeds is finished. Indeed, O Lord, please give me only a refuge.” Then the Buddha preached to Kisāgotamī this verse from the Dhammapada:

‘Taṃ puttapasusammattaṃ, vyāsattamānasaṃ naraṃ.
Suttaṃ gāmaṃ mahogho va, maccu ādāya gacchati.’

“Dear daughter Gotamī, that person who is intoxicated and negligent with children and cattle, whose mind is deeply attached to various acquired possessions—death carries that person away, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village, leaving not even a dog behind.”
139:
After the Buddha preached this verse, Kisāgotamī was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). (This is the explanation from the Aṅguttara Commentary).

According to the Kisāgotamī Therī Apadāna: When Kisāgotamī returned to the Buddha, the Buddha preached these verses:

‘Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ udayabbayaṃ.
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato udayabbayaṃ.’

(The meaning of this verse was already mentioned on page 80 in the story of Paṭācārā Therī).

‘Na gāmadhammo no nigamassa dhammo,
Na cāpiyaṃ ekakulassa dhammo.
Sabbassa lokassa sadevakassa,
Eseva dhammo yadidaṃ aniccatā.’

“Dear daughter Gotamī, this nature of impermanence (aniccatā) of the conditioned phenomena of mind and matter, which arise and perish in an instant, is not a law restricted to a single village that is defined as a village by common convention because it has no walls or market. It is not a law restricted to a single market town (nigama) that is defined as such because it has a market but no walls.
140:
“It is not a law restricted to a single household within a town or village. This nature of impermanence of mind and matter is the natural law (dhammatā) for the entire world of beings, including the six deva realms and twenty brahma realms, a law that cannot be resisted or denied.”

Whenever the two phenomena of mind and matter, the five aggregates, arise, they inevitably vanish and cease. This nature of conditioned things is not something that occurs separately or is restricted to a single town, village, or house. From the moment of arising (uppāda), through the stage of presence (ṭhiti), to the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga) and death (maraṇa), both mind and matter are constantly moving and ceasing. Everything that arises withers away—
It is purely impermanent (anicca).
It is purely suffering (dukkha).
It is purely non-self (anatta).

Upon hearing these two verses of Dhamma, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. This account from the Apadāna, where the Great Therī herself recounted her life and practice, should be specially noted.

After being established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and becoming a Sotāpanna, Kisāgotamī requested the Buddha to ordain her as a nun. The Buddha granted her permission to be ordained. Kisāgotamī circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid her respects, went to the nunnery, and received ordination as a bhikkhunī. From that time on, she was known as Kisāgotamī Therī.
141:
## Kisāgotamī Therī Attaining Arahantship

After becoming a nun, Kisāgotamī Therī strove diligently in the practice of Vipassanā. One day, while it was her turn at the Uposatha hall, she lit a lamp and sat watching the flame. Seeing the flames flickering and dying out, she took it as an object of meditation, reflecting: “Just as these lamp flames arise and perish, so too do these beings arise and perish; only those who have reached Nibbāna are no longer seen.”

The Buddha, while sitting in the Gandhakuṭī, sent forth a radiance and appeared as if sitting right in front of the Therī, saying: “Dear daughter Gotamī, what you have considered is true. These beings arise and perish like lamp flames; only those who have reached Nibbāna are no longer seen. For those who do not see the Dhamma of Nibbāna through the knowledge of the Path and Fruit, a single moment of life for one who sees Nibbāna is more praiseworthy and noble than living a hundred years.” Connecting the discourse, he preached this verse:

‘Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, apassaṃ amataṃ padaṃ.
Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, passato amataṃ padaṃ.’

“Dear daughter Gotamī, if someone should live for a hundred years without knowing or seeing with the two-fold Dhamma-eye of Path-knowledge and Fruit-knowledge the supreme Nibbāna, the unconditioned element which is the state of deathlessness (amataṃ padaṃ),
142:
rather than that person living for a hundred years with a continuous succession of aggregates, a single day of life for one who sees with the two-fold Dhamma-eye of Path-knowledge and Fruit-knowledge the supreme Nibbāna, the unconditioned element which is the state of deathlessness, is far more praiseworthy and noble.”

At the end of this verse, Kisāgotamī Therī reached the Fruit of Arahantship; she became an Arahant Therī whose taints were exhausted.

## (C) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

After becoming an Arahant, this Kisāgotamī Therī practiced with the utmost excellence in the use of sparse requisites (according to her past aspirations). She used to travel about wearing only robes that were (1) vatthulūkha—coarse and poor in the quality of the cloth, (2) suttalūkha—coarse and poor in the quality of the thread used to sew the robes, and (3) rajanalūkha—coarse and poor in the quality of the dye, using only enough dye to make it allowable.

Therefore, later, while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana Monastery and was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions of Etadagga, he placed the Arahant Kisāgotamī Therī in the position of—
143:
“Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who wear coarse robes, Kisāgotamī is the foremost.”

Having praised her thus, the Buddha appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “those who wear coarse robes” (lūkhacīvaradhara).

This is the account of Kisāgotamī Therī.
**********
## (13) The Account of Singālakamātu Therī
(Since the account of this Therī is only briefly explained in the Aṅguttara Commentary, I shall present it by combining the Aṅguttara Commentary with the Apadāna of Singālakamātu Therī.)

## (a) The Therī’s Past Aspiration
The future Singālakamātu Therī was born as the daughter of a minister during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Having accompanied her father to the monastery and heard the Buddha’s Dhamma, she gained great faith and became a bhikkhunī. She practiced the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) as purely as a polished conch shell. Furthermore, she was extremely respectful toward the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—and was particularly diligent in listening to the Dhamma. She possessed an intense desire to behold the Buddha (similar to the Elder Vakkali).

One day, she saw Padumuttara Buddha appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “those released through faith” (saddhādhimutta).
144:
Inspired by this, she made an aspiration for that foremost position of Saddhādhimutta and continued to develop the three trainings (sikkhā). At that time, Padumuttara Buddha, using three verses beginning with “Yassa saddhā tathāgate, acalā suppatiṭṭhitā,” taught that a person who possesses faith in the Triple Gem, virtue, and upright wisdom is called one who is not poor. Therefore, a wise person should repeatedly strive for these four qualities: faith (saddhā), virtue (sīla), clarity of faith in the Dhamma and Saṅgha (pasāda), and the vision of the Dhamma (dhammadassana). (These three verses should be noted in the Apadāna Pāḷi Vol. 2, page 286.)

Upon hearing this Dhamma, the young bhikkhunī was greatly delighted and asked the Buddha whether her aspiration would be fulfilled. Padumuttara Buddha then gave the prophecy (vyākaraṇa) that her aspiration would be fulfilled during the time of our current Buddha. Hearing the Buddha’s prophecy, the young bhikkhunī was overjoyed and served the Buddha with practice (paṭipatti) and loving-kindness (mettā) for the rest of her life. (To always maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward the Buddha and to practice the Dhamma correctly is indeed serving the Buddha through practice.)

## (b) Becoming a Bhikkhunī in Her Final Life
For a hundred thousand aeons, this noble lady did not fall into the four woeful states but wandered only through the realms of devas and humans. During the period when our Buddha appeared,
145:
she was born as the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the city of Rājagaha. When she reached the proper age, she married into the family of a merchant of equal status and gave birth to a son. The son was named “Singālaka.” Because of her son, the wealthy mother became known as “Singālakamātu” (Singālaka’s mother).

Her son, the young Singālaka, held wrong views and constantly performed the act of worshipping the various directions. One day, as the Buddha was entering Rājagaha for alms, he saw Singālaka worshipping the directions. Standing on the road, the Buddha gave a discourse of instruction to Singālaka.

At that assembly, two crores of men and women realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated. The wealthy Singālakamātu attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) at that assembly and became a bhikkhunī, becoming known as Singālakamātu Therī. From the time she ordained, she possessed the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) to an extraordinary degree (as per her past aspiration). Whenever the Therī went to the monastery to hear the Dhamma, she would spend her time merely gazing at the beauty of the Buddha’s physical form (rūpakāya). Knowing the Therī’s exceptional devotion, the Buddha primarily taught her Dhamma that was suitable for her and would inspire further faith. The Therī, taking faith as her primary basis, practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and
146:
attained the fruit of Arahantship. (She became an Arahant who was released through faith, a saddhādhura arahant.)

## (c) Receiving the Foremost Title
Later, while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana Monastery and appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective foremost positions, he spoke in praise of Singālakamātu Therī:

“Monks, among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs who are released through faith, Singālakamātu is the foremost.”

Having said this, he appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “those released through faith” (saddhādhimutta).

This is the account of Singālakamātu Therī.

## Here ends the Therī Apadāna (Chapter 44).

## Chapter 45
## Upāsakacarita
## (1) The Account of the Two Brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika
## (a) The Past Aspiration of the Lay Disciples
(I shall extract and present the account of the two brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika, from the Aṅguttara Commentary and the Commentary on the Theragāthā, Ekakanipāta.)

These two noble brothers, the future Tapussa and Bhallika Upāsakas, were born into noble families in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha’s Dhamma, they saw the Buddha appoint two lay disciples to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “those who first took refuge” (paṭhamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchantānaṃ). Inspired by this, they performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that foremost position. (From the Aṅguttara Commentary.)

## Lives in the Intermediate Period
Those two noble sons performed meritorious deeds for the rest of their lives. After passing away from that life, they did not fall into the four woeful states but wandered through the realms of devas and humans. The future Bhallika Upāsaka, thirty-one aeons before this present auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), during a time when no Buddha had appeared, offered various fruits to a Paccekabuddha named Sumana. Consequently, he wandered only in the happy realms (sugati).
148:
During the time of Sikhī Buddha, he was born as the son of a brahmin in the city of Aruṇavatī. That brahmin’s son heard the news that “after Sikhī Buddha had attained Buddhahood and spent the seven weeks (sattasattāha), upon reaching the eighth week, the two merchant brothers named Ujita and Ojita offered the first meal.” Accompanied by his friend (the future Tapussa), he went to pay homage to Sikhī Buddha. They invited the Buddha for a meritorious deed the following day and offered a great donation. They then made an aspiration: “Venerable Sir, may both of us friends become the first donors of the first meal to a Buddha like you in the future.”

Those two friends performed meritorious deeds together in various lives and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, they were born as the sons of a merchant named Gopāla and served the Saṅgha of monks with offerings of milk-rice for many years. (This section is from the Theragāthā Commentary.)

## (b) Becoming Lay Disciples in Their Final Life
Both of them wandered through the realms of devas and humans for an entire incalculable interval between Buddhas (buddhantara) from Kassapa Buddha until our Buddha. Shortly before our Bodhisatta attained Omniscient Buddhahood, they were born as the two sons of a merchant in the city of Asitañjana (according to the Theragāthā Commentary, the city of Pokkharavatī).
149:
The elder brother was named Tapussa, and the younger brother was named Bhallika.

Later, while these two merchant brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika, were managing their household, they traveled about constantly for trade with five hundred carts. At that time, our Bodhisatta had attained Omniscient Buddhahood and, after spending the seven weeks (sattasattāha, 49 days) at the site of the Great Bodhi tree, was sitting at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree at the beginning of the eighth week.

At that moment, the merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika arrived at that place with their five hundred carts. Their mother from a previous life had been reborn as a deity in that area. That deity thought, “It is now appropriate for the Buddha to receive food. Indeed, after this time, the Buddha will not be able to sustain himself without food (meaning: he had sustained himself for 49 days on the 49 morsels of thick milk-rice offered by the lady Sujātā; if the Buddha does not receive food today, he will not be able to sustain himself). My two sons are currently traveling on this road. It is best if I have my two sons offer a meal to the Buddha today.” Reflecting thus, she used her divine power to stop the oxen yoked to the five hundred carts from moving.

The merchant brothers searched and reflected on various signs and causes, wondering, “Why have the oxen stopped like this?” Then, their former mother, the terrestrial deity, appeared.
150: Knowing the exhaustion of the merchant brothers, a deity entered the body of a man and said: "Sons, why are you exhausted? There is no other yakkha, bhūta, peta, deva, or nāga possessing you to deceive you. In fact, I, who was your mother in a past life, am now a Bhummajo deity living in this place. The Blessed One, endowed with the ten powers, is currently residing at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Dear sons, offer the first meal to that Blessed One." Upon hearing the words of their former mother, the Bhummajo deity, the merchant brothers were filled with great joy. Thinking that preparing a fresh meal would take too long, they took rice cakes and honey balls, placed them in a golden tray, and went to the Blessed One. They said, "Venerable Sir, out of compassion, please accept this food." The Blessed One reflected on the practice of the previous Buddhas. At that time, the Four Great Kings offered four stone alms-bowls of the color of mung beans. With the intention that the Four Great Kings would receive great merit, the Blessed One resolved, "Let these four bowls become one." According to his resolution, the four stone bowls became a single bowl with four rims.
151:
151
At that moment, the two merchant brothers offered cakes of parched grain and honey-balls into the Buddha's bowl. After the Blessed One had partaken of the meal, they offered water for drinking and washing. When the meal was finished, they paid homage to the Buddha with great respect and sat in a suitable place. Then the Buddha preached the Dhamma to the merchant brothers. At the conclusion of the discourse, both merchant brothers were established in the two-fold refuge (dvevācika-saraṇagamana). (Regarding the establishment of these merchant brothers in the two-fold refuge, one should refer back to the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 2, starting from page 394.)

After being established in the two-fold refuge, the merchant brothers paid homage to the Buddha with great respect. Wishing to return to their own city, they requested the Buddha, "Blessed One, out of compassion, please grant us an object to worship and attend to daily."

The Buddha stroked his head with his right hand and granted the merchant brothers eight hair relics (kesadhātu). The merchant brothers placed the hair relics in golden caskets and brought them back to their city. At the gate of the city of Asitañjana, they enshrined the eight living hair relics and built a great stupa for worship. From that great stupa, blue rays of light would emanate and radiate on Uposatha days.

## (c) Receiving the Distinguished Title of Etadagga

Later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, he was conferring the titles of Etadagga upon the lay disciples (upāsakas) in order...
152:
When appointing them to their respective ranks, the Buddha praised the two merchant brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika, saying:

“Monks, among my lay disciples who first took refuge (saraṇagamana), the merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika are the foremost (etadagga).”

Thus, he placed them in the pre-eminent position of being “the first to take refuge.”

## The Path to Knowledge of the Two Brothers

These two merchant brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika, became the very first lay disciples (upāsakas) in the world to take refuge. Later, after the Blessed One had traveled to Vārāṇasī and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and while he was subsequently residing in Rājagaha, the merchant brothers arrived in Rājagaha for trade. They approached and paid homage to the Blessed One and sat in a suitable place. When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the two brothers, the elder brother, Tapussa, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and remained a lay disciple. The younger brother, Bhallika, however, entered the monkhood and became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña). (From the Commentary on Theragāthā, Vol. 1, page 60).

This is the account of the two brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika.
153:
## The Story of Anāthapiṇḍika

## (a) The Great Man’s Past Aspiration

This future Anāthapiṇḍika, the Great Man, was born into a noble family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha’s discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (etadagga) of being “the foremost among donors (dāyaka) who delight in giving.” Inspired and delighted, he performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made an aspiration for that very rank and position.

## (b) Becoming a Treasurer in His Final Life

That noble youth wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the era of our Buddha’s Dispensation, he was born as the son of the Great Treasurer Sumana in the city of Sāvatthī. His parents named him Sudatta.

## Acquiring the Name Anāthapiṇḍika

When the young treasurer Sudatta later took charge of the household and became its head, he took great delight in distributing food and alms to the destitute and helpless. Because of this virtuous quality, he became famous as “Anāthapiṇḍika” (Anātha = those without refuge + piṇḍika = one who gives food; thus, the Treasurer who feeds the destitute). (For a detailed account of this Great Treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika, one should review the Mahābuddhavaṃsa, Volume 3, Chapter 20, starting from page 180. Here, I shall present only a brief summary as it appears in the Aṅguttara Commentary).
154:
One day, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, carrying merchandise on five hundred carts for trade, arrived at the house of his friend, the merchant of Rājagaha. There, he heard the good news that the Buddha had appeared in the world. At the break of dawn, through the city gate opened by the power of devas, he went forth and approached the Buddha. Upon hearing the Dhamma, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The following day, he offered a great donation (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Having received the Buddha's promise to visit Sāvatthī, he returned. Along the 45-yojana journey, he entrusted his friends to build a monastery at every yojana, each worth one hundred thousand coins. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, he purchased Prince Jeta’s garden by covering the ground with gold coins, edge to edge, for eighteen crores. He spent another eighteen crores to construct the great monastery. When it was completed, he offered whatever was needed day and night, and spent another eighteen crores to celebrate the monastery dedication ceremony (libation ceremony). Regarding the duration of the dedication ceremony, teachers mentioned periods of nine months, five months, and three months respectively; however, all teachers agreed without dispute on the three-month period.
