## (c) Attaining the Foremost Title (Etadagga)

In this way, after donating fifty-four crores of wealth to this Dispensation, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika established the following daily offerings at his home:
155:
Every day, he offered five hundred meals by ticket (salāka-bhatta) [meals offered to five hundred monks who won the ticket lottery].

He offered five hundred fortnightly meals (pakkhika-bhatta) = twice a month, once during the waxing moon and once during the waning moon, he would specially prepare and offer meals to five hundred monks.

Every day, he offered five hundred portions of gruel by ticket = meaning he offered gruel daily to five hundred monks who won the ticket lottery.

He offered five hundred portions of fortnightly gruel = twice a month, once during the waxing moon and once during the waning moon, he would specially prepare and offer gruel to five hundred monks.

He offered five hundred regular meals (dhura-bhatta = nicca-bhatta). [Since the five hundred ticket-meals already referred to the communal regular meals (saṅghika-nicca-bhatta), this refers to offering five hundred individual regular meals (poggalika-nicca-bhatta)].

He offered daily five hundred meals for visiting monks (āgantuka), five hundred for departing monks (gamika), five hundred for the sick (gilāna), and five hundred for those attending the sick (gilānupaṭṭhāka) = meaning he offered meals daily to five hundred newly arrived monks unfamiliar with the routes, five hundred monks about to travel, five hundred unwell monks, and five hundred monks caring for the sick.

At Anāthapiṇḍika's house, five hundred seats were always prepared for the Saṅgha to sit.
156:
Consequently, at a later time while residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha, when appointing lay disciples to their respective foremost positions (Etadagga), declared regarding this merchant Anāthapiṇḍika (whose childhood name was Sudatta):

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ dāyakānaṃ yadidaṃ sudatto gahapati anāthapiṇḍiko = Monks, among my lay disciples who are donors, who delight in giving and generosity, the householder Sudatta, known as Anāthapiṇḍika, is the most excellent, the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) among donors.

## The Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta
## Greatly Cherished by the Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika

(In this section, for the benefit of the devout readers of the Buddha's life story, I shall present the Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta, which the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika deeply loved and cherished, in the most concise form possible. Those who wish for the full detail should consult page 306 of the Burmese translation of the Uparipaṇṇāsa).

While the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika was afflicted with illness, suffering, and was gravely ill = he was lying on his deathbed. At that time, Anāthapiṇḍika called a servant and said, “Friend, go to the Buddha and in my name say: ‘Venerable Sir, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika is ill, suffering, and gravely ill; that merchant Anāthapiṇḍika...’"
157: 'I pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One,' having said this, pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One (on my behalf). (Furthermore,) having approached the Venerable Sāriputta, in my words say, 'Venerable Sir, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; that Anāthapiṇḍika the householder pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta,' and pay homage at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta (on my behalf). Continue by saying, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to make a request: May the Venerable Sāriputta please come to the house of Anāthapiṇḍika the householder, out of compassion and kindness.' Thus, he gave instructions and sent him forth. (While Anāthapiṇḍika the householder was in normal health, he used to visit the Jetavana monastery at least once a day, or twice or thrice if circumstances permitted, to attend upon the Blessed One and the Great Elders without fail. Since he was now lying on his deathbed and could no longer go on foot, he sent a male servant to make this request). That male servant, replying 'Very well, master,' accepted the words of Anāthapiṇḍika the householder. He then approached the Blessed One as instructed, paid homage, and made the request. (After requesting the Blessed One, just as the sun was about to set,) he approached the Venerable Sāriputta, paid homage, and invited him as instructed by the householder. The Venerable Sāriputta accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
158:
Then, the Venerable Sāriputta adjusted his robes, took his bowl and robes, and with Venerable Ānanda as his companion monk, went to Anāthapiṇḍika's house. Sitting on the prepared seat, he asked Anāthapiṇḍika, “Householder, how is it? Are you able to endure (the painful feelings)? Are you keeping well? Are your postures (iriyāpatha) balanced? Are the painful feelings subsiding? Are they not increasing? Is there a sign of them subsiding rather than increasing?”

Then, Anāthapiṇḍika replied to Venerable Sāriputta at length with four metaphors, explaining that he was unable to endure the painful feelings, that he was not keeping well, that his postures were not balanced, that the painful feelings were only increasing and not subsiding, and that there was only a sign of increase rather than decrease.

Thereupon, Venerable Sāriputta reflected, “This present illness of the great merchant is a terminal illness (maraṇantika) that will only end in death; it cannot be averted. In this situation, other talk is of no benefit; I shall only preach the Dhamma to this merchant.” Having so considered, he preached the following detailed Dhamma discourse:

“Householder, (one who clings to the 6 doors, 6 objects, 6 consciousnesses, 6 contacts, 6 feelings, etc., with the three attachments of craving, pride, and views as 'this is mine', 'this I am', 'this is my soul', has no power to avert the terminal illness that arises in one's own continuum). Therefore, you should train yourself thus:”
159:
“I shall train so that I do not cling to the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) with the three attachments, and so that my mind does not depend on the eye-sensitivity (with subtle attachment/nikanti-taṇhā).” With such noble intention, you must practice and strive in the three trainings (sikkhā). (The section on the 6 doors is not yet finished).

(In this context: The phrase “I shall train so that I do not cling to the eye-sensitivity with the three attachments” conveys the meaning that one must contemplate the eye-sensitivity as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā). Truly, if one contemplates the eye-sensitivity as anicca, the clinging of pride (māna-gāha) as 'I' finds no footing (= one no longer clings with pride as 'I'). If one contemplates that eye-sensitivity as dukkha, the clinging of craving (taṇhā-gāha) as 'mine' finds no footing (= one no longer clings with craving as 'mine'). If one contemplates that eye-sensitivity as anattā, the clinging of views (diṭṭhi-gāha) as 'my soul' finds no footing (= one no longer clings with views as 'my soul'). Thus, the primary meaning is that one must repeatedly contemplate the eye-sensitivity as anicca, dukkha, and anattā so that these three attachments—craving, pride, and views—are severed from the eye-sensitivity.

These three types of clinging—taṇhā-gāha, māna-gāha, and diṭṭhi-gāha—are coarse states. Even when such clinging (gāha) is absent, the subtle craving and greed called nikanti, which delights in the eye-sensitivity, might still remain. Therefore, wishing to abandon even that nikanti-taṇhā, the Venerable Sāriputta further preached: “I shall train so that my mind does not depend on the eye-sensitivity (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).” This method should be understood for subsequent teachings as well.)
160:
After Venerable Sāriputta preached to Anāthapiṇḍika on abandoning the three great attachments and subtle craving (nikanti-taṇhā) regarding the eye-sensitivity, he continued to preach for the remaining states in the same manner:

“Householder, therefore you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to the ear-sensitivity (p)... the nose-sensitivity (p)... the tongue-sensitivity (p)... the body-sensitivity (p)... the mind-sensitivity (mano) with the three attachments, and my mind shall not depend on the mind-sensitivity (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).’ With such noble intention, you must practice and strive in the three trainings. (1)

Householder, therefore you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to various visible forms (rūpārammaṇa) (p)... various sounds (saddārammaṇa) (p)... various smells (gandhārammaṇa) (p)... various tastes (rasārammaṇa) (p)... various touches (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) (p)... various mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) with the three attachments, and my mind shall not depend on various mental objects (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).’ With such noble intention, you must practice and strive in the three trainings. (2)

Householder, therefore you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to the act of seeing = eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) (p)... the act of hearing = ear-consciousness (p)... the act of smelling = nose-consciousness (p)... the act of tasting = tongue-consciousness (p)... the act of touching = body-consciousness (p)... the act of knowing = mind-consciousness (mano-viññāṇa) with the three attachments, and my mind shall not depend on the act of knowing = mind-consciousness (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).’ With such noble intention...
161:
you must practice and strive in the three trainings (3).

Householder, therefore you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa) (p)... ear-contact (p)... nose-contact (p)... tongue-contact (p)... body-contact (p)... mind-contact (mano-samphassa) with the three attachments, and my mind shall not depend on mind-contact (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).’ With such noble intention, you must practice and strive in the three trainings (4).

Householder, therefore you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to the feeling (vedanā) born of eye-contact (p)... the feeling born of ear-contact (p)... the feeling born of nose-contact (p)... the feeling born of tongue-contact (p)... the feeling born of body-contact (p)... the feeling born of mind-contact with the three attachments, and my mind shall not depend on the feeling born of mind-contact (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).’ With such noble intention, you must practice and strive in the three trainings (5).

Householder, therefore you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) (p)... the water element (āpo-dhātu) (p)... the fire element (tejo-dhātu) (p)... the air element (vāyo-dhātu) (p)... the space element (ākāsa-dhātu) (p)... the consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu) with the three attachments, and my mind shall not depend on the consciousness element (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā).’ With such noble intention,
162:
162
One must strive and exert oneself in the practice of the Three Trainings (6).

Householder, therefore, you should train yourself thus: "I shall practice the Three Trainings with a noble intention so that I do not cling to form (...), feeling (...), perception (...), mental formations (...), consciousness with the three types of clinging, and so that my mind does not become attached to consciousness (through subtle nikanti-taṇhā)" (7).

Householder, therefore, you should train yourself thus: "I shall practice the Three Trainings with a noble intention so that I do not cling to the base of infinite space (...), the base of infinite consciousness (...), the base of nothingness (...), the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with the three types of clinging, and so that my mind does not become attached to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (through subtle nikanti-taṇhā)" (8).

Householder, therefore, you should train yourself thus: "I shall practice the Three Trainings with a noble intention so that I do not cling to this present world with the three types of clinging, and so that my mind does not become attached to this present world (through subtle nikanti-taṇhā)."

Householder, therefore, you should train yourself thus: "I shall practice the Three Trainings with a noble intention so that I do not cling to the world beyond with the three types of clinging, and so that my mind does not become attached to the world beyond."

(In this context, since the world of beings has been taught in the previous sections such as the first and second rounds, the term 'present world' refers to...)
163:
(It means the world of formations (saṅkhāra loka) such as the house, clothing, and food currently obtained in this life. The rest of the human world should be taken as the world beyond. The Venerable taught this to remove and prevent the arising of craving (taṇhā) in the great merchant's mind, such as: "May I be reborn in such and such a celestial realm, in such and such a place; may I eat such and such food, and wear such and such clothes.")

Merchant, therefore, you should train yourself thus: "I will not cling with the three types of clinging to all objects that are seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought, repeatedly sought, and explored by the mind. My mind shall not be attached (with subtle nikanti-taṇhā) to all those objects seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought, repeatedly sought, and explored by the mind." With such a noble intention, you must strive and practice the three trainings (9).

Thus, Venerable Sāriputta gave a detailed discourse to the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, adorning it with nine cycles (vāra). (In this regard, when one reaches the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), the three types of clinging are completely uprooted. Clinging to views (diṭṭhi) is uprooted at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Therefore, by teaching "you should practice so as not to cling with the three types of clinging," it is understood that the practice is for the attainment of Arahattaphala. Thus, Venerable Sāriputta taught the nature of emptiness (suññata) in detail to the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, culminating in Arahattaphala through the nine cycles: the sense bases, objects, consciousness, contact, feeling, elements, aggregates, formless jhānas, and all phenomena (sabba-dhamma)).

When Venerable Sāriputta had finished teaching this discourse, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika wept bitterly.
164:
Then, Venerable Ānanda and the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika spoke to each other as follows:

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Merchant, are you sinking into your possessions? Merchant, are you regressing in your merit?"

(Anāthapiṇḍika)
"Venerable Ānanda, I am not sinking into my possessions, nor am I regressing in my merit. Indeed, for a long time, I have served the Blessed One and have served the mind-developing (manobhāvanīya) monks. However, I have never before heard such a Dhamma discourse as this."

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Merchant, such a Dhamma discourse does not appear to laypeople clad in white. (Merchant, for laypeople, attachment and delight in fields, lands, silver, gold, female slaves, male slaves, children, and wives are very intense. For such people, a Dhamma discourse such as 'one should not be attached to these fields and lands, one should not have craving' does not appear—meaning they cannot appreciate such a discourse). Merchant, such a Dhamma discourse appears only to those who have gone forth (monks); they alone can appreciate such a discourse."

(Anāthapiṇḍika)
"Venerable Sāriputta, let me request and urge you: let such a Dhamma discourse also appear to laypeople clad in white. (Meaning, please teach such Dhamma to laypeople as well). Venerable Sir, there are many sons of good family whose eyes of wisdom have but little dust of defilements. Because they do not hear the Dhamma, they are losing the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma). If you teach it, there will be those who understand the Dhamma and reach Arahattaphala." This was their conversation.
165:
(In this regard, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika said, "I have never before heard such a Dhamma discourse even from the Blessed One." One might ask: Did the Blessed One never teach such subtle and profound Dhamma to Anāthapiṇḍika? The answer is: It is not that He did not teach it; He did. However, a discourse that details the 6 sense bases, 6 objects, 6 types of consciousness, 6 types of contact, 6 types of feeling, 6 elements, 5 aggregates, 4 formless jhānas, this world and the world beyond, each in its own cycle, and repeatedly applying them to the attainment of Arahattaphala through all things seen, heard, reached, and known—such a discourse as found in this Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta, the great merchant had never heard before. That is why he spoke thus.

Alternatively, this monastery donor was one whose mind was greatly inclined toward and delighted in the merit of giving (dāna). Whenever he went to the Blessed One or the mind-developing monks, he never went empty-handed. When going to the monastery in the morning, he would bring rice gruel and food. When going in the afternoon, he would bring butter, honey, molasses, and so on. At the very least, he would have his servants bring fine sand to spread within the precincts of the Gandhakuṭī monastery).
166:
Upon arriving at the monastery, he would give offerings, observe the precepts, and then return home. This monastery donor, Anāthapiṇḍika, was said to have a disposition like that of a Bodhisatta. Therefore, for twenty-four years, the Blessed One mostly taught him Dhamma related to giving, saying: "Lay follower, this merit of giving is the path of the Bodhisattas. I myself practiced giving for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. You are consistently following my path." Venerable Sāriputta and other great disciples also mostly taught him the discourse on giving (dāna-kathā) when he visited them. This is why Venerable Ānanda said, "Merchant, such a Dhamma discourse does not appear (is not appreciated) to laypeople clad in white."

In this context, one should not assume that the Blessed One never taught the practice of Insight (vipassanā) leading to the Paths and Fruits to Anāthapiṇḍika. He simply had not heard it explained in detail through the nine cycles as in this Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta. The merchant had indeed heard the practice of Insight that leads directly to the Noble Path. Therefore, it is specifically explained in the Ṭīkā (sub-commentary) of this Sutta: "Ujumaggāvahā vipassanā bhagavatā panassa kathikapubbā" = Indeed, the Blessed One had previously taught him the Insight that leads directly to the Noble Path. (This is a special point to note).

## The Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika
## Becoming a Deva in Tusita Heaven

Then, Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Ānanda, having exhorted the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika with this advice, rose from their seats and departed. Soon after,
167:
not long after the two Venerables had left, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.

Then, Anāthapiṇḍika the young deva, at midnight, came to the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. He addressed the Blessed One with the following verses (gāthās):

(The verses will be presented later. First, a special point to note: One might ask, "Why did Anāthapiṇḍika the deva come to the presence of the Buddha?" The answer is: As soon as he was reborn in Tusita heaven, seeing his celestial body shining like a mass of gold three gāvutas in height, and seeing the celestial gardens, mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees, the thought arose in his mind: "This prosperity of mine is truly great. What good deeds did I perform in the human world?" Reflecting with wisdom, he saw the meritorious deeds he had performed for the Triple Gem and thought: "This state of a deva is a place of negligence. Indeed, for me who is delighted and joyful with this celestial prosperity, forgetfulness (of mindfulness) could occur. I will go right now to praise the virtues of the great Jetavana monastery I built, the Sangha of monks, the Blessed One, the Noble Path, and Venerable Sāriputta, and only after returning from the human world will I enjoy this celestial prosperity." Thus, Anāthapiṇḍika the deva came to the presence of the Buddha. This is the answer).

## The 4 Verses Spoken by Anāthapiṇḍika the Deva

Idaṃ hi taṃ jetavanaṃ, isisaṅghanisevitaṃ.
Āvutthaṃ dhammarājena, pītisañjananaṃ mama.

Bhante = Exalted Blessed One. Idaṃ taṃ jetavanaṃ = This monastery called Jetavana.
168:
Isisaṅghanisevitaṃ = is the constant day and night dwelling place of the Noble Sangha and the ordinary Sangha, who have sought and are seeking special qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). Dhammarājena = By the King of Dhamma, the Buddha. Āvutthaṃ = It is the permanent residence where He dwells, having achieved the victory of the Deathless. (Tasmā = Therefore). Mama = For me, named Anāthapiṇḍika. Pītisañjananaṃ = It always generates joy (pīti).

(In this regard, the Jetavana monastery was very delightful and unlike other parks due to the Gandhakuṭī, the square pavilions, the decorated halls, the trees, vines, flowers, and living quarters. However, because those delights are based on the five cords of sensual pleasure, they cannot gladden the hearts of Noble Disciples as much as being the dwelling place of the Buddha and the Noble Sangha. Only the fact that it is the dwelling place of the Noble Sangha can exceedingly gladden the hearts of Noble Disciples like Anāthapiṇḍika. Therefore, he praised Jetavana monastery for the quality of being the residence of the Buddha and the Noble Sangha).

Kammaṃ vijjā ca dhammo ca, sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamaṃ.
Etena maccā sujjhanti, na gottena dhanena vā.

Kammaṃ = Volition (cetanā) associated with the Path. Vijjā ca = The two path factors of Right View and Right Thought included in the Noble Path. Dhammo ca = The three path factors of Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration included in the Noble Path. Sīlañca = The three path factors of Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood included in the Noble Path.
169:
(Established in this virtue of the Noble Path). 'Utamaṃ' = The supreme and blameless livelihood. 'Etena' = By this practice of the Eightfold Path. 'Maccā' = Beings. 'Sujjhandi' = Are purified and freed from the impurities of defilements. 'Gottana vā' = Neither by lineage. 'Dhanena' = Nor by wealth. 'Na sujjhandi' = Can they be purified or freed from the impurities of defilements.
(With this verse, the virtues of the Noble Path are praised.)

'Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano.
Yoniso vicine dhammaṃ, evaṃ tattha visujjhati.'

'Tasmā hi' = 'Tasmā eva' = Because one cannot be purified from defilements by lineage or wealth, but only by the Eightfold Path. 'Attano' = One's own. 'Atthaṃ' = The noble benefit that leads to Nibbāna. 'Sampassaṃ' = 'Sampassanto' = Discerning and seeing clearly. 'Paṇḍito poso' = A wise man of noble birth. 'Yoniso' = Through the proper means of developing the Path. 'Dhammaṃ' = The group of phenomena known as the five aggregates of clinging. 'Vicine' = Should investigate through Vipassanā, applying the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. 'Evaṃ' = When investigating in this way. 'Tattha' = Because of the causal sign which is the object of the Four Noble Truths, beginning with the five aggregates of clinging. 'Visujjhati' = He is purified from defilements, entering into the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa).

(In this context, it means: A wise person must practice Vipassanā on the group of mental and physical phenomena, the five aggregates of clinging. By practicing thus, when Vipassanā knowledge reaches its peak, Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) arises, and one penetrates the Truth of Suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha), the Truth of the Origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha), the Truth of Cessation through
170:
the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha), and the Truth of the Path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha), thereby becoming completely liberated and purified from defilements. With this verse, the virtues of Insight-knowledge and Noble Path-knowledge are praised.)

'Sāriputtova paññāya, sīlena upasamena ca.
Yopī pāraṅgato bhikkhu, etāvaparamo siyā.'

'Yo pi bhikkhu' = Whosoever monk. 'Pāraṅgato' = Has crossed over to the further shore, the city of Nibbāna. 'So pi' = That monk also. 'Etāvaparamo' = Has this attainment of Nibbāna as his highest limit. 'Siyā' = Is. 'Sīlena' = By the virtue of morality. 'Paññāya' = By the virtue of wisdom. 'Upasamena ca' = And by the virtue of the stilling of defilements. 'Sāriputtova' = Only the Elder Sāriputta, who received the title of Etadagga in wisdom among the many disciples in the Saṅgha. 'Seyyo' = Is especially praised and noble.

(With this verse, the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta are praised.)

The young deva Anāthapiṇḍika spoke these four verses. The Blessed One gave his consent (by remaining silent) to what the deva Anāthapiṇḍika had spoken. Then, the deva Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "The Blessed One has consented to my words," was joyful. He paid homage to the Blessed One, showing great respect, and vanished from that very spot.

Then, after that night had passed and the next day arrived, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, during this night,
171:
a certain deva came to me at midnight, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. He then addressed me with these verses." The Buddha then repeated the four verses spoken by the deva Anāthapiṇḍika to the monks.

(In this instance, the reason the Buddha did not explicitly mention the deva's name was that He wished to make manifest the power of Venerable Ānanda's inferential knowledge.)

Therefore, when the Blessed One finished speaking, Venerable Ānanda immediately addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, that deva must surely be Anāthapiṇḍika. Venerable Sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was one who had great devotion to the Elder Sāriputta." Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Ānanda: "Sādhu, Ānanda! Sādhu! Ānanda, you have reached as far as can be reached by reasoning. Ānanda, that deva was indeed Anāthapiṇḍika."

This is the account of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.

**********

## (3) The Story of Citta the Householder

(This Citta the Householder was a wealthy man just like Anāthapiṇḍika. However, in the terminology of the Sasana today, while Anāthapiṇḍika is known as "Anāthapiṇḍika the Merchant (Setthi)," this donor Citta is not commonly called "Citta the Merchant" but is better known as "Citta the Householder (Gahapati)." Therefore, in this text, he will be referred to as Citta the Householder.)
172:
## (a) The Householder's Past Aspiration

This future Citta the Householder, a virtuous man, was born into a noble family (the son of a merchant) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Dhamma of the Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a lay disciple to the rank of Etadagga in the field of being a "Dhammakathika" (an eloquent preacher of the Dhamma). Feeling inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position of Etadagga in Dhamma preaching.

## Life as a Hunter's Son

That noble son wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born in the house of a hunter (the son of a great hunter who killed animals). When he grew up and was capable of hunting in the forest, one day while it was raining, he took his spear and went into the forest to hunt. While searching here and there for animals, he saw a monk sitting on a stone slab in an unadorned mountain cave, with his rag-robe (paṃsukūla) covering his head. Realizing, "This noble one must be sitting there practicing the Dhamma of a monk," he quickly returned home. He had meat brought the previous day cooked on one stove and rice cooked on another (cooking the curry and rice simultaneously).

After having the rice and curry cooked together, he saw two monks coming to his house for alms.
173:
He went out to meet the two monks, took their bowls, and invited them to sit in the prepared seats. He said, "Venerable Sirs, please show me favor. Please sit here and accept this almsfood." After making this request for them to accept his alms, he instructed the other people remaining in the house, "Please look after these two noble ones with almsfood." He then took the cooked rice and curry, put them into a pot, tied the mouth of the pot with a banana leaf, and carried it toward the forest station. Along the way, he plucked various flowers and wrapped them in leaves. When he reached the place where the Elder was sitting, he set down the pot of almsfood in a suitable place and said, "Venerable Sir, please show me favor." He requested the Elder's bowl, filled it sufficiently with the rice and curry, and offered it into the Elder's hands. Then, he honored the Elder with the various flowers he had brought.

After making the offering, he stood in a suitable place and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, just as this offering of delicious almsfood and flowers brings great joy to my heart, so too, wherever I am born in the rounds of Saṃsāra, may thousands of gifts and presents come to me. May a rain of five-colored flowers also fall." The Elder, seeing that this hunter's son possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the Path and Fruit, favored him by preaching the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra) in detail. (The merit conducive to penetration, cultivated with the aim of Nibbāna, which is the end of the round of suffering, is called 'upanissaya'. From Aṅguttara Ṭīkā, Vol. 1, page 201.)
174:
That hunter's son performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. When he passed away from that existence, he was reborn in the celestial realm. In the place where he was born as a deva, a rain of celestial flowers fell so heavily that it reached up to his knees. That deva himself was endowed with a complexion more beautiful and radiant than other devas.

## (b) Becoming a Lay Disciple in the Final Life

That noble son wandered through the realms of devas and humans for an incalculable period between Buddhas (buddhantara). During the time when our Supreme Buddha appeared, he was born as the son of a merchant in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Magadha country. At the very moment of his birth, a marvelous rain of five-colored flowers fell throughout the entire city of Macchikāsaṇḍa, reaching up to the knees. Then, his parents said, "Our son has brought his own name with him. On the day of our son's birth, the entire city of Macchikāsaṇḍa became wonderful and extraordinary with five-colored flowers." Speaking these auspicious words, they named the boy "Citta Kumāra" (the Bright/Variegated Youth).

When the merchant's son Citta reached adulthood, he established a household. After his father, the great merchant, passed away, he attained the position of a merchant (Setthi) in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa. At that time, Venerable Mahānāma, who was one of the group of five monks (pañcavaggiya),
175:
arrived at the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa. Citta the Householder, being inspired by the peaceful demeanor of Venerable Mahānāma, went to meet him, took his bowl, and invited the Elder to his home to offer almsfood. After the meal, he invited the Elder to his own Ambāṭaka grove (a forest of hog-plum trees). He had a monastery built within that garden for the Elder to reside in. He then requested a promise from the Elder to always collect alms from his house and to reside in the Ambāṭaka grove monastery. Venerable Mahānāma, seeing that Citta the Householder possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) from past merits for attaining the Path and Fruit, preached to him. He frequently preached the Dhamma specifically concerning the detailed analysis and classification of the six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases. (This means he frequently taught in detail about the six internal bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the six external bases: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental objects. He taught these twelve sense bases because Citta the Householder was a person of medium wisdom, a 'majjhima' individual.)

Because Citta the Householder had practiced Vipassanā on the conditioned phenomena of mind and matter as impermanent, suffering, and non-self in previous lives (having crushed the conditioned phenomena with the knowledge of characteristics), when he strove and developed Vipassanā, he soon reached the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) and became an Anāgāmi Ariya. (Although it is not directly stated here which meditation subject he practiced to reach the Fruit of Non-returning,
176:
Considering the previous and subsequent accounts of Citta the Householder, it should be said that he attained the Path and Fruit by practicing the meditation on the sense bases (āyatana-kammaṭṭhāna).

(In this regard: Anāthapiṇḍika, the donor of the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, was a Sotāpanna Noble One devoted to giving. Citta the Householder, the donor of the great Ambāṭaka Grove Monastery in Macchikāsaṇḍa, was an Anāgāmī Noble One devoted to both giving and the Dhamma. This difference in the spiritual attainments of the two monastery donors should be noted beforehand).

## Citta the Householder's Devotion to Giving and the Dhamma

In this context, I shall present a brief excerpt from the Citta Saṃyutta to illustrate Citta the Householder's devotion to giving (dānābhirata) and his devotion to the Dhamma (dhammābhirata).

## Paṭhama Isidatta Sutta

On one occasion, many elder monks were staying at the great Ambāṭaka Grove Monastery, the meritorious work of Citta the Householder, in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa. Then, Citta the Householder went to the monastery, performed his duties to the elders, and after inviting them for a meal at his home the following day, he returned. On the next day, when the elders arrived at Citta the Householder's home for the meal and were seated on the prepared seats, Citta the Householder approached the elders, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He then addressed the most senior monk among them, named Ven. Thera: “Venerable Thera, it is said, ‘diversity of elements, diversity of elements’ (dhātunānatta). To what extent has the Blessed One explained the diversity of elements?”
177:
When he had asked this, the senior Ven. Thera, although he knew the answer, remained silent as he did not feel confident to reply. When asked a second time, he remained silent. When asked a third time, he remained silent as before.

At that time, among those monks, Ven. Isidatta, who was the most junior (saṅghanavaka), thought: “This senior Ven. Thera neither answers himself nor encourages others to answer. Citta the Householder, the lay follower, is being troubled (by the Sangha's inability to provide an answer). I shall answer this question and put the Sangha at ease.” Having thought so, he rose from his seat, went near the senior Ven. Thera, and asked permission: “Venerable Thera, may I answer Citta the Householder's question?” When the senior Ven. Thera gave permission, saying, “Friend Isidatta, you may answer Citta the Householder's question,” Ven. Isidatta returned to his seat and engaged in the following dialogue with Citta the Householder:

(Ven. Isidatta)
“Householder, did you not ask: ‘Venerable Thera, it is said, “diversity of elements, diversity of elements.” To what extent has the Blessed One explained the diversity of elements?’”

(Citta the Householder)
“Yes, venerable sir.”
178:
(Ven. Isidatta)
“Householder, the diversity of elements explained by the Blessed One is: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element; ... the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element. Householder, to this extent has the Blessed One explained the diversity of elements.”

Then, Citta the Householder was greatly delighted by Ven. Isidatta's answer and personally served the elders with choice food and delicacies. After the meal, when the elders returned to the monastery, the senior Ven. Thera said to Ven. Isidatta: “Friend Isidatta, this problem appeared clearly to your wisdom, but it did not appear to mine. Therefore, friend Isidatta, if other such questions arise, you yourself should answer them.”

## Dutiya Isidatta Sutta

In this Dutiya Isidatta Sutta, just as in the first, Citta the Householder invited the elder monks to his home for a meal. When they arrived, before serving the meal, he asked the senior Ven. Thera about the causes for the arising and non-arising of wrong views, such as “the world is eternal” or “the world is not eternal.” Although asked three times, the senior Ven. Thera remained silent (knowing but not feeling confident). Then, Ven. Isidatta asked permission from the senior Ven. Thera and—
179:
—answered Citta the Householder: “When there is self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), wrong views arise; when there is no self-identity view, wrong views do not arise.”

When Citta the Householder asked again about the manner in which self-identity view arises and does not arise, Ven. Isidatta explained it in detail. (For the full details of the questions and answers, one should refer to the Burmese translation of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta, 7. Citta Saṃyutta, 3. Dutiya Isidatta Sutta, starting from page 471).

After the discussion on the arising and non-arising of self-identity view, Ven. Isidatta and Citta the Householder conversed as follows:

(Citta the Householder)
“Venerable sir, from where has Ven. Isidatta come?”

(Ven. Isidatta)
“Householder, I have come from the Avanti country.”

(Citta the Householder)
“Venerable sir, there is a young man of good family named Isidatta from Avanti who is our friend, though we have never met (adiṭṭhasahāya), and he has gone forth as a monk. Have you ever seen him, venerable sir?”

(Ven. Isidatta)
“Householder, I have seen him.”

(Citta the Householder)
“Venerable sir, where is that venerable one living now?”

When asked this, Ven. Isidatta remained silent and did not give an answer.

(Citta the Householder)
“Venerable sir, are you our friend Isidatta whom we have never seen?”
180:
(Ven. Isidatta)
“Yes, householder.”

(Citta the Householder)
“Venerable sir, may Ven. Isidatta delight in Macchikāsaṇḍa. The Ambāṭaka Grove Monastery is delightful. I shall provide Ven. Isidatta with the four requisites: robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicine.”

(Ven. Isidatta)
“Householder, you have spoken well.” (Ven. Isidatta said this only to express appreciation for the householder's invitation; he did not say it with the desire to receive any of the four requisites).

Then, Citta the Householder was greatly delighted by Ven. Isidatta's answer and personally served the elders with choice food and delicacies. After the meal, when the elders returned to the monastery, the senior Ven. Thera spoke to Ven. Isidatta in the same manner as before (in the Paṭhama Isidatta Sutta).

Thereafter, Ven. Isidatta (thinking, “I should not stay here,” now that Citta the Householder had recognized him as the friend he had never seen in his lay life) put away his lodging, took his bowl and robes, and departed from Macchikāsaṇḍa, never to return.
181:
## Mahaka Pāṭihāriya Sutta

On one occasion, many elder monks were staying at the great Ambāṭaka Grove Monastery, the meritorious work of Citta the Householder, in Macchikāsaṇḍa. Then, Citta the Householder went to the monastery, performed his duties to the elders, and after inviting them for a meal at his cattle shed the following day, he returned. On the next day, when the elders arrived at Citta the Householder's cattle shed for the meal and were seated on the prepared seats, Citta the Householder personally served the elders with choice milk-rice mixed with ghee.

Citta the Householder's male servants and workers washed the golden bowl and served the milk-rice with ghee to the householder at the same time as the monks. After eating the milk-rice, Citta the Householder wished to accompany the elders and thought: “If this were at home, the mistress of the house could manage the remaining milk-rice as appropriate. But here at the cattle shed, if I do not give instructions, the workers will not manage it properly. If they do not, this choice milk-rice will go to waste without benefit.” Considering this, he instructed the workers, “Lads, distribute the remaining milk-rice as appropriate,” and then followed behind the monks.

At that time, the sun was scorching hot. The monks were walking with bodies that seemed sluggish and heavy, like those who had just finished a meal. Then, among those monks—
182:
—Ven. Mahaka, who was the most junior (saṅghanavaka), addressed the senior Ven. Thera: “Venerable Thera, would it not be good if a cool breeze blew, the sky became overcast, and rain fell drop by drop?” When the senior Ven. Thera replied, “Friend Mahaka, it would indeed be good if a cool breeze blew, the sky became overcast, and rain fell drop by drop,” Ven. Mahaka performed a miracle of psychic power so that a cool breeze blew, the sky became overcast, and rain fell drop by drop.

Then, the thought arose in Citta the Householder's mind: “How great is the psychic power and majesty of this junior monk!” Later, when they reached the monastery, Ven. Mahaka asked the senior Ven. Thera: “Venerable Thera, is this much sufficient?” The senior Ven. Thera replied with words of appreciation: “Friend Mahaka, this much is sufficient; friend Mahaka, this much has been done; friend Mahaka, this much has been offered as worship.” Then the monks went to their respective dwellings, and Ven. Mahaka also went to his own dwelling.

Thereafter, Citta the Householder approached Ven. Mahaka and requested him to perform a miracle. Ven. Mahaka said: “Householder, if that is so, spread your upper robe at the entrance of the dwelling and scatter a bundle of grass over it.” Citta the Householder replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” and as instructed by Ven. Mahaka, he spread his upper robe at the entrance and scattered the grass. Then, Ven. Mahaka—
183:
After entering the monastery, he closed the door-bolt and performed a psychic miracle (pāṭihāriya) where flames emerged from the keyhole and the gaps between the door panels, burning only the grass and not the ceiling. After the grass had been burned in this way, Citta the Householder shook out his upper robe, picked it up, and stood in a blameless spot, trembling with hair-raising awe.

Then, the Venerable Mahaka came out from the monastery and asked Citta the Householder, "Householder, is this much sufficient?" Citta the Householder replied, "Venerable Mahaka, this much is sufficient. Venerable Mahaka, this much has been done. Venerable Mahaka, this much has been offered as worship. Venerable Mahaka, please delight in staying at Macchikāsaṇḍa; the Ambāṭaka park monastery is delightful. I will take responsibility for the four requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicine—for the Venerable Mahaka." The Venerable Mahaka then gave words of appreciation (anumodanā), saying, "Householder, you have spoken well."

Afterward, the Venerable Mahaka, reflecting and considering, "I should not stay in this place," packed up his lodgings and bedding, took his bowl and robes, and departed from Macchikāsaṇḍa with a departure from which he would not return.

(In both these suttas—the second Isidatta Sutta and the Mahaka-pāṭihāriya Sutta—it should be specially noted that although Citta the Householder, having great faith in the Sasana, requested the Venerable Isidatta and the Venerable Mahaka to reside in his meritorious Ambāṭaka park monastery and offered to provide for the four requisites, from the perspective of the Elders, those four requisites
184:
were like requisites obtained through preaching or through showing miracles. Therefore, they renounced those four requisites and departed. The Commentaries and Sub-commentaries do not provide special explanations for this.

The reason for mentioning these two Isidatta Suttas and the Mahaka-pāṭihāriya Sutta here is merely to illustrate Citta the Householder's delight in the Dhamma (dhammābhirata). You, the virtuous readers of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, should make an effort to look into the 7th Citta Saṃyutta, which contains ten suttas, found in the second Saḷāyatana-vagga Saṃyutta of the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka Saṃyutta Nikāya).

## A Brief Account of the Venerable Sudhamma

One day, the two Chief Disciples, accompanied by a thousand follower monks, arrived at the Ambāṭaka park monastery. (At that time, the Venerable Sudhamma was the presiding elder in charge of that monastery). The monastery donor, Citta the Householder, prepared a great offering of honor for the thousand monks headed by the two Chief Disciples (without consulting the Venerable Sudhamma). The resident monk, Venerable Sudhamma, could not tolerate this and insulted Citta the Householder by saying, "Among these offerings, one thing is still missing: a sesame cake" (insulting the householder based on his birth). (In Citta the Householder's lineage, an ancestor had once been a cake-seller. Therefore, wishing to insult the householder regarding his birth, he spoke thus).

At that time, because Citta the Householder countered with an 'Okkali' rebuke—which was neither the speech of a monk nor the speech of a layman, like the cackling of a hen or the cawing of a crow—the Venerable Sudhamma became extremely
185:
angry and went to report the matter to the Blessed One. After receiving the Blessed One's admonition and established in that advice, he apologized and asked for forgiveness from Citta the Householder. While staying at that very Ambāṭaka park monastery, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and attained the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). (This is the explanation in the Aṅguttara Commentary; for the detailed story, one should look at the Story of Citta the Householder starting from page 327 of the first volume of the Dhammapada Commentary, and the Vinaya Cūḷavagga, 4-Paṭisāraṇīyakamma, starting from page 35 of the Burmese translation).

## Citta the Householder's Journey to Visit the Buddha

(I shall now extract and write the account of Citta the Householder's journey to visit the Buddha from the Dhammapada Commentary)—After the Venerable Sudhamma had become an Arahant, Citta the Householder reflected, "I have attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) without even seeing the Blessed One. I have been established in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) without even seeing the Blessed One. It is only proper that I should now go to pay homage to the Blessed One." Having so considered, he had five hundred carts fully loaded with sesame, rice, ghee, molasses, honey, clothes, and so on. Then he sent out an invitation to the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa, saying, "Those who wish to see the Buddha, please come along with me. I will take responsibility so that you will not be weary for lack of food and sustenance."

According to that invitation, five hundred monks, five hundred nuns, five hundred laymen, and five hundred laywomen departed together with Citta the Householder to visit the Buddha.
186:
Citta the Householder made preparations so that for the 2,000 people who followed him to see the Buddha and his own 1,000 attendants—a total of 3,000 people—there would be no lack of gruel, rice, food, and so on during the journey of thirty leagues (yojanas). However, as soon as they knew that Citta the Householder was coming to visit the Buddha, at every league's distance, devas created temporary pavilions and camps, waiting to serve those 3,000 people with celestial gruel, food, rice, and drinks. Not a single person lacked any kind of food or drink.

In this manner, being served and entertained by the devas, and traveling steadily at one league per day, Citta the Householder arrived at the city of Sāvatthī within one month. The five hundred carts remained as full as when they were first loaded. Along the way, he even distributed and donated the gifts sent by devas and humans, and thus reached Sāvatthī.

On the day Citta the Householder was to arrive at Sāvatthī, the Blessed One and the Venerable Ānanda spoke in advance as follows:

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, this evening, Citta the Householder, surrounded by five hundred laymen, will arrive and pay homage to me."

(Venerable Ānanda)
"Exalted Buddha, when this Citta the Householder comes to pay homage to the Blessed One, will any miracles occur?"
187:
(The Buddha)
"They will occur, Ānanda."

(Venerable Ānanda)
"What kind of miracles will occur, Exalted Buddha?"

(The Buddha)
"Ānanda, when Citta the Householder arrives and pays homage to me, a massive rain of five-colored celestial flowers will fall heavily over an area of about eight karīsas (mìn-pè), deep enough to sink one's knees."

Hearing these words, the citizens of Sāvatthī discussed among themselves, "It is said that a householder named Citta, who is so greatly meritorious, will arrive today to pay homage to the Blessed One. It is said that such miracles will also occur. We too shall have the opportunity to see this meritorious Citta the Householder today." They each took gifts and stood waiting along both sides of the road.

When Citta the Householder's group of pilgrims arrived near the Jetavana monastery, the five hundred monks who accompanied them went ahead first. Citta the Householder told the five hundred laywomen, "Mothers, you come later," and leaving them behind, he approached the Blessed One surrounded by the five hundred laymen. (Notably, those who stand or sit in the presence of the Buddhas do not do so haphazardly or without order; they stand and sit calmly and steadily on both sides of the path, leaving the middle open for the Buddha to walk).
188:
Citta the Householder entered the great path where the Buddha walks. As the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka), who had attained the three lower fruits, looked around, every place he gazed upon seemed to stir and vibrate. The multitude of people sitting in every direction he looked gazed at Citta the Householder as if he were a marvel, saying, "This is Citta the Householder." Citta the Householder approached the Blessed One, entered within the six-colored Buddha-rays, and fervently grasping the two ankles, he paid homage to the Buddha's feet with great devotion. At that very moment, the aforementioned massive rain of five-colored celestial flowers fell profusely. Thousands of 'Sādhu' acclamations from the people arose.

Citta the Householder remained in the presence of the Blessed One for a whole month. During his stay, he requested all the monks of the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, to remain only in the monastery and offered a great donation. He also kept those who had followed him to see the Buddha inside the monastery and provided for them without lack. In doing so, not even for a single day did he have to take any item from what he had carried in his own carts; he was able to give his donations solely with the gifts sent by devas and humans.

When the month was completed, Citta the Householder paid homage to the Blessed One and said:

"Exalted Buddha, I came with the thought, 'I shall give offerings to the Blessed Ones,' and a month has passed during the journey. For me,
189:
another month has passed here at this Jetavana monastery. I have not had the opportunity to take and donate any of the gifts I brought with me. For this duration of two months, I have been able to give donations only with the gifts sent by devas and humans. If I were to continue staying in this place for a year, I still would not get the chance to donate my own offerings. I wish to return after unloading and donating the offerings contained in the five hundred carts to the Saṅgha. Please direct me to a place where I may unload and store those offerings, Exalted Buddha."

The Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, vacate a place for Citta the Householder." Following the Blessed One's command, the Venerable Ānanda vacated a place. Citta the Householder unloaded and stored the five hundred cartloads of offerings in the Kappiya-bhūmi building cleared by the Venerable Ānanda. After donating them to the Saṅgha, he set out on his return journey toward Macchikāsaṇḍa with the three thousand monks and laypeople who had come with him, using the empty carts. Devas and humans repeatedly arose and said, "Venerable Citta the Householder, have you performed the kind of merit that requires you to travel with empty carts?" Unable to bear it, they loaded the carts with the seven jewels until they were full.
190:
Citta the Householder, providing for the entire group of monks and laypeople who had accompanied him on the pilgrimage with the gifts offered to him by devas and humans, traveled comfortably back to the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa.

Venerable Ānanda, having paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, said:

"Venerable Sir, it took Citta the Householder a month to travel here to the presence of the Blessed One. He has also stayed here at the Jetavana Monastery for a full month. During this long period, he has performed great acts of dana (charity) using only the gifts offered to him by devas and humans. Now, having emptied his five hundred carts, he must travel back to his city, which will also take a month. Notably, devas and humans have repeatedly arisen and said, 'O Noble Citta, have you performed deeds that require you to travel with empty carts?' Unable to bear this, they have filled his carts with the seven kinds of jewels. Citta the Householder will now travel comfortably back to Macchikāsaṇḍa, once again providing for the monks and laypeople with him using the gifts offered by devas and humans.

Venerable Sir, I wish to ask: does this honor and hospitality occur for Citta the Householder only when he comes to the presence of the Blessed One, or does it also occur when he travels to other places?"
191:
Thus he inquired. Then, the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda:

"Dear Ānanda, for this Citta the Householder, whether he comes to my presence or goes to any other place, honor and hospitality will surely arise. Indeed, Ānanda, this lay disciple Citta is one who possesses unwavering faith in kamma and its results, both mundane and supramundane, and he is one who has the highest devotion to the Triple Gem through supramundane faith. For a person of such nature, wherever they go, it is the natural law that gains, honor, and hospitality will arise."

Having said this, the Buddha preached this verse from the Pakiṇṇakavagga of the Dhammapada:

Saddho sīlena sampanno,
Yasobhogasamappito.
Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati,
Tattha tattheva pūjito.

Ānanda = Dear Ānanda. Saddho = One who is fully endowed with the two types of faith, mundane and supramundane. Sīlena = With the training of virtue (sīla) that laypeople should practice. Sampanno = One who is perfectly endowed and complete. Yasobhogasamappito = The noble disciple who is abundantly endowed with both worldly wealth and the wealth of a virtuous person (sappurisa-dhana), along with a large retinue of five hundred noble lay followers. Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ = To whatever region—East, West, South, or North—without distinction.
192:
Bhajati = he goes. So = that noble disciple of the Buddha. Tattha tattheva = in whatever place he arrives. Pūjito = is honored and revered by humans and devas, overwhelmed by their loving-kindness, faith, and devotion.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1, page 330).

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

From that time on, Citta the Householder traveled and lived surrounded by five hundred noble lay followers. Later, when the Blessed One was appointing lay disciples to their respective positions of Etadagga (the foremost) (referencing Saṃyutta Nikāya 2, page 474), based on the events in the Citta Saṃyutta of the Saḷāyatana Vagga, He praised Citta the Householder, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ citto gahapati = Monks, among my lay disciples who are preachers of the Dhamma, Citta the Householder is the most excellent, the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha appointed him to the position of Etadagga, the foremost in the category of "Dhammakathika = those who are skilled in preaching the Dhamma." (In this regard, Citta the Householder's skill in preaching the Dhamma should be noted by looking at the Saṃyojana Sutta on page 469 and the First Kāmabhū Sutta on page 475 of the Saḷāyatana Vagga Saṃyutta, Second Volume of the Burmese Translation of the Saṃyutta Nikāya).
193:
## Citta the Householder Preached Even Near Death

## Gilānadassana Sutta

Since Citta the Householder was a Noble One of the stage of Anāgāmī (Non-returner), even when he was about to pass away, he preached the Dhamma befitting one who held the title of Etadagga in Dhamma preaching. One should note the summary of the 10th Sutta of the Citta Saṃyutta, the Gilānadassana Sutta, provided below. (For the detailed account, see the Burmese translation of Saṃyutta Nikāya, Vol. 2, starting from page 484).

At one time, when Citta the Householder was afflicted with a terminal illness (māraṇantika-roga), many deities of the parks, forests, trees, and those presiding over medicinal herbs, grass, and forest vegetation gathered and urged Citta the Householder, saying, "Householder, make a wish: 'May I become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) in the future.'"

Then, Citta the Householder said to that assembly of deities, "That state of a Universal Monarch is also impermanent. It is unstable. That state of a Universal Monarch—the glory of a Cakkavatti—is something that must ultimately be abandoned."

When Citta the Householder spoke thus, his friends, companions, and relatives, thinking he was delirious, said to him, "Noble sir, be mindful; do not talk incoherently."

Because they said this, Citta the Householder asked, "What did I say that caused you to tell me, 'Noble sir, be mindful; do not talk incoherently'?" Then his friends, companions, and relatives replied:
194:
"Noble sir, you said: 'That state of a Universal Monarch is also impermanent. It is unstable. That state of a Universal Monarch—the glory of a Cakkavatti—is something that must ultimately be abandoned.'"

When they replied thus, Citta the Householder explained to his friends, companions, and relatives: "Friends, deities of the parks, forests, trees, and those presiding over medicinal herbs, grass, and forest vegetation came and urged me, saying, 'Householder, make a wish: "May I become a Universal Monarch in the future."' I told those deities, 'That state of a Universal Monarch is also impermanent. It is unstable. That state of a Universal Monarch—the glory of a Cakkavatti—is something that must ultimately be abandoned.' (I was not talking incoherently)."

Then his friends, companions, and relatives asked, "Noble sir, what benefit did those deities see that they urged you, saying, 'Householder, make a wish: "May I become a Universal Monarch in the future"'?"

Citta the Householder replied to those friends, companions, and relatives: "Friends, in the minds of those deities, they thought: 'This Citta the Householder is virtuous and of good conduct. If this Citta the Householder makes a wish, "May I become a Universal Monarch in the future," for this virtuous Citta the Householder, because he is pure in virtue, this mental aspiration will surely and certainly be fulfilled. One who possesses the Dhamma can see the results that are in accordance with the Dhamma.' Because they had such thoughts,
195:
those deities, seeing this special benefit, urged me, saying, 'Householder, make a wish: "May I become a Universal Monarch in the future."' I told those deities, 'That state of a Universal Monarch is also impermanent. It is unstable. That state of a Universal Monarch—the glory of a Cakkavatti—is something that must ultimately be abandoned.' (I was not talking incoherently)."

When his friends, companions, and relatives requested, "Noble sir, if that is so, please also admonish us," Citta the Householder preached his final sermon to those friends, companions, and relatives as follows:

"Friends, companions, and relatives, if that is so, you should train yourselves thus:

'We will be endowed with unwavering faith in the Blessed One: (1) He is called Arahant because He is worthy of special offerings. (2) He is called Sammāsambuddha because He rightly knew all things by Himself. (3) He is called Vijjācaraṇasampanna because He is perfect in knowledge and conduct. (4) He is called Sugata because He speaks only what is good. (5) He is called Lokavidū because He knows the world. (6) He is called Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi because He is the incomparable leader of those to be tamed. (7) He is called Satthādevamanussānaṃ because He is the teacher of gods and humans.
196:
(8) He is called Buddho because He has realized the Four Noble Truths. (9) He is called Bhagavā because He possesses the six supreme glories.'

Thus, we shall be endowed with unwavering faith in the Blessed One.

And: '(1) The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One. (2) It is to be seen for oneself. (3) It gives results without delay. (4) It invites one to come and see. (5) It is worthy of being applied within oneself. (6) It is to be personally experienced by the wise.'

Thus, we shall be endowed with unwavering faith in the Dhamma.

And: '(1) The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's noble disciples is practicing the good way. (2) The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's noble disciples is practicing the straight way. (3) The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's noble disciples is practicing the true way. (4) The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's noble disciples is practicing the proper way. (These are the four causal qualities). This Saṅgha of the Blessed One's noble disciples, consisting of four pairs of persons, eight types of individuals—'
197:
‘The community of disciples is worthy of gifts brought from afar (5). They are worthy of hospitality (6). They are worthy of offerings dedicated for the hereafter (7). They are worthy of being saluted with joined palms (8). They are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world (9).’—

“In this way, we shall be endowed with such unwavering faith in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, you should practice thus: ‘Whatever gifts we have in our home, we shall share them without discrimination with those who are virtuous and of good conduct.’”

This was the final teaching he gave. Thereafter, Citta the Householder, having established his friends, companions, and relatives in these four states—the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and generosity—passed away.

(Note: Regarding this, although there is no specific mention in the scriptures as to which realm Citta the Householder was reborn after his death, since he was an Anāgāmī Ariya, he would have been reborn in one of the fifteen Rūpāvacara Brahma realms, excluding the Asaññasatta realm. Specifically, it should be noted that he was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm.)

This is the account of Citta the Householder.

## (4) About Hatthaka Āḷavaka the Lay Disciple

## (A) The Lay Disciple’s Past Aspiration

This noble person, the future Hatthaka Āḷavaka the lay disciple, was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. On one occasion, while listening to the Buddha’s discourse,
198:
he saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being endowed with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha also gave him a prophetic declaration.

## (B) Becoming Prince Āḷavaka in the Final Life

That noble son wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time when this Buddha appeared, he became Prince Āḷavaka, the son of King Āḷavaka in the city of Āḷavī, within the kingdom of Āḷavī.

(From this point onwards—starting from King Āḷavaka going out for a hunt, until Prince Āḷavaka attained the stage of Anāgāmī and became a lay disciple learned in the Tipiṭaka, surrounded by five hundred lay disciples—the full and detailed biography has already been written in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 4, from page 257 to 307. Please refer back to those pages.)

## (C) Attaining the Etadagga Title

One day, Hatthaka Āḷavaka the lay disciple, together with five hundred lay disciples, went to the Buddha, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Buddha, seeing the very disciplined and refined assembly of Hatthaka Āḷavaka, asked: “Dear Āḷavaka, your assembly is indeed large. How do you, dear son, treat and support this assembly?” Hatthaka Āḷavaka replied to the Buddha:
199:
“Venerable Sir, I support and treat with generosity (dāna) those who would be pleased and satisfied by receiving gifts (1). I support and treat with pleasant speech (piyavācā) those who would be pleased and satisfied by hearing kind words (2). When various matters arise, I support and treat with beneficial conduct (atthacariyā) those who would be pleased and satisfied by having their affairs successfully managed and looked after (3). I support and treat with impartiality (samānattatā) those who would be pleased and satisfied by being treated as equals (4).”

Based on this matter, later, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, when the Buddha was appointing lay disciples to various pre-eminent positions, he declared regarding Hatthaka Āḷavaka:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi parisaṃ saṅgaṇhantānaṃ yadidaṃ hatthako āḷavako = Monks, among my lay disciples who support their assembly through the four bases of sympathy (namely dāna, piyavācā, atthacariyā, and samānattatā), Hatthaka Āḷavaka is the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and appointed him to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) in the category of supporting an assembly (parisa-saṅgaṇhaka).

This is the account of Hatthaka Āḷavaka the lay disciple.
200:
## (5) About Mahānāma the Sakyan King

## (A) The Sakyan King’s Past Merit

This noble person, the future Mahānāma the Sakyan king, was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha’s discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of “giving choice food and medicine (paṇītarasadāna).” Inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha also gave him a prophetic declaration.

## (B) Becoming Mahānāma the Sakyan King in the Final Life

That noble son wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time when this Buddha appeared, he was born into the Sakyan royal clan in the city of Kapilavatthu as a Sakyan prince named Mahānāma (the elder brother of Venerable Anuruddha). Upon reaching maturity, as soon as he saw the Buddha for the first time, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and became a Sotāpanna Ariya.

## (C) Attaining the Etadagga Title

One day, after the Buddha had spent the rainy season retreat in the city of Verañjā and was traveling on a dhammadūta journey, he arrived at the royal city of Kapilavatthu and was residing at the Nigrodhārāma monastery, surrounded by a company of monks.
201:
Mahānāma the Sakyan heard the news that “the Buddha has arrived,” went to the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He then addressed the Buddha: “Venerable Sir, I have heard news that ‘the company of monks suffered great hardship and exhaustion while going for alms in the city of Verañjā.’ Venerable Sir, please grant me the commitment to serve and provide for the Saṅgha of monks daily for four months. I wish to restore the physical strength of the Saṅgha, Venerable Sir.” The Buddha accepted Mahānāma the Sakyan’s request by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, Mahānāma the Sakyan, starting from the next day, served the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the five kinds of excellent food, catumadhu medicine, and so on every day. When the four months were completed, he again requested a commitment to serve for another four months. After those four months were completed, he again requested a commitment to serve for another four months, thus completing one full year of service. When the year was completed, he requested a commitment to serve once more, but the Buddha no longer granted the request.

(Note: Beyond one year, because the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada prohibits accepting or consenting to an invitation for medicinal requisites, the Buddha did not grant the commitment/permission to serve further. To elaborate—on the third occasion, Mahānāma the Sakyan had said, “Venerable Sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha with medicinal requisites for the rest of my life =
202:
I wish to invite them.” Then the Buddha had said, “Sādhu, sādhu, Mahānāma! Mahānāma, if that is so, you may invite the Saṅgha with medicinal requisites for the rest of your life,” thus granting the commitment/permission. After this permission was given, the Buddha heard that the Chabbaggī monks were harassing Mahānāma the Sakyan with insistent demands that could cause distress and the decline of faith. Having rebuked those monks, the Buddha laid down the training rule (found in Vinaya II, 136-137): “A monk who is not ill, excluding a further invitation or a permanent invitation, may accept an invitation for medicine for only four months. If he accepts beyond that, it is an offence of Pācittiya.” (This training rule is known as the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada. The detailed background of this rule can be found in the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Pācittiya Pāḷi, starting from page 153). Therefore, although permission was initially granted, it is said that “he no longer granted the commitment” because it was later prohibited by the training rule.)

From that time onwards, Mahānāma the Sakyan served every monk who came to him in the same manner with the five kinds of very excellent and delicious food and catumadhu medicines. Thus, the reputation of Mahānāma the Sakyan for “serving the Saṅgha with the five kinds of very excellent and delicious food and catumadhu medicines” became famous throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa.

For this reason, later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery and appointing lay disciples to pre-eminent positions in order, he declared regarding Mahānāma the Sakyan:
203:
“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ paṇītadāyakānaṃ yadidaṃ mahānāmo sakko = Monks, among my lay disciples who give choice food and medicinal requisites, Mahānāma the Sakyan is the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and appointed him to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) in the category of “giving choice things (paṇītadāna).”

This is the account of Mahānāma the Sakyan king.

**********

## (6) About Ugga the Householder

## (A) The Householder’s Past Merit

This noble person, the future Ugga the householder, was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha’s discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of “giving what is pleasant (manāpadāna).” Inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha also gave him a prophetic declaration.

## (B) Becoming Ugga the Householder in the Final Life

That noble son wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time when this Buddha appeared, he was born into a wealthy merchant family in the region of Vesālī.
204:
## Being Named Ugga the Merchant
After this merchant's son was born, he was not given a specific name. In his later years, the merchant's son's physical body (attabhāva) became full, tall, and prominent, appearing as beautiful as a decorated archway pillar or a hoisted golden cloth. His virtues and reputation also became more prominent and widespread day by day. Thus, because of his lofty physical stature and prominent virtues, he later became known among the four classes of people as "Ugga the Merchant."

Notably, this Ugga the Merchant established himself in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) upon his first meeting with the Buddha, and later realized the three lower Paths and three lower Fruits (becoming an Anāgāmī, a Non-returner).

When Ugga the Merchant reached an older age, while sitting in a secluded place, he reflected: "I shall offer to the Buddha whatever objects I find pleasing and delightful. I have heard from the presence of the Buddha that 'the giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.'" Then, a special thought arose in Ugga the Merchant's mind: "Indeed, may the Buddha, knowing my thought, come to the door of my house."
205:
The Buddha, knowing Ugga the Merchant's thought, arrived at the merchant's house door in a wondrous manner, surrounded by a company of monks. Hearing that the Buddha had arrived, Ugga the Merchant was exceedingly encouraged and joyful. He went to the Buddha, paid respects with the fivefold prostration, received the Buddha's bowl, and invited him inside. He seated the Buddha on the prepared seat and the company of monks on the remaining seats. After serving the Saṅgha led by the Buddha with various delicious foods and completing the meal duties, he sat in a suitable place and addressed the Buddha thus:

"(1) Venerable Sir, I have heard and received this teaching from the presence of the Buddha: 'Manāpadāyī labhate manāpaṃ = The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.' Venerable Sir, my delicacies which have the color of Sal flowers are pleasing to me. May the Buddha, out of compassion, accept these delicacies of mine." The Buddha accepted them out of compassion.

Again, "(2) Venerable Sir, I have heard and received this teaching from the presence of the Buddha: 'Manāpadāyī labhate manāpaṃ = The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.' Venerable Sir, my pork prepared with jujube fruits...
206:
...is pleasing to me. (Etc.) (3) My fried water spinach is pleasing to me. (Etc.) (4) Venerable Sir, my Sāli rice, from which the black grains have been removed and which is served with many soups and curries, is pleasing to me. (Etc.) (5) Venerable Sir, my garments made in the Kāsika country are pleasing to me. (Etc.) (6) Venerable Sir, my couch with long-haired rugs, flower-embroidered covers, antelope skin rugs, a red canopy, and red pillows at both ends is pleasing to me. Venerable Sir, we know that 'these items are indeed not allowable for the Buddha.' Venerable Sir, this sandalwood stool of ours is worth over a hundred thousand; I wish the Buddha to accept these items of mine out of compassion." The Buddha accepted them out of compassion.

(A special note here: Ugga the Merchant, after the Buddha had finished the gruel and before the main meal was served, wished to offer these gifts and spoke as mentioned above.

The phrase "The Buddha accepted them out of compassion" is merely the focus of the teaching. In reality, Ugga the Merchant offered those gifts to both the Buddha and the five hundred monks.

Regarding the statement in item (6), "We know that these items are indeed not allowable for the Buddha," he spoke of the allowable gifts as "not allowable" by association with the unallowable gifts. In truth, Ugga the Merchant had all the bedding and furniture...
207:
...brought and piled up. He sent the unallowable items to his house shop and offered the allowable, proper (kappiya) bedding and furniture to the five hundred monks led by the Buddha.

Regarding the "sandalwood stool worth over a hundred thousand" mentioned in item (6), it was not very large, measuring about two and a half cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. Because it was solid and considered a noble material by worldly convention, it was worth over a hundred thousand. The Buddha, after accepting the sandalwood stool, had it cut into pieces and donated it to the monks for grinding eye-ointment. This is a special point to note.)

Then the Buddha gave a teaching of appreciation (anumodanā) to Ugga the Merchant with these following verses:

"The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing,
Who gives with intention to those who are upright.
Clothing, bedding, food, and drink,
And various kinds of requisites.

Householder Ugga, the giver who offers pleasing gifts with pure intention and faith, definitely receives various pleasing fruits of giving. Whosoever gives with a strong and longing wholesome desire to the noble Arhats who are upright in body, speech, and mind—offering clothing, bedding, food, drink, and various other...
208:
...requisites with faith.

Having known the Arhats who are like fertile fields,
Giving, releasing, and without attachment,
That virtuous person, having given what is hard to give,
The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.

Whosoever, having clearly known with wisdom the noble Arhats who are like excellent fertile fields, gives, releases, and does not hold back with a clinging mind; that virtuous person of soft heart, having given the gift that is difficult for those with ordinary resolve and lack of faith to give, or because of such giving, definitely receives various pleasing fruits of giving."

The Buddha, having performed the appreciation with these verses for Ugga the Merchant, rose from his seat and departed. (This collection of words is extracted from the Manāpadāyī Sutta, Anguttara Nikāya, Burmese Translation, Volume 2, pages 53-55.)

At that very offering ceremony, Ugga the Merchant informed the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, I have heard and received this teaching from the presence of the Buddha: 'Manāpadāyī labhate manāpaṃ = The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.'
209:
Venerable Sir, whatever pleasing property of mine exists, I have already offered those various items to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha." Having informed him thus, from that time onwards, he constantly offered his various pleasing gifts to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha.

## (C) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
For this reason, later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery and was appointing lay followers to the respective positions of Etadagga, he praised Ugga the Merchant, saying:

"Monks, among my disciples, the lay followers who are givers of pleasing things (manāpadāyakānaṃ), Ugga the Merchant of Vesālī is the foremost."

Thus, he placed him in the position of Etadagga, the foremost, in the category of "giving pleasing things."

## The Future Existence of Ugga the Merchant
Later, Ugga the Merchant of Vesālī passed away. After passing away, he was reborn in one of the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Brahma realms. At that time, the Buddha was still residing and dwelling at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. Then, at midnight, Ugga Brahma, having a very pleasing appearance and making the entire Jetavana monastery...
210:
...shine and glow, approached the Buddha, paid respects, and stood in a suitable place. The Buddha asked Ugga Brahma:

"Ugga, how is it? Is your wish fulfilled according to your desire?"
