Ugga Brahma replied to the Buddha:

"Venerable Sir, my wish is indeed fulfilled according to my desire."

(Here, one might ask: "What was asked and what was answered?" The answer should be understood as: He asked about the Fruit of Arhatship (Arahatta-phala) and he answered about the Fruit of Arhatship. To clarify further—Ugga Brahma, while he was a human, had a strong desire to attain the Fruit of Arhatship. Therefore, referring to that Fruit of Arhatship, the Buddha asked, "Is your wish fulfilled according to your desire?" Since Ugga Brahma had reached the Fruit of Arhatship by that time, he replied, "My wish is indeed fulfilled according to my desire," referring to that Fruit of Arhatship.)

Then the Buddha taught the Dhamma to Ugga Brahma with these two following verses:

"The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing,
The giver of the best receives the best again.
The giver of the excellent becomes a receiver of the excellent,
The giver of the foremost reaches the foremost state."

The giver of what is pleasing receives what is pleasing,
The giver of the noble receives the noble again...
211:
211
He who gives what is desired obtains what is desired;
He who gives what is praised reaches the state that is praised.

Yo aggadāyī varadāyī,
seṭṭhadāyī ca yo naro.
dīghāyu yasavā hoti,
yattha yatthūpapajjati.

Whoever is in the habit of giving the foremost thing, the excellent thing; whoever is in the habit of giving what is desired, and whoever is in the habit of giving what is praised—that person, in whatever realm or existence they are reborn, becomes long-lived and possesses a great following.

This is the account of Ugga the Merchant.

## (7) The Account of Uggata the Merchant
## (a) The Merchant's Past Merits
This noble person, the future Uggata the Merchant, was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a lay follower to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Saṅghupaṭṭhāna = serving the Saṅgha with an impartial mind." Inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made a resolution for that very position. The Buddha then delivered a prophecy (byādita) concerning him.
212:
212
## (b) Becoming Uggata the Merchant in His Final Life
That noble person wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the period when this current Buddha appeared, he was born into a merchant family in the village of Hatthigāma. He was named "Young Uggata." Later, when he reached adulthood and his father passed away, he succeeded to the position of Merchant.

At that time, while the Buddha was wandering through the country accompanied by a large assembly of monks, he arrived at Hatthigāma and resided in the garden named Nāgavana. Then, Uggata the Merchant, who had been indulging in intoxicants for seven days and was surrounded by dancers, went to the Nāgavana garden to enjoy himself. Upon seeing the Buddha, he was overcome with great shame and fear. When he approached the Buddha, his intoxication completely vanished. Uggata the Merchant respectfully paid homage to the Buddha and sat in a suitable place. The Buddha then preached the Dhamma to him. At the conclusion of the discourse, Uggata the Merchant attained the three lower paths and fruits (= he became an Anāgāmī, a Non-returner).

From that time on, Uggata the Merchant released the dancers, saying, "You may go happily wherever you wish." He became one who delighted only in giving and spent his time offering dāna to the Saṅgha. Devas would come to him during the latter part of the night and say to Uggata the Merchant:
213:
213
"Merchant, this particular monk is a Tevijja Arahant, endowed with the three types of higher knowledge. This particular monk is a Chaḷabhiñña Arahant, endowed with the six types of supernormal powers. This monk is virtuous; this monk is immoral (dussīla)."

Even upon hearing the words of the devas, Uggata the Merchant did not lose his faith because of the immoral ones; instead, he recognized and focused only on the true virtues of the virtuous monks and the Noble Ones with devotion. (He did not focus on the faults of the immoral ones; this is truly exemplary). He offered alms with an equal mind of faith to both the virtuous and the immoral. Even when sitting near the Buddha, he never reported or spoke of the faults of the immoral ones, but only spoke words of praise regarding the virtues of the virtuous monks.

## (c) Receiving the Foremost Title
For this reason, later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery and appointing lay followers to their respective foremost positions, he declared regarding Uggata the Merchant:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ saṅghupaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ hatthigāmako uggato gahapati = Monks, among my lay disciples who serve the Saṅgha with an impartial mind, Uggata the householder of Hatthigāma is the foremost.”
214:
214
Thus, the Buddha appointed him to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Saṅghupaṭṭhāna = serving the Saṅgha with an impartial mind."

Special Note:
(The village of Hatthigāma, where this Uggata the Merchant resided, is located in the Vajjī country. This Uggata the Merchant of Hatthigāma (No. 7) and the Ugga the Merchant of Vesālī (No. 6) mentioned previously are both extraordinary individuals who each possess eight wonderful qualities. The detailed accounts can be found in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka, Aṅguttara Nikāya, Book Three, Aṭṭhakanipāta, Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka, 3-Gahapati Vagga, First Sutta and Second Sutta, starting from page 47. Here, however, a summary will be provided.)

## The Eight Wonderful Qualities of Ugga the Merchant (No. 6)
On one occasion, while the Buddha was residing at the Kūṭāgārasālā monastery in the Mahāvana forest near Vesālī, he briefly addressed the monks, saying, "Monks, you should regard Ugga the Merchant of Vesālī as one endowed with eight wonderful qualities," and then entered his fragrant chamber (Gandhakuṭī).

Later, a certain monk went to Ugga the Merchant's house in the morning and sat on a prepared seat. (In Ugga the Merchant's house, five hundred seats were always kept ready so that five hundred monks could sit). Then, that monk asked Ugga the Merchant, who had come to pay homage and was sitting in a suitable place, "Merchant, the Buddha has declared that you are endowed with eight wonderful qualities. Merchant, what are those eight wonderful qualities that the Buddha spoke of?"

Ugga the Merchant replied, "Venerable Sir, I do not know which eight wonderful qualities the Buddha was referring to. However, Venerable Sir, there are eight wonderful qualities present in me. Please listen to these eight qualities and pay close attention; I shall speak." The monk agreed, saying, "Very well, Merchant." Then Ugga the Merchant addressed the monk as follows:
215:
215
(1) Venerable Sir, as soon as I first saw the Buddha from a distance, my mind felt absolute faith and devotion toward him. (No doubt arose as to whether he was the Buddha or not; my mind was filled with great devotion, thinking, 'This noble one is certainly the Buddha.' There was no turbidity at all). Venerable Sir, this first wonderful quality of "absolute faith and devotion toward the Buddha upon first sight" is evident in me.

(2) Venerable Sir, with a mind overflowing with faith and devotion, I approached the Buddha. The Buddha preached to me the graduated discourse (anupubbīkathā), which is the noble path to the attainment of the paths and fruits: (1) Dānakathā = discourse on giving, (2) Sīlakathā = discourse on virtue, (3) Saggakathā = discourse on the heavenly realms, and (4) Maggakathā = discourse on the noble practice leading to the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna. While he was preaching thus, when the Buddha knew that my mind was ready, softened, free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa), uplifted, and clear, he preached the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā, the Four Noble Truths: Suffering (Dukkha), the Origin (Samudaya), the Cessation (Nirodha), and the Path (Magga). At that time, I attained the Dhamma-eye (dhamma-cakkhu) reaching the fruit of Anāgāmī; I became an Anāgāmī. After becoming an Anāgāmī, I took the supramundane refuge and undertook the practice of the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth (Brahmacariyapañcamakasīla).
216:
216
(In the ordinary five precepts commonly practiced, where one undertakes "Kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi," the five precepts practiced by substituting that with "Abrahmacariyā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi" is called Brahmacariyapañcamakasīla).

Venerable Sir, this second wonderful quality of "becoming an Anāgāmī upon first seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma, and undertaking the supramundane refuge along with the Brahmacariyapañcamakasīla" is evident in me.

(3) Venerable Sir, I had four wives who were young and in their prime. Venerable Sir, after I became an Anāgāmī, I returned home, called those four wives, and said, "Sisters, I have undertaken the practice of the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth. Any sister who wishes may remain in this house, enjoy these riches, and perform meritorious deeds. If you wish to return to the homes of your relatives and parents, take enough wealth for your use and return there. Or, if you desire another husband, tell me to which man I should give you."

Venerable Sir, when I spoke thus, the eldest wife said, "My lord, please give me in marriage to such-and-such a man." Venerable Sir, I then sent for that man, and holding my eldest wife with my left hand and a water pitcher with my right hand, I gave her away in marriage to that man. Venerable Sir, while I was thus giving away my young and beautiful eldest wife, I was not aware of any change or disturbance in my mind (meaning, his mind did not waver or become upset). Venerable Sir, this third wonderful quality of "having no mental disturbance even when giving away my eldest wife to another man" is evident in me.
217:
(4) Venerable sir, whatever wealth and possessions I have in my house, I do not distinguish them from the virtuous ones who possess good conduct. (One who thinks, 'I will give this much, I will not give that much; I will give these items, I will not give those items,' is said to distinguish his wealth from the virtuous ones. For me, such a thought does not arise; rather, I maintain the mind that all my wealth and possessions belong to the virtuous ones, just like the property of the Saṅgha or the property of a group). Venerable sir, this is the fourth wonderful quality that is present in me: 'maintaining the mind that all my wealth and possessions belong to the virtuous ones without distinction.'

(5) Venerable sir, whenever I approach or serve a monk, I do so only with respect and attend to him personally; I never approach or serve without respect. Venerable sir, this is the fifth wonderful quality that is present in me: 'serving the noble monks with respect.'

(6) Venerable sir, if that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen to the Dhamma only with respect. I do not listen without respect. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach the Dhamma to that venerable one. Venerable sir, this is the sixth wonderful quality that is present in me: 'listening respectfully when a noble monk teaches the Dhamma, and teaching the Dhamma oneself if the noble monk does not.'

(7) Venerable sir, deities approach me and say, 'Householder, the Blessed One has well-taught the Dhamma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, endowed with all good qualities.' Venerable sir, when they speak thus, I reply to those deities, 'Whether you deities speak thus or not,
218:
the Blessed One has indeed well-taught the Dhamma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, endowed with all good qualities.' It is not a wonder that deities approach me and speak thus. However, venerable sir, because of the fact that deities approach me and I get to converse with them, I have never known any elation of mind such as 'Deities approach me' or 'I get to converse with deities.' Venerable sir, this is the seventh wonderful quality that is present in me: 'the absence of elation of mind despite deities approaching me and my conversing with them.'

(8) Venerable sir, among the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) taught by the Blessed One that lead to the lower realms (kāma-bhūmi), I do not see any single fetter that I have not yet abandoned. (By this statement, he declares his status as an Anāgāmī Ariya). Venerable sir, this is the eighth wonderful quality that is present in me: 'being an Anāgāmī Ariya.'

Venerable sir, these eight wonderful qualities are present in me. However, I do not know which eight wonderful qualities the Blessed One was referring to when he spoke of me.

Then that monk, having received alms-food from Ugga the householder's house, departed from that place. After finishing his meal, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga the householder. Then the Blessed One addressed that monk:

'Monk, well done, well done! One who wishes to answer and speak rightly should answer and speak just as Ugga the householder has spoken.'
219:
'Monk, I declare that Ugga the householder is endowed with the eight wonderful qualities that he himself explained. Monk, you should remember Ugga the householder as one endowed with these eight wonderful qualities.' (These are the eight wonderful qualities of Ugga the householder).

## (7) The Eight Wonderful Qualities of Uggata the Householder

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was staying at Hatthigāma (Elephant Village) in the Vajjī country, he briefly addressed the monks, saying, 'Monks, you should remember Uggata the householder of Hatthigāma as one endowed with eight wonderful qualities,' and then entered the monastery.

Then a certain monk, as in the previous method, went to the house of Uggata the householder in the morning and questioned him just as the previous monk had. Uggata the householder, replying in the same manner as the previous Ugga, explained his eight wonderful qualities as follows:

'(1) Venerable sir, while I was indulging in and intoxicated by the five cords of sensual pleasure in my Nāgavana Garden (Ironwood Forest Garden), as soon as I saw the Blessed One from afar for the first time, my mind immediately gained absolute faith and devotion in the Blessed One, and my intoxication vanished. Venerable sir, this is the first wonderful quality that is present in me: "the immediate gaining of absolute faith in the Buddha upon seeing him and the cessation of intoxication."

(2) Venerable sir, with a mind overflowing with faith and devotion, I approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me a progressive discourse on the path to the Path and Fruit, namely: (1) Discourse on Giving (dāna-kathā), (2) Discourse on Virtue (sīla-kathā), (3) Discourse on Heaven (sagga-kathā), and (4) Discourse on the Path (magga-kathā). While he was teaching thus, when the Blessed One knew that I had a ready mind, a soft mind, a mind free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa), an uplifted and joyful mind, and a clear mind,
220:
the Blessed One then taught and revealed to me the Four Noble Truths—Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path—which is the teaching special to the Buddhas (sāmukkaṃsika dhammadesanā). At that time, I attained the Dhamma-eye, reaching the fruit of Anāgāmī; I became an Anāgāmī Ariya. Having become an Anāgāmī Ariya, I took the supramundane refuges and undertook the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth (brahmacariya-pañcamaka-sīla). Venerable sir, this is the second wonderful quality that is present in me: "becoming an Anāgāmī Ariya upon first seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma, and undertaking the supramundane refuges along with the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth."

(3) Venerable sir, I had four wives who were young and in their prime. Venerable sir, after I became an Anāgāmī Ariya, I returned home, called those four wives, and said, "Sisters, I have undertaken the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth. Any sister who wishes may remain in this house, enjoy the wealth, and perform meritorious deeds. If you wish to return to the house of your relatives and parents, take enough wealth for your use and return. Or, if you desire another man, tell me to which man I should give you." I gave them this broad permission. Venerable sir, when I spoke thus, the eldest wife said, "My lord, please give me to such-and-such a man." Venerable sir, I then sent for that man, and taking the eldest wife with my left hand and a water pitcher with my right hand, I poured the water and gave the eldest wife to that man. Venerable sir, while I was thus giving away my young and beautiful eldest wife, I did not experience any change or disturbance in my mind. Venerable sir, this is the third wonderful quality that is present in me: "the absence of any mental disturbance even when giving away the eldest wife to another man."
221:
(4) Venerable sir, whatever wealth and possessions I have in my house, I do not distinguish them from the virtuous ones who possess good conduct. Venerable sir, this is the fourth wonderful quality that is present in me: 'maintaining the mind that all my wealth and possessions belong to the virtuous ones without distinction.'

(5) Venerable sir, whenever I approach or serve a monk, I do so only with respect and attend to him personally; I never approach or serve without respect. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen to the Dhamma only with respect; I do not listen without respect. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach the Dhamma to that venerable one. Venerable sir, this is the fifth wonderful quality that is present in me: 'serving the noble monks with respect, listening respectfully when a noble monk teaches the Dhamma, and teaching the Dhamma oneself if the noble monk does not.'

(6) Venerable sir, when I have invited the Saṅgha, deities approach me and say, 'Householder, this monk is one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta); this monk is one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta); this monk is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī); this monk is one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta); this monk is one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta); this monk is a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī); this monk is a faith-follower (saddhānusārī); this monk is virtuous and of good conduct; this monk is immoral and of evil conduct.' It is not a wonder that deities come and speak thus. Venerable sir, while I am serving the Saṅgha, I do not think, 'Because this person is immoral, I will give him only a little...'
222:
222
'I will give to this person; but to this person, because he is virtuous, I will give much'—I do not recall such a thought ever arising in me. Indeed, Bhante, I give with an equal mind to both the virtuous and the immoral. Bhante, this is the sixth marvelous and wonderful quality found in me.

(7) Bhante, deities approach me and say: 'Householder, the Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end.' When they speak thus, Bhante, I reply to those deities: 'Whether you deities speak thus or not, the Dhamma has indeed been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end.' Yet, I do not recall any elation of mind arising because deities approach me or because I converse with deities, thinking, 'Deities approach me' or 'I converse with deities.' Bhante, this is the seventh marvelous and wonderful quality found in me.

(8) Bhante, if I were to pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare of me: 'There is no fetter remaining for the householder Uggata of Hatthigāma by which he would return again to this sensual world.' (By this statement, he reveals his attainment as an Anāgāmī). Bhante, for me...
223:
223
...this is the eighth marvelous and wonderful quality found in me: that there is no fetter (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) remaining that would lead back to this sensual realm.

Bhante, these eight marvelous and wonderful qualities are found in me. However, I do not know which eight marvelous qualities the Blessed One was referring to when He spoke of me.'

Thus he spoke. (The subsequent details are identical to the previous story of Ugga the Householder. These are the eight marvelous qualities of the householder Uggata. Although in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhaka Nipāta, both householders are referred to simply as 'Ugga', based on the context of this Etadagga-vagga Pāḷi, the householder from Vesālī is presented as 'Ugga' and the householder from Hatthigāma as 'Uggata'. Although only a brief summary of the eight qualities was intended for these two householders, the detailed account is provided here due to its inspiring nature. This is a special note to be remembered).

This is the account of the householder Uggata.

## (8) The Story of the Householder Sūrambaṭṭha
## (a) The Past Deeds of the Householder
This noble person, the future Sūrambaṭṭha, was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a lay disciple to the foremost position (Etadagga) of those who possess 'unwavering confidence' (aveccappasāda) in the Dispensation. Inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position.
224:
224
The Blessed One also granted him the prophecy. 

## (b) Becoming Sūrambaṭṭha in his Final Birth
That noble man wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was born into a wealthy merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī. He was named 'the youth Sūrambaṭṭha'. When he reached maturity, he established a household and lived as a supporter and follower of heretics (titthiyas) outside the Dispensation.

## Sūrambaṭṭha Becoming a Stream-Enterer
Then one day, at dawn, the Blessed One surveyed the world of beings and saw the past merits of the householder Sūrambaṭṭha that would lead to the attainment of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). At the time for alms-round, the Buddha went to the door of Sūrambaṭṭha's house. Upon seeing the Blessed One, Sūrambaṭṭha thought: 'The ascetic Gotama is indeed born of a noble warrior clan and is very famous in the world. Therefore, it would not be proper if I do not approach him.' Having thought thus, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage at His feet, took the alms-bowl, and invited Him inside. He offered a seat on a couch worthy of noble ones, served Him with food, and sat down in a suitable place.
225:
225
The Blessed One delivered a discourse to the householder Sūrambaṭṭha that was suitable to his temperament. At the conclusion of the teaching, Sūrambaṭṭha was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala); he became a Noble Stream-enterer. Having encouraged and guided Sūrambaṭṭha to the attainment of the Fruit of Stream-entry, the Blessed One returned to the monastery.

## Māra Coming to Test Him
Thereafter, Māra the Evil One thought: 'This man named Sūrambaṭṭha was our property—one of our people (as a disciple of the heretics). However, the Buddha went to his house today. I wonder if Sūrambaṭṭha, having heard the Buddha's Dhamma, has realized the Noble Path. I shall investigate to clearly know whether he has escaped from my domain of the five cords of sensual pleasure.' Being a powerful being capable of creating any form he desired, Māra created a psychic image identical to the Blessed One. He mimicked the manner of holding the robes and the bowl exactly like the Buddha, appearing with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), and stood at the door of Sūrambaṭṭha's house.

Sūrambaṭṭha, hearing that 'the Buddha has come again,' thought: 'There is no reason for Buddhas to come without a cause. For what reason has the Blessed One returned?' He quickly went to the Māra disguised as the Buddha, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place.
226:
226
He respectfully asked: 'Bhante, you have only just finished your meal at my house and departed. For what reason have you returned?'

Māra said: 'Lay disciple Sūrambaṭṭha, while I was preaching the Dhamma, I spoke a certain word without careful reflection. It is true that I taught that all five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self (anicca, dukkha, anatta). However, not all of these five aggregates are of such a nature. Indeed, among those five aggregates, there are some that are permanent, stable, and eternal.' Thus he spoke these testing words.

## Sūrambaṭṭha's Unwavering Faith
Then the Stream-enterer Sūrambaṭṭha thought: 'This is a very serious and weighty matter. Indeed, there is never any instance where the Buddhas speak or teach without careful reflection. It is said that Māra is an adversary of the Buddha. Surely, this person must be Māra.' Having reflected thus, he asked directly: 'Are you not Māra?' For Māra, these words spoken by a Great Noble Disciple were like being struck by an axe. Consequently, Māra could no longer maintain his disguise and spoke honestly: 'Yes, Sūrambaṭṭha, I am Māra.'
227:
227
Then the Stream-enterer Sūrambaṭṭha said: 'O Māra! Even if hundreds or thousands of Māras like you were to come, you would not be able to shake my faith. When the Great Buddha of the Gotama lineage preached to me, He taught me up to the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry that "Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā—all conditioned things are impermanent." Do not stand at my door!' Saying this, he snapped his fingers and drove him away. Upon hearing Sūrambaṭṭha's words, Māra could not utter another word and vanished on the spot. In the evening, Sūrambaṭṭha went to the Blessed One, reported everything Māra had done, and said: 'Magnificent Blessed One, in this way, Māra attempted to shake my faith.'

## (c) Receiving the Foremost Title
Taking this event as the occasion, while the Blessed One was later residing at the Jetavana monastery and appointing lay disciples to their respective foremost positions, He declared of the householder Sūrambaṭṭha:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ aveccappasannānaṃ yadidaṃ sūro ambaṭṭho—Monks, among my lay disciples who have unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda) in the Dispensation, Sūrambaṭṭha is the foremost."
228:
228
Thus, praising him, the Buddha appointed him to the foremost position (Etadagga) of those who possess 'unwavering confidence' (aveccappasāda) in the Dispensation.

This is the account of the householder Sūrambaṭṭha.
**********
## (9) The Story of Jīvaka the Physician
## (a) The Past Deeds of Jīvaka
This noble person, the future Physician Jīvaka, was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a lay disciple to the foremost position (Etadagga) of those who possess 'devotion to the person' (puggalappasāda—faith based on the person of the Buddha). Inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. The Blessed One also granted him the prophecy.

## (b) Becoming Jīvaka in his Final Birth
That noble man wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was conceived in the womb of a courtesan named Sālavatī in the city of Rājagaha, through Prince Abhaya. 

It is the custom of courtesans that when they give birth, if the child is a boy, they usually discard him in a remote place; if it is a girl, they usually nurture and raise her.
229: Therefore, the courtesan Sālavatī had a maidservant secretly discard the newborn child in a trash heap using an old winnowing basket so that no one would know. At that time, as Prince Abhaya was going to pay respects to his father, King Bimbisāra, he saw the child from afar and sent his attendants, saying, "Friends, what is that object surrounded by crows?" Upon inspection, the attendants said, "Prince, it is a newborn child." The prince asked again, "Friends, is he still alive?" When the attendants replied, "Prince, he is still alive," the prince had the child brought to his palace and raised him comfortably. Because the attendants had reported "Jīvati = He is still alive," the child was named Jīvaka, according to the derivation 'Jīvatīti Jīvako'. To this original name Jīvaka, the epithet 'Komārabhacca' was added because he was raised by Prince Abhaya, and thus he became known as 'Jīvaka Komārabhacca', meaning 'Jīvaka, the foster son of Prince Abhaya'. When Jīvaka, the foster son of Prince Abhaya, reached the age of sixteen, he went to the city of Takkasilā and mastered the science of medicine. After receiving remuneration and honors from King Bimbisāra (and becoming the king's royal physician), he successfully treated the illness of King Caṇḍapajjota. King Caṇḍapajjota sent to the great physician Jīvaka five hundred carts of grain,
230:
230
He sent sixteen thousand pieces of currency, a thousand pieces of surrounding cloth, and a pair of cloths from the Sivi kingdom of priceless value as an offering for the physician's wisdom.

At that time, the Blessed One was residing at the Gijjhakūṭa Hill monastery in the city of Rājagaha. When the great physician Jīvaka treated the Blessed One by administering a gentle purgative for the excess of humors (dosa-mala) in His body, he thought, "May the four requisites used by the Blessed One be my own offerings alone." He then requested the Blessed One to reside in his own Mango Grove monastery (Ambavana monastery). After treating the Blessed One, he offered that pair of Siveyyaka cloths (from the Sivi kingdom) and requested, "Venerable Sir, may only the Blessed One use this pair of Siveyyaka cloths." He then donated the thousand pieces of surrounding cloth to the Saṅgha of monks.

(This is a brief account of the physician Jīvaka as written in the commentary on the Etadagga-vagga, first volume of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, in this Great Chronicle of Buddhas. For the detailed story, one should refer to the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, 8. Cīvarakkhandhaka, starting from page 381.)

## (C) Receiving the Foremost Title
Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery and appointing lay disciples to the positions of 'Foremost' (Etadagga), He addressed the physician Jīvaka—
231:
231
“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ puggalappasannānaṃ yadidaṃ jīvako komārabhacco = Monks, among my lay disciples who are devoted to individuals, Jīvaka Komārabhacca, the foster son of Prince Abhaya, is the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and appointed him to the position of 'Foremost' (Etadagga) in the category of "those devoted to individuals" (puggalappasāda).

This is the story of the physician Jīvaka.

## (10) The Story of the Householder Nakulapitā
## (A) His Past Merits
This noble person, the future householder Nakulapitā, was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a lay disciple to the position of 'Foremost' (Etadagga) in the category of "those who are intimate (vissāsaka) in speech with the Buddha." Inspired, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position. The Buddha also gave him a prophecy (byādika).

## (B) Becoming the Householder Nakulapitā in His Final Life
That noble man wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the period when this Buddha appeared, he was born into a wealthy family in the city of Susumāragira within the Bhagga country.
232: (Both the husband and wife were named after their son 'Nakula'; the father was known as 'Nakulapitā' and the mother as 'Nakulamātā'). When the Buddha was traveling on a journey surrounded by a company of monks, he arrived at the city of Susumāragira and stayed in the Bhesakaḷā Grove. (The city was named Susumāragira because a crocodile made a sound when the city was being founded. The grove was named 'Bhesakaḷā' because it was governed by an ogress of that name). At that time, when the householder Nakulapitā and his wife came to the Buddha along with the people of Susumāragira, as soon as they saw the Buddha for the first time, both husband and wife perceived the Buddha as their own son, thinking, "This is our eldest son." They prostrated at the Buddha's feet and said in unison, "Dear son, where have you been wandering and staying all this time, abandoning us, your parents?" (In the past, the householder Nakulapitā had been the Buddha's father for five hundred lives. He had been his younger uncle for five hundred lives, his elder uncle for five hundred lives, and his maternal uncle for five hundred lives. The householder's wife, Nakulamātā, had also been the Buddha's mother for five hundred lives. She had been his younger aunt for five hundred lives, his elder aunt for five hundred lives, and his paternal aunt for five hundred lives. Because the element of love and affection had been established for such a long time throughout the cycle of rebirths,
233: upon seeing and meeting the Buddha, they perceived him as their son and, unable to restrain themselves, spoke to him with such intimacy. The Buddha did not say "Move aside" until the merchant couple reached a state of satisfaction. He only waited for the time when they would be satisfied. Later, when these former parents regained their composure and reached a state of equanimity, the Buddha, knowing their underlying tendencies (āsaya), preached the Dhamma to them. At the conclusion of the discourse, both of them were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and became Sotāpanna Ariyas. At another time, when the householder Nakulapitā and his wife were advanced in age, the Buddha visited the city of Susumāragira again. Upon hearing the news that the Buddha had arrived, the couple went to pay respects to him and invited him for a meritorious deed the following day. On the next day, they served the Buddha and the Saṅgha in their home with various kinds of delicious alms-food and delicacies. After the meal, they approached the Buddha and sat in a suitable place. The householder Nakulapitā said to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, since I married the young Nakulamātā when I was young, I am not aware of ever having been unfaithful to her even in thought; how much less so in body? Venerable Sir, we wish to see each other in this present life, and we also wish to see each other in the life hereafter."
234: The householder's wife, Nakulamātā, also addressed the Buddha in the same way: "Venerable Sir, since the householder Nakulapitā married me when I was young, I am not aware of ever having been unfaithful to him even in thought; how much less so in body? Venerable Sir, we wish to see each other in this present life, and we also wish to see each other in the life hereafter." (The commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 1, mentions only this much; I shall now provide the full discourse). Then the Buddha said to the householder Nakulapitā and his wife, "Lay disciples, if a husband and wife wish to see each other in this life and also wish to see each other in the life hereafter, both should have: (1) equal faith (saddhā), (2) equal virtue (sīla), (3) equal generosity (cāga), and (4) equal wisdom (paññā). If they possess such equal faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom, then that husband and wife will see each other in this life and also in the life hereafter." After saying this, the Buddha further preached these Dhamma verses: (1) Ubho saddhā vadaññū ca, saññatā dhammajīvino. Te honti jānipatayo, aññamaññaṃ piyaṃvadā.
235: (Gahapatayo = Lay disciples). Both husband and wife are endowed with faith (saddhā). They understand the words of those in need (vadaññū). They are self-controlled in body, speech, and mind (saññatā). Those spouses speak affectionately to one another (piyaṃvadā) and live righteously (dhammajīvino). (2) Atthāsaṃ pacurā honti, phāsukaṃ upajāyati. Amittā dummanā honti, ubhinnaṃ samasīlinaṃ. For such a couple, benefits (attha) increase abundantly. They live happily and free from danger. Enemies become unhappy and envious because the couple is filled with prosperity. This happens to the couple who are equal in virtue (samasīlinaṃ). (3) Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, samasīlabbata ubho. Nandino devalokasmim, modanti kāmakāmino. Having practiced the Dhamma in this world, both being equal in virtue and vows (samasīlabbata), they rejoice in the deva world, obtaining the sensual pleasures they desire. (Samasīlabbata = Equal in...)
236:
Being of virtuous conduct, both husband and wife, having practiced the Dhamma in this very life, and being filled with joy, they rejoice in the celestial realm. (Excerpted from Anguttara Nikāya, Vol. 1, pp. 386-7; Burmese Translation pp. 372-3).

## (c) Attaining the Title of Etadagga

The discourse taught based on the request made by the wealthy householder Nakulapitā and his wife is called the Pathama-samajīvī Sutta. If one reflects deeply on the essence of this Sutta, it is evident that both the wealthy householder Nakulapitā and his wife Nakulamātā possessed a heart of extreme intimacy, trust, and affection toward the Buddha, much like that toward their own son. Because they possessed such an extremely intimate and trusting heart, they were able to open up and speak everything in their hearts without any shame or fear.

Therefore, at a later time, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery and was assigning the titles of Etadagga (the foremost positions) to the lay disciples in order, He took the occasion of the words spoken by Nakulapitā and his wife out of their intimate affection and trust as the origin of the matter, and addressed the wealthy householder Nakulapitā:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ vissāsakānaṃ yadidaṃ nakulapitā gahapati = Monks, among my lay disciples...
237:
Among my lay disciples (upāsakas) who speak with intimacy and trust (with me), the householder Nakulapitā is the most excellent, the foremost."

Thus, praising him, the Buddha placed him in the position of Etadagga—the most excellent—in the category of "Vissāsaka = those who speak with intimacy and trust with the Exalted One."

This is the account of the householder Nakulapitā.

## Here ends the section on the Conduct of Laymen (Upāsakacarita).

* Upāsakacarita = The practice and conduct of laymen.
238:
## Conduct of Laywomen (Upāsikācarita)

## (1) The Account of the Wealthy Lady Sujātā

## (a) The Past Meritorious Deeds of the Wealthy Lady

This future wealthy lady Sujātā was born into a noble family (the daughter of a merchant) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Dhamma of the Buddha, she saw the Buddha appoint a certain laywoman to the position of Etadagga—the most excellent—in the category of being the first to take refuge (saraṇagam). Inspired by this, she performed extraordinary meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made a formal aspiration for that very position. The Buddha also granted her a prophecy (byādika).

## (b) Becoming the Wealthy Lady Sujātā in Her Final Life

That noble lady wandered through the celestial and human realms for a hundred thousand aeons. Before our Buddha appeared, she was born as Sujātā, the daughter of the wealthy merchant Seniya in the village of Senānigama near the Uruvelā forest. When she reached maturity, she made a vow at a banyan tree (addressing the tree deity): "If I am married into a family of equal status and if my first pregnancy results in a son, I shall perform an annual sacrificial offering (bali) to you." This wish of the merchant's daughter Sujātā was fulfilled.

(When Sujātā reached maturity, she was married to the son of a wealthy merchant from Vārāṇasī and gave birth to a son named Yasa in her first pregnancy. From that time on, because her wish was fulfilled,
239:
she came every year to the banyan tree where she made the vow to perform the sacrificial offering to the tree deity.

While she continued these offerings, by the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā Sakkarāj), the year the Buddha was to attain Enlightenment, it should be estimated that she had performed the offering at least twenty times. Indeed, around the year 103 ME when the Buddha was to attain Buddhahood, the wealthy lady Sujātā's son, the young merchant Yasa, was already married and enjoying the five sensual pleasures in rotation within his three palaces. This specific note is made because people often mistakenly estimate Sujātā, who offered the thick milk-rice on the day of the Buddha's Enlightenment, as a very young merchant's daughter.

On the full moon day of Kason in the year 103 ME, marking the completion of the six years of the Bodhisatta's practice of austerities (dukkara-cariyā), the wealthy lady Sujātā thought, "I shall perform the sacrifice early." At the break of dawn after midnight, she rose and had her servants milk the cows. On that day, the calves did not approach the udders of their mothers (as if they knew). As soon as the milking vessel was placed near the udders, the milk began to flow out continuously on its own by its own nature, without needing to be milked. Seeing this miracle, Sujātā took the milk herself, placed it in a new pot, and began to cook the thick milk-rice (ghana-pāyāsa) by lighting the fire herself.

While the thick milk-rice was being cooked, very large bubbles appeared, circling to the right and revolving only within the pot; not a single drop spilled outside. The Great Brahmā held a white umbrella over it, and the Four Great Guardian Kings
240:
stood guard holding their swords. Sakka, the King of Devas, adjusted the firewood and blew the fire, and the deities collected the essence (ojā) from the four continents and placed it into the pot of milk-rice. In this manner, they performed the service (veyyāvacca).

Having witnessed these miracles in a single day, the wealthy lady Sujātā called her maid Puṇṇā and said, "Mother Puṇṇā, today our tree deity seems very pleased. In all this time, I have never seen such miracles before. Go quickly and clean the banyan tree, the deity's abode." The maid Puṇṇā replied, "Very well, my lady," and obeying the lady's words, she went quickly to the foot of the banyan tree.

The Bodhisatta, awaiting the time for alms, had gone early and was sitting at the foot of the banyan tree. The maid Puṇṇā, who went to clean the area, returned home and said to Sujātā in amazement, "My lady, the banyan tree deity has descended in person and is sitting at the foot of the tree."

Sujātā said, "Hey maid, if what you say is true, I shall release you from slavery." She then dressed in her full finery, placed the milk-rice into a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, covered it with another golden bowl, wrapped it in fine cloth, and hung garlands of fragrant flowers around it. Carrying it on her head, she went there. Upon seeing the Bodhisatta, she was filled with great joy and approached him, bowing her body repeatedly from the moment she saw him.

After approaching,
241:
she lowered the bowl from her head, opened it, and offered the milk-rice along with the golden bowl into the hands of the Bodhisatta. After paying homage, she spoke words of blessing: "May your heart's desire be fulfilled just as my heart's desire has been fulfilled," and then she departed.

The Bodhisatta went to the banks of the Nerañjarā River, placed the golden bowl on the bank, bathed, and returned to the shore. He then divided the milk-rice into forty-nine morsels and consumed it. After floating the golden bowl in the current of the Nerañjarā River, he proceeded to the Mahābodhi Maṇḍala (the Great Seat of Enlightenment) and attained the state of the All-Knowing Buddha, the Supreme One of the Three Worlds. After spending the seven weeks (Satta-sattāha) near the Mahābodhi Maṇḍala, He traveled to the Isipatana Migadāyavana and preached the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Seeing the past supportive conditions (upanissaya) for the attainment of the Path and Fruit of the young merchant Yasa, the son of Sujātā, the Buddha went to the foot of a certain tree and sat there.

As for the young merchant Yasa, on the following night, he saw his harem and was filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He lamented, "Upadduṭaṃ vata bho = Alas, it is distressed! This wretched body of all beings, including myself, is afflicted and oppressed by various defilements. Upassaṭṭhaṃ vata bho = Alas, it is oppressed! This wretched body of all beings, including myself, is tormented and oppressed by various defilements." Thus lamenting, he left his home and went to the Buddha outside the city. Upon hearing the Dhamma, he realized and attained the Path and Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga-phala). (According to the Anguttara Commentary, Vol. 1,
242:
page 310, he realized and attained the three lower Paths and Fruits).

Thereafter, Yasa's father, the wealthy merchant, followed his son's footsteps and arrived at the Buddha's presence, where he inquired about Yasa. The Buddha used His psychic power to hide Yasa and preached the Dhamma to the father. At the conclusion of the discourse, the father was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), while the young merchant Yasa attained the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala). Then, the Buddha called Yasa with the "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, Monk) ordination. At that moment, Yasa's lay appearance vanished, and he became an Ehi Bhikkhu monk, adorned with psychic-made robes and bowl. The wealthy merchant invited the Buddha for a meal. The Buddha, with Venerable Yasa as His attendant monk, went to the merchant's house. After the meal, He preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, Venerable Yasa's mother, the wealthy lady Sujātā, and his former wife from his lay life were both established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. On that very day, the lady Sujātā, together with her daughter-in-law, was established in the Threefold Refuge (Te-vācika-saraṇagam). (This is a brief summary. For a detailed account, one should refer to the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 2, pages 271 to 277, and pages 500 to 527).
243:
## (c) Attaining the Title of Etadagga

Later, when the Blessed One was assigning the female lay disciples to their respective foremost positions (etadagga), he praised the great lay disciple Sujātā, the merchant's wife, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ paṭhamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchantīnaṃ yadidaṃ sujātā seniyadhīta = Monks, among my female lay disciples who first went for refuge to the Triple Gem, the most prominent is Sujātā, the daughter of the merchant Seniya.”

Thus, he appointed her to the foremost position (etadagga) in the category of “those who first took refuge” (paṭhamaṃ saraṇagamana).

This is the account of Sujātā, the merchant's wife.

**********

## (2) The Story of the Great Lay-Supporter Visākhā

## (a) Visākhā’s Past Meritorious Deeds

In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, this noble lady-to-be was born as the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī. Later, while listening to the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, she saw the Blessed One appoint a certain laywoman to the foremost position (etadagga) in the category of “those who delight in giving” (dāyikā). Inspired by this, she performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made a solemn wish for that very position. The Blessed One also gave her the prophecy (byādita).
244:
## Life as the Youngest Daughter of King Kikī

This noble lady wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), in the time of Kassapa Buddha, she became the youngest of the seven sisters, the daughters of King Kikī, the ruler of the Kāsi kingdom. At that time—

Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā ca, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhadāyikā.
Dhammā ceva, Sudhammā ca, Saṅghadāsī ca sattamā—

According to this summary verse (saṅgaha-gāthā), King Kikī had seven daughters: (1) Princess Samaṇī, (2) Princess Samaṇaguttā, (3) Princess Bhikkhunī, (4) Princess Bhikkhadāyikā, (5) Princess Dhammā, (6) Princess Sudhammā, and (7) Princess Saṅghadāsī. These seven sisters, in the time of our current Buddha—

Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā ca, Paṭācārā ca, Gotamī.
Dhammadinnā, Mahāmāyā, Visākhā ceva sattamī—

According to this summary verse, they respectively became: (1) Khemā Therī, (2) Uppalavaṇṇā Therī, (3) Paṭācārā Therī, (4) the foster mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Therī, (5) Dhammadinnā Therī, (6) the mother Queen Mahāmāyā, and (7) the great lay-supporter Visākhā.

## (b) Becoming Visākhā in Her Final Life

Princess Saṅghadāsī, the youngest of King Kikī’s seven daughters, wandered through the realms of devas and humans for an entire incalculable interval between Buddhas (buddhantara). During the period when our Blessed One appeared in the world,
245:
she was conceived in the womb of Sumanādevī, the chief consort of the merchant Dhanañjaya, who was the son of the great merchant Meṇḍaka in the city of Bhaddiya, Aṅga kingdom. Her parents and relatives named the merchant's daughter Visākhā. When Visākhā was seven years old, the Blessed One, seeing that the Brahmin Sela and other beings worthy of being tamed possessed the past merit to attain the Paths and Fruits, traveled on a journey accompanied by a large assembly of monks and arrived at the city of Bhaddiya in the Aṅga kingdom.

## The Five People of Great Merit

At that time, the merchant Meṇḍaka was living as the leader of the “Five People of Great Merit” in the city of Bhaddiya. These five people were: (1) the great merchant Meṇḍaka, (2) his chief wife named Candapadumā, (3) his son, the merchant Dhanañjaya, (4) Dhanañjaya’s wife named Sumanādevī, and (5) Meṇḍaka’s slave named Puṇṇa. (I shall briefly present the greatness of their merit as described in the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume 2, Chapter 18, Malavagga, Story 10: The Story of Meṇḍaka, pages 237–238)—

1. The Power of the Great Merchant Meṇḍaka: One day, wishing to test his merit, the great merchant Meṇḍaka had 1,250 granaries cleaned. After washing his head, he sat at the doorway and looked up at the sky. At that moment, a heavy rain of red sali rice poured down, and all 1,250 granaries were filled with red sali rice.
246:
The great merchant also wished to test the merit of the other members of his household. He encouraged his wife, son, daughter-in-law, and slave, saying, “You too should test your merit.”

2. The Power of the Great Merchant’s Wife, Candapadumā: Then, Candapadumā, dressed in all her finery, had a measure (about one pyi) of rice measured out while a crowd of people watched. She had that rice cooked and sat at a seat prepared at the gateway. Holding a golden ladle, she announced, “Let those who desire rice come!” To everyone who came, she gave a full bowl of rice. Although she gave all day long, only the place where the ladle dipped into the rice was visible, and the rest of the rice pot remained undiminished.

The Reason for the Name Candapadumā: In the times of previous Buddhas, she had offered alms to the Saṅgha by lifting the rice pot with her left hand and holding a ladle or spoon with her right hand, filling the bowls in this manner. Because of this, a clear mark of a Paduma lotus appeared on her left palm, and a clear mark of the moon (Canda) appeared on her right palm. Furthermore, in the times of previous Buddhas, she had taken a water filter (dhamakaroṇa) with her left hand, filtered drinking water, and offered it, moving tirelessly here and there to where the Saṅgha was. Therefore, on this great merchant's wife,
247:
a clear mark of the moon appeared on her right sole, and a clear mark of a Paduma lotus appeared on her left sole. Because of these reasons, her parents and relatives named her “Candapadumā.”

3. The Power of the Son, the Merchant Dhanañjaya: The merchant Dhanañjaya, Meṇḍaka’s son, after washing his head, took a bag containing a thousand coins and said, “Let those who desire coins come!” To everyone who came, he gave a full bowl of coins. Even though he gave in this way, there remained exactly one thousand coins in the bag.

4. The Power of the Daughter-in-law, the Merchant’s Wife Sumanādevī: Sumanādevī, the daughter-in-law of the great merchant Meṇḍaka, also dressed in all her finery, took a basket of grain and sat in an open space, saying, “Let those who desire provisions and rice come!” To everyone who came, she gave a full bowl. Even though she gave in this way, the basket containing the grain remained as full as before.

5. The Power of the Trusted Slave, Maung Puṇṇa: Maung Puṇṇa, the trusted slave of the great merchant Meṇḍaka, dressed in finery suitable for a servant, yoked oxen with golden ropes to golden yokes. Holding a golden goad, he marked the oxen with five-finger marks of perfume, placed golden caps on their horns, went to the field, and demonstrated plowing. At that time, miraculously,
248:
seven furrows branched out: three on the left, three on the right, and one in the center.

People living throughout Jambudīpa took whatever they desired—whether rice, provisions, silver, or gold—only from the house of the great merchant Meṇḍaka. This is the account of the Five People of Great Merit.

Within the domain of King Bimbisāra in Rājagaha, besides the great merchant Meṇḍaka, there were four other great merchants: Jotika, Jaṭila, Puṇṇa, and Kākavaliya. Including Meṇḍaka, there were five great merchants of “Inexhaustible Wealth” (amitabhoga) within King Bimbisāra’s domain. (Among these five, the story of the merchant Puṇṇa will be explained in the story of Uttarā; the brief accounts of the remaining four merchants will be presented near the conclusion of this sixth volume).

When the great merchant Meṇḍaka, one of the five merchants of inexhaustible wealth, heard the news that the Blessed One had arrived in their city of Bhaddiya, he called his granddaughter Visākhā (the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya) and encouraged her, saying: “Dear granddaughter, the matter I am about to tell you is a blessing and a meritorious deed for you, and it is also a blessing and a meritorious deed for us. Along with your five hundred young companions, each of you ride in one of five hundred carriages, accompanied by five hundred slave-girls, and go to welcome the Blessed One.”
249:
## Visākhā Becoming a Sotāpanna at Age Seven

Upon hearing her grandfather’s encouragement, the young Visākhā joyfully did as he said and went to welcome the Blessed One. Notably, although her grandfather Meṇḍaka, out of his pride as a merchant, had told her to ride the carriage right up to the presence of the Buddha, Visākhā was wise and well-mannered in knowing what was appropriate. She rode the carriage only as far as the ground was suitable for a carriage, and then (reaching a point where continuing by carriage would be disrespectful), she alighted and approached the Blessed One on foot. She paid homage and stood at a respectful distance.

Then, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the young Visākhā in a way that was suitable to her temperament. At the conclusion of the teaching, Visākhā, along with her five hundred companions, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala); she became a Sotāpanna Noble One.

The great merchant Meṇḍaka also went to visit the Blessed One, paid homage with great respect and devotion, and stood at a respectful distance. Then, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the great merchant Meṇḍaka in a way that was suitable to his temperament. At the conclusion of the teaching, the great merchant Meṇḍaka was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and became a Sotāpanna Noble One. He then invited the Blessed One for a meritorious meal the following day, and on the next day, at his home,
250:
He served the Saṅgha led by the Buddha with excellent food and delicacies. In this manner, the great merchant Meṇḍaka performed a great act of almsgiving for a full fortnight (fifteen days). The Blessed One stayed in the city of Bhaddiya as long as there were beings to be guided, and when there were no more to be guided at that time, he departed from Bhaddiya.

## Visākhā’s Family
## Moving to the City of Sāketa

In the city of Sāvatthī, King Pasenadi of Kosala (since there was not a single merchant of limitless wealth in his kingdom) sent a message to King Bimbisāra, requesting: “In the territory of the Kosala kingdom where my authority extends, there is not a single household of a merchant of limitless wealth. Therefore, I wish for one such household to be sent to our country.”

King Bimbisāra discussed this matter with his ministers. The ministers deliberated, saying, “We cannot possibly send a household of a great merchant of limitless wealth. However, let us send a merchant’s son (to satisfy King Pasenadi).” They agreed and requested Dhanañjaya, the son of the great merchant Meṇḍaka, to go and reside in the Kosala kingdom. Upon hearing the ministers' words, King Bimbisāra requested Dhanañjaya, the son of Meṇḍaka, to go and live in Kosala and sent him there.

(Note: According to the Dhammapada Commentary, King Kosala and King Bimbisāra were brothers-in-law, related as husbands of each other's sisters.
251:
When King Kosala went to King Bimbisāra and requested a great merchant to be sent to his Kosala kingdom, King Bimbisāra, unable to unsettle or disturb the great merchants, urged Dhanañjaya, the son of Meṇḍaka, to go and live in Kosala. Dhanañjaya agreed, and thus his household accompanied King Kosala.)

Dhanañjaya moved from the city of Bhaddiya. When he reached a place seven leagues away from Sāvatthī that seemed pleasant to live in, he asked King Kosala, “Whose kingdom is this?” King Kosala replied, “Merchant, it is my kingdom.” Dhanañjaya then asked, “How far is Sāvatthī from here?” King Kosala said, “Sāvatthī is more than seven leagues away.” Dhanañjaya then requested, “The interior of Sāvatthī is too narrow for us to live in. Our retinue is very large. If it pleases Your Majesty, let us establish a city and live right here.” King Kosala agreed, saying, “Very well.” He created a new city at that spot, handed it over to Dhanañjaya, and departed. Because he himself took up residence in that place, the city was named “Sāketa.”

In the city of Sāvatthī, the young Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, son of the great merchant Migāra, had reached maturity. At that time, his father, the great merchant Migāra, considered, “My son has come of age. Now is the time to bind him with a household.” He gave instructions, saying, “Search for a maiden from a family of the same caste as ours,” and sent out
252:
men who were skilled and wise in discerning the truth of matters. Those searching for a maiden did not find any maiden they liked in Sāvatthī, so they went to the city of Sāketa to search.

On that day, Visākhā, the merchant’s daughter, went to a large pond outside the city for a water festival, accompanied by five hundred maiden friends of the same age. The men from Sāvatthī searching for a maiden also wandered through Sāketa, but not finding any maiden to their satisfaction, they stood at the city gate. At that time, a heavy rain began to fall. Then, the five hundred maidens who had come out of the city with Visākhā, fearing they would get wet, ran quickly and entered a rest house for shelter. The searchers did not find any maiden among those five hundred who satisfied them.

Notably, behind those five hundred maidens, Visākhā, the merchant’s daughter, disregarding the rain, walked without haste (with great composure) and entered the rest house last, allowing herself to get wet. When the elders from Sāvatthī searching for a maiden saw Visākhā, they thought, “In this world, a maiden with such beautiful appearance must be of the highest degree (there can be no maiden more beautiful than this one). This beauty might be as delicate as a ripe pomegranate for some maidens. Only by initiating a conversation
253:
can we know whether this maiden has a sweet voice or not.” After considering this, the elders and Visākhā exchanged words as follows:

(The Elders)
“Daughter, you walk like a very old woman.”

(Visākhā)
“Fathers, what did you see that makes you say this?”

(The Elders)
“The other maidens who are your playmates, fearing the rain, ran swiftly and took shelter in this rest house. But you, dear daughter, did not walk faster than an old woman. You did not even care that your sarong would get wet. If a lion or a horse were chasing you, dear daughter, would you still act so slowly?”

(Visākhā)
“Fathers, sarongs are not rare things in this world. In my house, sarongs are easily obtained. Women of noble families who have reached maturity are like merchandise; if by chance they run and break a hand or a foot, men will look upon a physically impaired woman with disgust and merely spit and walk away. Therefore, I came slowly.”
254:
Then the elders thought, “In the whole of Jambudīpa, there is no woman equal to this maiden. Just as she is endowed with beauty, her voice is also very pleasant and sweet. She speaks knowing the truth of the matter. She is sufficient in both quality, appearance, and voice.” Having considered this, they threw a flower garland over Visākhā. Then Visākhā thought, “Previously, I was one who had not been claimed. Now, I have been claimed.” With a refined manner, she sat down on the ground right there. Then the elders surrounded Visākhā with a curtain. After the curtain was placed and she knew she was properly covered, Visākhā went to her home accompanied by her group of maidservants. The elders of the merchant Migāra also followed along with Visākhā to the presence of the great merchant Dhanañjaya.

Then, the great merchant Dhanañjaya and the elders spoke to each other regarding the proposal:

(Great Merchant Dhanañjaya)
“Friends, in which village do you live?”

(The Elders)
“Lord Merchant, we are the elders of the merchant Migāra who lives in Sāvatthī. Our merchant heard that there is a maiden of age in your house and sent us to speak about a proposal.”
255:
(Great Merchant Dhanañjaya)
“Very well, friends. Although your merchant is not equal to us in terms of wealth, he is equal in terms of caste (being of the merchant class). It is very rare in the world to find someone endowed with the quality of being equal in all aspects, both wealth and caste. Friends, you may return. Just tell your merchant that we have accepted.”

After hearing the words of the great merchant Dhanañjaya, the elders of the merchant Migāra returned to Sāvatthī. They spoke words of joy and prosperity to the merchant Migāra, saying, “Lord Merchant, we have obtained the maiden Visākhā in the house of the great merchant Dhanañjaya in the city of Sāketa.” Hearing this, the merchant Migāra, with a heart full of joy and satisfaction, thinking, “We have obtained a maiden from a great and noble family,” immediately sent a message to the great merchant Dhanañjaya: “We will come to fetch the maiden very soon. We wish for the necessary preparations to be made.” The great merchant Dhanañjaya sent back a message to Migāra: “Making these necessary preparations is no burden for us; it is not a problem. Indeed, we only wish for the merchant himself to perform the duties he must perform.”

## Accompanying King Kosala to the Wedding Ceremony

The merchant Migāra went to King Pasenadi and said, “Your Majesty, an auspicious occasion has arisen for me. For the sake of your servant, the young Puṇṇavaḍḍhana
256:
256
"I must go and fetch the maiden named Visākhā, the daughter of the wealthy merchant Dhanañjaya. Please grant me permission to go to the city of Sāketa." King Kosala asked, "Very well, Great Merchant. Is it necessary for us to accompany you?" Migāra the merchant replied, "Great King, how could people like us ever hope for the company of such as Your Majesty?" (meaning it is not easy to obtain). Then, King Kosala, wishing to honor both noble families, promised, "Let it be so, Great Merchant. I too shall accompany you," and he went to Sāketa together with the merchant Migāra.

When the wealthy merchant Dhanañjaya heard the news, "Now the merchant Migāra is coming to our city of Sāketa, bringing King Kosala with him," he went out personally to welcome them, received the King with great respect, and went to his home. Upon reaching the house, he immediately arranged everything—lodging, flowers, perfumes, rice, and so forth—for the King, for the King's army, and for the merchant Migāra and his people. Dhanañjaya himself considered and fulfilled all the needs for everyone, thinking, "This person should receive this object; that person should receive that object." All those people thought and noted, "The merchant Dhanañjaya is attending to and honoring only us."

One day, King Pasenadi Kosala sent a message to the merchant Dhanañjaya, saying, "Because our people are so numerous, the merchant
257:
257
will not be able to provide care and food for us for a long time. Therefore, I want you to consider the time for the maiden to depart for Sāvatthī." Dhanañjaya also sent a message back to the King, saying, "Now the rainy season has arrived; the army will not be able to travel for four months. Let all the requirements for Your Majesty's army be my responsibility. Indeed, I wish for Your Majesty to return to the city of Sāvatthī only when I send you."

From that time on, the entire city of Sāketa became like a large village constantly holding a festival. In this way, the three months of the rainy season passed and the full moon of Thadingyut (Assayuja) was reached. In particular, the Great Creeper Ornament (Mahālatā-pasādhana) that the merchant Dhanañjaya was preparing for his daughter Visākhā to wear was not yet finished. Then, the supervisors of the merchant Dhanañjaya came to him and said, "Lord Merchant, there is no lack of other remaining materials; however, the firewood for cooking rice for the army and the retinue is insufficient." Then the merchant ordered, "Friends, go and dismantle the elephant and horse stables and use them as firewood to cook the rice." Following the merchant's orders, the supervisors dismantled the stables and used them as firewood to cook rice, and half a month (15 days) passed again.
258:
258
After half a month (15 days) had passed, the supervisors again told the merchant, "Lord Merchant, the firewood is insufficient." Then Dhanañjaya said, "Friends, at this time during the rainy season, firewood will not be obtainable. What I want you to do is to open our cloth warehouses, take the coarse cloths and fabrics, make them into wicks, soak them in large jars of oil, and cook the rice." In this manner, they continued to cook rice until four full months had passed and the full moon day of Tazaungmon (Kattika) arrived. At that time, the Great Creeper Ornament was also completed.

Then, the merchant Dhanañjaya, hearing that the Great Creeper Ornament for his daughter Visākhā was finished, on the day he said, "Tomorrow the maiden must be sent to the bridegroom's house," had his daughter Visākhā sit near him and gave her advice (ovāda), saying, "Dear daughter, a housewife living in the home of her husband and masters should learn and master such and such practices." At that time, the merchant Migāra was sitting in an adjacent room and was listening intently to the advice given by Dhanañjaya to his daughter Visākhā. Dhanañjaya instructed his daughter Visākhā as follows:

"Dear daughter, a daughter-in-law living in the father-in-law's house—
(1) Must not take the indoor fire outside.
(2) Must not bring the outdoor fire inside.
259:
259
(3) Must give only to those who return.
(4) Must not give to those who do not return.
(5) Must give to both those who return and those who do not.
(6) Must sit happily.
(7) Must eat happily.
(8) Must sleep happily.
(9) Must tend the fire respectfully.
(10) Must revere the household deities."
Thus he taught and advised these ten admonitions. (The meaning and intent of these ten admonitions should be looked up in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 4, pages 479-480).

After giving these ten admonitions to his daughter Visākhā, the merchant Dhanañjaya gathered all his associates the next day and, in the midst of the King's army, had eight wise householders act as guarantors, saying, "If any fault should arise concerning my daughter in the place where she goes, may you eight wise householders clear and resolve it." After giving these instructions, he had his daughter Visākhā adorned with the Great Creeper Ornament worth ninety million. He gave his daughter wealth amounting to one hundred and fifty-four (154) carts for the cost of perfumes. He also gave five hundred maids who would always accompany her, five hundred chariots yoked with noble horses, and various utensils, one hundred of each kind. After giving these, he sent King Kosala and the merchant Migāra to go ahead first.
260:
260
After that, when it was time for his daughter Visākhā to depart, the merchant Dhanañjaya called the head cowherds and ordered, "Friends, my daughter will need milch cows to drink milk and bulls to yoke to vehicles in the place where she goes. Therefore, open the cattle pens on the path my daughter will travel, and let the space be filled with cattle to the extent of eight usabhas (one usabha is 20 ta) in width. At a distance of three gāvutas, there is a large ravine eroded by water of such a name; when the front of the cattle herd reaches that place, give a signal by the sound of drums and close the cattle pens." The head cowherds agreed and carried out the merchant's orders. When the gates of the cattle pens were opened, only the milch cows with large and healthy bodies went out. When the gates were closed, due to the power of Visākhā's past merit (the merit of offering more than requested to the Saṅgha during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, saying, "Venerable sirs, this food and delicacies are especially good for phlegm, bile, and wind disorders," making them want to eat), the strong bulls and oxen also jumped over the fences, went outside, and followed along the journey.

## Visākhā's Entry into the City of Sāvatthī
Then, when the lady Visākhā reached the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, she considered, "Should I enter the city sitting in a covered vehicle, or should I enter standing in a chariot, showing myself clearly?" Then, in the mind of the lady Visākhā, the thought arose:
261:
261
"If I enter the city in a covered vehicle, the extraordinary excellence of my Great Creeper Ornament will not be apparent." The lady Visākhā entered the city standing in a chariot, showing herself clearly to the whole of Sāvatthī. The citizens of Sāvatthī, seeing Visākhā's glory, praised her, saying, "This is the lady Visākhā; she is indeed endowed with such beauty and glory. This wealth and glory are truly suitable and fitting for this lady alone." In this way, the lady Visākhā entered the house of the merchant Migāra with great wealth and glory.

On the very day the lady Visākhā arrived, all the citizens thought, "The merchant Dhanañjaya treated us with great honor and care when we were in his city (Sāketa)," and they sent gifts to the lady Visākhā according to their means. The lady Visākhā had all those gifts redistributed to other houses throughout the city until they reached everyone. (In this way, on the day of her arrival, Visākhā won the hearts of the citizens of Sāvatthī through the practice of generosity and hospitality.)

Then, for Visākhā, in the period immediately following the first watch of the night, an event occurred in the house of the merchant Migāra where a noble mare gave birth to a foal. The lady Visākhā had her maids hold torches and went to the place where the mare was giving birth, had the mare bathed with warm water,
262:
262
had her anointed with oil, and only then returned to her own quarters.

## The Reception of the Merchant Migāra
The merchant Migāra held a wedding reception for his son for seven days. While doing so, although the Blessed One was residing in the Jetavana monastery at the head of their own city, he did not pay any attention (being of wrong view). On the seventh day, he invited the naked ascetics (Acelakas), who were unclothed and bare, to fill his entire house, gave them seats, and sent a message to Visākhā, saying, "Let my daughter come and pay respects to the Arahants." When the lady Visākhā heard the word "Arahants," being a Sotāpanna noble disciple, she was filled with joy and went to the place where the naked ascetics were sitting. Upon seeing those naked ascetics, she was greatly disappointed, thinking, "How can such persons be Arahants? Why did my father-in-law call me to these naked ascetics who are completely devoid of shame and fear (hiri-ottappa)?" Saying "Dhi, dhi!" (an expression of disgust), she returned to her own room.

The unclothed naked ascetics, seeing that behavior, all spoke in unison to the merchant Migāra, "Merchant, can you not find another daughter-in-law? Why did you bring this great wretched female disciple of the ascetic Gotama into your house? Quickly expel this 'Kāḷakaṇṇī' (bringer of ill-luck), this wretched woman, from this house." Then the merchant Migāra thought—
263:
Thinking, "I cannot expel this daughter-in-law Visākhā just because of the words of these naked ascetics; she is the daughter of a great family," he considered the matter and spoke words of appeasement to the naked ascetics, saying, "Teachers, young people, whether knowingly or unknowingly, are prone to act and speak impulsively. Please remain silent," and then dismissed them.

## Migāra the Financier Becoming Unable to Endure

Thereafter, Visākhā (as a wise daughter-in-law) had her father-in-law, Migāra the financier, sit on a noble seat. Holding a golden ladle herself, she respectfully served him by filling a golden bowl with sweet, undiluted milk-rice. Migāra the financier, receiving the care and attention of his wise daughter-in-law Visākhā, sat enjoying the sweet, undiluted milk-rice served in the golden bowl. At that time, an elder monk on his alms round arrived at the door of Migāra the financier's house. Visākhā saw the monk and thought, "It is not appropriate for me to speak directly to my father-in-law (who is a great wrong-believer)." Thus, she stood aside so that the financier could see the elder monk. However, Migāra the financier, being a foolish person, even though he saw the elder, pretended not to see him and continued eating the milk-rice with his head bowed.

Visākhā the financier’s daughter, realizing, "Even though he sees the elder, my father-in-law, that great fool of a man, does not make even a sign of recognition," went to the elder and, paying homage, said, "Please proceed, Bhante. My father-in-law is only eating stale food."
264:
Migāra the financier could still tolerate what the naked ascetics had said. However, when it was said that he was "only eating stale food," at that moment he could no longer bear it. Removing his hand from the golden bowl, he gave the order, saying, "Take this milk-rice away from here! And expel this Visākhā from this house! Drag her out! Indeed, while I am eating auspicious milk-rice in such an auspicious house, this Visākhā speaks and acts as if I were an eater of filth!"

Even though Migāra the financier spoke thus, all the servants and workers in that house were Visākhā’s own people. Therefore, who would dare to seize Visākhā by the hands or feet? No one dared to touch her. Far from seizing her, there was not a single person who could even speak against her.

## Visākhā Demands Justice

Then, Visākhā the financier’s daughter, having heard her father-in-law's words, said, "O Father, I cannot leave this house based on such an unlawful sequence of words. I was not brought here by you, Father Financier, like a slave girl carrying a water pot from the landing place. Daughters of noble families with living parents do not leave a house for such reasons. For this very reason, on the day my father was coming to Sāvatthī, he summoned eight wise elders and householders and entrusted me to them, saying, 'If any fault arises concerning my daughter, you must investigate and clear it.' Please summon those eight wise householders and let them investigate whether I am at fault or not."

Thus she spoke words that were full of reason and polite.
265:
265
I wish for you to clarify whether this is true or not," he said in a polite and reasonable manner.

## Holding the Inquiry
At that time, the treasurer Migāra thought, "This Visākhā speaks only what is good." He then summoned eight wise householders and opened the case, saying, "Gentlemen, before this young lady Visākhā has even been in this house for seven days, she said to me, who lives in this auspicious house, 'You are eating filth'."

Then, the manner in which the elders, the lady Visākhā, and the treasurer Migāra questioned, clarified, and reported was as follows:

(The Elders)
"Daughter, did you say what this great treasurer has just reported?"

(Visākhā)
"Fathers, it may be that my father-in-law wishes to eat filth. I did not say that my father-in-law eats filth in that way. In truth, when a Thera who observes the dhutaṅga of alms-round arrived and stood at the door of this house, this great treasurer Migāra (my father-in-law) did not pay attention to that venerable one while he was eating undiluted milk-rice. For this reason, I went to the Thera and said, 'Please move on, Venerable Sir; my father-in-law is not performing new meritorious deeds in this present life; he is only consuming the fruits of his old, past merits.' I only said this much."
266:
(The Elders)
"Lord Financier, in this matter, our daughter is not at fault. Our daughter spoke the truth. Why are you angry, Lord Financier?"

(Migāra)
"Sponsors, let this matter be if it is not a fault. However, this young woman Visākhā, on the very day she arrived at this house, went wherever she pleased without regarding my son."

(The Elders)
"Daughter, did you go as the financier has now charged?"

(Visākhā)
"Fathers, I did not go wherever I pleased as this financier charges. The truth is, on that day, a thoroughbred mare in this house was in labor. I thought to myself, 'It is not proper for me to remain indifferent while this thoroughbred mare is giving birth.' Thus, I had torches carried and, surrounded by my maidservants, I went to the place of birth and ensured that the mare was cared for during labor."

(The Elders)
"Lord Financier, our daughter has performed a task in your house that even the maidservants could not do. Why do you see this as a fault? Is such an action not a great service?"
267:
(Migāra)
"Sponsors, let such actions be considered a virtue. But I wish to present specifically: when this young woman Visākhā’s father gave her admonitions on the day she was to come to this house, he said, '(1) The indoor fire must not be taken outside.' How can we manage without giving fire to our neighbors on both sides?"

(The Elders)
"Daughter, is it true that your father, the great financier Dhanañjaya, gave such an admonition as the financier has now presented?"

(Visākhā)
"Fathers, my father, the great financier Dhanañjaya, did not speak regarding ordinary fire as my father-in-law now presents.
