In truth, secret matters or conversations concerning the father-in-law and others within the house should not be told to maidservants, manservants, and so on. Indeed, if such talk spreads, it can lead to quarrels and disputes. My father gave this admonition referring to this 'indoor fire'."

(Migāra)
"Sponsors, let this matter be if it is not a fault. This young woman Visākhā’s father also admonished, '(2) The outdoor fire must not be brought into the house.' If our indoor fire is extinguished, how can we manage without bringing in fire from outside? We must surely bring it in."
268:
(The Elders)
"Daughter, is this true as the financier has presented?"

(Visākhā)
"Fathers, my father, the great financier Dhanañjaya, did not mean the ordinary fire as my father-in-law presents. In truth, faults spoken by servants and workers should not be told to the people inside the house. If such talk spreads, it can cause quarrels. My father gave this admonition referring to this 'outdoor fire'.

Furthermore, my father the financier gave the admonition, '(3) Give only to those who return.' This was meant in the sense that one should lend household items only to those who return them. 

Regarding the admonition, '(4) Do not give to those who do not return,' it was meant in the sense that one should not again lend or give household items to those who do not return what was borrowed. 

Regarding the admonition, '(5) Give whether they return or not,' it was meant in the sense that when poor relatives and friends come to one, it is proper to give to them whether they are able to return it or not. 

Regarding the admonition, '(6) One should sit happily,' it was meant in the sense that when one sees one's father-in-law or mother-in-law,
269:
it is not proper to remain sitting where one should stand up; one must rise first and show respect. 

Regarding the admonition, '(7) One should eat happily,' it was meant in the sense that one should not eat before serving the father-in-law, mother-in-law, and husband. It is only proper to eat after serving them and seeing for oneself whether all the food and delicacies are available. 

Regarding the admonition, '(8) One should sleep happily,' it was meant in the sense that one should not go to bed and sleep before the father-in-law, mother-in-law, and husband. It is only proper to sleep after performing the major and minor duties that should be done for them. 

Regarding the admonition, '(9) One should respectfully tend the fire,' it was meant in the sense that one should look upon and treat one's father-in-law, mother-in-law, and husband with great respect, as if they were a great mass of fire or a king of nagas."

(Migāra)
"Sponsors, let these nine points that have been spoken be considered virtues rather than faults. However, this young woman Visākhā—"
270:
270

"My father commanded me to worship the household deities. What is the meaning of this?"

(The Elders)
"Daughter, is it true as the wealthy merchant has stated?"

(Visākhā)
"Fathers, it is true that my father, the merchant, commanded me to worship the household deities. Indeed, regarding this instruction, '(10) The household deities must be worshipped,' my father gave this command with the meaning: 'From the time you begin to manage your own household, if you see a monk arriving at your door, you should eat only after you have offered as much as you can from the food and delicacies available in your home to those monks.'"

Thereupon, the elder guarantors remarked in a tone of condemnation, "Merchant, it seems that for your part, you only take pleasure in not giving or offering anything when you see the monks." Finding no other words to offer in rebuttal, the merchant Migāra sat with his head bowed.

## Visākhā’s Success in the Subsequent Dispute

Then, the eight elder guarantors, the merchant Migāra, and his daughter-in-law Visākhā continued their dispute as follows:

(The Elders)
"How is it, Merchant? Are there any other faults regarding our daughter?"

(Migāra)
"There are no more, sirs."
271:
271

(The Elders)
"Merchant, if that is the case, why did you attempt to expel our faultless daughter from your home without cause?"

(At that moment, Visākhā stood up and said:)
"Fathers, it is not appropriate for me to leave this house immediately just because of the (inconsiderate) words spoken by my father-in-law. In truth, on the day I came to this house, my father, the merchant, entrusted me to you so that you might investigate and clear my name should any question of my fault arise. (Now, the investigation into my faultlessness is complete.) At this time, it is a pleasure for me to go."

Having said this, Visākhā (went to her private quarters) and commanded her male and female servants, "Prepare the carriages and other necessaries." Then, the merchant Migāra called the eight elder guarantors and apologized to his daughter-in-law Visākhā, saying, "Daughter, I have spoken wrongly out of ignorance and lack of consideration. Please forgive me."

Visākhā, seeing that the right opportunity had arrived, said, "O fathers, I have long since forgiven what should be forgiven of you. However, I wish to state specifically: I am a daughter of a family with unwavering faith and devotion in the Sāsana of the Exalted Buddha. It is impossible for us to live apart from the Sangha of monks. If I am allowed to attend to and serve the Sangha of monks according to my wish, I shall continue to stay in this house. If not, I cannot stay."

The merchant Migāra then gave his consent graciously, saying, "Dear daughter, you may...
272:
272

...attend to and serve your monks as you desire."

## The Merchant Migāra Becomes a Sotāpanna

Thereafter, the lady Visākhā invited the Exalted Buddha (to accept a meal offering the next day). On the following day, the Sangha led by the Buddha sat filling the great merchant's house. The naked ascetics (Acelakas), having heard the news that the Exalted Buddha had arrived at the merchant Migāra's house, went there and sat surrounding the house.

After pouring the water of libation for the offering, the lady Visākhā sent word to her father-in-law, the merchant, saying, "All the preparations for the offerings are complete. I wish for my father-in-law to come and personally attend to and serve the Exalted Buddha." Following the advice of the naked ascetics, the merchant Migāra sent back an evasive reply, saying, "Let my daughter herself serve the Exalted Buddha."

After the lady Visākhā had served the Exalted Buddha with a great variety of delicious foods and the meal was finished, she again sent word to her father-in-law, saying, "The offering of the meal is complete. I wish for my father-in-law to come and listen to the Dhamma discourse."

At that time, prompted by his past wholesome kamma, the merchant Migāra reflected, "It would indeed be most unreasonable for me not to go now." With a strong desire to hear the Dhamma, he went to the place where the Exalted Buddha was to preach.
273:
273

As the merchant Migāra was going, the naked ascetics advised him, "If you listen to the Dhamma of the Monk Gotama, sit and listen from outside the curtain." According to their words, the merchant's men went ahead and surrounded the area with a curtain.

The Exalted Buddha, as if saying, "Merchant Migāra, whether you wish to stay outside the curtain, or on the other side of a wall, or on the other side of a mountain, or even on the other side of the universe, I am truly the Buddha; I am able to make you hear my voice no matter how great the distance," preached the Dhamma discourse that leads to the attainment of the Path and Fruit—such as the discourse on giving (dānakathā), virtue (sīlakathā), and heaven (saggakathā)—to the merchant Migāra, just like shaking a great mango tree laden with ripe golden fruit by its trunk.

(It is specifically to be noted: When the Exalted Buddha preaches the Dhamma, those standing in front of Him, those standing behind Him, those standing beyond a thousand universes, and those in the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm all say, "The Exalted Buddha is looking only at me; He is preaching the Dhamma only to me." Indeed, when the Exalted Buddha is preaching, it is as if He is looking at each member of the audience and as if He is conversing with each one of them.

To elaborate slightly: The Buddhas are like the moon. Just as the moon, while staying in its path in the middle of the sky, appears to every person as if "the moon is directly above me, the moon is directly above me," so too when the Buddhas preach the Dhamma,
274:
274

...it appears to all the audience in the left, right, front, back, and above as if He is facing them directly.

This occurrence is the result of the meritorious deed of giving (dāna) performed by the Buddhas during their fulfillment of the Perfections (pāramīs), when they generously sacrificed their heads, their eyes, their hearts, and even their children like Prince Jālī and Princess Kaṇhājinā, and wives like Maddī Devī, to be servants of others, giving them to those who asked. (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1, page 256).

At the conclusion of the discourse, the merchant Migāra was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and became a Sotāpanna Ariya. He lifted the curtain, paid homage to the feet of the Exalted Buddha with the fivefold prostration, and in the presence of the Buddha, spoke words of joy to his daughter-in-law Visākhā, saying, "Dear daughter, from this day forward, you are my mother," thus placing her in the position of his mother. From that time on, the lady Visākhā became known as "Migāramātā" (the Mother of Migāra).

This is the explanation from the Anguttara Commentary. In the Dhammapada Commentary, however, following the tradition of the Reciters (Bhāṇakas), it is explained: "After the merchant Migāra became a Sotāpanna Ariya, he came and lifted the edge of the curtain, took his daughter-in-law's breast into his mouth and said, 'From today, you are indeed my mother,' thus placing her in the position of his mother. From that time on, Visākhā became known as 'Migāramātā.' Later, when she had a son, (in accordance with the name Migāramātā), that son was named 'Migāra the Merchant's Son,'" and so forth.

In this matter, since the Anguttara Commentary explains only the essential summary of Visākhā's story, for the sake of the virtuous readers of the Buddha's life,
275:
I shall further present other noteworthy matters concerning Visākhā, extracted from the first volume of the Dhammapada Commentary.

## The Mother-in-law also Becoming a Stream-enterer

After the Great Treasurer Migāra had placed his daughter-in-law in the position of a mother, he went to the presence of the Blessed One. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, massaged the feet with his hands, and kissed them with his mouth, announcing his name three times: “Venerable Sir, I am Migāra; Venerable Sir, I am Migāra.” He then addressed the Buddha: “Exalted One, for all this time that has passed, I did not know in which recipient a gift given would yield great fruit. Now, however, I have come to know it through my daughter-in-law. I have been liberated from all the sufferings of the four woeful states. The arrival of my daughter-in-law Visākhā at this house was for my benefit and happiness.” Having said this, he recited the following verse:

“So'haṃ ajja pajānāmi, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.
Atthāya vata me bhaddā, suṇisā gharamāgatā.”

“Venerable Sir, today I have clearly understood in which recipient a gift given bears great fruit. Indeed, the virtuous and wise daughter-in-law Visākhā has come to the house of me, known as Migāra, for my own benefit.”
276:
276

"Indeed, she has arrived due to the support of past wholesome kamma."

The wise daughter-in-law Visākhā again invited the Exalted Buddha for the next day. On that day, the merchant's wife, the mother-in-law of Visākhā, also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and became a Sotāpanna Ariya. From that time on, the house of the merchant Migāra became one with its doors wide open for the Sāsana of the Exalted Buddha.

When a noble person reaches a home,
For the many people dwelling there,
To enter quickly the palace of Nibbāna,
Open is the door of the Eightfold Path.

## The Merchant’s Honor to Visākhā

Thereafter, the merchant Migāra reflected, "Oh, my daughter-in-law has been of great service to me. For this wise daughter-in-law, I shall perform the acts of honor that are customary for those who have gained faith. This wise daughter-in-law of mine cannot always wear the very heavy Mahālatā ornament. I shall make an ornament for her that she can wear during all four postures, day and night."

Having so reflected, he commissioned the "Ghanamatthaka" (solid and smooth) ornament worth one hundred thousand. When the ornament was finished, he invited the Sangha led by the Buddha, respectfully offered a meal, and had the wise daughter-in-law Visākhā bathed with sixteen pots of scented water. He then had her adorned with the ornament in the presence of the Exalted Buddha and made her pay homage to the Buddha. After the Exalted Buddha had preached the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), He returned to the monastery.
277:
From that time onwards, the wealthy lady Visākhā performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) as she desired. Having received the *eight boons from the Exalted One, she became as exceptionally prominent as the moon in the sky and attained prosperity through her sons and daughters. To make it clear: Visākhā had ten sons and ten daughters. Among those twenty children, each one in turn had ten sons and ten daughters (thus, Visākhā had four hundred grandchildren). Among those four hundred grandchildren, each one again had ten sons and ten daughters, resulting in eight thousand great-grandchildren. Therefore, the ancient Elders composed and praised her with this verse:

Visākhā vīsati puttā,
nattā ca caturo satā.
panattā aṭṭhasahassā,
jambudīpe supākaṭā.

Visākhā = Visākhā, the wise daughter-in-law of the wealthy merchant Migāra. Vīsati puttā = having twenty children. Caturo satā nattā ca = having four hundred grandchildren. Aṭṭhasahassā panattā ca = and having eight thousand great-grandchildren.

* The eight boons are: (1) the right to offer rain-cloths to the Saṅgha for as long as she lived; (2) the right to offer food to incoming (āgantuka) monks; (3) the right to offer food to monks setting out on a journey; (4) the right to offer food to sick monks; (5) the right to offer food to monks attending the sick; (6) the right to offer medicine to sick monks; (7) the right to offer a constant supply of rice-gruel; (8) the right to offer bathing cloths to the community of bhikkhunīs. These are the eight. For the detailed account of these eight boons, one should refer to the Visākhā-vatthu starting from page 407 of the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi.
278:
Jambudīpe = throughout the island known as Jambudīpa. Supākaṭā = she was very famous and well-known.

Thus, they composed this verse in her praise.

## Special Characteristics of Visākhā
Visākhā lived to the age of one hundred and twenty (120) years. Not a single grey hair grew on her head. She always appeared youthful, as if she were sixteen (16) years old. When people saw Visākhā going to the monastery surrounded by her sons, daughters, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, she was so youthful that they had to ask, "Who among these women is Visākhā?"

Those who saw Visākhā walking would think, "Let her walk slowly for now; our lady Visākhā is most beautiful only when she is walking." Those who saw Visākhā standing, (p), sitting, (p), or lying down would think, "Let her lie down a little longer; our lady Visākhā is most beautiful only when she is lying down." In this way, among the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—Visākhā was so beautiful that there was no room to say, "She is not beautiful in such-and-such a posture."

(She possessed the strength of five noble elephants)—Visākhā could bear the strength of five noble elephants. At one time, King Pasenadi of Kosala heard the report that "Visākhā possesses the strength of five noble elephants." Wishing to test her strength, he ordered a great noble elephant to be released at the time when Visākhā was returning from the monastery after listening to the Dhamma.
279:
The noble elephant, raising its trunk, came charging directly toward Visākhā with the intent to kill. Among Visākhā’s five hundred female attendants, some fled in fear. (In the sentence following this, the Sri Lankan edition has 'ekaccā na pariccajitvā,' while the Sixth Council edition has 'ekaccā na parissajjitvā.' The reading 'ekaccā pana parissajjitvā' is more logical, and I shall translate accordingly). Some attendants, however, surrounded and clung to Visākhā. When Visākhā asked, "Why is this happening?" they replied, "My lady... the King, wishing to test your strength, has ordered the noble elephant to be released."

The wealthy lady Visākhā thought, "What benefit is there in fleeing upon seeing this elephant? (There is none). How should I catch this elephant?" She then reflected, "If I were to seize this elephant as firmly as my strength allows, the elephant would surely be destroyed and die." Thus, when the elephant reached her, she merely pinched its trunk with two fingers and gently pushed it over. The elephant was unable to keep itself upright. (It fell down flat). The crowd of people shouted "Sādhu" in applause. Visākhā then returned home safely with her retinue.

## The Circumstances for Building the Pubbārāma Monastery
At that time in the city of Sāvatthī, the wealthy lady Visākhā, the mother of Migāra, having many children and grandchildren, and having healthy and strong children and grandchildren, was recognized and designated by everyone as a "most auspicious noble lady."
280:
Among her many children and grandchildren, not a single one had ever passed away in the interim. The citizens of Sāvatthī would first invite and feed Visākhā at auspicious festivals. Later, on a certain festival day, while many people were dressed in full finery and going to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma, Visākhā also, after eating at the place where she was invited, wore her Mahālatā ornament and accompanied the people to the monastery. As she was about to enter the monastery grounds, she reflected, "It is not appropriate to go into the presence of the Buddhas in such an appearance of vanity." She then removed the Mahālatā ornament, wrapped it in a bundle, and handed it to her maidservant, who possessed the strength of five noble elephants—a strength born of her own merit—to carry it.

(Only that maidservant could carry or lift that Mahālatā ornament; others could not. Therefore, Visākhā said to the maid, "Mother... take this ornament; I shall wear it only when I return after listening to the Dhamma from the Exalted One," and handed it to her.)

After handing the Mahālatā ornament to the maid, Visākhā wore the Ghanamaṭṭhaka ornament, approached the Exalted One, and listened to the Dhamma. When the sermon was over, Visākhā paid respectful homage to the Exalted One, rose from her seat, and departed. The maidservant, however, forgot the Mahālatā ornament right at the place where the Dhamma was heard. It was the custom of the Venerable Ānanda to collect and keep any object left behind by the audience after listening to the Dhamma. Thus, on that day, Venerable Ānanda found Visākhā’s Mahālatā ornament.
281:
Upon finding it, he informed the Buddha, "Exalted One, Visākhā has forgotten her Mahālatā ornament and left it behind." The Exalted One said, "Ānanda, my son, keep it in a suitable place." Thus, Venerable Ānanda lifted the Mahālatā ornament and hung it on one side of the staircase.

The wealthy lady Visākhā, together with the laywoman *Suppiyā, wandered within the Jetavana monastery to find out what needed to be done for incoming monks, traveling monks, sick monks, and so on. In particular, when the young monks and novices saw the great donors Visākhā and Suppiyā wandering within the monastery, those who desired ghee, honey, oil, and such,

* The laywoman Suppiyā was the wife of the lay disciple Suppiya from the city of Bārāṇasī. Both husband and wife had great faith in the Triple Gem. They were accustomed to offering the four requisites to the Saṅgha and performing all duties for the Saṅgha. At one time (while the Buddha was staying in the Isipatana Deer Park in Bārāṇasī), the great donor Suppiyā went to the monastery and, seeing a sick monk, asked, "Venerable sir, what nutriment do you require?" When the monk replied, "I require meat broth," she said, "Very well, venerable sir, I shall send it," and returned home. The next day, being unable to obtain suitable meat, she cooked meat broth from her own thigh flesh for the monk and offered it. Because of her intense faith in the Buddha, she later became one who had a normal body without even a scar. The detailed account can be found starting from page 311 of the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi.
282:
would approach those great donors while holding their bowls, plates, and so on. On that day, they did the same.

The great donor Visākhā, after looking after the sick monks, young monks, and novices and donating what was needed, exited the Jetavana monastery through another gate. While standing in the monastery precincts, she said to her maidservant, "Mother, bring the Mahālatā ornament; I shall wear it." Only then did the maidservant clearly remember that she had forgotten it and left the monastery, saying, "Oh, my lady... I have forgotten it and left it behind."

Then the wealthy lady Visākhā said, "If that is the case, go and get it and return. However, if the Venerable Ānanda has lifted that Mahālatā ornament and kept it in another place, do not bring it back. I have already relinquished and offered that ornament to the Venerable Elder." She sent the maidservant with these instructions. Visākhā said this because she already knew that Venerable Ānanda would collect and keep the belongings forgotten and left behind by people of the four classes within the monastery so that they would not be lost.

As soon as Venerable Ānanda saw the maidservant, he asked, "For what purpose have you come?" When the maidservant replied, "I have come because I forgot my lady's Mahālatā ornament," he said, "I have hung it on the side of such-and-such a staircase. Go and take that ornament." The maidservant said, "Venerable sir, an object that has been touched by the hands of your reverences, my lady—"
283:
“I have already made the object something that cannot be taken back (having established the intention of donation), Venerable Sir,” she had said. The servant returned to Visākhā empty-handed. When Visākhā asked, “How was it, mother?”, she reported the matter to Visākhā.

Then Visākhā said to the servant, “Mother, I shall no longer wear the Mahālatā ornament that has been handled by the Noble One. It has indeed been relinquished by me. However, it would be very burdensome and difficult for the Noble Ones to look after and maintain it. I shall sell that ornament and offer the proceeds as allowable requisites to the Saṅgha. Go, bring that Mahālatā ornament back.” The servant went to the monastery and brought the Mahālatā ornament back. Visākhā did not wear the Mahālatā ornament but instead called for goldsmiths to have it valued. The goldsmiths valued it, saying, “This ornament is worth nine crores, and the workmanship is worth one hundred thousand.” Visākhā had the ornament placed on a carriage and said, “If that is so, sell this Mahālatā ornament.”

No one else would be able to pay such a price to purchase it. Indeed, women worthy of wearing such a Mahālatā ornament are very rare. Truly, in this world, only these three women obtained the Mahālatā ornament: (1) the great lay-devotee Visākhā, (2) Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, and (3) the daughter of the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī.
284:
Therefore, the treasurer’s daughter Visākhā herself paid the price of the Mahālatā ornament (nine crores and one hundred thousand). She had those nine crores and one hundred thousand coins loaded onto carts and taken to the monastery. After paying homage to the Buddha, she said: “Venerable Sir, my noble Elder Ānanda touched my Mahālatā ornament with his hand to keep it safe from loss. From the moment the Elder touched it, I have no longer been able to wear that ornament. Therefore, I intended to sell the Mahālatā ornament and offer the proceeds as allowable requisites (kappiya-vatthu) to the Saṅgha. However, I could find no one else capable of buying that ornament, so I have brought the value of the ornament (nine crores and one hundred thousand) myself. Among the four requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicine—which would be most appropriate to offer, Venerable Sir?”

The Blessed One replied: “Visākhā, it would be appropriate for you to build a monastery near the East Gate of this city of Sāvatthī for the residence of the Saṅgha.” Visākhā replied, “It is well, Venerable Sir,” and with a joyful heart, she purchased the land for the Pubbārāma monastery for ninety million (90,000,000) coins. With another ninety million, she began the construction of the great Pubbārāma monastery complex.

## The Construction of the Great Pubbārāma Monastery in Nine Months under the Supervision of Ven. Moggallāna

One day, at dawn, when the Blessed One surveyed the world of beings, he saw a certain being who had passed away from the celestial realm...
285:
(Note: As a matter of regular practice, when the Blessed One accepted alms at Visākhā’s house, he would depart by the southern gate and reside at the Jetavana monastery. When he accepted alms at Anāthapiṇḍika’s house, he would depart by the eastern gate and reside at the Pubbārāma monastery. Whenever the Blessed One was seen heading towards the northern gate, everyone knew, “He will be setting out on a journey.”) 

On that day, the lay-devotee Visākhā heard the news that “The Blessed One is heading towards the northern gate.” She quickly went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and asked, “Do you wish to set out on a journey, Venerable Sir?” The Blessed One replied, “Yes, Visākhā.” She then pleaded, “Venerable Sir, I am in the midst of building a monastery for you, having relinquished so much wealth (nine crores). Please turn back, Venerable Sir.” The Blessed One said, “Visākhā, this journey is one from which I cannot turn back.” Visākhā, considering that “The Blessed One must surely have seen someone endowed with past merits for the Paths and Fruits,” then requested, “Venerable Sir, if that is the case, please leave behind one monk who can distinguish and manage what has been done and what remains to be done in the construction of the monastery before you depart.” Then the Blessed One,
286:
said to Visākhā, “Visākhā, take the bowl of whichever monk you prefer.”

Although Visākhā naturally loved and preferred the Venerable Ānanda, she thought, “Venerable Mahāmoggallāna possesses great psychic power. If I can rely on that Elder, my monastery construction will be completed quickly.” Thus, she requested the bowl of Venerable Moggallāna. The Elder looked towards the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said, “Dear Moggallāna, take your retinue of five hundred monks and stay behind.” Following the Blessed One’s command, the Elder stayed behind with his five hundred disciple monks.

Through the Elder’s psychic power, people who went for timber and stones as far as fifty or sixty leagues were able to bring back large timbers and stones and return on the very same day. They did not suffer exhaustion while loading timber and stones onto carts, nor did any cart axles break. Before long, the great two-storied mansion (pasāda) was completed. That great mansion was adorned with a total of one thousand rooms: five hundred rooms on the lower floor and five hundred rooms on the upper floor. The great lay-benefactress Visākhā had the mansion built on a clean plot of land as wide as eight karīsas. Furthermore, thinking, “A single great mansion alone is not beautiful,” she surrounded it with five hundred meditation huts,
287:
five hundred small mansions, and five hundred long halls, completing the construction.

## The Great Dedication Ceremony Lasting Four Months

Thereafter, the Blessed One returned to Sāvatthī after wandering for nine months. In the Pubbārāma mansion of the great lay-benefactress Visākhā, all necessary tasks were completed within nine months due to the supervision of Venerable Moggallāna. For the mansion’s pinnacle (thūpikā), the benefactress had it made of solid red gold (tambaloha) large enough to hold about sixty pots of water. When Visākhā heard the news that “The Blessed One has arrived at the Jetavana monastery,” she went to welcome him and invited him to her monastery, saying: “Venerable Sir, please reside only in this Pubbārāma monastery of mine for these four months of the rainy season, together with the Saṅgha. I shall perform the monastery dedication ceremony.” She obtained the Blessed One’s consent to reside there. The Blessed One accepted Visākhā’s request.

From that day on, Visākhā gave great offerings to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha at the monastery itself. Then, a friend of Visākhā brought a piece of cloth worth one hundred thousand and came to Visākhā, saying: “Friend,
288:
I wish to offer this cloth as a floor covering in your mansion. I would like you to tell me where it should be spread.” Then the great benefactress Visākhā said, “Very well, friend. If I were to tell you the truth that ‘there is no place to spread it,’ you might misunderstand me as ‘not wanting to give you the opportunity.’ Therefore, go and look through all one thousand rooms on both the upper and lower floors of the great mansion yourself and find a place to spread it.” Having been given permission, the friend took the cloth worth one hundred thousand and wandered through various places on the upper and lower floors. Finding no floor covering of lesser value than the cloth she brought, she thought, “I can no longer obtain a share of merit in this friend’s meritorious mansion,” and becoming unhappy, she stood in one spot weeping.

At that time, Venerable Ānanda saw the friend and asked, “Why are you weeping?” When she explained the reason, Venerable Ānanda said, “Do not be troubled by such thoughts. I shall tell you a place to spread it.” He advised her, “At the foot of the staircase, near the place where the monks wash their feet, spread this cloth of yours as a foot-wiper. After washing their feet, the monks will first wipe their feet on your cloth before entering the monastery. If this is done, it will be of great benefit to you.”
289:
This was a place that Visākhā had inadvertently overlooked.

## Offering the Four Requisites Completely

For the duration of the four months of the rainy season, the great lay-benefactress Visākhā gave great offerings to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha within the monastery. On the final day (the full moon of Tazaungmon), she offered cloth for robes to the Saṅgha. Even the cloth for robes received by the most junior monk (saṅghanava) was worth one thousand. She offered catumadhura medicine, filling the bowls of all the monks. During the four-month dedication ceremony, ninety million (90,000,000) coins were spent.

Thus, Visākhā spent nine crores on purchasing the monastery land, nine crores on building the monastery, and nine crores on the four-month dedication ceremony—a total of twenty-seven crores of wealth donated to the Buddha’s Dispensation. There is no other woman who, while remaining in the state of a woman and living in the house of a father-in-law with wrong views, has made such a great sacrifice and donation.

On the evening of the day the great dedication ceremony was completed, the great lay-benefactress Visākhā, surrounded by her sons, daughters, grandsons, and great-grandsons, reflected with joy, “All that I have yearned for and all that I have prayed for has reached its pinnacle and completion.” As she circumambulated the great mansion,

293
medicines used by physicians, consisting of clear ghee, fresh butter, honey, sesame oil, and sweet molasses? (Thus), the cycle of meritorious deeds and the aspirations of mine, Visākhā, the mother of Migāra (Migāramātā), which began since the time of Padumuttara Buddha, have now been fulfilled in this human history, just as I intended, while humans and devas rejoice and cry 'Sādhu'. (This collection of verses is extracted from the Dhammapada Commentary).

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
The house of the great donor Visākhā was always bright and shining with the color of robes in the morning (due to the many monks entering and leaving), and it was fragrant with the scent of the breeze and the dye from the robes of the monks moving about. Just like in the house of the millionaire Anāthapiṇḍika, in the house of the great donor Visākhā, various kinds of food, such as food for guests and food for travelers, were always prepared and ready.

In the morning, after offering the appropriate food to the Saṅgha, the great donor would have her attendants carry medicinal requisites such as ghee, fresh butter, honey, oil, and molasses, as well as the eight kinds of drinks (made from rose-apple, mango, grape, banana, etc.), and go to the monastery where the Buddha resided. There, she would offer the medicinal requisites and drinks to the Saṅgha as needed.
294:
294
After that, she would listen to the Dhamma from the Buddha and then return home. (This was Visākhā's regular practice of meritorious deeds).

Therefore, later on, when the Buddha was assigning the various titles of Etadagga (foremost positions) to the female lay disciples (upāsikā) in order, he praised Visākhā, the mother of Migāra, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ dāyikānaṃ yadidaṃ visākhā migāramātā" — "Monks, among my female lay disciples who delight in giving and charity, the millionaire Visākhā, the mother of Migāra, is the most excellent, the foremost."

Thus, he appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "donors" (dāyikā), those who delight in giving.

This is the account of the great donor Visākhā.
