## (3-4) About Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī
## (a) Past Aspirations of the Two Lay Disciples
Both of these noble women, the future Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī, were daughters of good families (millionaires' daughters) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. One day, they went to the monastery to listen to the Buddha's Dhamma teaching. While there, the future Khujjuttarā saw the Buddha appoint a female lay disciple
295:
Seeing the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (etadagga) of being “foremost among those of great learning (bahussuta),” she was inspired and performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra), making an aspiration for that very rank and position. The Blessed One also granted her a prophecy.

The future Sāmāvatī, also a treasurer’s daughter, saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (etadagga) of being “foremost among those who dwell in loving-kindness (mettāvihārī).” Inspired, she performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that rank and position. The Blessed One Padumuttara also granted her a prophecy.

Those two treasurer’s daughters performed meritorious deeds for the rest of their lives. After passing away from that life, they were reborn in the celestial realm. While wandering between the deva and human worlds, a hundred thousand aeons passed, and they reached this Bhadda-kappa.

At that time, when our Buddha appeared in the world, the Great Treasurer Ghosaka and his wife in the city of Kosambī established a practice of regular alms-giving (nibaddha-dāna), giving away one thousand coins every single day. (For a detailed account of the Great Treasurer Ghosaka and his wife, one should review the Mahābuddhavaṃsa, Volume 3, Chapter 27, from pages 693 to 712).

## (b) Becoming Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī in Their Final Life

While the Great Treasurer Ghosaka and his wife were performing their regular alms-giving, among the two aforementioned fulfillers of perfections...
296:
296
the goddess who was to become Khujjuttarā passed away from the deva world and was conceived in the womb of a head nurse in the house of the millionaire Ghosaka. When the girl was born, her body was slightly hunchbacked. (The past kamma reasons for being born as a servant girl to a nurse and being hunchbacked despite being a possessor of perfections will be explained later). Because her body was hunchbacked, she was named Khujjuttarā. (Khujja = having a hunchbacked body + Uttarā = the girl Uttarā).

## The Millionaire's Daughter Sāmāvatī
At that same time, the goddess who was to become Sāmāvatī also passed away from the deva world and became the daughter of the millionaire Bhaddavatiya in the city of Bhaddiya in the kingdom of Bhaddavatiya. Her parents named her "Sāmā". Later on, a great famine (dubbhikkha) occurred in the city of Bhaddiya. The citizens, fearing the famine, fled to other places where they might find relief.

Then, Sāmā's father, the millionaire Bhaddavatiya, consulted with his wife, saying, "Dear wife, the end of this famine currently affecting Bhaddiya is unknown. (It is not known on which day or month this famine will end). Let us go to our friend, the millionaire Ghosaka, in the city of Kosambī. When he sees us, he will not forget us."
297:
He was an unseen friend (adiṭṭhasahāya) of the wealthy merchant Bhaddavatiya; therefore, they consulted each other in this manner. After discussing this, the merchant Bhaddavatiya left the others behind and, taking his wife and daughter Sāmāvatī, set out toward the city of Kosambī. All three family members suffered greatly during the journey and eventually reached the city of Kosambī, where they took up residence in a public rest house (catudisā-sarap).

## Sāmāvatī’s Encounter with Misfortune

The merchant Ghosaka also had a great daily (nibaddha) alms-distribution established at his house gate for the destitute, travelers, and beggars. At that time, the merchant Bhaddavatiya thought, “I do not dare to present myself to my friend, the merchant Ghosaka, in this current state of poverty. We shall meet the merchant Ghosaka only after we have recovered our physical well-being and are properly dressed.” Thus, the merchant Bhaddavatiya and his wife sent their daughter Sāmāvatī to the merchant Ghosaka’s alms-pavilion to ask for rice.

Sāmāvatī, the merchant’s daughter, went to the alms-pavilion holding a bowl. Not daring to push through the crowded mass of people, she stood in a place apart from the crowd with a modest and bashful demeanor. Seeing Sāmāvatī standing there with such composure and modesty, the supervisor of the alms-distribution thought, “Other people make loud noises in every direction, like fishermen scrambling for fish in a place where fish are being distributed—”
298: After reflecting thus, he asked the merchant's daughter Sāmāvatī, 'Dear, why do you not take [the food] and go like the others?' Sāmāvatī said, 'Father, how can a modest girl like me enter such a crowded and narrow place? It is impossible.' When the manager of services asked, 'Dear, how many people are there in your family?' the merchant's daughter Sāmāvatī replied, 'O father, there are three in our family.' The manager of services then gave her three portions of rice. Sāmāvatī gave that rice to her parents. Because the father, the Great Merchant, had been hungry for a long time, he ate excessively and passed away that very day. On the next day, Sāmāvatī went to the alms shed and asked for only two portions of rice. On that day, the mother, the merchant's wife, passed away after midnight due to both the lack of food and her grief over the merchant's death. On the following day, the merchant's daughter Sāmāvatī asked for only one portion of rice.
299: The manager of services, wishing to investigate Sāmāvatī's behavior, asked, 'Dear, on the first day you took rice for three people, on the second day for two, and today, the third day, you ask for only one. What is the reason for this?' When Sāmāvatī explained that her father had passed away on the first day and her mother after midnight on the second day, and therefore she was asking for only one portion for herself today, the third day, the manager of services asked again, 'Dear, in which city or village did you live?' When Sāmāvatī fully explained that their family of three had come from the city of Bhaddiya due to the danger of famine, the manager of services said, 'Dear, if that is the case, you are one who should be called the daughter of our Great Merchant Ghosaka. I also have no other daughter. Therefore, from this day forward, you are my daughter, dear,' and he adopted her as his daughter. Sāmāvatī, the adopted daughter of the manager, heard the loud shouting of the alms-seekers in the alms hall and asked, 'O father, why is there such a high and loud noise now?' When her father, the manager, said, 'Daughter, it is not possible to make the noise less or to make it quiet among so many people,' Sāmāvatī said, 'O father, I have thought of a method to make the noise less or to make it quiet in this matter.' The manager asked, 'What should be done, daughter?' Sāmāvatī said, 'O father, after putting up a fence all around and leaving only two gates—an entrance and an exit—you should arrange for the alms-seekers to enter through the entrance gate, receive their food in their vessels placed inside the enclosure, and then leave through the exit gate.'
300:
“—Dear father, please arrange it so that the recipients enter through an entrance gate, receive their food, and then leave through an exit gate.” When she gave this advice, her father, the supervisor of the work, agreed, saying, “Very well, daughter.” From the next day onward, he had it done according to Sāmāvatī’s instructions. From that time on, the great alms-pavilion became very pleasant and quiet, like a great Padumā lotus pond.

## Sāmāvatī Becoming the Daughter of the Merchant Ghosaka

Then one day, the merchant Ghosaka, who used to hear loud and boisterous voices at his alms-pavilion but no longer heard such sounds, sent for the supervisor of the alms-distribution and they questioned and answered each other as follows:

(Merchant): “My man, are you not giving alms today?”
(Supervisor): “I am giving them, my lord merchant.”
(Merchant): “If you are giving them, why do I not hear the loud and boisterous sounds at the alms-pavilion as I did before?”
(Supervisor): “It is true, my lord merchant. I have a wise daughter. By following the method and means she suggested, I have been able to make the alms-pavilion quiet.”
(Merchant): “You have no daughter (as far as I know). Where did you get this wise daughter?”
301:
When questioned thus, the supervisor could no longer hide the truth and revealed the full story of how the daughter Sāmāvatī had arrived. Then the merchant Ghosaka said to the supervisor, “My man, why did you commit such a burdensome act? You did not tell me that my friend's daughter was staying with you for all this time. Send my daughter to my house immediately.” Hearing the merchant’s words, the supervisor, though unwilling, had to send Sāmāvatī to the merchant’s house. From that time on, the merchant Ghosaka treated Sāmāvatī as his own daughter. Thinking, “I shall provide for my daughter,” he gathered five hundred young women of the same social class and age as Sāmāvatī to be her attendants.

## King Udena Appointing Sāmāvatī as Queen

One day, while King Udena, the ruler of Kosambī, was touring the city, he saw the merchant’s daughter Sāmāvatī playing, surrounded by her five hundred attendants. Feeling a deep affection for her, he asked, “Whose daughter is this young woman?” Upon hearing, “She is the daughter of the merchant Ghosaka,” he asked again whether she had a master or husband. When told she had no husband, he said, “Go and tell the merchant Ghosaka: ‘The King desires your daughter Sāmāvatī,’” and he dispatched his ministers to the merchant Ghosaka. Hearing this news, the merchant thought, “We have no other daughter besides this Sāmāvatī; my only beloved daughter will be among many enemies (rival queens)—”
302: When King Udena heard those words, he became very angry and, after turning the Great Merchant Ghosaka and his wife out of their house, he had the royal seal placed on the entire house, effectively closing it. When the daughter Sāmāvatī returned home after playing and found her parents sitting outside the house in despair, she asked, 'O mother and father, why are you sitting outside the house?' When the Merchant Ghosaka and his wife told her the reason, the clever daughter Sāmāvatī said, 'O mother and father, why did you not know to reply with these words: "Our daughter cannot live alone if she must stay in the golden palace surrounded by rivals. However, if you allow her five hundred maiden attendants to stay with her as well, our daughter will stay"? O mother and father, now send such a reply to the Great King.' Then the merchant and his wife said, 'Very well, daughter. We simply did not know your mind,' and they sent the reply to King Udena as Sāmāvatī had instructed. When King Udena heard those words, he was exceedingly pleased and said, 'Even if there are a thousand, all of them must be taken and brought.' Then, after choosing an auspicious constellation and an auspicious time, they escorted the merchant's daughter Sāmāvatī along with her five hundred maiden attendants to the golden palace.
303: King Udena appointed all five hundred maidens as Sāmāvatī's attendants, consecrated Queen Sāmāvatī with the ceremonial water, and had her reside magnificently in a golden palace. At that time, in the city of Kosambī, three merchant friends—Merchant Ghosaka, Merchant Kukkuṭa, and Merchant Pāvāriya—learned from the five hundred ascetics they had been supporting that the Buddha had appeared and was currently residing in the city of Sāvatthī. They went to Sāvatthī, listened to the Dhamma, and became Noble Ones who have attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpanna). After offering great alms to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for fifteen days, they requested the Buddha to visit Kosambī and received His promise. They returned to Kosambī, and each built a great monastery. Then they sent an invitation to the Buddha. The Buddha, saying, 'I shall go to Kosambī,' set out on His journey surrounded by many monks. On the way, seeing the past merits of the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife, who were destined to attain the Fruit of Arahantship, He diverted His path toward Kosambī and went to the market town of Kammāsadamma in the Kuru country. After guiding and admonishing the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife, He continued His journey toward Kosambī. Eventually arriving at Kosambī, He accepted the three great monasteries donated by the three merchants. On the following day, at the invitation of the merchants, He entered the city of Kosambī surrounded by the assembly of monks. As soon as He entered the city—
304:
304
According to the plan of Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, who harbored a grudge, drunkards were hired to insult the Buddha in various ways. When the Venerable Ānanda suggested moving to another town, the Buddha preached the Attadaṇḍa-vatthu from the Dhammapada to him. The Buddha then continued to reside and grace the three great monasteries donated by the three wealthy merchants in rotation. (For a detailed account of this matter, one should review the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume III, pages 712 to 727).

## Khujjuttarā Becoming a Stream-Enterer
The three great merchants of Kosambī, in their respective turns, offered grand alms-givings to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha for an entire month. Afterwards, they magnanimously allowed the townspeople to perform meritorious deeds as well. Consequently, people from various streets, wards, and associations also offered great alms-givings.

One day, the Buddha, surrounded by a company of monks, sat in the house of a master florist upon his invitation. At that moment, Khujjuttarā, a trusted servant of Queen Sāmāvatī, arrived at that house to buy flowers, bringing eight kahāpaṇas as she did daily. Upon seeing Khujjuttarā, the florist said, “O mother Uttarā, today I cannot give you flowers yet. I am serving the Saṅgha led by the Buddha. I would like you to be a companion in serving the meal. By performing such voluntary service (veyyāvacca)...”
305:
305
“...if you perform this, you will be liberated from the life of a servant who must perform the service of others,” he advised. Then, after eating her own food, Khujjuttarā assisted in the voluntary service of preparing and offering the meal to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha.

She memorized the entire Dhamma preached by the Buddha as an Upanisinnakathā (a discourse for those seated nearby). Upon hearing the Anumodanā (discourse of appreciation), she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and became a Noble Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna).

## Sāmāvatī and Her Group Becoming Stream-Enterers
On other days, Khujjuttarā used to buy flowers for only four kahāpaṇas and would hide the other four for herself. However, on that day, because she had realized the Four Noble Truths and become a Noble One (Ariya), she no longer had the desire to steal others' property. She bought flowers worth all eight kahāpaṇas, filled her basket, and returned to Queen Sāmāvatī. Then, Queen Sāmāvatī and Khujjuttarā spoke to each other as follows:

(Sāmāvatī)
“Mother Uttarā, on other days you did not bring so many flowers. Today, however, there are many flowers indeed. Why is this? Has the King become more faithful and gracious toward us?”

Because Khujjuttarā had become a Noble One who was not fit to tell lies, she did not hide her past deceptions of previous days, months, and years, but confessed and revealed everything.
306:
306
She confessed everything without concealment.

(Sāmāvatī)
“If so, why did you bring so many flowers today?”

(Khujjuttarā)
“I have heard the Dhamma of the Buddha today and have realized the Deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, I will no longer lie to or deceive my ladies.”

Then, Queen Sāmāvatī along with her five hundred attendants stretched out their hands and requested, “Mother Uttarā, please give us also the Dhamma of the Deathless Nibbāna that you have obtained.”

(Khujjuttarā)
“Ladies, this cannot be given from one hand to another like a physical object. In truth, I will preach the Dhamma to you according to the method taught by the Buddha. If you possess the previous merit which is the cause for the Path and Fruit, you will attain that Deathless Nibbāna.”

(Sāmāvatī and others)
“If that is so, Mother Uttarā, please preach it right now.”

(Khujjuttarā)
“It is not proper to preach like this (with me in a low place and you ladies in high places). You must prepare a high seat for me, and you must sit in low places.”

Then, the five hundred court ladies led by Sāmāvatī gave Khujjuttarā a high seat, while they themselves...
307:
307
...took low seats and remained sitting. Khujjuttarā (being a trainee Noble One, a Stream-enterer who had attained the analytical insights), established herself in the Sekhapaṭisambhidāñāṇa (the analytical insight of a trainee) and preached the Dhamma to the five hundred court ladies led by Sāmāvatī. At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching, all five hundred court ladies, with Queen Sāmāvatī at their head, were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry; they became Noble Stream-enterers. From that time on, they relieved Khujjuttarā of her menial duties and said, “Mother Uttarā, after you have heard the Buddha’s Dhamma, please learn and memorize it, and then preach it to us in turn.” From then on, Khujjuttarā did as the court ladies requested (every day she listened to the Dhamma from the Buddha, memorized it, and preached it in turn to the court ladies in the golden palace).

## Khujjuttarā’s Past Wholesome and Unwholesome Kamma
(In this matter, one might ask: “Why did this Khujjuttarā become a servant?” The answer is: During the era of the Dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, she made a novice nun (sāmaṇerī) perform her own menial tasks. Due to that unwholesome kamma, she had to be a servant of others for five hundred consecutive births.

Again, one might ask: “Why did she become a hunchback?” The answer is: Before the Buddha appeared, the woman who was to become Khujjuttarā was a court lady in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī. While there, she saw a hunchbacked Paccekabuddha entering the palace for alms. Wanting to mock him in front of her fellow court ladies, she walked around with a stooped posture. Because of that, she became a hunchback.
308:
308
One might ask again: “What wholesome merit did Khujjuttarā perform to become a wise person in this life?” The answer is: Before the Buddha appeared, while the woman who was to become Khujjuttarā was living in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī, she saw eight Paccekabuddhas departing from the palace carrying alms-bowls filled with hot milk-rice. She said, “Venerable Sirs, please place your bowls upon these bracelets (donated by me) and proceed.” She then removed eight gold bracelets she was wearing and offered them (to be used as bowl-stands). As a result of that kamma, she became a wise person. These are the past kammas of Khujjuttarā to be specially noted. From Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, page 338).

## Queen Māgaṇḍiyā’s Incitements of Malice
Thereafter, although the five hundred court ladies who were attendants of Queen Sāmāvatī had themselves become Noble Stream-enterers who realized the Four Noble Truths, they did not get the opportunity to go to the Buddha and pay homage frequently because King Udena was one who lacked faith in the Dispensation. (Being Stream-enterers, they desired very much to see the Buddha). Therefore, when the Buddha walked along the streets within the city of Kosambī, because the latticed windows were too few for five hundred women to look through, they made holes in their respective bedchambers and gazed upon the Buddha through those holes.

One day, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā came out from her palace and was walking about. When she reached the quarters of those court ladies and saw the holes in the chambers, she asked, “What is this?” The five hundred court ladies, not knowing Queen Māgaṇḍiyā’s grudge against the Buddha, replied honestly, “The Buddha...
309:
309
...has arrived in this city of Kosambī. We stand near these chamber holes and both gaze upon the Buddha and pay him homage.” When they spoke thus honestly, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā thought with clenched teeth, “Now I shall know what to do to the ascetic Gotama. These women are also the servants and disciples of the ascetic Gotama. I shall also know what to do to these women.”

Having gone from there, when she was in a private place with King Udena, she incited him with malicious words, saying, “Great King, the court ladies of Queen Sāmāvatī have desires for those outside of your majesty. Within two or three days, they will plot and assassinate your majesty. Queen Sāmāvatī, along with her attendants, has no love or affection for your majesty at all. They even watch the ascetic Gotama as he walks through the city streets. Because the latticed windows were not enough, they broke the windows and made holes in their chambers, doing whatever they could to get a look at him.” King Udena thought, “Those women would not do such a thing,” and he did not accept or believe Queen Māgaṇḍiyā’s words. Even when she spoke a second time, he remained unbelieving. Then, when she spoke for the third time to the unbelieving King Udena, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā said, “Great King, if you do not believe my words, go to the chambers of those women yourself and investigate.” King Udena went, and in the chambers...
310:
310
...when he saw the holes, he asked, “What are these holes?” When the court ladies replied honestly about the matter, he did not become angry with them and said nothing at all, but simply had the holes closed. From that time on, King Udena had latticed windows made for the palace of those five hundred court ladies that had openings only at the top. (This was the first instance of inciting malice).

Because Queen Māgaṇḍiyā was unable to make the King angry by that means, she said, “Great King, shall we investigate to see whether these five hundred court ladies led by Sāmāvatī have affection for your majesty or not? Please have eight live chickens sent to them and order them to be cooked for your majesty.” After hearing Queen Māgaṇḍiyā’s words, the King said, “I want these chickens cooked and sent to me,” and he sent eight live chickens to Sāmāvatī. How could a Noble Disciple (Ariyasāvikā) who is a Stream-enterer cook live chickens? (She would rather die than take life; she would not cook them). Thus, Sāmāvatī said, “It is not proper,” and she did not even wish to touch those live chickens with her hands.

Then Māgaṇḍiyā said, “Let it be, Great King. Order those same chickens to be cooked for the ascetic Gotama.” King Udena did as Queen Māgaṇḍiyā said. Queen Māgaṇḍiyā had the chickens killed while they were on the way and sent them to Sāmāvatī with the instruction, “I want these chickens cooked and offered to the ascetic Gotama.”
311:
The very honest Sāmāvatī, because the chickens were already dead and because they were being sent as an offering to the Buddha, had the dead chickens cooked and sent to the Buddha. Queen Māgaṇḍiyā said, "Look, Your Majesty..." but even with this, she was unable to make King Udena angry. (This was the second attempt at causing discord).

## The Third Attempt at Causing Discord

King Udena had three queens: (1) Queen Sāmāvatī, (2) Queen Vāsuladattā, the daughter of King Caṇḍapajjota of Ujjenī, and (3) Queen Māgaṇḍiyā. Each queen had five hundred female attendants. King Udena was accustomed to staying for seven days at a time in the palace of each of these three queens in rotation. Then, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā had a small cobra placed in a bamboo tube and kept it near her quarters. As for King Udena, it was his custom to take his elephant-charming lute (Hatthikanta-vīṇā) wherever he went. When the King came to her, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, without the King's knowledge, placed the small cobra inside the cavity of the lute and blocked the opening.

Later that night, as the King was about to go to Queen Sāmāvatī's quarters, she spoke to him (pretending to be concerned for his welfare): "Your Majesty, this Queen Sāmāvatī is a partisan of the ascetic Gotama. She does not respect Your Majesty even as much as a blade of grass. Having done something, she is only plotting to harm Your Majesty.
312:
Please remain vigilant and mindful."

King Udena spent seven days in Queen Sāmāvatī's palace and then went to Queen Māgaṇḍiyā's palace for another seven days. As soon as the King arrived, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā spoke as if concerned for his welfare, saying, "Your Majesty, how is it? Has Queen Sāmāvatī not been looking for an opportunity against you?" She took the lute from the King's hand, shook it, and said, "How is this, Great King? Something is moving and crawling inside this lute!" She then opened the hole for the snake to come out (opening the hole she had originally made) and cried out, "Abbhummē! Oh, it is my ruin! Anto sappo! There is a great snake inside the lute!" and she threw the lute away and ran. (Māgaṇḍiyā's attempt at causing discord was successful). At that moment, King Udena, crackling with rage like a burning bamboo grove or a furnace into which salt has been thrown, gave the order: "Quickly, bring Sāmāvatī along with her attendants!" The king's men went and summoned them.

"When another is angry and harsh,
If one remains steadfast in Dhamma,
And practices loving-kindness in one's heart,
Where can there be defeat?"
— Dhammupadesa.

Queen Sāmāvatī, knowing the King was angry, gave a Dhamma instruction to the other women: "The King summons you because he wishes to kill you. Throughout this entire day, spray the King with loving-kindness by radiating directed loving-kindness (odhissaka-mettā)." King Udena, along with Queen Sāmāvatī...
313:
After having those five hundred women summoned, he lined them all up in order. He then took up a great bow, fitted a poison-tipped arrow, drew the bowstring, and stood ready.

At that moment, all five hundred women, led by Sāmāvatī, focused on the King and radiated directed loving-kindness (odhissaka-mettā). The King was unable to shoot the arrow, nor was he able to lower it. Perspiration poured from his body in streams. His whole body trembled, and saliva flowed from his mouth. He could not see what he should hold or what was worth holding.

Then Sāmāvatī asked the King, "Great King, are you weary?" The King replied, "Yes, Queen, I am very weary. Please be my refuge." Queen Sāmāvatī said, "Very well, Your Majesty. Please point the arrow toward the great earth." The King did as Queen Sāmāvatī said. Then Queen Sāmāvatī made an asseveration (adhiṭṭhāna): "May the arrow be released from the King's hand." At that very moment, the arrow was released from the King's hand.

At that instant, King Udena felt as if he had been submerged in water and returned. With wet hair and wet clothes, he prostrated at Sāmāvatī's feet and apologized, saying, "Queen, please forgive me. I have committed this wrong without investigation or reflection, based on the words of the slanderer Māgaṇḍiyā." When Queen Sāmāvatī spoke words of forgiveness, saying, "I forgive you, Your Majesty," King Udena said, "Very well, Queen. In this way, you have truly forgiven me.
314:
From this time today, according to your wishes, Queen, offer alms to the Buddha. In the afternoon, go to the monastery and listen to the Dhamma. From today onwards, I shall provide you with protection." Then, Queen Sāmāvatī, taking the opportunity, said, "Your Majesty, if that is so, from today onwards, please request and invite a monk from the Buddha to teach us the Dhamma." King Udena went to the Buddha and requested a monk, and he obtained the Venerable Ānanda Thera. From that time on, the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī invited Venerable Ānanda Thera, offered him alms-food daily, and after he had finished his meal, they learned the Dhamma from him.

One day, the five hundred women led by Queen Sāmāvatī, having developed faith and devotion during the Elder's sermon of appreciation (anumodanā), offered five hundred upper robes to the Elder (one robe each).

(In a past life, when the Elder was a tailor, he offered a needle and a palm-sized piece of coarse cloth to a Paccekabuddha. Due to the merit of offering the needle, he became a person of great wisdom in this life. Due to the merit of offering the piece of cloth, he received robes and cloth in this manner five hundred times.)
315:
## The Burning of Sāmāvatī and Others

Thereafter, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, seeing no other way, one day suggested to King Udena, "Your Majesty, let us go to the park for recreation." King Udena, unaware of Māgaṇḍiyā's plot, agreed, saying, "Very well, Queen." Queen Māgaṇḍiyā then summoned her uncle, the brahmin Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, and secretly instructed him: "Uncle, when we go to the park, go to Sāmāvatī's palace. Put Sāmāvatī and her five hundred attendants inside the palace, lock the doors saying it is the 'King's command,' surround it with straw, and set Sāmāvatī's palace on fire." The foolish brahmin Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, when King Udena and Queen Māgaṇḍiyā had gone to the park for recreation, set fire to Sāmāvatī's palace exactly as Queen Māgaṇḍiyā had instructed.

On that day, due to the power of their past obstructive unwholesome kamma (upapīḷaka-akusala-kamma), all five hundred women were unable to enter meditative attainment (samāpatti). Sāmāvatī and all five hundred women perished in the fire simultaneously, like a heap of chaff. The king's men who were guarding the women went to the King and reported, "Your Majesty, such an act (the burning of Sāmāvatī's palace) has been committed."

## King Udena's Stratagem

King Udena, while investigating to find the culprit who had set the fire...
316:
learned that Queen Māgaṇḍiyā had caused it to be done. He summoned Queen Māgaṇḍiyā to his presence and spoke with a royal stratagem: "Māgaṇḍiyā, you who have done what I ought to have done, have performed a good deed. You have caused the death of Queen Sāmāvatī, who was constantly striving to kill me. I am very pleased with you. I shall grant you rewards and wealth. Summon your relatives."

When Queen Māgaṇḍiyā heard King Udena's words, she was greatly delighted and summoned even those who were not her relatives, claiming them as such. When King Udena knew that all the criminals had gathered, he had those criminals buried in pits as deep as their necks in the palace courtyard, covered them with earth, had their heads that remained above ground smashed, and had the ground plowed with plows fitted with iron shares and iron blocks. As for Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, he had her body cut into pieces and fried in a frying pan.

## The Past Unwholesome Kamma of Sāmāvatī and Others

(Here, one might ask: "What was the past unwholesome kamma that caused Queen Sāmāvatī and her five hundred attendants to be trapped in a burning building and die?")

The answer is: In a life before a Buddha had appeared, the woman who was to become Queen Sāmāvatī, together with those five hundred women, was playing in the water of the Ganges. While standing outside the landing place, they felt a severe cold. Seeing a small leaf-roofed hut of a Paccekabuddha nearby, they set fire to it from the outside to warm themselves, without investigating or reflecting whether the Paccekabuddha was inside.
317:
Inside the leaf-hut, the Paccekabuddha was still seated, dwelling in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). When the flames subsided, those women saw the Paccekabuddha. (In this instance, although there was no fault because they had no intention to kill or cause death during the previous fire, they lacked proper reflection and were overcome with fear.) They thought, "Friends, what have we done? We have committed a great mistake. This Paccekabuddha is the one who goes to the King's golden palace daily for alms. If the King sees that this Paccekabuddha has passed away, he will be greatly enraged with us. Now, before the King hears of this, it is proper that we cremate this Paccekabuddha until he turns to ashes so that all traces disappear." Having made this wrong consultation and plan, they added more firewood and mistakenly set fire to him again. (This second act of setting fire was a grave offense because it involved the intention to kill.)

When the flames (from the second fire) subsided again, the Paccekabuddha rose from the attainment of cessation. While those women were watching, he shook his robes and flew up into the sky, departing. Due to that evil unwholesome kamma, those women suffered in hell, and as a remaining result (vipāka), they met their end by being burned to death in this present life. This is the answer.

## (c) Attainment of the Title of Etadagga

After Queen Sāmāvatī and the five hundred palace women had perished, words of praise arose in the midst of the four assemblies—1. Bhikkhu (monks), 2. Bhikkhunī (nuns), 3. Upāsaka (laymen), and 4. Upāsikā (laywomen)—as follows. The manner in which it arose was:
318:
“Khujjuttarā is indeed very learned (bahussuta). Although she is a woman, she preached the Dhamma to five hundred palace women and established them in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

Queen Sāmāvatī also was able to ward off the arrow shot at her by King Udena by radiating specific loving-kindness (odissaka-mettā).”

In this way, words of praise arose.

Later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery, as he was sequentially appointing laywomen to the positions of Etadagga, he praised the lady Khujjuttarā, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ khujjuttarā — Monks, among my female disciples, the laywomen who are learned (bahussuta), Khujjuttarā is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “being very learned (bahussuta).”

(She truly deserved to be praised with the title of Etadagga. To clarify further: after Queen Sāmāvatī and the five hundred palace women became Noble Ones (Ariyas) as Stream-enterers, they said to Khujjuttarā, “Mother Uttarā, please go to the Buddha every day, listen to all the Dhamma the Buddha preaches, and then preach it back to us.” She did as the palace women requested and later became a woman who was a bearer of the Three Baskets (Tipitakadhara). That is why the Buddha,
319:
placed Khujjuttarā in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of being learned (bahussuta) in later times.

Thus, among the laywomen (upāsikā), the noble disciple Khujjuttarā, who was very learned and had attained the analytical knowledge of a trainee (sekha-paṭisambhidāpatta), was appointed to the Etadagga position by the Buddha himself. While the Buddha was residing in the city of Kosambī, she went to the Buddha regularly to listen to the Dhamma. Upon returning to the palace, she preached the Dhamma she had heard to the five hundred noble female disciples led by Sāmāvatī, exactly as the Buddha had taught, beginning with the introduction: “Vuttaṃ hetaṃ bhagavatā, vuttaṃ arahatāti me sutaṃ” (This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard).

The Elders who conducted the Council (Saṅgāyana) compiled the sequence of the Buddha's words (Jinavacana) consisting of 112 discourses (suttas) preached by Khujjuttarā under the name “Itivuttaka Pali.” (From Itivuttaka Commentary, page 29).

At the great assembly for appointing Etadagga titles, the Buddha praised Queen Sāmāvatī, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ mettāvihārīnaṃ yadidaṃ sāmāvatī — Monks, among my female disciples, the laywomen who dwell in loving-kindness (mettāvihārī), Sāmāvatī is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed her to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “dwelling in loving-kindness (mettāvihārī).”

This is the account of Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī.
320:
## (5) The Story of the Laywoman Uttarā Nandamātā

## (a) Uttarā's Past Merits

This future laywoman Uttarā Nandamātā was a daughter of a good family (a wealthy man's daughter) in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. One day, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, she saw the Buddha appoint a laywoman to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “delighting in meditative absorption (jhānābhirata).” Inspired, she performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made a prayer for that same position. The Buddha also granted her a prophecy (byādika).

## (b) Becoming the Daughter of the Wealthy Man Puṇṇa in her Final Life

## The Birth of Uttarā

That noble lady wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time when our Buddha appeared, she was born in the city of Rājagaha as the daughter of a laborer named “Puṇṇa Sīha,” who depended on the wealthy man Sumana, and his wife Uttarā. The daughter was also named “Uttarā,” similar to her mother's name.

## When Puṇṇa Sīha Became Wealthy

Then one day, on a festival day, the wealthy man of Rājagaha summoned Puṇṇa and said, “Friend Puṇṇa, what use is a festival or observing the Uposatha to poor people (like you)? However, would you like to take the festival wages and provisions to enjoy the festival, or will you take the strong oxen,
321:
plows, and plowshares to plow the field? Tell me what you prefer.” Then the poor man Puṇṇa said to the wealthy man, “Lord, let me consult with my wife first.” He then told his wife Uttarā what the wealthy man had asked. His wife Uttarā encouraged him, saying, “O Lord, the wealthy man is our master and ruler. Therefore, when speaking with him, whatever he says is fitting. However, my lord, do not abandon your work of plowing.” The poor man Puṇṇa listened to his wife's words, took all the necessary equipment such as the plow, plowshare, and oxen, and went to the field to plow.

It so happened that on that day, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera rose from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and reflected, “Whom should I bless today?” He saw the *past merit (upanissaya) of this poor man Puṇṇa, and at the time for alms-round, he took his bowl and robes.

* By the phrase “seeing the past merit (upanissaya),” it is shown that although there must be a combination of present causes to be fulfilled in this life to attain the Path and Fruit, one must certainly be endowed with past merit. Similarly, for kamma that yields results in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya kamma), one must be endowed with past merit (upanissaya) just as much as present causes. Therefore, even if (present) causes such as the supreme association with a virtuous person (sappurisūpanissaya) and wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) are fully present,
322:
for a person who lacks the past merit (upanissaya) which is the cause for attaining the Path and Fruit, the attainment of the Path and Fruit cannot be fulfilled. (From Ṭīkā, 208).

Venerable Sāriputta took his bowl and robes and went to the place where the poor man Puṇṇa was plowing, showing himself at a short distance. When Puṇṇa saw the Elder, he stopped plowing for a moment, went to the Elder, and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. Venerable Sāriputta looked at Puṇṇa (wishing to bless him) and asked for a place where there was cool water. Puṇṇa thought, “The Great Elder likely wishes to wash his face.” He went quickly, brought a tooth-stick, prepared it properly, and offered it to the Elder. While Venerable Sāriputta was chewing the tooth-stick, Puṇṇa brought out the water-strainer (dhamakaroka) along with the bowl and brought back a full vessel of water.

After Venerable Sāriputta washed his face, he set out on his alms-round. At that time, the poor man Puṇṇa reflected, “On other days, the Elder does not come this way. Today, however, he must have come to bless me. Oh, if only my wife would pour the food she brings for me into the Elder's bowl as an offering, how good it would be!”

Then, the poor man Puṇṇa's wife, thinking, “Today is a festival day,” prepared snacks and food early with the provisions she had received for herself. As she was bringing them to the field where her husband Puṇṇa was plowing,
323:
Seeing the Elder on the way, she thought: "Oh, on other days when I see the Elder, I have no offerings. When I have offerings, I do not see my noble lord. Today, however, both the offering and the recipient are present before me. I will go back home and cook again for my husband, but first, I must offer this food I have brought to the Elder." Reflecting thus with the three stages of volition (cetanā), she poured the rice she had brought into the alms-bowl of the Venerable Sāriputta and made a wish, saying, "Venerable Sir, may I be liberated from such a miserable way of living."

The Elder also said to the woman, "May your wish be fulfilled," and after giving words of appreciation (anumodanā) to gladden her, he turned back from that spot and went to the monastery.

(In this regard, when a wholesome deed of giving is performed, many thought-processes of great wholesome impulsions (mahākusala-javana-vīthi) arise. In each thought-process, seven wholesome impulsions occur. Among these seven impulsions, the wholesome volition (kusala-cetanā) contained in the first impulsion is called 'kamma to be experienced in this very life' (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma). This is because, if conditions are met, it can produce results in the present life in the form of non-living (anupādinṇaka) material things such as gold and silver.

For this diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma to bear fruit, four conditions must be met: (a) Vatthu-sampadā = the recipient must be an Anāgāmī or an Arahant; (b) Paccaya-sampadā = the offering must be righteously obtained; (c) Cetanā-sampadā = the donor must be endowed with the three stages of volition; (d) Guṇātireka-sampadā = the recipient must have just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). When these four conditions are met, and the donor is also endowed with past merit (upanissaya)—
324:
—only when these causes coincide can the results be given in the present life.

In the case of the poor man Puṇṇa and his wife, their act of giving was endowed with the four conditions for the present life mentioned above. Furthermore, Puṇṇa himself was one who possessed the past merit (upanissaya) to become a treasurer (seṭṭhi). Therefore, on that very day, it produced non-living (anupādinṇaka) material results in the form of inexhaustible blocks and nuggets of gold, making him a great treasurer of immense wealth.

Puṇṇa's wife returned home, cooked food for her husband, and brought it to the place where Puṇṇa was plowing. She was afraid of her husband's potential anger, fearing that if he became angry, the merit of the alms-offering would become ineffective (ahosi-kamma) and bear no fruit. Thus, she said in advance, "My lord, for just this one day, please guard and restrain your mind from anger."

When Puṇṇa asked, "For what reason?", his wife explained the circumstances fully, saying, "My lord, while I was bringing your portion of food today, I saw the Venerable Sāriputta on the way. I offered your share of rice into the Elder's bowl, then went back home to cook fresh rice and have only now arrived late."

## The clods of earth turned into gold

Puṇṇa said, "My dear, you have done a delightful thing. I too have already offered a tooth-stick and water for washing the face to the great Elder earlier this morning. Today is indeed a good dawn for us."
325:
"Everything the Elder used today for his personal needs was our property alone," he said joyfully. Wholesome thoughts, identical in nature, arose repeatedly in the minds of both husband and wife.

Then, after Puṇṇa had finished his meal, he laid his head on his wife's lap and rested for a while. At that time, the process of sleep—the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness—descended upon Puṇṇa's continuity of aggregates (i.e., he fell asleep). After sleeping for a short while, Puṇṇa woke up and looked at the area he had plowed. Wherever Puṇṇa looked, it was shining with bright yellow gold, as if scattered with large yellow luffa flowers.

Puṇṇa said to his wife, "My dear, what are those things? (pointing to the clods of earth). Today, this entire area of the field I have plowed appears to me to have the color of gold."

The wife said, "My lord, I think your eyes are playing tricks on you because you have been so exhausted all day."

Puṇṇa replied, "My dear, if you do not believe me, look for yourself."

Only then, after looking at the field, did the wife say, "My lord, you are speaking the truth. These things must indeed be nuggets of gold as you say."

Puṇṇa went there himself, picked up a clod of earth, and struck it against the head of the plow. The large clod of earth became a solid nugget of gold and remained stuck to the plow-head like a large lump of molasses. Puṇṇa—
326:
—called his wife and said, "My dear, seeds sown by others bear fruit only after three or four months. But the seed of faith (saddhā) sown in the excellent field of merit that is our noble lord Sāriputta has surely and certainly borne fruit this very day. In this entire measure of land (pe), there is not a single clod of earth even the size of a wood-apple that is not gold."

When the wife asked, "What shall we do now, my lord?", Puṇṇa replied, "My dear, we cannot possibly hide and consume this much gold in any way." Leaving his wife there, he filled the bowl he had brought with gold nuggets and went to the royal palace. He had the King informed, "A man has arrived at the palace gate carrying a bowl of gold."

The King had Puṇṇa brought into his presence, and the King and Puṇṇa questioned and answered each other as follows:

(The King)
"My good man, where did you get this gold?"

(Puṇṇa)
"Great King, today the entire area of the field I plowed has turned into solid gold. I wish for your officials to be sent to collect it as royal property."

(The King)
"What is your name?"

(Puṇṇa)
"Great King, my name is Puṇṇa."
327:
Then the King said, "Men, go! Yoke the carts and bring the gold from the place where Puṇṇa plowed his field." He sent the royal officials along with the carts.

## Puṇṇa's Family

## Becoming Treasurers and Sotāpanna Ariyas

The royal officials who went with the carts began picking up the gold nuggets, saying, "This is by the King's merit." However, all the gold nuggets they picked up turned back into ordinary clods of earth. The officials went back to the palace and reported this to the King. King Bimbisāra suggested, "Men, if that is the case, pick them up while saying, 'This is by the merit of Master Puṇṇa'."

The officials went back again and, as instructed by the King, picked them up while saying, "This is by the merit of Master Puṇṇa." Every piece they took remained pure gold.

The officials transported all that gold in many hundreds of carts and, by the King's command, piled it in the palace courtyard. The great heap of gold nuggets was about the height of a palm tree. The King summoned the merchants to that spot and asked, "In this city, in whose house is there this much gold?"

The merchants replied, "Great King, there is no such amount of gold in anyone's house." The King then asked, "To Master Puṇṇa, who is the owner of this much wealth—
328:
—what should be done for him?"

The merchants unanimously submitted, "Great King, this Puṇṇa should be appointed as a great treasurer with the title 'Dhana-seṭṭhi'." King Bimbisāra then decreed, "If that is so, let Master Puṇṇa be designated with the title 'Dhana-seṭṭhi' in this city of Rājagaha and be appointed to the position of a great treasurer." He then gave all that gold back to Master Puṇṇa and, on that very day, honored him with the position of a Great Wealthy Treasurer (Mahādhana-seṭṭhi) along with grand royal regalia.

When the great treasurer Puṇṇa-sīha, also known as Dhana-seṭṭhi, held the auspicious ceremony for his appointment, he offered a great donation for seven days to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. On the seventh day, upon hearing the Buddha's discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), all three members of the family—(1) the great treasurer Puṇṇa, (2) his wife, and (3) his daughter Uttarā—were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and became Sotāpanna Ariyas. This is the account of the great treasurer Puṇṇa-sīha (who held the title Dhana-seṭṭhi), one of the five great treasurers of immeasurable wealth (amitabhoga) within the realm of King Bimbisāra's authority.

## The Great Treasurer Puṇṇa-sīha

## Becoming related by marriage to the (heretical) Great Treasurer Sumana

Later, the great treasurer of Rājagaha (Sumana) heard the news that "there is a grown daughter in the house of the great treasurer Puṇṇa." Wishing to marry her to his son, he sent a messenger to the house of the great treasurer Puṇṇa.
329: When the wealthy merchant Puṇṇasīha heard the message sent by the merchant Sumana, he replied firmly, "I cannot give my daughter under any circumstances." Sumana, unable to bear this due to his own pride as a merchant, sent another message: "Do you refuse to give me your daughter because you have suddenly become a high-ranking official after living under the shadow of my house?" Puṇṇasīha, refusing to yield, replied: "Even if what your master Sumana says about the current situation is true, one should not assume that a man will always remain in such a state (of poverty). Indeed, I am now capable of even taking people like Sumana as my servants. In truth, I am not disparaging the lineage or ancestry of the merchant Sumana; however, my daughter is a Sotāpanna Ariyasāvikā (a Noble Disciple of the Buddha) who daily offers flowers worth one kahāpaṇa to the Triple Gem. I can by no means send such a daughter to the house of one who holds wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) like you." Upon learning of Puṇṇasīha's firm refusal, Sumana softened his tone and sent another message: "I do not wish to destroy our long-standing friendship. I will arrange for flowers worth two kahāpaṇas daily for my daughter-in-law." Only then did the merchant Puṇṇasīha, being a grateful (kataññū) person,
330:
Therefore, he consented, saying, “Very well,” and sent his daughter Uttarā to the house of the merchant Sumana.

## Uttarā’s Great Faith and Desire

One day, Uttarā, the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇa, pleaded gently with her husband, the merchant’s son: “My lord, in my parents' house, I used to observe the eightfold Uposatha precepts regularly eight times a month. Now, if you would agree and accept, I wish to undertake and practice the eightfold Uposatha precepts.” The merchant’s son refused flatly, saying, “I cannot grant permission.” Uttarā, unable to make the merchant’s son gain the right understanding, had to remain silent. Another time, during the Vassa (rainy retreat), she planned to become an Uposatha observer and asked for permission again, but she still did not receive it.

When two and a half months of the three-month Vassa had passed and only half a month (15 days) remained, Uttarā sent a message to her parents: “Mother and Father, since you placed me in this cage called a household, I have not had the opportunity to undertake and practice the Uposatha precepts for even a single day during all this time. I would like you to send fifteen thousand (15,000) coins to me.” Upon hearing the news sent by their daughter, the parents did not even ask for the reason and sent the fifteen thousand (15,000) kyats/coins immediately.
331: Uttarā took those coins and sent for a courtesan named Sirimā (the sister of Jīvaka) in the city of Rājagaha. She said, "Sister Sirimā, I wish to observe the Uposatha for this half-month (15 days). I want you to take these fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas and attend to, care for, and entertain the merchant's son for these fifteen days." Sirimā accepted Uttarā's proposal, saying, "Very well, noble lady." From then on, the merchant's son, thinking "I shall enjoy myself with Sirimā," agreed to Uttarā's observance of the Uposatha for the half-month. Knowing that her husband had agreed, Uttarā, surrounded by her maidservants, personally prepared hard and soft foods for the Buddha every day. After offering them to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and after the Buddha had finished his meal and returned to the monastery, she would ascend to the noble mansion, undertake the Uposatha precepts, and sit reflecting on her own virtue (sīla). Thus, when the day arrived to conclude the fifteen-day Uposatha (the day after the full moon of Thadingyut), she was moving about early in the morning, personally supervising the cooking of rice gruel and other foods. "The nature of sensual objects is such that if used for a long time, due to the accumulation of negligence (pamāda), one regards another's property as one's own." (Dhammupadesa). At that time, the merchant's son, while enjoying himself with Sirimā in the mansion, opened the lattice window and stood looking into the courtyard.
332: At that moment, Uttarā happened to look up toward the lattice window. (Their eyes met). Looking at Uttarā, the merchant's son thought, "How like a woman of hell this Uttarā is! Abandoning such merchant's wealth, she wanders about aimlessly among the servants, soiled and stained with cooking pots, curry pots, and charcoal soot," and he smiled. Uttarā, knowing the merchant's son was negligent, reflected, "This fool must think his wealth will last forever," and she too smiled. Then Sirimā, becoming angry, thought, "This servant girl smiles at the master even while I am here!" and she ran downstairs. From the way Sirimā ran down, Uttarā realized, "This foolish woman, having stayed in this house for only half a month, has mistakenly come to think 'This is my house'." At that very moment, she entered into the attainment of loving-kindness (mettā-appanā-jhāna) and remained standing with her faculties composed. Sirimā ran through the servants, seized a ladle, scooped it full of boiling oil from a cauldron where cakes were being fried, and poured it with all her might over Uttarā's head. Because Uttarā had suffused herself with the jhāna of loving-kindness, the boiling oil poured over her head simply slid off like water poured onto a lotus leaf.
333: At that moment, Uttarā's maidservants who were standing near Sirimā looked at her and rebuked her to her face: "Hey, woman! You came here receiving a fee from our mistress, yet after staying in this house for fifteen days, you strive to act as if you were our mistress's equal!" Only then did the (negligent) Sirimā clearly realize and reflect that she was merely a guest. Having realized her mistake, Sirimā went and prostrated herself at Uttarā's feet, pleading, "Noble lady, I have acted wrongly without consideration. Please forgive me." Then Uttarā said, "Sister Sirimā, I cannot accept your apology here. I am a daughter who has a father. If you make my father, the Buddha, forgive you, then I shall forgive you." At that very moment, the Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, arrived and sat in the place prepared in Uttarā's home. Sirimā went to the Buddha, prostrated herself at his feet, and said, "Venerable Sir, I have committed a fault against the noble lady Uttarā. She says she will forgive me only if the Exalted One forgives me. O Blessed One of great glory, please forgive me." When the Buddha said, "Sirimā, I forgive you," Sirimā went to Uttarā and asked for her forgiveness as well. Furthermore, on that day, after hearing the Buddha's discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal—
334:
Akkodhena jine kodhaṃ, asādhuṃ sādhunā jine.
Jine kadariyaṃ dānena, saccenālikavādinaṃ.

Conquer anger with non-anger (metta); conquer the wicked with goodness. Conquer the stingy with giving; conquer the liar with truth.

At the end of this Dhamma verse, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and became a Sotāpanna Ariya. After becoming a Sotāpanna, Sirimā invited the Blessed One and, on the following day, offered a great alms-giving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. In this way, the life story of Uttarā, the merchant’s daughter, who was the mother of the youth named Nanda and thus called Nandamātā, arose.

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery and was appointing female lay disciples to Etadagga positions, he spoke in praise of Uttarā Nandamātā:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ jhāyīnaṃ yadidaṃ uttarā nandamātā — Monks, among my female lay disciples who are meditators (jhāyī), Uttarā Nandamātā is the foremost.”
335:
“Among my female lay disciples (sāvikā upāsikā) who are frequent practitioners of meditative absorption (jhāna), Uttarā the lay disciple, mother of the youth Nanda, is the foremost.”

With these words of praise, he placed her in the pre-eminent position (etadagga) of being “foremost among those who practice jhāna (jhāyī).”

This is the account of the lay disciple Uttarā Nandamātā.
**********
## (6) The Story of Princess Suppavāsā (Koliyan)

## (a) The Princess’s Past Deeds

This future Princess Suppavāsā of the Koliyan Sakyans was born into a noble family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha’s teaching, she saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay disciple to the pre-eminent position (etadagga) of being “foremost among those who give choice alms (paṇītadāyikā).” Inspired, she performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made an aspiration for that rank and position.

## (b) Becoming the Koliyan Sakyan Princess Suppavāsā in Her Final Life

That noble lady wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the period when this Buddha appeared, she was born as a Sakyan princess in the Koliyan country. She was named Suppavāsā. When Princess Suppavāsā reached the proper age, she married a Sakyan prince...
336:
336

While living as a housewife after following her husband to his home, she heard the Buddha's teaching upon her first meeting with Him and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). That Suppavāsā, the Sakyan princess, later gave birth to the youth Sīvali. (For the detailed account of this, one should refer to the Thera-apadāna section in the first part of this sixth volume, starting from page 305).

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

On one occasion, this Suppavāsā, the Koliyan Sakyan princess and mother of the Venerable Sīvali, offered and served various kinds of abundant and delicious choice food (paṇīta-bhojana) to the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head. After the Buddha had finished His meal and was delivering the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), He addressed Princess Suppavāsā:

"Bhojanaṃ Suppavāse dentī ariyasāvikā paṭiggahakānaṃ pañca ṭhānāni deti—Suppavāsā, a noble female disciple who gives food and nutriment gives five things to the recipients. She is said to give the gift of life (āyu), the gift of beauty (vaṇṇa), the gift of happiness (sukha), the gift of strength (bala), and the gift of intelligence and wit (paṭibhāna).

By giving the gift of life, she becomes a partaker of life—whether as a long-lived deity or a long-lived human. (etc.) By giving the gift of intelligence and wit, she becomes a partaker of intelligence and wit—whether as a wise deity or a wise human."
337:
337

This was the discourse He preached. Thus, the circumstances for conferring the Etadagga title arose.

Later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, He appointed the female lay disciples (upāsikās) to their respective foremost positions (Etadagga). Regarding this Suppavāsā Upāsikā, the daughter of the Koliyan Sakyan King, He declared:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ paṇītadāyikānaṃ yadidaṃ suppavāsā koliyadhīta—Monks, among my female lay disciples who give choice and exquisite things, Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyan Sakyan, is the foremost."

Thus, praising her, He placed her in the foremost position (Etadagga) as the "Foremost Giver of Choice Things" (Paṇītadāyikā).

This is the account of Princess Suppavāsā.

**********

## (7) The Account of Suppiyā Upāsikā

## (a) Suppiyā's Past Merit

This future Suppiyā Upāsikā was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's teaching, she saw the Buddha declare a certain laywoman as the foremost in "attending to sick monks" (gilānupaṭṭhākī). She then performed great meritorious deeds and made a resolution for that very position.
338:
“—the most excellent and supreme in providing extraordinary care,” she performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position.

## (b) Final Life as the Laywoman Suppiyā

That woman of good family wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time when this Blessed Buddha appeared, she was reborn as the daughter of a merchant in a wealthy family in the city of Vārāṇasī. She was named Suppiyā. When the merchant’s daughter Suppiyā reached maturity, she went to the house of a young man of good family named Suddhiya (and became the mistress of the house).

Later, the Blessed One, surrounded by a company of monks, arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī and resided at the Isipatana Migadāvuna monastery. When the merchant’s wife Suppiyā saw the Blessed One for the first time and heard the Dhamma, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry and became a Sotāpanna Ariya.

## Suppiyā’s Amazing Devotion in Alms-giving

One day, the laywoman Suppiyā went to the Migadāvuna monastery, and after listening to the Dhamma, she walked around the monastery cells. She found a monk who was weak and unwell after taking a purgative. She paid respects to him, spoke with him intimately, and asked, “Venerable sir, what should you receive for your health to be restored?” The sick monk replied, “Laywoman, it would be suitable if I could get some meat broth (māṃsarasa).”
339:
339

Suppiyā Upāsikā replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I shall send it to you." After paying respects and returning to the city, she sent her maidservant to the market the next day to obtain meat that was available (paṃsukūla-māṃsa, i.e., meat not specifically slaughtered for her). The maidservant searched the entire city but could not find any such meat and returned to inform Suppiyā Upāsikā.

Suppiyā, the merchant's wife, thought: "I have promised the Venerable Sir that I would send meat broth. If I do not send it because I cannot find meat, the Venerable Sir will not receive meat broth from elsewhere and will suffer greatly. I must do something to send it." Thinking thus, she went into her bedroom, cut a piece of flesh from her own thigh, and gave it to the maidservant, saying: "Dear girl, take this meat, mix it with the necessary ingredients for broth (such as ginger, onion, cumin, bay leaf, etc.), prepare the meat broth, and take it to the monastery to offer it to the sick monk. If that sick monk asks about me, tell him that I am unwell."

The maidservant did exactly as Suppiyā had instructed. The Buddha, knowing of this matter, went to Suppiyā Upāsikā's house the next day at the time of almsround, accompanied by a company of monks. (His visit was at the invitation of the lay disciple Suppiya, her husband).
340:
340

The Buddha sat on the prepared seat and engaged in a conversation with the lay disciple Suppiya as follows:

(Buddha)
"Where is the laywoman Suppiyā?"

(Suppiya)
"She is unwell, Blessed One."

(Buddha)
"Even if she is unwell, let her come."

(Suppiya)
"She is unable to come, Blessed One."

(Buddha)
"If she is unable to come, then bring her here, even by carrying her."

Then Suppiya carried Suppiyā and brought her. The moment Suppiyā Upāsikā saw the Buddha, that great wound healed, and new flesh, normal skin, and hair appeared. At that moment, both husband and wife exclaimed, "Friends, how wonderful is the greatness of the Buddha's power! How extraordinary! The moment she saw the Buddha, that great wound healed, and new flesh, normal skin, and hair appeared!" With joyful and uplifted minds, they served the Saṅgha with the Buddha at their head with exquisite food and offerings.

After the Buddha had finished His meal, He preached the Dhamma to Suppiya and Suppiyā and returned to the monastery. He then convened the Saṅgha of monks and, in that assembly, He asked:

(Buddha)
"Monks, who asked Suppiyā Upāsikā for meat?"
341:
341

(The Monk)
"Blessed One, I asked Suppiyā Upāsikā for meat."

(Buddha)
"Monk, was it delivered?"

(The Monk)
"It was delivered, Blessed One."

(Buddha)
"Monk, did you consume it?"

(The Monk)
"I did consume it, Blessed One."

(Buddha)
"Monk, did you inquire (what kind of meat it was)?"

(The Monk)
"I did not inquire, Blessed One."

Then the Buddha rebuked that monk in many ways and declared:

"Monks, people who have faith and devotion will even sacrifice their own flesh. Monks, human flesh is not to be eaten. For a monk who eats it, there is a Thullaccaya offense. Monks, meat should not be eaten without inquiring. For a monk who eats it, there is a Dukkaṭa offense."

Thus He laid down the training rule. (For the detailed account, one should refer to the Myanmar translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, starting from page 311). In this way, the circumstances for Suppiyā Upāsikā's Etadagga title arose.
342:
342

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

Later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, He appointed the female lay disciples to their respective foremost positions (Etadagga). Regarding this Suppiyā Upāsikā, He declared:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ gilānupaṭṭhākīnaṃ yadidaṃ suppiyā upāsikā—Monks, among my female lay disciples who attend to the sick, Suppiyā Upāsikā is the foremost."

Thus, praising her, He placed her in the foremost position (Etadagga) as the "Foremost Attendant to the Sick" (Gilānupaṭṭhākī).

This is the account of Suppiyā Upāsikā.

## (8) The Account of Kātiyānī Upāsikā

## (a) The Upāsikā's Past Merit

This future Kātiyānī Upāsikā was born into a good family (a merchant's family) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Seeing the Buddha declare a certain laywoman as the foremost in "unwavering confidence in the Dispensation" (aveccappasanna), she felt inspired, performed great meritorious deeds, and made a resolution for that very position.

## (b) Final Life as the Merchant's Daughter Kātiyānī

Having wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was born as a merchant's daughter in the city of Kuraraghara during the time this Buddha appeared.
343:
343

Her parents named her "Kātiyānī." When the merchant's daughter Kātiyānī reached maturity, she became very close friends with the merchant's wife Kāḷī, who was the mother of the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa (as mentioned in the Thera-apadāna section below).

## The Unwavering Faith of the Merchant's Daughter Kātiyānī

Later, when the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa returned from the presence of the Buddha, his mother, the merchant's wife Kāḷī, requested him, "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to me just as you recited it to the Buddha." Accordingly, during the night, he sat on the decorated Dhamma-throne (dhammāsana) in the preaching pavilion in the center of Kuraraghara and began to preach the Dhamma, with his mother Kāḷī seated before him as the primary listener. At that time, this merchant's daughter Kātiyānī went along with Kāḷī and stood at the edge of the assembly, listening to the Dhamma with great respect.

At that same time, five hundred thieves, following the marks they had made during the day, dug a tunnel from the edge of the city and reached the house of this merchant's daughter Kātiyānī. Then the thief leader (bandit chief), instead of entering the tunnel with his subordinates, went to the place where the Venerable Soṇa was preaching to investigate why the crowd had gathered. He stood at the edge of the assembly, right behind Kātiyānī.

At that moment, Kātiyānī said to her maidservant, "Go, girl, enter the house and bring some oil for the lamps. We shall light the lamps and continue listening to the Dhamma."
344: (According to the Sinhalese version) 'Let us light the lamps, friends, and share in the merit of our friend Kāḷī,' she said and sent her. That maid reached the house and saw the thieves (dacoits) inside the tunnel. She did not dare even to take the oil for the lamps and returned to the Dhamma assembly, telling her mistress, 'Mistress, thieves (dacoits) have dug a tunnel into the house and are staying there.' The thief leader heard these words and thought, 'If this merchant woman Kātyāyanī follows her maid's words and goes to her house, I will cut her into two pieces with my sword right here. But if she continues to listen to the Dhamma with the same focused attention as before, I will have the stolen goods returned.' Kātyāyanī, upon hearing the maid's words, said, 'Dear, do not make a sound; be quiet. If thieves steal, they will only take the physical objects they see. I am now listening to the Dhamma, which is very difficult to hear. Dear, do not create an obstacle to the Dhamma (dhammantarāya).' The thief leader, hearing Kātyāyanī's words from behind, reflected, 'If we steal the property from the house of one who remains with such great wholesome intention and disposition, we will surely sink into the great earth; we will certainly be swallowed by the earth.' Thinking thus, he immediately went to Kātyāyanī's house, made the thieves leave all the stolen goods, and then came with the thieves to listen to the Dhamma, standing at the edge of the assembly.
345:
The lay disciple Kātiyānī, the treasurer’s wife, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) at the conclusion of the Dhamma discourse by the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa; she became a Sotāpanna. Then, at dawn, the bandit leader bowed down at the feet of the lay disciple Kātiyānī and pleaded, “Noble Lady, please forgive all of us.” When Kātiyānī asked, “What offense have you committed against me?” the bandit leader recounted all the crimes he had committed and intended to commit. Kātiyānī said, “Friends, if that is so, I forgive you.” The bandit leader then said, “O Noble Lady, it is not enough to be forgiven merely by words. Indeed, we wish for all five hundred of us to be ordained as monks under your son, the noble Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.” The lay disciple Kātiyānī took all five hundred bandits and had them ordained under the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, acting as their sponsor. Those five hundred bandits, having been ordained under the Elder, strove and practiced the Dhamma diligently, and all five hundred of them attained the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala); they became Arahants. Thus arose this story concerning the unwavering faith (aveccappasāda) and confidence of the lay disciple Kātiyānī in the Dispensation.

## (c) Receiving the Pre-eminent Title

Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery, he was sequentially appointing lay disciples...
346:
When the Buddha was conferring the titles of Etadagga (the foremost), He praised the female lay disciple Kātiyānī, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ aveccappasannānaṃ yadidaṃ kātiyānī = Monks, among my female lay disciples who possess unwavering faith, Kātiyānī is the foremost.”

Thus, He appointed her to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) in the category of “those with unwavering faith” (aveccappasanna).

This is the account of the female lay disciple Kātiyānī.
**********
## (9) The Account of the Female Lay Disciple Nakulamātā
(The account of this female lay disciple Nakulamātā should be understood according to the method already described in the section on male lay disciples, Chapter 10—The Account of the Male Lay Disciple Nakulapitā. Specifically, in the place of Nakulapitā, Nakulamātā should be understood as the primary subject.)

Both the husband and wife, Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā, lived during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Just as the future Nakulapitā, as a young man of good family, saw the Padumuttara Buddha appoint a male lay disciple to the Etadagga position of being the most intimate (vissāsaka) and performed great meritorious deeds to aspire for that position, the future Nakulamātā, as a young woman of good family, also saw the Padumuttara Buddha appoint a female lay disciple to the Etadagga position of being the most intimate (vissāsikā) and performed great meritorious deeds to aspire for that position. Since the story follows a similar course, it is not explained in detail in the Commentary.

This Nakulamātā, just like Nakulapitā, was addressed by the Blessed One as: “Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ
347:
upāsikānaṃ vissāsi-kānaṃ yadidaṃ nakulamātā gahapatānī = Monks, among my female lay disciples who are intimate and familiar (vissāsikā), the Treasurer's wife Nakulamātā is the foremost.” Thus, she received the appointment to the Etadagga position in the category of being intimate.

This is the account of the female lay disciple Nakulamātā.
**********
## (10) The Account of the Female Lay Disciple Kāḷī of Kuraraghara
## (a) The Past Merit of the Upāsikā
The future Kāḷī Upāsikā was also a daughter of a good family (a Treasurer's daughter) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's discourse, she saw the Padumuttara Buddha appoint a female lay disciple to the Etadagga position of “Anussavappasanna = those who possess faith through hearsay, having gained confidence in the Buddha's virtues by hearing about Him without having seen Him personally.” Inspired to emulate her, she performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that pre-eminent position.

## (b) Becoming the Treasurer's Daughter Kāḷī in Her Final Birth
That daughter of good family wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time when this Buddha appeared, she was born as the daughter of a Treasurer in the city of Rājagaha. Her parents named her “Kāḷī.”

When the Treasurer's daughter Kāḷī reached the age of maturity, she was married to a family in the city of Kuraraghara in the Avanti Dakkhināpatha region (Southern India).
348: ...a merchant's son living in the city of Kuraraghara in the Avanti Dakkhiṇāpatha region (Southern India), and she had to go to the house of that merchant's son in Kuraraghara. Later, the young merchant's wife Kāḷī became pregnant. When her pregnancy reached maturity, she reflected, 'It is not appropriate to give birth in the home of others in a distant land, away from one's parents.' She returned to her parents' home in her birthplace, Rājagaha. One night at midnight (at the midnight hour of the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era, the day the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta was preached), she heard the conversation of the Deva Kings Sātāgira and Hemavata, who were standing in the sky above her palace discussing the virtues of the Triple Gem. Through hearsay, she repeatedly developed faith in the Dispensation and, without having seen the Buddha, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala); she became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). (These events have been fully described on page 457 of the second volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas; they should be reviewed and noted from there.) That woman Kāḷī was the first among women and noble ladies to become a Stream-enterer and a noble disciple (ariyasāvikā), becoming like an elder sister among the women. That very night, Kāḷī gave birth to a son (the future Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa). After staying at her parents' home as long as she wished, she returned to Kuraraghara.
349:
## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title
Later, while the Blessed One was seated gracefully among the monks at the Jetavana monastery, conferring various Etadagga titles upon the female lay disciples, He spoke concerning Kāḷī, the Treasurer's wife of Kuraraghara:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvikānaṃ upāsikānaṃ anussavappasannānaṃ yadidaṃ kāḷī upāsikā kuraraghari-kā = Monks, among my female lay disciples who possess faith through hearsay (anussavappasanna), the Treasurer's wife Kāḷī of Kuraraghara is the foremost.”

Thus, praising her, He appointed her to the Etadagga position in the category of “those with faith through hearsay.”

This is the account of Kāḷီ Upāsikā of Kuraraghara.
