## Appendix
## Accounts of the Treasurers of Immense Wealth (Amitabhoga)
## (1) The Account of the Treasurer Jotika
## (a) His Life as a Sugarcane Field Owner
In the distant past (before the time of Vipassī Buddha, ninety-one aeons ago from this present aeon), there were two brothers who were householders in the city of Bārāဏasī. They had their workers plant a sugarcane field. One day, the younger brother went to the sugarcane field and thought, “I will give one stalk to my elder brother, and one will be for me.” He cut two sugarcane stalks and, to prevent the juice from leaking out, he tied the cut ends with leaves and other materials before carrying them back.

In those days, there was no need to crush sugarcane with machinery as is done today. When a sugarcane stalk was cut from the base or the tip and held up, the juice would flow out spontaneously, just as water drips from a water-strainer (dhammakaraka).

As the householder was returning home with the two sugarcane stalks, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana in the Himālayas arose from meditative attainment (samāpatti). Reflecting, “Whom shall I bless today?”, he saw the younger brother in his net of knowledge and, knowing the householder's capacity to perform an act of generosity (dāna-sangaha), he took his bowl and robes and arrived there by psychic power.
351:
He stood before the householder. Upon seeing the Paccekabuddha, the householder was filled with devotion. He spread his upper robe on a high piece of ground and said, "Venerable Sir, please sit here." After seating the Paccekabuddha, he requested, "Venerable Sir, please tilt your bowl slightly." He then untied the bundle of sugarcane stalks and pressed them over the bowl. The sugarcane juice flowed out naturally and filled the bowl.

After the Paccekabuddha had consumed the sugarcane juice, the householder thought, "It is truly wonderful that the Venerable One has consumed my sugarcane juice. If my elder brother wants the price, I shall give him the price. If he wants the share of merit, I shall give him the share of merit. (I shall also offer the sugarcane juice I brought for my brother)." Having thought thus, he requested, "Venerable Sir, please tilt your bowl toward me a little," and untying the second bundle of sugarcane, he poured and offered that juice as well. (In this matter, the elder brother did not know what he had brought for him. Nevertheless, the householder's mind was free from any deceit or crookedness, thinking only, 'My brother will take and eat other sugarcane from the field').

Since the Paccekabuddha had already consumed the first portion (of the juice from the first stalk), he did not consume the second offering of juice but remained seated, intending to share it with other Paccekabuddhas.
352:
Wishing to share the second offering of sugarcane juice with other Paccekabuddhas, he merely accepted it and remained seated without consuming it. The householder, perceiving the Paccekabuddha's intention, paid homage with the five-fold prostration and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this offering of excellent sugarcane juice, may I enjoy prosperity in the celestial and human worlds, and in my final existence, may I attain the same Dhamma that you have realized and witnessed."

The Paccekabuddha said, "Evaṃ hotu—May it be as you have aspired," and after performing the appreciation (anumodanā) with the two verses beginning with "Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ," he made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) so that the householder could see him, and traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana. There, he offered the sugarcane juice to five hundred fellow Paccekabuddhas.

After witnessing that miracle, the younger brother went to the elder brother. When the elder brother asked, "Where have you been?" he replied, "I went to see whether the sugarcane field was doing well or not." Then the elder brother rebuked him, saying, "What is the use of someone like you going to the sugarcane field? (He rebuked him because he brought no sugarcane). Truly, should you not have brought a stalk or two?" The younger brother then said, "O brother, I did take two stalks. However, I met a Paccekabuddha on the way. After offering the juice from my own stalk to him,
353:
I thought, 'I will give my brother either the price he desires or the share of the merit,' and so I also offered the juice from the stalk I brought for you to that Paccekabuddha. How is it? Will you take the price of the sugarcane brought for you, or will you take the share of the merit?" he asked honestly.

Then the elder brother asked, "What did the Paccekabuddha do?" The younger brother replied exactly as he had seen, "O brother, the Paccekabuddha consumed the juice from my stalk, but he took the juice from your stalk respectfully and traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana to offer it to five hundred Paccekabuddhas."

Even as the younger brother was speaking, the elder brother was overwhelmed with a surge of joy (pīti) throughout his body. He made an aspiration, saying, "May I alone attain that extraordinary Dhamma realized by that Paccekabuddha!" Thus, the younger brother aspired for the three types of attainments—human, celestial, and Nibbāna. The elder brother, with a single aim, aspired for the Fruit of Arahatship. This was the previous meritorious deed of those two brothers.

## Their Lives as Brothers Again
Those two brothers lived out their life span, and when they passed away from that life, they were reborn in the celestial world. Between the times of Phussa Buddha and Vipassī Buddha, they spent an interval of an incalculable aeon (buddhantara asaṅkhyeyya kappa)
354:
only in the celestial world. While those two were residing in the celestial world, Vipassī Buddha appeared in the world. Those two also passed away from the celestial world and were reborn in the city of Bandhumatī in the house of a wealthy householder of good family. The elder brother remained the elder, and the younger brother remained the younger. The parents named the elder brother Sena and the younger brother Aparājita.

When the two brothers reached adulthood and were well-established in their households, they heard the voice of the Dhamma-ghosaka (the Dhamma announcer) roaming through the city of Bandhumatī, proclaiming: "O virtuous ones! The Buddha-treasure, the Dhamma-treasure, and the Sangha-treasure have appeared in the world like the sun and the moon. Give alms! Perform meritorious deeds! Today is the eighth day, the Aṭṭhamī Uposatha day. Today is the fourteenth day, the Cātuddasī Uposatha day. Today is the fifteenth day, the Pannarasī Uposatha day. Observe the Uposatha! Listen to the Dhamma!" Seeing the multitude of people giving alms in the morning and going to listen to the Dhamma in the afternoon, the elder brother, Sena the householder, asked, "Where are you all going?" When the people replied, "We are going to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha," he said, "Let me follow as well." He went along with the crowd and sat at the edge of the assembly to listen to the Dhamma.
355:
Vipassī Buddha, knowing the inclination and disposition of Sena the householder, preached the graduated discourse, such as the discourse on giving (dānakathā) and the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā). After Sena the householder heard the Buddha's Dhamma, a very intense effort to ordain arose in him. He requested Vipassī Buddha to ordain him. Then the Buddha asked, "Lay disciple, do you have relatives who should be asked for permission?" When Sena replied, "I have, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "If that is so, come back after asking permission from your relatives."

That night, Sena the householder went to his younger brother, Aparājita the householder, and the two brothers consulted as follows:

(Sena)
"Dear brother, let all the wealth and property in this house be yours."

(Aparājita)
"Noble brother, and what will you do?"

(Sena)
"I shall ordain in the presence of the Buddha."

(Aparājita)
"Noble brother, what are you saying? After our mother passed away, I found in you a mother; after our father passed away, I found in you a father. This house has many resources. We can perform meritorious deeds while remaining in the house. Please do not ordain like this."
356:
(Sena)
"I have heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha. One who remains in the midst of a household is unable to fulfill that Dhamma. Therefore, I shall certainly ordain. Dear brother, you remain here."

Sena the householder spoke thus, and after making his younger brother Aparājita turn back, he was initiated in the presence of Vipassī Buddha. Later, he attained full ordination. By practicing and striving in the Dhamma of a monk, he reached the Fruit of Arahatship before long and became an Arahant.

## The Construction and Offering of the Gandhakuṭī
The younger brother, Aparājita the householder, thinking, "I shall celebrate my brother's initiation and ordination," offered alms to the Sangha headed by the Buddha for seven days. Then, paying respectful homage to his elder brother, the Venerable Sena, he said, "Venerable Sir, you have completed the work for your own liberation. As for me, I am bound by the five cords of sensual pleasure and am unable to renounce the world to ordain. I wish for you to tell me of a great meritorious deed that would be suitable for me while I remain at home." Then the Venerable Sena advised Aparājita, "Very well, very well, wise man. Build and offer a Gandhakuṭī (Perfumed Chamber) for the Buddha."

Aparājita the younger brother accepted, saying, "Very well." He had various types of timber brought and had them sawn and split for pillars and other parts.
357:
He had pillars made and adorned with the seven kinds of jewels—one pillar adorned with gold, one with silver, one with rubies, and so on. With these pillars, he had a great Gandhakuṭī built, and he had the great chamber roofed with tiles also adorned with the seven kinds of jewels.

## The Nephew Aparājita Offers a Portico
Specifically, while the great brick Gandhakuṭī was being built, a nephew of the same name (the son of his sister), also called Aparājita, came to the householder Aparājita and requested, "Uncle, I also wish to perform a meritorious deed. I would like you to give me a share in this merit." The uncle, Aparājita the householder, rejected him plainly, saying, "I cannot give it, nephew. I shall perform a meritorious deed that is not shared with others."

Although the nephew Aparājita requested many times, he could not obtain a share in the great brick Gandhakuṭī by any means. He then thought, "It would be best if I could get the portico (reception hall) directly in front of the great brick Gandhakuṭī," and he had a portico made of the seven kinds of jewels constructed. This nephew Aparājita became the great merchant Meṇḍaka during the time of our Buddha. (The details of this story will become clear later).
358:
## The Scenery and Splendor of the Great Gandhakuṭီ Brick Monastery
Notably, in the great Gandhakuṭī brick monastery, there were three large windows made of the seven kinds of gems. Directly in front of these three large windows, the householder Aparājita had three square ponds constructed on the ground, finished smoothly with plaster. He had them filled with water scented with four types of perfumes and planted five kinds of lotuses in these three ponds, intending for the lotus pollen, carried by the wind, to be sprinkled upon the Blessed One while He sat inside the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery.

The layers of the four sides of the Gandhakuṭī monastery's pinnacle (thūpikā) were made of red-gold plates, and the crest was made of coral. The roofing tiles below the pinnacle were made of emerald. Thus, the pinnacle of the great Gandhakuṭī brick monastery was as beautiful as a dancing peacock. Furthermore, the donor of the Gandhakuṭī monastery, the householder Aparājita, took gems that were suitable for setting and those that were not (using them in their raw, solid form) and filled the entire precinct surrounding the Gandhakuṭī monastery with the seven kinds of gems to a height nearly reaching the knees.

## Offering the Great Gandhakuṭီ Brick Monastery to the Buddha
Having thus completed and beautified the great Gandhakuṭī brick monastery, the donor, householder Aparājita, went to his elder brother, the Venerable Sena Thera.
359:
—and addressed him: “Venerable Sir, the great Gandhakuṭī brick monastery is now complete. I desire that the Blessed One make use of this brick monastery. I have heard that great merit arises from such use, Bhante.” The elder brother, Venerable Sena Thera, went to the Blessed One and said: “Exalted Buddha, this merchant Aparājita has completed the construction of the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery for the sake of the Blessed One. He now desires that the Blessed One make use of it.”

The Blessed One Vipassī rose from His seat and proceeded toward the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery. Looking at the heap of seven kinds of gems scattered throughout the precinct to a height almost knee-deep, He stood only at the entrance. Although the merchant Aparājita invited Him, saying, “Blessed One, please enter,” the Blessed One did not enter but remained standing at that very entrance. When invited for the third time, He looked at the merchant’s elder brother, the Venerable Sena Thera.

The Thera, understanding the Blessed One’s intention by His manner of looking, instructed his younger brother, the merchant: “Go, dear brother, and say to the Blessed One: ‘The responsibility of guarding it shall be mine alone; may the Blessed One dwell comfortably as He wishes.’” Upon hearing the Thera’s words, the merchant approached the Blessed One with the fivefold prostration—
360:
—and addressed Him: “Blessed One, just as people enter the shade of a tree and then depart without any lingering concern, or just as they cross to the other side of a river and abandon the raft without concern, even so, may the Blessed One dwell comfortably as He wishes, without any concern or anxiety whatsoever.”

(In this regard, one might ask: “Why did the Blessed One remain standing without entering the monastery?” The answer is: The Blessed One reflected, “Many people come to the Buddha in the morning and in the afternoon. If those people were to pick up the gems and leave, I could not forbid them. If the monastery donor, the merchant Aparājita, were to harbor resentment toward Me, thinking, ‘Even though so many gems are scattered within the monastery precinct and he sees his own attendants stealing them, the Buddha does not forbid it,’ he would be headed for the states of misery (apāya).” Therefore, He remained standing. This is the answer.)

When the merchant Aparājita thus addressed Him (taking responsibility), saying, “Blessed One, the guarding shall be my responsibility alone; may the Blessed One dwell in comfort,” the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery. The merchant donor of the monastery then stationed guards around the area and instructed them: “Friends, forbid those who take gems away in their laps, baskets, or bags. However, do not forbid those who take them away by the handful.”
361:
Within the city, the monastery donor, the merchant Aparājita, also had a proclamation made from house to house: “I have scattered the seven kinds of gems knee-deep within the precinct of the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery. Let the poor who return from listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One take two handfuls of gems. Let the wealthy also take one handful of gems.” The merchant’s intention was this: “Those with faith will surely go because they wish to hear the Dhamma. Those without faith will also go out of greed for wealth, and by hearing the Dhamma, they will be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra).” It was for the sake of benefiting the multitude that he had this proclamation made.

Following the merchant Aparājita’s words, the people took the gems—the poor by two handfuls and the wealthy by one handful. When the gems scattered the first time were exhausted, he scattered them a second time to the same knee-deep height. When those were exhausted, he scattered them a third time to the same knee-deep height.

Furthermore, the merchant Aparājita thought, “For the people who behold both the golden radiance emanating from the Blessed One’s body and the radiance of the precious gem, it will be an experience they can never have enough of.” With this thought, he placed at the feet of the Blessed One a priceless great precious gem the size of a large cucumber.
362:
The multitude of people, just as the householder had intended, gazed upon the radiance of the Buddha's body and the radiance of the precious gems with insatiable delight.

## A Brahmin Openly Stealing the Great Gem
One day, a Brahmin of wrong view thought, “It is said that a very valuable precious gem is placed at the feet of the Buddha. I will steal that gem.” With this intention, he went to the monastery and entered before the Buddha from among the people who had come to pay their respects. The donor of the monastery, the householder, sensed the Brahmin's dishonest manner of entry and realized, “He wants to steal the gem.” He thought, “Oh, it would be good if this Brahmin does not steal the gem.”

However, the Brahmin, as if bowing to the Blessed One, lowered his hands to the Buddha's feet, picked up the large gem, hid it in his waist-cloth, and walked away. The donor, householder Aparājita, could not maintain a clear and peaceful mind regarding the Brahmin's action. After the Buddha had finished preaching the Dhamma, he approached the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, three times I have scattered the seven kinds of gems to a height nearly reaching the knees throughout the entire precinct of the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery. My mind never felt any dissatisfaction toward the people who took those gems; instead, my faith and clarity only increased. Today, however, I thought, ‘Oh, if only this Brahmin...’"
363:
“If I do not steal the great gem, it would be good,” I thought, yet when that Brahmin stole the great gem and left, I could not keep my mind clear in any way, Bhante,” he addressed.

## Aparājita the Householder Following the Buddha's Guidance
## Making an Aspiration

Upon hearing the householder's words, Vipassī Buddha gave a subtle hint: “Lay follower, are you not able to act so that others cannot steal or destroy your property?” The householder, following the guidance given by the Buddha, paid homage with deep respect and made this aspiration:

“Bhante, starting from today, may it be that even a single thread of a fringe of my property cannot be taken, plundered, or stolen by hundreds of kings or thieves through force or intimidation. May hundreds of kings and thieves be unable to seize, plunder, or steal it. May fire not burn my property, and may water not wash it away.”

Thus he made his aspiration. The Buddha then gave the blessing of appreciation (anumodanā) to the householder, saying, “Evaṃ hotu—May it be as you have now aspired.” When Aparājita the householder held the water-pouring ceremony for the Gandhakuṭī brick monastery, there were 6,800,000 monks...
364:
For nine months, he offered a great donation to six million eight hundred thousand monks within the monastery grounds. On the day the water-pouring ceremony for the donation was completed, he offered a set of triple robes (ti-cīvara) to each of the monks. Even the cloth intended for the robes offered to the youngest monk was worth one hundred thousand.

## The Final Life as Jotika the Treasurer

That householder Aparājita, the donor of the monastery, performed meritorious deeds in this manner throughout his life. After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. For a long period of ninety-one aeons, he did not fall into the four woeful states. During the time when our Supreme Buddha appeared in the world, he took conception in the womb of a treasurer’s wife in a household of the treasurer class in the city of Rājagaha, where he remained for nine and a half months. On the day this son of the treasurer was born, all the weapons throughout the city of Rājagaha blazed brilliantly like a roaring fire. The ornaments worn on the bodies of all the people also emitted radiance as if they were releasing flames. Thus, the entire city of Rājagaha was filled with a solid mass of brilliant light.

The father of the child, the treasurer, went early to pay his respects to King Bimbisāra. At that time, King Bimbisāra and the treasurer questioned and answered each other as follows:

(The King)
“Today, all weapons are blazing with brilliance, and the entire city is filled with a solid mass of light. Do you, Treasurer, know the reason for this?”
365:
(The Treasurer)
“I know, Your Majesty.”

(The King)
“For what reason, Great Treasurer?”

(The Treasurer)
“A servant of Your Majesty has been born in my house. It is due to the power of the merit of my son that this (the entire city being covered in brilliance) has occurred.”

(The King)
“Treasurer, how is it? Will that son of yours be a thief?”

(The Treasurer)
“Your Majesty, there is no reason for my son to be a thief. He is one of great glory and possesses extraordinary merit performed in the past.”

(The King)
“If that is so, it is proper to look after and raise that child well. Let these one thousand coins be for the child’s milk-money.”

Having spoken thus, King Bimbisāra ordered one thousand coins to be given daily as milk-money. Later, on the day the child was named, he was given the name “Jotika Kumāra” (Young Jotika) because of the solid mass of brilliant, flickering light that had appeared throughout the city.

## Sakka Creating the Mansion for Jotika the Treasurer

Later, when Jotika Kumāra reached the age of maturity, the ground was cleared to build a house for him. At that moment, Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of becoming hot. When Sakka investigated, thinking, “Why has this (the heating of the Paṇḍukambala) happened?”, he realized that they were taking a site for Jotika’s house.
366:
Knowing this, Sakka thought, “This Jotika is not one who should live in a house built by those men. It is proper that I go to that place.” Having so planned, he went to that place in the guise of a carpenter and asked, “Friends, what work are you doing?” When the people replied, “We are taking a site for a house for Jotika Kumāra,” Sakka said, “Friends, move aside. This Jotika the Treasurer is not one who should live in a house built by you.” He then gazed intently at a plot of land sixteen karīsa in extent. At that very moment, that plot of land became as level as a kasiṇa-disk. (1)

Sakka then thought, “Let a seven-storied palace made of the seven kinds of gems emerge here, breaking through the earth,” and he gazed intently again. At that very moment, a seven-storied palace emerged, breaking through the earth. (2)

Sakka then thought, “Let seven walls made of the seven kinds of gems appear surrounding this great palace,” and he gazed intently again. At that very moment, seven great walls made of the seven kinds of gems emerged, breaking through the earth. (3)

Then Sakka thought, “Let wish-fulfilling trees (padesā-bin) appear in the intervals between the seven walls,” and he gazed intently again. At that very moment, wish-fulfilling trees appeared just as Sakka had intended. (4)

Then again, Sakka thought, “Let four great golden pots appear at the four corners of the seven-storied palace,”
367:
and he gazed intently again. Everything happened exactly as Sakka had intended. (Specifically, the size of the mouths of the four great golden pots that appeared for the Bodhisatta: one was one yojana, another was three gāvutas, another was two gāvutas, and another was one gāvuta in diameter. They reached down to the edge of the great earth. The size of the mouths of the four great golden pots that appeared for Jotika the Treasurer is not specifically explained in the ancient Commentaries. All four appeared full of gems, like palm fruits placed across the mouth; this is the distinction). (5)

At the four corners of the palace, four great golden sugarcane trees grew, with trunks the size of young palm trees. The leaves of these sugarcane trees were made of emeralds, and the stems were made of gold. These great sugarcane trees appeared to manifest the past meritorious deeds of Jotika the Treasurer. (6)

At the seven gates, seven Yakkha generals took up guard (i.e., they protected the gates). (1) At the first gate, the Yakkha general named Yamakoḷī guarded together with his retinue of one thousand (1,000) Yakkhas. (2) At the second gate, the Yakkha general named Uppala together with his retinue of two thousand (2,000) Yakkhas. (3) At the third gate, the Yakkha general named Vajira together with his retinue of three thousand (3,000) Yakkhas. (4) At the fourth gate, the Yakkha general named Vajirabāhu together with his retinue of four thousand (4,000) Yakkhas.
368:
(5) At the fifth gate, the Yakkha general named Kasakanda stood guard together with his retinue of five thousand (5,000) Yakkhas. (6) At the sixth gate, the Yakkha general named Kaṭattha stood guard together with his retinue of six thousand (6,000) Yakkhas. (7) At the seventh gate, the Yakkha general named Disāmukha stood guard together with his retinue of seven thousand (7,000) Yakkhas.

Yamakoḷī ca uppalo,
Vajiro vajirabāhu.
Kasakando kaṭattho ca,
Disāmukho ca sattamo.
Ete gaṇhiṃsu ārakkhaṃ,
Jotikassa nivesane. (Verse of spontaneous inspiration)

## King Bimbisāra Appointing Him as Treasurer by Sending the White Umbrella
Upon hearing the news that “a seven-storied mansion made of the seven kinds of gems has emerged from the earth for the young Jotika, along with seven walls, seven gates, and four large jars of gold,” King Bimbisāra sent the white umbrella of a Treasurer and the ceremonial regalia to Jotika. From that time on, the young man became famous as “Treasurer Jotika.”

## Deities Bringing the Treasurer's Wife Satulakāyီ from the Northern Island
The woman who had performed meritorious deeds together with Treasurer Jotika was at that time living in the island of Uttarakuru.
369:
When Jotika Kumāra became the Treasurer, deities brought that woman of the Northern Continent, “Satulakāyī,” who was his partner in merit, from the Northern Continent and placed her in the auspicious chamber of Jotika’s seven-storied mansion. When the Treasurer’s wife, Satulakāyī, came from the Northern Continent, she brought only one salay of rice and three fire-stones. For that couple, rice was produced from that single salay of rice throughout their lives. Even if people were to pour a hundred cartloads of rice (into that vessel), that one salay of rice would remain as exactly one salay. (How wonderful!)

When they wished to cook rice, they would put the rice in a pot and place it on top of the three fire-stones. At that moment, the stones would blaze brilliantly, and as soon as the rice was cooked, the flames would extinguish. By the sign of the fire extinguishing, they knew that the rice was cooked. When cooking curries and so on, it was the same way. Thus, for Jotika the Treasurer and his wife, food was cooked only by means of those fire-stones. (They did not have to cook with firewood, etc.). They lived only by the light of emerald gems; they knew nothing of the light of fire or the light of oil lamps.

The news that “The wealth and luxury of Jotika the Great Treasurer is indeed so magnificent” spread throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Multitudes of people prepared their vehicles and came in a constant stream to see the wealth of Jotika the Treasurer. Whenever people came, Jotika the Treasurer had them fed with rice from the Northern Continent cooked on the fire-stones.
370: "Take whatever clothes and ornaments you desire from the wish-fulfilling trees, O friends and mothers," they were urged. Furthermore, opening the mouth of a large gold pot measuring a gāvuta, they were encouraged, "Take as much gold, silver, and wealth as you need, O friends and mothers." Even though all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa took as much gold and silver as they desired and returned, the large gold pot did not decrease even by a finger's breadth; it remained as full as ever. This occurrence was the result of the meritorious deed of the householder Aparajita—who later became the treasurer Jotika—when he had white sand spread within the precinct of the great brick monastery of the Gandhakuṭī and gave alms by scattering the seven kinds of jewels knee-deep three times. ## King Bimbisāra Visiting to View Jotika’s Mansion While the multitude of people were taking clothes, ornaments, wealth, gold, and silver as they desired, King Bimbisāra wished to view Jotika’s mansion but did not have the opportunity as the crowds were still coming. Later, when those who took what they desired had left and the number of visitors had dwindled, King Bimbisāra said to the great treasurer, Jotika’s father, "We wish to see your son’s mansion." The father treasurer replied, "Very well, your Majesty," and went to his son, saying, "Dear son, the King wishes to view your mansion." The son, Jotika the treasurer, also accepted, saying, "Very well, father. Let the King come."
371:
King Bimbisāra, accompanied by a large retinue, went to the mansion of Jotika the Treasurer. At the first gateway, a maidservant who was sweeping and discarding rubbish reached out her hand to the King. The King, thinking she was the Treasurer’s wife, felt embarrassed and did not place his hand upon her arm. In the same manner, at the other gateways, he mistook the maidservants for the Treasurer’s wife and did not place his hand upon their arms. (In this way, even the maidservants in Jotika’s mansion were so magnificent and beautiful that they could be mistaken for the Treasurer’s wife).

Jotika the Treasurer came out to welcome the King, paid him respectful homage, and followed behind the King, saying, “Please proceed ahead, Your Majesty.” To the King, the floor paved with emeralds appeared like a deep chasm a hundred cubits deep. The King, misunderstood and thought, “This Treasurer Jotika has dug a great pit to capture me,” and did not dare to step forward. Jotika the Treasurer said, “Your Majesty, this is not a pit; please follow after me,” and he walked ahead of the King. Only when Jotika the Treasurer stepped forward did the King tread upon the emerald floor, and starting from the ground floor, he toured and inspected the mansion.

**The Thought of the Young Prince Ajātasattu**
At that time, the young Prince Ajātasattu, while walking along holding his father’s finger, thought: “Oh, how foolish and ignorant my father is! This householder, who is of a lower caste than us, lives in a great mansion made of the seven kinds of jewels, while my father, though a true universal monarch, lives in a palace made of wood. If I were to become King, I would by no means allow this Treasurer to live in such a great jewel mansion.”
372:
For the King, while he was ascending to the upper floors of the mansion, the time for the morning meal arrived. The King said to Jotika the Treasurer, “Great Treasurer, we shall eat our morning meal right here.” Jotika the Treasurer replied, “I understand, Your Majesty; the morning meal has already been prepared for Your Majesty.”

Then, King Bimbisāra bathed with sixteen pots of scented water and sat upon the Treasurer’s own throne prepared within the pavilion where Jotika resided. At that time, after giving the King water to wash his hands, they first brought and placed before the King soft milk-rice (pāyāsa) in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand. The King, thinking it was the food to be eaten, prepared to eat it. Then Jotika the Treasurer said, “Your Majesty, this is not yet for consumption; this is only soft milk-rice prepared to provide a pleasant aroma.” Only after saying this did Jotika’s attendants bring rice cooked from Uttarakuru grain in another golden bowl worth a hundred thousand and placed it on top of the previous golden bowl of milk-rice. (It is said that by doing so, the steam from the milk-rice in the lower bowl continuously warmed the Uttarakuru rice in the upper bowl, making it hot and pleasant to eat from beginning to end).
373: When the King ate the extremely sweet and delicious Uttarakuru rice, he did not know the limit (because it was so good). Then Jotika the Treasurer paid homage to the King with joined palms and said, “That is enough, Your Majesty; I wish for you to eat only this much. If you exceed this, you will not be able to digest it.” When King Bimbisāra asked, “What is this, Great Treasurer? Are you speaking thus to honor (boast of) your own food?” Jotika the Treasurer replied, “Your Majesty, it is not at all that I speak to honor my own food. Indeed, even for all of Your Majesty’s soldiers and attendants, there is this Uttarakuru rice and exquisite curry. In truth, I am afraid of losing my reputation (receiving bad news).” When the King asked, “For what reason?” Jotika the Treasurer replied, “If Your Majesty’s body should feel even slightly heavy or sluggish (because the food is so rich), people might wrongly blame me, saying, ‘The King ate a meal at Jotika the Treasurer’s house yesterday; Jotika must have done something.’ I am afraid of such blame, Your Majesty.” Only then did the King command, “If that is so, take away the meal and offer clear water.” At the conclusion of the King’s meal, the entire retinue of the King’s attendants and soldiers also ate that same Uttarakuru rice.
374: ## The Treasurer’s Wife Satulakāyī Appearing Before the King Thereafter, while King Bimbisāra was engaging in pleasant conversation and inquiring about his well-being, he asked the treasurer Jotika: (The King) "Great Treasurer, is there no wife of the treasurer in this house?" (Jotika) "There is, your Majesty." (The King) "Where is the treasurer’s wife now?" (Jotika) "She is sitting in the auspicious inner chamber; it is because she does not know of your Majesty’s arrival." (Indeed, although the King had arrived early with his retinue, the treasurer’s wife Satulakāyī truly did not know that the King had arrived). Then, the treasurer Jotika, considering that "The King wishes to see my wife," went to her and asked, "The King has arrived at our house; is it not proper for you to go and see the King?" Satulakāyī, while reclining in the auspicious inner chamber, asked, "Lord, what kind of person is this one called 'King'?" When Jotika replied, "A King is one who rules over us," Satulakāyī, wishing to clearly express her dissatisfaction, said, "Alas, we must have performed our meritorious deeds poorly! That there should still be someone who rules over us! We must have performed meritorious deeds with insincere faith,
375: and although we have attained great wealth and prosperity, we are born in a place under another's rule. Surely, we must have given alms without believing in Kamma and its results. Being born in a place ruled by another is the result of such merit performed without faith, merely as a matter of routine," she lamented. Then she asked, "Lord, what must I do now?" The treasurer Jotika replied, "Take a palm-leaf fan and go fan the King." Following Jotika’s instructions, the treasurer’s wife Satulakāyī took a palm-leaf fan and came to fan the King. While she was fanning, the breeze carrying the scent from the King’s turban struck both her eyes. At that moment, tears began to flow steadily from her eyes. Seeing this, the King said to Jotika, "Great Treasurer, womenfolk are of little wisdom; she probably thinks, 'The King might seize my husband’s wealth,' and is weeping out of fear that it will be taken as royal property. Tell your wife, 'I have no desire for your wealth,' and comfort her; let her be at ease." ## Jotika the Treasurer Giving a Gem the Size of a Large Cucumber to King Bimbisāra Then Jotika the treasurer said, "Your Majesty, this lady is not weeping." When the King asked, "If she is not weeping, why are
376: tears flowing now?" the treasurer explained, "Your Majesty, it is because of the scent of your Majesty’s turban that tears have formed in her eyes. Indeed, this lady does not look at the light of lamps or ordinary fire; she is one who eats, lives, and sleeps only by the light of jewels. Your Majesty, however, lives by the light of oil lamps." The King said, "Ah, that is true, Treasurer." Then Jotika the treasurer said, "Your Majesty, if that is so, from today onwards, please live only by the light of jewels," and he presented a priceless gem the size of a large cucumber. King Bimbisāra, after thoroughly inspecting the seven-storied mansion of Jotika, praised him, saying, "The wealth of the treasurer Jotika is truly grand and magnificent," and returned to the golden palace. ## Jotika the Treasurer Becoming Disillusioned and Attaining Arahantship due to King Ajātasattu’s Unjust Conduct At another time, Prince Ajātasattu, having associated with the evil friend Devadatta, plotted and killed his father King Bimbisāra by roasting him with acacia embers. Upon ascending the throne, with the intention of "attacking and seizing Jotika’s mansion," he set out with a great army. When he saw his own reflection along with his surrounding army in the jewel-encrusted wall surrounding Jotika’s mansion, he thought, "The treasurer Jotika, having raised a great army..."
377:
377
Thinking, "He has come out with his army to attack me," the King did not even dare to approach the wall.

On that day, the Great Treasurer Jotika was observing the Uposatha. Having eaten his morning meal early, he went to the monastery, listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, and was sitting peacefully.

"When unwholesome greed arises and spreads, and when blind, cruel, and wicked people are afflicted with suffering, the virtuous person who dwells in the Dhamma remains joyful in mind and peaceful in body." (Dhammupadesa)

When King Ajātasattu arrived with his great army, the Yakkha guardian named Yamakoḷi, who was guarding the first gate of Jotika's mansion, shouted and threatened, "Where do you think you can escape?" He attacked and destroyed King Ajātasattu's great army, causing it to break, and pursued them in every direction and corner. At that time, King Ajātasattu, his army defeated, fled directly toward the monastery.

When the Great Treasurer Jotika saw King Ajātasattu, he rose from his seat and stood, saying, "Great King, what is the matter?" King Ajātasattu spoke resentfully, "Treasurer, why do you sit here as if listening to the Dhamma at this monastery after ordering your men to fight against me?" The Great Treasurer Jotika asked, "Oh, Great King, did you go to seize my house?" When King Ajātasattu replied angrily, "Yes, I went there," the Great Treasurer Jotika said, "Great King, if I do not wish it (do not consent), my house...
378:
378
...cannot be seized even by a thousand kings (let alone by the Great King alone)," he replied calmly and courageously.

Then King Ajātasattu, becoming furious, said, "Are you going to be the king? (Do you think you are the king?)" The Great Treasurer Jotika calmly replied, "I am not a king. However, if I do not wish it, not even a single thread of the fringe of my property can be seized or taken by kings or thieves." King Ajātasattu, filled with royal pride, said, "Must I take your property only with your consent? Since I am the king, I can take your property even if you do not wish it."

Then the Great Treasurer Jotika courageously said, "Great King, if that is so (extending the backs of both hands), there are these twenty rings on my ten fingers. I do not give these rings to the Great King. If you are able, please remove them."

King Ajātasattu was a man of such strength that if he jumped from a crouching position on the ground, he could ascend eighteen cubits; if he jumped from a standing position, he could ascend eighty cubits. Despite being so powerful, although he twisted and turned the rings on the Treasurer's fingers from left and right repeatedly, he could not remove even a single ring, only losing his royal dignity. Then the Great Treasurer Jotika said, "Great King, if you desire them, please spread out your royal robe to receive them," and he straightened his fingers, pointing them downward. At that moment, the twenty rings...
379:
379
...fell off easily. Thereafter, the Great Treasurer Jotika said to King Ajātasattu, "Great King, just as you have seen, if I do not wish it, my property cannot be seized." Having developed great spiritual urgency (saṃvega) due to King Ajātasattu's rude behavior, he said, "Great King, please grant me permission to become a monk."

King Ajātasattu, thinking, "If this Treasurer Jotika becomes a monk, I will be able to seize his mansion easily," readily agreed with a single word of request, saying, "If you wish to become a monk, do so."

The Great Treasurer Jotika, filled with great spiritual urgency, was ordained in the presence of the Buddha. Before long, through the practice of meditation, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship and became well-known as the Elder Jotika. At the very moment the Elder Jotika attained Arahantship, all his wealth, including the celestial mansion, vanished completely. The devas also took the Treasurer's wife, named Satulakāyī, back to the continent of Uttarakuru.

One day, the monks asked the Elder Jotika, "Friend Jotika, do you still have any attachment or craving for that great mansion or for the Treasurer's wife Satulakāyī?" When the Elder Jotika replied, "No longer, friends," the monks reported to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, this monk Jotika speaks untruthfully and claims to have attained Arahantship." At that time, the Buddha said:
380:
380
"Monks, in the mental and physical continuity of my son, the Arahant Jotika, there is certainly no attachment or craving for that celestial mansion, wealth, or the Treasurer's wife." Having said this, he spoke this verse of Dhamma:

"He who, having abandoned craving in this world, wanders forth as a homeless one, in whom craving and existence are exhausted—him I call a Brahmin."

(Bhikkhave = O monks. Yo = whoever. Idha = in this present world. Taṇhaṃ = craving that arises depending on the six doors. Pahantvāna = having abandoned and cut off by the Path of Eradication. Anāgāro = having no desire for household life. Paribbaje = has gone forth into the monkhood. Taṇhābhavaparikkhīṇaṃ = in whom the six types of craving and the three types of existence are completely exhausted. Taṃ-tādisaṃ = such a noble Arahant. Ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds. Brāhmaṇaṃ = call a Brahmin, a noble person who has put away and abandoned all evil. Brūmi = I declare in praise.)

At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.

This is the story of the Treasurer Jotika.

## (2) The Story of the Treasurer Meṇḍaka
## The Treasurer's Past Merits
This noble person, the future Treasurer Meṇḍaka, ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of the Buddha Vipassī...
381:
381
...was a man named Aparājita, the nephew (sister's son) of the householder Aparājita (the future Jotika), sharing the same name as his uncle. Later, his uncle, the householder Aparājita, began building a brick Gandhakuṭī monastery for the Buddha.

The nephew Aparājita went to his uncle and said, "Uncle, let us build the brick Gandhakuṭī monastery together as uncle and nephew." When the uncle refused, saying, "I will build the brick Gandhakuṭī monastery alone, without involving others," the nephew reflected, "If a brick Gandhakuṭī monastery is built here, it would be appropriate to have a reception hall in the open space in front of the monastery." He then had timber brought from the forest and had a reception hall built for the Buddha in front of the brick Gandhakuṭī monastery. He had one pillar decorated with gold, one with silver, one with rubies, and one with the seven kinds of gems, and so on. All parts, including the beams, rafters, eaves, door leaves, windows, laths, and roof tiles, were decorated with gold, silver, and other precious materials.

On top of that hall, he installed roof tiles made of solid red gold and pinnacles made of coral. In the center of the reception hall, he erected a jeweled pavilion (Dhamma pavilion) and had a Dhamma seat (Dhammāsana) prepared. The design of that Dhamma seat was as follows:
382:
382
(1) The four legs and the four frames were made of solid red gold. (2) He had four golden goat statues cast and placed under the four legs of the seat. (3) He had two other golden goat statues cast and placed under the footstool. (4) He had six other golden goat statues cast and placed surrounding the Dhamma pavilion. (5) The seat for preaching was first woven with small threads, then overlaid with golden threads in the middle, and finally woven with strings of pearls on top. (6) The backrest of that Dhamma seat was made of sandalwood.

When the construction of the reception hall was completed and the water-pouring ceremony was held, he invited the Buddha along with 6,800,000 monks and gave alms daily for four months. On the final day, he offered a set of three robes (Ticīvara) to each. In that alms-giving ceremony, even the robe offered to the most junior monk (saṅghanava) was worth one hundred thousand (one thousand according to the Sri Lankan version).

## Life as the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī
Thus, the future Treasurer Meṇḍaka, having performed meritorious deeds during the time of the Buddha Vipassī, passed away from that life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. When he reached this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), he was born into a wealthy family in the city of Bārāṇasī and became the Great Treasurer of Bārāṇasī upon reaching adulthood. One day, as the Great Treasurer was going to serve the King...
383:
383
...he saw the Chaplain (Purohita) and asked, "Teacher, how is it? Have you examined the constellations, the times, and the moments?" The Chaplain replied, "Yes, I have examined and reflected on them. For teachers like us, what other duty is there besides examining the constellations, times, and moments?" The Treasurer continued, "If so, what will happen in the countryside?" Then they continued their conversation as follows:

(Chaplain)
There will be a peril.

(Treasurer)
What kind of peril, Teacher?

(Chaplain)
There will be the peril of famine (hunger), Treasurer.

(Treasurer)
Around what time will it occur, Teacher?

(Chaplain)
It will occur three years from now, Treasurer.

Hearing this, the Great Treasurer expanded his farming activities extensively. With the wealth he had at home, he bought only grain and built 1,250 granaries. He stored all the granaries full of paddy. The grain that exceeded the capacity of the granaries was stored in large jars. The grain that still exceeded those was buried in pits in the ground. The grain that remained even after that was mixed with fine clay and used to plaster the walls of the house. (This is a worthy example to note.)
384:
At a later time (when the chief chaplain had spoken), when the peril of famine (dubbikkha-bhaya) struck, the great merchant Mahābhoga consumed the grain he had stored for many days. When the grain stored in the granaries and large jars was exhausted, he summoned his attendants and servants and said, “Friends, go now. Enter the foot of the mountains and sustain yourselves as best as you can. When rice and grain become plentiful and abundant again, those who wish to return to me may do so. Those who do not wish to return may live wherever they please.” Those people wept and wailed, their tears flowing freely. They paid their respects to the merchant, stayed with him for seven days, and then did as he had instructed.

Only one servant named Puṇṇa remained with the merchant to perform the household duties. Including this servant Puṇṇa, there were only five members in the household: the merchant’s wife, the merchant’s son, the merchant’s daughter-in-law, and the merchant himself. When the grain buried in the ground was also exhausted, these five members of the merchant’s household scraped off the fine clay used for plastering the walls, soaked it in water, and sustained themselves with the grain obtained from it. Later, as the peril of famine increased, overwhelmed, and became more severe, and the clay from the walls was nearly gone, the merchant’s wife scraped the clay remaining at the base of the walls, soaked it in water, and obtained about one pasata (a measure) of paddy. When she husked it, she obtained one salay of rice. Thinking, “When the peril of suffering arrives, thieves are very numerous,”
385:
fearing the danger of wicked thieves, she placed that one salay of rice into a small pot for safekeeping, covered it, and buried it in the ground.

Then one day, the merchant returned from serving the king and asked his wife, “Lady, I am very hungry. Is there anything to eat?” The merchant’s wife did not say “there is nothing” when there was. The conversation between the merchant and his wife was as follows:

(The Wife)
“My lord, there is one salay of rice.”

(The Merchant)
“Where is that one salay of rice now?”

(The Wife)
“Fearing the danger of thieves, I have buried it in the ground.”

(The Merchant)
“If that is so, dig up that one salay of rice and try to cook something.”

(The Wife)
“My lord, if I make gruel (yāgu) with this one salay of rice, it can serve for two meals. If I cook it as rice (bhatta), it can serve for only one meal. Between these two, gruel and rice, which should I prepare? Shall I make gruel or cook rice, my lord?”

(The Merchant)
“Lady, there is no other support for us. Let us eat our fill of rice and die. Just cook the rice.”

Following the merchant’s command, the wife cooked the rice, divided it into five portions, served the merchant’s portion, and placed it ready before him. At that moment,
386:
on Mount Gandhamādana, a Paccekabuddha had just emerged from meditative attainment (samāpatti).

(Specifically, while dwelling in meditative attainment, hunger cannot oppress due to the power of the attainment. However, for the Noble Ones who have emerged from meditative attainment, hunger becomes powerful and intense, as if burning the layer of the stomach. Therefore, it is the natural custom of Paccekabuddhas who have emerged from meditative attainment to survey where alms-food may be obtained and proceed to that place. Furthermore, those who are able to offer any kind of alms-dana to these Noble Ones on the day they emerge from such attainment invariably receive some form of prosperity, such as the position of a general and so on).

Therefore, that Paccekabuddha also surveyed with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and saw: “The peril of famine (dubbikkha) has broken out throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. In the house of the great merchant Mahābhoga of Bārāṇasī, however, rice cooked from one salay for five people is ready. Do the members of this merchant’s household have faith? Are they able to perform an act of favor (offering) to me?” Upon reflecting, he saw that all five of them possessed faith and were capable of making the offering. Taking his bowl and robes, he appeared at the merchant’s door, standing clearly before him.

When the merchant saw the Paccekabuddha, his heart was filled with shimmering faith and devotion. He thought, “Because I did not give alms-dana in the past, I am now facing such a peril of famine. This rice for me now, if consumed, might sustain me for only a single day. But if it is offered to the Noble One,
387:
it will be able to bring about my welfare and happiness for many billions of aeons.” Having thought thus, he had the bowl of rice set aside, went to the Paccekabuddha, and after paying homage with the five-fold prostration, invited him inside. When the Paccekabuddha was seated in his place, the merchant washed and wiped his feet. He then placed the Paccekabuddha on a golden-footed stool, brought the bowl of rice, and poured it into the Paccekabuddha’s alms-bowl.

When half the rice had been poured and only half remained in the bowl, the Paccekabuddha covered the alms-bowl with his hand. Then the merchant said to the Paccekabuddha, “Venerable Sir, this rice is one person’s portion from the rice cooked for five people with one salay of rice. It is not possible to make two portions of this rice; it cannot be divided for two people. Please do not favor me for this present world alone (but favor me for the world hereafter as well). I wish to offer it all without leaving any remainder.” Having spoken thus, he poured the entire portion and made these five aspirations: “Venerable Sir, in whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, may I be one who never sees or encounters such a peril of famine again. From this day forward, may I be one who is able to provide food and provisions to all the people living in the island of Jambudīpa. May I not have to make a living by working with my own hands. After having one thousand two hundred and fifty (1,250) granaries cleaned, and having washed my head, at the very moment I sit at the entrance of those granaries and look up at the sky, may showers of red sāli rice
388:
fall abundantly and fill all my granaries. In whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, may this current wife of the merchant be my wife, this current son be my son, this current daughter-in-law be my daughter-in-law, and this current servant be my servant.” Thus he made these five aspirations.

## The Extraordinary Volition of the Entire Household

The merchant’s wife also thought and reflected, “While my lord the merchant is being oppressed by the peril of famine, there is no way I can eat my portion (selfishly).” Having offered her portion to the Paccekabuddha, she made this aspiration: “Venerable Sir, in whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, may I be one who never sees or encounters such a peril of famine again. For my part, even if I must give food to all the people living in the island of Jambudīpa by placing a bowl of rice before me, may the place from which I take the food always remain full as long as I do not rise from my seat. In whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, may this merchant be the master of my house, this son be my son, this daughter-in-law be my daughter-in-law, and this servant be my servant.”

The merchant’s son also offered his portion to the Paccekabuddha and made this aspiration: “Venerable Sir, from this day forward, may I be one who never sees or encounters such a peril of famine again. For my part, even if I must give coins to all the people living in the island of Jambudīpa while holding a bag of a thousand coins, may this bag of a thousand
389:
always remain full. In whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, may these two parents be my mother and father. May this wife be my wife, and this servant be my servant.”

The merchant’s daughter-in-law also offered her portion to the Paccekabuddha and made this aspiration: “Venerable Sir, from this day forward, may I be one who never sees or encounters such a peril of famine again. For my part, even if I must give food and provisions to all the people living in the island of Jambudīpa by placing a basket of grain before me, may it never appear to be exhausted. In whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, may these in-laws be my in-laws. May this merchant’s son be the master of my house, and this servant be my servant.”

The servant named Puṇṇa also offered his portion to the Paccekabuddha and made this aspiration: “Venerable Sir, from this day forward, may I be one who never sees or encounters such a peril of famine again. May all these masters be my masters in whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra. For my part, when I plow once, may three furrows on the left, three furrows on the right, and one furrow in the middle—thus seven furrows—be accomplished, sufficient to sow one ambaṇa (four baskets) of seed.”

(Although Puṇṇa could have aspired for the position of a general on that day, because of his great affection for his masters, he only aspired to be their servant, saying: “May these masters
390:
be my masters in whatever future existence or realm I may be born throughout the cycle of saṃsāra.”)

When all of them had finished speaking, the Paccekabuddha said, “Evaṃ hotu—May it be so (as you have aspired),” and then recited:

“May all that you wish and desire be quickly fulfilled.
May all your intentions be fulfilled like the full moon on the fifteenth day.”

“May all that you wish and desire be entirely fulfilled.
May all your intentions be fulfilled like the wish-fulfilling gem (maṇi-jotirasa).”

After performing the act of appreciation (anumodanā) with these verses of blessing, the Paccekabuddha thought, “It is proper that I further increase the faith of these people.” He then made a determination, “May these people see me until I reach Mount Gandhamādana,” and departed. The members of the merchant’s household
391:
The five of them also stood there watching. When the Paccekabuddha reached Mount Gandhamādana, he shared and partook of that alms-food together with five hundred other Paccekabuddhas. Due to the spiritual power of the Paccekabuddha, that portion of food meant for five people was sufficient for all five hundred. The five members of the merchant’s household also remained standing, watching with great devotion.

## Giving Results within the Same Day

In particular, after the sun had passed noon, the merchant’s wife washed the rice pot, covered it, and set it aside. The merchant, being severely oppressed by intense hunger, lay down and fell asleep. Waking up in the evening, he said to his wife, “My dear, I am very hungry. Are there any crusts or grains of rice left sticking to the pot? (Please go and look).” Although the merchant’s wife knew she had washed the pot clean and set it aside, she did not say “There is none.” Instead, thinking, “I will look in the pot before I speak,” she rose, went to the rice pot, and opened it.

At that very moment, the rice pot was filled with rice having the appearance of jasmine buds, and it stood there lifting the lid upwards. Upon seeing this, the merchant’s wife, her entire body suffused with joy (pīti), said to the merchant, “My lord, please get up! I had washed the rice pot clean before covering it and setting it aside. Now, however, that rice pot
392:
is filled with rice having the appearance of jasmine buds. Indeed, the nature of meritorious deeds is that they should be performed; indeed, the nature of almsgiving is that it should be performed. My lord, please get up and eat happily.”

The merchant’s wife first served and fed the father and the son. Only after the father and son had finished eating and left did she sit down with her daughter-in-law and eat herself. Then she gave rice to the servant, Puṇṇa. No matter how much was taken, the place from which it was taken remained inexhaustible. Only the mark where the first ladle of rice was scooped out could be seen. On that very day, the granaries, large jars, and so on were once again filled with grain just as they had been before. The merchant had a proclamation made throughout the city: “Abundant provisions of rice have appeared in the house of the Mahābhoga merchant. Let those who wish for seed-grain and rice come and take as much as they desire.” People took as much seed-grain and rice as they wished from the merchant’s house. All the people living in the island of Jambudīpa obtained their livelihood by depending on that Mahābhoga merchant.

## Becoming Meṇḍaka the Merchant in the Final Life

When that Mahābhoga merchant passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering through the celestial and human realms, he was born into a merchant family in the city of Bhaddiya during the time when our Exalted Buddha appeared. His wife was also born into a Mahābhoga merchant family, and when she reached the proper age, she became the chief wife of that merchant.
393:
## Being Named Meṇḍaka the Merchant

In the area behind the merchant’s house, about eight karīsas in extent, large golden goats (rams) the size of elephants, horses, and bulls emerged from the earth, their backs touching one another. This was due to the power of the merit he had performed by making and offering a golden goat during the time of Vipassī Buddha. In the mouths of these golden goats, balls of five-colored thread were already placed. Whenever there was a need for ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, or for clothing, gold, silver, and so on, the balls of thread had to be removed from the mouths of those golden goats. From the mouth of just one golden goat, enough ghee, oil, honey, molasses, clothing, gold, and silver would come forth for all the people living in Jambudīpa. From that time on, the merchant’s name became famous as “Meṇḍaka the Merchant.” (Meṇḍaka means the merchant who owns golden goats).

The son of this merchant couple in their past life became their son in this life as well (that son was the merchant Dhanañjaya, the father of Visākhā). The daughter-in-law from the past life became the daughter-in-law in this life as well. The servant from the past life became the servant in this life as well. (The chief wife of Meṇḍaka the Merchant was named Candapadumā; the daughter-in-law, the wife of Dhanañjaya the Merchant, was named Sumanadevī; and the servant of Meṇḍaka the Merchant was named Puṇṇa).

(The account of the spiritual power of Meṇḍaka the Merchant, his wife, his son Dhanañjaya, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, and his faithful servant Puṇṇa, as well as the events leading up to Meṇḍaka the Merchant becoming a Sotāpanna, should be reviewed again starting from page 245 in the section on Visākhā in the Chapter on the Lives of Laywomen in Volume VI of this Great Chronicle of Buddhas).
394:
Furthermore, after Meṇḍaka the Merchant had listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha and became a Sotāpanna, he informed the Buddha about how the heretics (titthiyas) had spoken ill of the Buddha and tried to prevent him from coming to the Buddha’s presence. At that time, the Buddha said to Meṇḍaka the Merchant, “Lay disciple, these beings do not see their own great faults. They speak of the faults of others, even making them up where none exist, scattering them about like chaff in various places.” After saying this, He preached this verse of Dhamma:

Sudassaṃ vajjaṃ aññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ.
Paresaṃ hi so vajjāni, opunāti yathā bhusaṃ.
Attano pana chādeti, kaliṃva kitavā saṭho.

(Gahapati = O lay disciple known as Meṇḍaka. Imesaṃ sattānaṃ = Of these beings. Aññesaṃ = of others. Vajjaṃ = the fault. Sudassaṃ = is easily seen. Attano pana = But one's own. Vajjaṃ = fault. Duddasaṃ = is difficult to see, even if it is very great. Hi = Indeed. So = that person who ignores his own faults and habitually looks for the faults of others. Paresaṃ = of others. Vajjāni = the faults. Bhusaṃ yathā = like chaff. Opunāti = speaks of them by scattering them about. Attano pana = But one's own. Vajjaṃ = fault. Kitavā = a crafty. Saṭho = bird-hunter. [Alternatively] Saṭho = a crafty bird-hunter.)
395:
Kitavā-kitavāya = with branches and so on. Kaliṃ = his own body. Chādeti iva = as if covering. Chādeti = he covers up.

At the conclusion of this verse of instruction, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so on. (From Dhammapada Commentary Vol. 2, p. 232 onwards).

This is the story of Meṇḍaka the Merchant.
