## (3) The Story of Jatila the Merchant

## Jatila’s Past Karma

This future Jatila the Merchant was a goldsmith during the era of the Dispensation of Kassapa Buddha. After the parinibbāna of Kassapa Buddha, while the great relic stupa (dhātu-cetiya) was being built, an Arahant Elder went to the site of the stupa and asked, “Friends, why is the northern portal of the stupa not being raised?” When the people replied, “Venerable sir, it is because there is not enough gold,” the Arahant Elder said, “I will go into the city and encourage the people to donate gold. You all should perform the work with reverence.” Having spoken these words of encouragement, he entered the city and exhorted the multitude, saying, “Mothers and brothers, there is not enough gold for the northern portal of your stupa. Please provide gold.” He then arrived at the house of the goldsmith.

At that time, the goldsmith was sitting there after having had a quarrel with his wife. Then the Elder said to the goldsmith, “Lay disciple, for the
396:
northern portal for which you all have taken responsibility, there is not enough gold. Therefore, it would be proper if you provide gold.” The goldsmith, being angry with his wife, spoke rudely, saying, “Just go and throw your Buddha into the water!” Then his wife said to the goldsmith, “You have committed a very cruel and evil deed. If you are angry with me, you should only abuse me or beat me. Why do you show hostility toward the Buddhas of the past, future, and present?” Thus she spoke, pointing out his fault.

At that very moment, the goldsmith was struck with great urgency (saṃvega) and pleaded, “Venerable sir, please forgive me.” The Arahant Elder said, “Friend, you have not said anything offensive to me; you have only spoken offensively against the Buddha. Therefore, ask forgiveness from the Buddha himself.” When the goldsmith asked, “Venerable sir, how should I ask for forgiveness?” the Arahant Elder gave him instructions, saying, “Friend, make three golden flower pots, place them inside the relic chamber, and ask for forgiveness with wet clothes and wet hair.”

The goldsmith replied, “Very well, venerable sir.” When he began making the golden flowers, he called his eldest of three sons and said, “Come, dear son. I have mistakenly spoken words of hostility against the Buddha. Therefore, I must make these three golden flower clusters, place them in the relic chamber, and ask for forgiveness.
397:
Dear son, you too should be my companion in this.” The eldest son said, “I did not ask you to speak words of hostility; (you spoke them of your own accord). Therefore, you alone should do it.” Thus he did not wish to help in making the golden flower clusters. He called the middle son and spoke to him in the same way. The middle son also spoke like the first and did not wish to do it. When he called the youngest son and spoke to him in the same way, the youngest son said, “All matters that arise for my father are the responsibility of the son.” Saying this, he became his father’s companion and helped in making the golden flower clusters.

The goldsmith made three golden flower pots (including the flower clusters) about a span in height, placed them in the relic chamber, and (as instructed by the Arahant Elder) asked for forgiveness from the Buddha with wet clothes and wet hair. (This is the account of Jatila the Merchant’s past karma).

## Becoming Jatila the Merchant in the Final Life

Because of that aforementioned verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita), that goldsmith was cast into the water for seven times (seven lives). In this final existence, he became the son of a merchant’s daughter in Bārāṇasī. To elaborate—during the time of our Exalted Buddha, there was a very beautiful daughter of a merchant in the city of Bārāṇasī. When that merchant’s daughter was fifteen or sixteen years old, her parents gave her a maidservant to look after her and had her live in a magnificent chamber on the topmost floor of a seven-storied palace.
398:
One day, a Vijjādhara traveling through the air saw the merchant's daughter looking out through an open casement window. Overcome with intense passion, he entered through the window and shared an intimate union with her.

Due to her association with the Vijjādhara, the merchant's daughter soon became pregnant. When I, her maid, saw her condition and asked, "Mistress, what is this? What has happened?", she replied, "Let it be; do not tell anyone," and swore me to secrecy. Thus, out of fear, I remained silent. In the tenth month, she gave birth to a son. She had a new pot brought to her, placed the infant inside, covered it with a lid, and placed flower garlands and wreaths on top. She then commanded me, "Carry this pot on your head and set it adrift in the Gaṅgā River. If anyone asks, 'What is this?', say, 'It is a ritual offering for my mistress.'" I did exactly as the merchant's daughter commanded.

At that time, two women bathing downstream in the Gaṅgā saw the pot floating by. One said, "That pot is mine." The other said, "The contents inside that pot are mine." As they spoke, the pot reached them. They retrieved it, placed it on the bank, and upon opening it, they saw the infant. One said, "Because I claimed the pot, the infant belongs to me." The other said, "Because I claimed the contents inside the pot...
399:
the infant belongs to me, as I claimed the contents inside the pot." The two women, arguing, went to the court of justice and reported the matter. When the ministers of justice were unable to reach a decision, they went before the King. After hearing the words of both women, the King decreed to the second woman, "You shall own the child," and to the first woman, "You shall own the pot."

Among those two women, the one who received the child was a close devotee and supporter of Venerable Mahākaccāyana. Therefore, she raised the child with the intention, "I will have this boy ordain under the Elder." Because the impurities of birth had not been washed away on the day he was born, his hair remained tangled like matted locks. For this reason, they named the boy "Jaṭila."

When the boy Jaṭila was old enough to walk steadily, Venerable Mahākaccāyana entered that house for alms. The devotee offered the Elder a seat and served him food. Seeing the boy Jaṭila, the Elder asked, "Great devotee, how is this? Did you obtain a child?" The devotee replied, "I did, Bhante. I have raised this boy with the intention of having him ordain under you.
400:
Please ordain this boy, Bhante," she said, offering him to the Elder.

Venerable Mahākaccāyana accepted, saying "Very well." While taking the boy away, he examined with his supernormal knowledge, "Does this boy have the merit to enjoy human prosperity?" He perceived, "He is a being of great merit and will enjoy immense wealth. This boy is still young, and his wisdom is not yet mature." Considering this, he took the boy Jaṭila to the city of Takkasilā and went to the house of a close lay supporter.

The supporter, after paying homage to the Elder, saw the boy while standing and asked, "Bhante, did you obtain a child?" Venerable Mahākaccāyana replied, "Yes, lay follower, I did. This boy will eventually ordain as a monk, but he is still young. Let him stay with you for now." When the Elder said this, the supporter accepted, saying "Very well, Bhante," and raised the boy, treating him as his own son.

That supporter was a merchant. In his house, there was a vast amount of merchandise that had remained unsold for twelve years. One day, as the merchant was about to travel to another village, he brought all those unsold goods to the shop, had the boy (Jaṭila) sit in the shop, explained the prices of the various goods, and
401: "Take this much wealth for such and such merchandise and give it," he instructed before departing on his journey. ## Goods Unsold for Twelve Years Being Sold in a Single Day On that day, the guardian deities of the city caused even those customers who wished to buy as little as chili or cumin to come directly to the shop where the youth Jaṭila was sitting. Jaṭila sold in a single day all the merchandise that had remained unsold and piled up for twelve years. When the householder merchant returned and found not even a small amount of merchandise left in the shop, he asked, "Dear son, did you destroy all the goods?" Jaṭila replied, "I did not destroy them; I have sold all the goods according to the instructions you gave. This money is the price for such and such goods; this money is the price for such and such goods," and he handed over the exact accounts. The merchant was extremely satisfied and thought, "He is a man of priceless worth; he is one who can live comfortably in any place or any occupation." He then married his daughter, who was of age and ready, to the youth Jaṭila. He commanded his men, "Build a large house for this youth Jaṭila," and when the house was completed, he handed it over, saying, "Sons and daughters, go; live happily in your own home."
402:
## Jaṭila Becoming a Treasurer, Owner of a Golden Mountain

Afterward, during the house-warming ceremony for the youth Jaṭila, as soon as he stepped on the threshold with one foot, a great mountain of gold about eighty cubits high burst through the earth at the back of the house. When the King heard the news that "a great mountain of gold has burst through the earth at the house of the youth Jaṭila," he sent the treasurer's white parasol to the youth Jaṭila, honored him with the regalia of a treasurer, and appointed him to the position of a Great Treasurer. From then on, he became famous by the name "Jaṭila the Great Treasurer."

## Searching Throughout Jambudīpa

Jaṭila the Great Treasurer had three sons. When those sons reached adulthood, the Treasurer's mind inclined toward ordaining as a monk. He thought, "If there are other treasurer families with wealth equal to ours, the King will grant me permission to ordain; if not, he will not. Are there any treasurer families or houses in Jambudīpa with wealth equal to ours?" To investigate this, he had gold bricks, gold staffs, and gold sandals cast. He handed them to his trusted men and instructed them, "Friends, go. Take these items and travel throughout Jambudīpa as if looking at various sights. Find out whether there are treasurer families with wealth equal to ours, and then return."

As those trusted men traveled through the regions, they arrived at the city of Bhaddiya. At that time, the Great Treasurer Meṇḍaka saw those men and asked, "Friends, for what purpose
403:
are you traveling?" When they replied, "We are traveling because we wish to see a certain object," the Great Treasurer Meṇḍaka realized, "These people have no reason to travel just to see these gold bricks, gold staffs, and gold sandals; they are traveling to investigate the country." He said, "Friends, enter the back of our house and look."

In the backyard of the Great Treasurer Meṇḍaka's house, in an area of land about eight karīsas wide, those men saw life-sized golden goats the size of elephants, horses, and bulls, emerging from the earth with their backs touching. They walked among those golden goats and then came back out. Then the Great Treasurer Meṇḍaka asked them, "Friends, have you seen the object you were traveling to find?" When the men replied, "We have seen it, Great Treasurer," he said, "If that is so, friends, go wherever you wish."

Jaṭila the Great Treasurer's men returned to their treasurer from the city of Bhaddiya. When Jaṭila the Great Treasurer asked, "Friends, did you see a treasurer family with wealth equal to ours?", they prefaced their words by saying, "Lord Treasurer, what wealth do you have? In the city of Bhaddiya, the wealth of the Great Treasurer Meṇḍaka is of such and such a nature," and they reported everything they had seen in full. Hearing this, Jaṭila the Great Treasurer was pleased and satisfied, thinking, "I have found one treasurer family. Might there
404:
be others as well?" He gave them a woolen blanket worth one hundred thousand and instructed those trusted men again, "Friends, go. Investigate other treasurer families as well," and sent them off.

Those men went to the city of Rājagaha and stood near the palace-mansion of the Great Treasurer Jotika, not far away, where they gathered wood and built a fire. When people asked, "What is this? What are you doing?", the men of Treasurer Jaṭila replied, "We have a woolen blanket worth a great price for sale, but there is no one who can buy it. If we carry it back to our city, we are afraid of the danger of thieves and robbers. Therefore, we will burn this blanket and then go."

At that time, Jotika the Great Treasurer saw those men and asked, "What are these people doing?" When he heard the reason, he had the men called and asked, "Friends, how much is this blanket worth?" When the men replied, "It is worth one hundred thousand, Great Treasurer," Jotika the Great Treasurer had his people give those men one hundred thousand coins. Then he instructed, "Friends, give this blanket to my maidservant who sweeps my gateway and throws away the rubbish," and he handed it over to the men of Treasurer Jaṭila to deliver it.

Jotika the Great Treasurer's maidservant took the blanket and, while weeping (in front of those men), went to her master, the Great Treasurer Jotika, and said, "Lord Treasurer...
405:
“How so? If I, your servant, have committed a fault, is it not proper to beat me? (meaning: you should beat me). Why have you sent such a coarse blanket to me? How can I, your servant, wear or wrap myself in such a coarse blanket? (meaning: I cannot wear or wrap myself in it).” Thus, she complained with dissatisfied words. Then, the wealthy man Jotika said, “Mother... I did not send this for you to wear or wrap yourself in. In fact, I sent this to you so that you might roll it up and place it at the foot of your bed, and when it is time for you to sleep, you may use it to wipe your feet after they have been washed with scented water. How so? Are you not even capable of doing this? (meaning: can you not even wipe your feet with it?)” Only after he explained this did the servant girl feel satisfied and said, “I shall be able to perform this task of wiping my feet,” and she took the blanket and left.

The trusted messengers of the wealthy man Jatila also witnessed this event personally. Upon returning to their master, Jatila the wealthy man asked, “Friends... have you seen any wealthy family whose fortune is equal to ours?” They replied, “Lord... what is your fortune compared to theirs? In the city of Rājagaha, the fortune of the wealthy man Jotika is of such and such a nature.” After introducing the subject in this way, they described the glory and abundance of Jotika’s mansion and then recounted the story they had personally seen regarding the servant girl and the blanket.
406: ## The Great Treasurer Jaṭila Testing the Merit of His Three Sons When the great treasurer Jaṭila heard the words of those trusted men, his heart was filled with joy and satisfaction. He reflected, "Now I shall have the opportunity to become a monk," and went to the King, saying, "Your Majesty, I wish to ordain as a monk." (In this regard, although the Commentary does not directly state which king it was, the Visākhāvatthu in the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume 1, page 243, explains: "Bimbisārarañño pana vijite pañca amitabhogā nāma ahesuṃ Jotiko, Jaṭilo, Meṇḍako, Puṇṇaka, Kāḷavaḷiyo ti = Specifically, in the kingdom where King Bimbisāra’s authority extended, there were five treasurers of immeasurable wealth: Jotika, Jaṭila, Meṇḍaka, Puṇṇaka, and Kāḷavaḷiya." Therefore, it should be understood as King Bimbisāra). The King also graciously granted permission, saying, "Very well, Great Treasurer, ordain as you wish." The great treasurer Jaṭila returned to his home, summoned his three sons, and placing a diamond-tipped goad with a golden handle in the hand of the eldest son, said, "Dear son, go to the mountain of gold at the back of the house and dig out a block of gold." The eldest son took the diamond goad and went to strike the mountain of gold with all his might. It was as if he were striking a solid slab of rock. The great treasurer Jaṭila took the diamond goad from the eldest son’s hand, gave it to the middle son, and sent him in the same manner. For the middle son as well, when he struck the mountain of gold with the diamond goad, it was just as if he were striking a solid slab of rock. Thereafter, he placed the diamond goad in the hand of the youngest son and sent him to strike it. For the youngest son...
407:
when he took the diamond pickaxe and struck the golden mountain, gold came out easily in layers and clusters, as if he were striking soft earth that had been pounded into powder and piled up. Then, the wealthy man Jatila said to the youngest son, “Come, dear son, this much is enough.” He then said to the eldest and middle sons, “Dear sons, this golden mountain did not arise because of your merit; it arose because of the merit of myself and your younger brother. Therefore, live in unity with this younger brother and enjoy this wealth together.”

(Note: Here, one should reflect on the previous account of Jatila the wealthy man’s life as a goldsmith. Because of the unwholesome verbal kamma of speaking rudely to an Arahant, saying, “Throw your Buddha into the water and go,” he was not only cast into the water after birth for seven lifetimes, but even in this final existence, he was cast into the water immediately after birth due to that same unwholesome verbal kamma.

Because only the youngest son had assisted him when he made golden flowers to worship and ask for forgiveness at the great relic stupa of Kassapa Buddha, this current great mountain of gold appeared for the wealthy man Jatila and his youngest son.)

In this way, after Jatila the wealthy man had instructed and advised his sons, he went to the Buddha and became a monk. After practicing the Dhamma with great diligence, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship within two or three days; he became an Arahant.

Later, when the Buddha was wandering for alms together with five hundred monks,
408:
He arrived at the door of the house where the three sons of the wealthy man Jatila lived. Those three sons offered alms to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha for half a month (15 days).

In the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a question: “Friend Jatila, even today, do you still have attachment and desire for the great golden mountain, eighty cubits high, and for your three sons?” When the Arahant Elder Jatila replied, “Friends, I no longer have any attachment or affection for that golden mountain and my sons,” the monks criticized him, saying, “This Elder Jatila is speaking untruth and claiming the attainment of Arahantship.” The Buddha, hearing the words of those monks, said, “Monks, in the heart of my son, the monk Jatila, there is no longer any attachment or affection for that golden mountain and his sons.” He then preached this Dhamma verse:

Yo’dha taṇhaṃ pahantvāna, anāgāro paribbaje.
Taṇhābhavaparikkhīṇaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

(The meaning of this verse was already written below in the story of the wealthy man Jotika.)

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. (Extracted and written from the Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, page 441 onwards.)

This is the story of the wealthy man Jatila.
409:
## (4) The Story of the Wealthy Man Kāḷavaḷiya

The story of this wealthy man Kāḷavaḷiya is found in brief in the Commentary to the Uparipaṇṇāsa, 1. Devadaha Sutta, page 4. The account is as follows:

During the time of the Buddha, there was a poor man named Kāḷavaḷiya in the city of Rājagaha. One day, Kāḷavaḷiya’s wife boiled some sour gruel mixed with leaves for their meal. (Being very poor, they could not afford to cook rice and had to boil gruel mixed with leaves instead). On that day, the Elder Mahākassapa emerged from the Attainment of Cessation (Nirodha-samāpatti) and reflected, “Whom shall I favor today?” Seeing the poor man Kāḷavaḷiya in his vision, he went to the door of his house and stood for alms.

Kāḷavaḷiya’s wife took the bowl from the Elder’s hand and poured all the sour gruel mixed with leaves, which she had just boiled, into the bowl and offered it to the Elder. (This kind of gift is called “Niravasesa-dāna,” a gift given without leaving anything for oneself). The Elder Mahākassapa went to the monastery and offered that gruel to the Buddha. The Buddha took only as much as was sufficient for Himself. The remaining gruel was enough for five hundred monks. The poor man Kāḷavaḷiya also arrived at that place (where the gruel was being distributed) to ask for leftovers and received a small amount of gruel to eat.

Elder Mahākassapa asked the Buddha about the benefit that would be gained by the donor of the gruel, Kāḷavaḷiya.
410:
The Buddha replied, “On the seventh day from today, Kāḷavaḷiya will receive the white umbrella of a wealthy man; he will become a wealthy man (Setthi).” The poor man Kāḷavaḷiya heard these words spoken by the Buddha clearly, returned home, and told his wife about it.

At that time, while King Bimbisāra was touring the city, he saw a criminal who had been placed alive on a stake (impaled). When the criminal saw the King, he took a risk and shouted loudly, “Great King... I wish for you to send me the rice from your royal meal.” The King said, “Yes, very well, I shall have it sent.” When the evening meal was served, he remembered the words requested by that criminal and said to the relevant officials, “Find someone who can deliver this meal to the stake outside the city.”

Because the outskirts of the city of Rājagaha were a place where very fierce ogres (yakkhas) roamed, no one dared to go outside the city at night easily. Therefore, the officials had a bag of a thousand coins carried through the city (announcing that whoever dared to go and deliver the meal to the stake outside the city should take this bag of a thousand coins). When it was carried around for the first and second time, no one appeared who dared to take the bag of coins. Only when it was carried around for the third time did the wife of Kāḷavaḷiya
411:
take that bag of a thousand coins from the hands of the king’s men (a case of ‘if you fear, you miss; if you are brave, you become a noble’). 

The king’s men presented her to the King. She took the appearance of a man (by wearing men’s clothes), equipped herself with the five kinds of weapons, took the royal meal, and bravely departed from the city. When she reached the outskirts of the city, an ogre (yakkha) named Dīghatāla, who resided in a palm tree, saw her passing near the tree and threatened her, saying, “Stop, stop! You have become my food!” Then, the ogre and she spoke back and forth as follows:

(She)
“I am not your food; I am the King’s messenger.”

(Ogre)
“Where are you going now?”

(She)
“I am going to the criminal who is on the stake alive.”

(Ogre)
“Would you be able to carry a message of mine as well?”

(She)
“Yes, I can.”

(Ogre)
“If that is so, shout and proclaim along the way: ‘The goddess named Kāḷī, daughter of the great celestial king Sumana and wife of the ogre Dīghatāla, has given birth to a son.’ There are seven pots of gold at the base of this palm tree. Take those pots of gold as your fee for proclaiming the news.”
412:
She went along the way shouting and proclaiming, “The daughter of the Deva King Sumana, the wife of the Yakkha Dīghatāla, named the ogress Kāḷī, has given birth to a son!” King Sumana, while sitting in the assembly of Yakkhas, heard that voice and said, “A human brings very pleasant news for us; call that human.” Having called and heard the news, he became filled with faith and devotion, saying, “There are pots of gold in the area where the shadow of this tree spreads; I give those pots of gold to you.”

She went to the place of the impaling stake and fed the prisoner. After the prisoner had finished eating, when she wiped his mouth with her hand, he realized it was a woman’s touch and bit her hair-knot with all his might. Being a brave woman, she cut off her hair-knot with a sword and returned only to the King.

Then the King asked, “Dear woman, by what sign or token shall I know that you have finished feeding him?” She replied, “You may know by the sign of my hair-knot,” and she reported all the events she had encountered to the King and had the pots of gold brought. The King had the pots of gold brought and asked his ministers, “Is there such a vast amount of wealth belonging to any other person?” The ministers replied, “There is not, Your Majesty.” Then the King—
413:
—appointed her husband Kāḷavaḷiya to a position of high status and ceremony in the city of Rājagaha, bestowing upon him the title of “Dhana-Seṭṭhī” (Wealthy Merchant).

This is the story of the merchant Kāḷavaḷiya.

## The account of the immensely wealthy merchants ends.

at 11:00 AM.

Dhamma-nāda Monastery, Mingun Hill Range.
414:
## Nine Verses of Aspiration at the Conclusion of the Work
## Pali and Word-by-word Meaning

(1) Tisatekasahassāmhi,
Sāke’kattiṃsatādhike.
Aḍḍhateyyasahassāmhi,
Jinacakke tu terase.

(2) Paṭhamāsāḷhamāsassa,
Kāḷe terasame dine.
Sorivāramhi pubbaṇhe,
Ekādasaghaṭikkhaṇe.

Ekattiṃsatādhike = with thirty-one in excess. Tisatekasahassāmhi sāke = in the Burmese Era of one thousand three hundred. (Or), Ekattiṃsatādhike tisatekasahassāmhi sāke = in the Burmese Era 1331. Jinacakke tu = as for the Era of the Conqueror (Buddhist Era). Terase = with thirteen in excess. Aḍḍhateyyasahassāmhi = in the year two thousand five hundred. (Or), Terase aḍḍhateyyasahassāmhi = in the glorious Buddhist Era of two thousand five hundred and thirteen.

Paṭhamāsāḷhamāsassa = of the first month of Āsāḷha, when ordination ceremonies are grandly held and the Punnaga flowers bloom in the deep forests. Kāḷe terasame dine = on the thirteenth day of the waning moon. Sorivāramhi = on Saturday, the day of the Nagas' delight.
415:
Pubbaṇhe ekādasaghaṭikkhaṇe = in the morning at the eleventh hour, when the sun's rays are rising.

(3) Siddhipatto mahābuddha-
vaṃso buddhatthadīpako.
Chabhāgehi sukhaṃ chaṭṭha-
saṅgītisahajātako.

Buddhatthadīpako = which illustrates the life of the Buddha by comparing his Perfections (Pāramīs) and his years of ministry (Vassa). Chaṭṭhasaṅgītisahajātako = which is worthy of being called the 'twin-born' companion of the Sixth Buddhist Council, being the legitimate son born from the heart of the State Buddha Sāsana. Mahābuddhavāṃso = this scripture named the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, which is complete with exemplary models. Chabhāgehi = in six volumes divided accordingly. Sukhaṃ = easily and without hardship. Siddhipatto = has reached successful completion, filled with profound meaning, to spread the light of wisdom to all people in accordance with Buddhist texts.

(4) Pañcatālīsavassāni,
Ṭhatvā lokaṃ sadevakaṃ.
Uttāresi mahāvīro,
Dhammanāvāya yo jino.

Mahāvīro = He who possesses great energy (viriya) and right exertion (sammappadhāna), fulfilling the fivefold duties of a Buddha day and night. Yo jino = that Blessed One who conquered the five Maras. Pañcatālīsavassāni = for a period of forty-five years (Vassa).
416:
Ṭhatvā = having remained firm like a golden mountain. Sadevakaṃ lokaṃ = the world of beings including Brahmas and Devas. (Or), Sadevakaṃ lokaṃ = the inhabitants of the three realms: Brahmas, Devas, and humans. Dhammanāvāya = by means of the boat or raft of the Dhamma, which is the Noble Eightfold Path. Uttāresi = has rescued and ferried them across to the shore of Nibbāna.

(5) Taṃ jinaṃ pañcatālīsa-
khaṇḍena pūjayāmahaṃ.
Sakkaccaṃ buddhavāṃsena,
Gantheneha sagaṇṭhinā.

Ahaṃ = I, who am known as a Mahā-Visiṭṭha Tipiṭakadhara Elder, who has had the opportunity to live with the eye of scripture and constant mindfulness from youth until now due to past merit conducive to wisdom. Idha = in this present Buddha Sāsana. Pañcatālīsakhaṇḍena = with forty-five sections, aspiring to the forty-five years of the Buddha's ministry. Sagaṇṭhinā = together with the Ganthi (decisive interpretations) and Anu-dīpanī. Buddhavāṃsena ganthena = with this scripture named the Great Chronicle of Buddhas. Taṃ jinaṃ = that Blessed One who conquered the five Maras. Sakkaccaṃ pūjayāmi = I worship and honor with a humble heart, subduing pride, without coarse bodily or verbal actions.

(6) Yaṃ pattaṃ kusalaṃ tassa,
Ānubhāvena pāṇino.
Sabbe saddhammarājassa,
Ñatvā dhammaṃ sukhāvahaṃ.

Maya = by me, who am called a Tipiṭakadhara Elder. Yaṃ kusalaṃ = that great merit known as the Great Chronicle of Buddhas,
417:
which was achieved through effort, wisdom, and faith in composing this scripture. Pattaṃ = has certainly been attained and received, based on wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). Tassa kusalassa = of that great merit involving effort, wisdom, and faith in the work of this scripture. Ānubhāvena = by the power and influence of that merit, which is the rightful inheritance of Kamma. Sabbe = all without exception. Pāṇino = living beings who maintain their life-faculty and exist until now. Saddhammarājassa = of the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, who delights beings with faith through his Perfections, generosity, conduct, and the extraordinary qualities of a Buddha. Sukhāvahaṃ = which brings about the three types of happiness: human, celestial, and Nibbāna. Dhammaṃ = the excellent teaching spoken and instructed. Ñatvā = having clearly and truly understood through the three types of wisdom: learning, reflection, and meditation, like a swift horse—

(7) Pāpuṇantu visuddhāya, sukhāya paṭipattiyā.
Asokamanupāyāsaṃ, nibbānasukhamuttamaṃ.

Visuddhāya = which is pure and clean, being far removed from the two low extremes of sensual indulgence and self-mortification. Sukhāya = which is easy and pleasant for abandoning the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that obstruct the Path and Fruit. Paṭipattiyā = by the noble practice of the Middle Way, which is the pure Eightfold Path. Asokaṃ = which is entirely free from the sorrow and grief caused by the five types of misfortune (vyasana).
418:
Anupāyāsaṃ = which is free from the burning danger of despair (upāyāsa) that seethes within without overflowing. Uttamaṃ = which is supreme and excellent due to the aforementioned qualities. Nibbānasukhaṃ = the happiness of Nibbāna, which is the liberation from the thirst of craving (taṇhā) that binds various lives, great and small. Pāpuṇantu = may they reach it through the swift realization of the ten types of insight-wisdom (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

(8) Ciraṃ tiṭṭhatu saddhammo,
Dhamme hontu sagāravā.
Sabbepi sattā kālena,
Sammā devo pavassatu.

Saddhammo = the three aspects of the Sāsana known as Saddhamma: Learning (pariyatti), Practice (paṭipatti), and Realization (paṭivedha). Ciraṃ = for a long time, for five thousand years. Tiṭṭhatu = may it endure and shine like the sun, free from the interference of those who argue perversely (vitaṇḍavādī). Sabbepi = all without exception. Sattā = beings: humans, Devas, and Brahmas. Dhamme = in the Dhamma taught and proclaimed by the Lord Buddha. Sagāravā hontu = may they hold it in high esteem like a royal umbrella, lighting the lamp of wisdom with deep and sincere faith, regarding it as the true refuge. Devo = the rain-deity known as Pajjunna, who is the source of benefit for the prosperity of all people. Kālena = at the proper time during the night. (Or) Kālena = every five days in poor soil areas, every ten days in medium soil areas,
419:
every fifteen days (once a fortnight) in good soil areas, at the proper time during the night. Sammā pavassatu = may it rain abundantly and heavily so that the towns and villages may be pleasant, beautiful, and prosperous.

(9) Yathā rakkhiṃsu porāṇā,
Surājāno tathevimaṃ.
Rājā rakkhatu dhammena,
Attanova pajaṃ pajaṃ.

Porāṇā = of ancient times. Surājāno = the ancient good kings such as Mahāsammata, who were Bodhisattas and whose glory and power shone brightly. Pajaṃ = the citizens and all the people. Dhammena = by means of the Tenfold Virtue of Kings (rājadhamma). Rakkhiṃsu yathā = just as they protected and guarded them to be free from hunger and enemies by standing in the position of parents. Tatheva = in the same manner as those ancient good kings. Rājā = the noble King (Sammuti-deva) who rules the Union of Burma with intellectual, physical, and administrative strength. Imaṃ pajaṃ = these people of the Union, bound by the bond of loving-kindness as brothers. Dhammena = by means of the Tenfold Virtue of Kings. Attano pajaṃ iva = as if they were his own children born from his breast. Rakkhatu = may he be able to protect and support them by spreading loving-kindness and compassion, pouring down the rain of the Brahma-vihāras to make the country pleasant, and raising the banner of wisdom.
420:
The commentator Ven. Mahā Buddhaghosa made aspirations with the four verses beginning with “Yaṃ pattaṃ kusalaṃ tassa” at the conclusion of the Aṭṭhasālinī and Pañcapakaraṇa commentaries, which are the commentaries on the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

We also make our aspirations with great devotion using the same aspiration verses of that commentator Ven. Mahā Buddhaghosa. By doing so:

“Saccaṃ punapi saccanti, bhujamukkhippa vuccate.
Sakattho natthi nattheva, parassattha’makuubbatoti—
Vacanato parattho va sappurisehi kattabbo, paratthe sampādite pana sakattho sampannova nāma.

For one who does not work for the benefit (attha) of others, his own benefit (sakattha) cannot exist. It truly cannot exist. (This word) is true. Again, it is true. Thus, raising the arm, it is said (or: say it).

Because of such words spoken by various wise poets, all good people (sappurisa) should perform the benefit of others (parattha) as their priority. When the benefit of others is fulfilled, one’s own benefit is indeed said to be fulfilled.”

(May this be in perfect accordance with the concluding remarks of Ven. Saṅgharakkhita Mahāsāmi found in the Sāratthavilāsinī, the Pañcikā-ṭīkā.)

## Here ends the entire Great Chronicle of Buddhas.
